      account that already exists into a group — "Administrators by role, everybody else by
      default" — so every database that upgraded into user groups has a working administrator, and
      only a database created *after* `032` does not. The dev database is one of the former: its
      `admin` is in `Administrators [is_admin]`, which is why the same request that answers
      `AUTH_FORBIDDEN` on a fresh box answers `OBJECT_NOT_FOUND` there. Two environments, one of
      them the one we ship, and the divergence is exactly the thing under test.

      Found by `F-08`'s install smoke test, which builds the only fresh installation this project
      makes — and which could not see it either until `U-20` gave it a credential to be refused
      with. It had been asserting `GET /sensors/999999/state` answers `OBJECT_NOT_FOUND`; it
      answered `AUTH_FORBIDDEN`, and that assertion is sound again now rather than needing to be
      weakened. Tests: 1 new in `accounts.test.ts`, resolving `full` on an arbitrary object id and
      asserting `viaAdminGroup` — the right answer for the wrong reason would be a per-object
      grant. Mutation 1/1.

- [x] **P-184 — six pause-precedence tests fail on a tree that was green eight hours earlier** · M ·
      `packages/core/test/pause-precedence.test.ts` fails six of its twenty-nine cases, all of them
      the `schedule` source: "holds a sensor by schedule", the two combinations that report
      schedule, the resume refusal, the dependency release on a schedule edit, and the
      all-four-holders report. **Deterministic, not flaky** — six of six on every run, in isolation
      and in the full suite.

      **Nothing in the repository changed between green and red.** The full suite passed on this
      same core source at about 02:00 on 2026-09-07 and failed at about 10:00; `git stash` confirms
      the failures are present on `5568fc8` without any local edit. So the variable is time or the
      environment, not the code, which makes this a test that was passing for a reason nobody
      stated. The suspicion to start from: the fixture pins `OUTSIDE = 2026-08-24T03:00:00.000Z`
      and creates its schedule *now*, so anything in the schedule path that is evaluated relative
      to creation rather than to the instant passed in would drift away from the pinned date as
      real time moves — two weeks by now. `SchedulePauses.recompute` itself takes `now` and calls
      the pure `isActiveAt`, so if that suspicion is right the drift is upstream of it, in what
      `list` or `anyWork` returns.

      **P-184 outcome. The drift was real and the direction was the other one.** The fixture
      drives `recompute` and `sweep` at the pinned `OUTSIDE` — Monday 03:00 UTC — but three
      service paths reach the schedule at the *real* clock and cannot be told otherwise:
      `ObjectService.pauseState` computes schedule holding live, `resume` evaluates the same way
      before deciding whether to refuse, and `ScheduleSync` recomputes at the mutation's own
      timestamp. So the window `mo:08:00-mo:18:00` was closed at `OUTSIDE` and **open for ten
      hours of every real week**, and during those ten hours the row said "held by schedule" while
      every live path said "open".

      **Green was the accident.** Ten hours in a hundred and sixty-eight is a 6% chance per run,
      and the run that caught it was a Monday morning. The failing assertion is the one whose own
      comment states the invariant — "the view an operator reads has to agree with the row a probe
      is filtered by, or one of them is lying about the same sensor" — and for a fortnight it had
      been asserting that agreement at two different instants.

      Fixed in the fixture, not in the product: the office window is pinned to a weekday that is
      not today, which closes it on both clocks at once, at any hour, without asking `pauseState`
      to accept an instant it has no other reason to take. It stays closed at `OUTSIDE` whichever
      day is chosen — either the weekday differs, or the day is Monday and 03:00 is still before
      08:00. An injectable `now` on `pauseState` was written first and reverted: it fixed the view
      and left `resume` and `ScheduleSync` on the real clock, which is a seam that buys a third of
      a fix.

      Mutations 2/2, both run inside the window that exposes this. Restoring the fixed Monday
      window reproduces exactly the six original failures; a window that is always *open* fails
      fifteen, which is what says the fixture is doing the work rather than the cases passing
      regardless. Full suite green at 3,875 — measured on a Monday morning, which is the only time
      that number means anything for this file.

- [x] **P-185 — the pause view and the probe's filter disagree at every window edge** · S ·
      P-184 · Falls out of `P-184`'s diagnosis and is a property of the product, not of a test.
      `paused_by_schedule` in `sensor_runtime` is what the probe configuration filters on and is
      moved by the sweep; `pauseState` computes schedule holding live from the definition, because
      it must — a group or a device carrying a schedule has no `sensor_runtime` row to read a flag
      from. Between a window edge and the next sweep, armed at the next wall-clock minute, the two
      disagree.

      The direction that matters is the close: at 18:00 the row still says not-paused, so the
      probe keeps scanning and an alarm can still fire, while the operator's view already reports
      the sensor held by its maintenance window. Somebody is told the window has started while it
      pages them. The open edge is the milder inverse — the UI says live, nothing is scanning it —
      and both are bounded by the sweep, so this is a minute, not an outage. Worth deciding
      deliberately rather than by accident: either the view reads the flag where there is one, or
      the sweep is armed off the next window edge rather than off the next minute.

      **P-185 outcome. The premise was wrong by three orders of magnitude, and both proposed fixes
      were wrong with it.** The sweep is not armed on the minute: `#arm` computes
      `MINUTE - (now % MINUTE) + 50`, so it fires fifty milliseconds *past* every wall-clock
      minute — and schedules have minute resolution, so every possible boundary is acted on
      within 50 ms of itself. The method's own comment says exactly this: "a boundary at 09:00:00
      is acted on at 09:00:00 and not at 08:59:59.998". I filed a ticket about a sixty-second
      exposure without reading the twenty lines that set it, and then proposed arming off the next
      window edge — which the class comment above rejects, with a better argument than mine: a
      deadline computed an hour ago is an hour wrong the moment a country changes its clocks, and
      the transitions that matter most are the ones nobody is awake for.

      So no product change. What was genuinely missing is that **nothing asserted the agreement at
      all** — which is what `P-184` had just demonstrated, since the one assertion that claimed to
      was comparing two clocks. `schedules.test.ts` now asserts all three parties at one instant,
      in both window states: the view says held, the row says held, and the probe is not given the
      sensor — then the same three the other way round. Mutations 2/2: a view that stops reporting
      schedule holding fails it, and a "closed" window that quietly covers the present fails it.

      It also adds `farFromNow()`, the missing complement of the `aroundNow()` helper that was
      already in that file. Its absence is what `P-184` was made of: a test that wants "closed"
      reaches for a fixed window like `mo:08:00-mo:18:00`, which is closed at whatever instant the
      author had in mind and open for ten hours of every real week.

      The residual exposure is 50 ms plus the sweep's own duration. **`P-186` measured that second
      term**: 73.5 ms for five thousand sensors moving at once, so the disagreement is about
      **125 ms**, twice a day — three orders of magnitude from the minute this ticket claimed.

- [x] **P-186 — the schedule sweep has no measured budget** · S · P-185 · Every installation with
      a schedule runs `ScheduleSweep.sweep` once a minute, for ever, and nothing measures it. The
      perf suite has budgets for ingestion, rollups, history, clone and tree build; this is the
      one periodic loop without one. It matters twice: it is the term that bounds how long the
      pause view and the probe's configuration can disagree after a window edge (`P-185`), and a
      sweep that grows with the sensor count is a minute-by-minute cost on exactly the large
      installations `P-15` sizes for. `recompute` opens with a `LIMIT 1` that returns nothing when
      no schedule is assigned, so the floor is already known to be near zero — what is unknown is
      the shape above it. Wants a `test:perf` case at the 5,000-sensor scale with every sensor
      under a schedule, run on a quiet machine with `ms-server` stopped, and the number in
      `docs/findings/`.

      **P-186 outcome.** Measured at the v1 target, in a tree of the shape an installation has,
      with the schedule assigned at the probe so the inheritance walk runs the full depth:
      `docs/findings/2026-09-07-schedule-sweep-budget.md`.

      | pass | median | samples | budget |
      | --- | --- | --- | --- |
      | no schedule assigned | **0.8 ms** | 2.4, 0.8, 0.8 | 50 ms |
      | a window closing, 5,000 moving | **73.5 ms** | 247.2, 73.5, 66.0 | 1,000 ms |
      | an ordinary minute | **10.4 ms** | 11.6, 10.4, 10.0 | 600 ms |

      **The always-paid cost is 10.4 ms a minute at five thousand sensors — a duty cycle of
      0.017%.** An installation that does not use schedules cannot tell the feature exists: 0.8 ms
      is `anyWork`'s `LIMIT 1` returning nothing. What makes the steady state cheap is that
      `applyPauses` writes only where the flag differs, so the walk runs, the answer is discarded,
      no `sensor_state` row is written and no probe is pushed to.

      **It also finishes `P-185` with a number instead of an argument.** That ticket claimed the
      pause view and the probe's filter could disagree for up to a minute after a window edge; the
      arming answered half of it (50 ms past the minute, and boundaries have minute resolution) and
      this is the other half. The disagreement is 50 ms + 73.5 ms ≈ **125 ms**, twice a day.

      Three samples of each rather than one, because the machine was not exclusively mine —
      `ms-server` and the Vite container were stopped per `CLAUDE.md` and the rest were idle under
      2.2%, but two containers from unrelated work were up. The first pass of each case is visibly
      dearer (cold buffers, an unplanned query) and is reported rather than averaged away, because
      that cost is paid once per process start and not once a minute.

      Budgets are set at roughly ten times the measured value, so a change that makes this
      materially worse fails rather than drifts. What is **not** measured is the shape above five
      thousand: the walk should be about linear in the sensor count, but that is an expectation,
      and an installation an order of magnitude larger is `P-15`'s question to re-measure rather
      than to extrapolate.

      the defect either until `U-20` gave it a credential to be refused with. A development
      database that has been migrated forward for weeks is not the thing we ship, and the ways it
      differs are invisible precisely because nobody chose them.

      What would help is being able to get a *fresh* one cheaply and routinely — a documented
      teardown-and-rebuild for `dev/`, so the shipped first-boot path is exercised by ordinary
      work rather than only by a smoke test somebody remembers to run. Note the constraint before
      designing it: `docker compose down -v` deletes the dev Postgres volume, which is the whole
      point here but is also how somebody loses a fixture they wanted; and `dev/data` holds the
      vault key and `first-admin-password`, so "fresh" means those too. Not urgent, and worth
      doing before the next thing that only reproduces on a virgin database.

      three things a fresh install has none of — the vault key, the generated password and the
      probe's spool — then starts the core so it migrates and bootstraps.

      **Surgical, not a directory wipe**, and that is the design constraint: `dev/data` is also
      where somebody's own notes and scratch files live — `api.txt`, `smoke-api.sh`, `spike/`,
      `test-logs/` — so the state is named one item at a time and everything else is left. It does
      not touch the container, its volume, or any other database, including the `ms_test_*`
      scratch ones the suites make. `docker compose down -v` would have been the obvious mechanism
      and is the wrong one twice over: it takes the whole volume, and it is the command that loses
      a fixture somebody wanted.

      It names what it will destroy and then asks — `--yes` for a script, a typed `y` for a
      person, a refusal when there is no terminal to ask on — which is `P-188`'s pattern applied to
      the other destructive thing in `scripts/`.

      **`CREATE DATABASE` inherits `timescaledb` from `template1`**, which is where the image's own
      initialisation puts it and is why a plain `CREATE DATABASE` works for the scratch databases
      in `test/support/database.ts`. Migration `003` checks for the extension and cannot install
      it, so the reset checks too rather than trusting it: if the image ever stops seeding
      `template1`, the failure is a sentence at the point the assumption was made instead of a
      migration abort three steps later.

      **Run for real, which is what it was for.** The dev database was 5,051 sensors migrated
      forward for weeks; it is now one root object, no samples, one account — and that account
      reads `admin | admin | Administrators [is_admin]`, which is `P-183`'s fix confirmed on a

      The 5,000-sensor load is reproducible with `scripts/soak.sh --sensors 5000`, and the tree is

- [x] **P-189 — approving a connected probe does not start it scanning** · M · R-01, P-187 ·
      The first thing an operator does after installing is approve the probe waiting in the queue.
      Nothing happens. It keeps sitting there, scanning nothing, until something makes it
      reconnect.

      `ProbeEndpoint` sets `session.approved` **once, at admission**:

          // **An unapproved probe is sent nothing**, which is the whole of what approval means
          if (session.approved) this.#queueConfig(session, logger, hello.configVersion ?? '');

      A probe that connected while pending has `session.approved === false` for the life of that
      session, and `ProbeRegistry.approve` writes `probe_registration`, writes `probe_config`, logs
      "a probe was approved" and tells the live session nothing. `ConfigChangeNotifier` rides the
      audit sink, so later object mutations do flush — to a session that is still marked
      unapproved.

      **The API reference promises the opposite**, in the approve route's own description: "A probe
      that is already connected starts scanning without reconnecting." That sentence is not
      implemented.

      Measured on a fresh install (`P-187`'s reset, which is how this was found): probe pending,
      `POST /probes/dev-local-probe/approve` answers `status=approved objectId=2`, then five
      thousand sensors created under it — and eleven minutes later the probe had logged nothing
      since its handshake and `sample` was empty. Restarting it: `probe applied its
      configuration`, `scheduled: 5000`, readings within seconds.

      Two ways to make it true, and they are not equivalent. **Implement the promise** — on
      approval, find the live session, re-evaluate it and queue its configuration. Note what else
      is bound to the handshake before choosing this: the probe's own key is issued "at its next
      handshake, not here", so a session that never re-handshakes also never gets its key, and
      `hasOwnKey` stays false. **Or close the session on approval** and let the probe reconnect on
      its own retry, which it does in seconds — cruder, one line, and it makes the documented
      sentence true in effect while keeping the key issue on the handshake where the design put it.
      The second looks right; the first is what the sentence literally says.

      **P-189 outcome. Closed the session, and the key settled it.** The endpoint now indexes
      pending sessions by gid — `#sessions` deliberately holds approved ones only, which is why a
      decision had nothing to act on — and `ProbeRegistry.approve` calls `disconnect(gid)` through
      a narrow `ProbeConnections` interface, late-bound from `main.ts` the way
      `ConfigChangeNotifier.attach` already is.

      **Reviving the session in place would have left the probe scanning without a key**, which is
      the argument that decided it. A key is issued only when a probe presents the *enrolment*
      key, in the welcome — `approve` nulls the stored hash precisely so the next handshake
      re-issues one (`P-37`). Flipping `approved` on a live session and pushing it a configuration
      skips the welcome, so the probe would have been scanning happily on a credential the core
      had just invalidated, and would have been refused whenever it did eventually reconnect.

      Measured on the dev stack: approve at `08:20:25.081`, then `a probe was approved` →
      `closing a probe connection so a decision reaches it` → `link to core closed` →
      `reconnecting to core` → reconnected at `08:20:26.222`, **1.1 seconds**, with
      `issued this probe a key of its own` on the core and `issuedKey: true` on the probe, and
      `scheduled: 5000` behind it. `hasOwnKey` stays false for one more handshake, which is `P-37`
      working as designed: issuing repeats until the probe comes back *using* the key.

      The approve route's description said "A probe that is already connected starts scanning
      without reconnecting", which was not implemented. It now says what happens and why, and
      names this ticket — a sentence that was wrong for long enough to be quoted in a bug report
      is worth marking rather than quietly correcting.

      **An existing test claims this property and does not test it.** `probe-endpoint.test.ts`
      has "reaches a probe that was enrolled after it had already connected", whose comment reads
      "If the session only resolved its branch at the handshake, approving it would do nothing
      until someone restarted the probe" — exactly this defect. It drives an *already approved*
      session whose branch is claimed later, which is a different property, and it passed
      throughout. Left in place, because what it tests is worth testing; the real case is two new
      tests beside it. Tests: 4 new. Mutations 2/2 — approve not telling the connection, and
      pending sessions not being indexed.

- [x] **P-190 — the README's "making it scan something" documents a flow that R-01 replaced** · S ·
      P-189 · It tells the reader to claim a branch with
      `PATCH /objects/2 {"kind":"probe","gid":"dev-local-probe"}`, and says so under a note that

      `R-01` has landed: there is a queue, and `POST /probes/{gid}/approve` binds the identity to

      **P-190 outcome.** The section documents the enrolment flow: list the queue, create an
      object for the probe to own, approve it onto that object. Three commands where there was
      one, and the one it replaces could not work on the installation it was written for.

      It also says what happens next, because `P-189` changed it: the probe's connection is closed
      as it is approved and it comes back about a second later, through the handshake that issues
      its key and its first configuration. Without that sentence the reader watches a probe
      disconnect immediately after they approve it and reasonably concludes they broke something.

      **Walked end to end on a fresh install, using nothing but what the page says.**
      `scripts/dev-reset.sh` (`P-187`) back to empty, then the four commands extracted from the
      README itself rather than typed from memory: the token minted from the bootstrap password;
      `GET /probes` answering with one entry, `pending`, `objectId: null`; the object create
      returning **`id: 2`**, which is why the page can state that number rather than hedge; and
      the approve answering `status=approved objectId=2`. The `P-189` sequence — approved,
      connection closed, reconnecting, key issued, connected — all landed inside the same second,
      so "about a second later" is conservative.

      Then the last sentence of the section, which needed a sensor to be true of: a device and one
      `icmp.ping` under the new probe object, first reading in about twenty seconds, sensor `up`

      scanning one, which is the only claim that matters here and the one that could not be made
      before `P-187` existed.

- [x] **P-197 — no smoke test approves a probe, so nothing proves a decision reaches one in the
      packaged build** · M · P-189, P-196 · Approving a connected probe (`P-189`) and withdrawing
      one (`P-196`) are both proved only by unit tests. `smoke-install.sh` deliberately stops at
      "connected, pending approval" and hands off to `smoke-enrol.sh`, which never approves — so
      the one path an operator actually walks on a fresh install, *approve it and watch it start
      scanning*, is not exercised anywhere against a packaged install.

      **What that leaves uncovered is the wiring, which is where all four of these bugs lived.**
      `main.ts` binds the registry to the endpoint with `probeRegistry.attach(probeEndpoint)`, and
      neither `withdraw` nor `remoteAddressOf` is reached by any test that runs the real services.
      Both halves are unit-tested; the line joining them is not. `P-189` and `P-196` were each a
      decision that wrote its rows and never reached the probe — exactly the class of defect a
      unit test cannot see.

      **Where it goes: `smoke-enrol.sh`, not `smoke-install.sh`.** The two-box shape is the point.
      Approving a probe binds it to a branch and issues it a key in the welcome, and a bundle that
      quietly depended on a path only the core host has is the failure this file already exists to
      catch. `smoke-install.sh` should keep stopping where it does.

      The sequence, and each step is an assertion:

      1. Approve the pending probe onto a branch — create a probe object, `POST
         /probes/:gid/approve` with `local: false` (it is on the other box). Assert `applied
         configuration` appears in the probe's journal and `systemctl show ms-probe -p NRestarts`
         is still `0`. **The restart count is half the assertion**: bouncing the service would
         prove the handshake works, which was never in doubt, and hide whether the decision
         reached a live connection.
      2. Revoke it with a note. Assert `stopped scanning` in the probe's journal, `NRestarts`
         still `0`, and that the operator's own sentence — not the word "revoked" — reached that
         journal. The last one is what proves the reason travelled rather than a bare close.
      3. Optionally re-approve and assert it comes back, which is the only end-to-end check on
         `P-37`'s key re-issue after the hash was cleared.

      **Three things that will bite whoever writes it:**

      - **The API needs authentication now.** Use `ms_docker_curl` from `scripts/lib/api-auth.sh`,
        which `smoke-install.sh` already does; the older helpers predate it and used bare `curl`.
      - **A poll under `set -euo pipefail` aborts on its first failure.** `gid="$(curl -sf … |
        …)"` takes the pipeline's status, so a core that has not opened its port yet ends the
        script instead of being retried. `|| true` inside the substitution, and silence the
        parser's stderr on that one call so an expected non-answer does not print a stack trace
        that reads like a crash.
      - **Order matters, or step 2 makes step 1 vacuous.** Both assert on the probe's journal, and
        `stopped scanning` after `applied configuration` is only meaningful in that order. A
        third block that stops the probe (a narrowed `allow-from`, say) has to come after both or
        it hollows them out.

      Working versions of the approve and revoke helpers exist at `f8ccb54:scripts/smoke/` — they
      predate the auth requirement and would need `ms_docker_curl`, but the API sequence and the
      poll handling are right. They are on an unreferenced commit, so retrieve them early or write
      them fresh.

      **P-197 outcome. Three steps in `smoke-enrol.sh`, and one of them proved nothing until a
      mutation said so.** Approve onto a branch with `local: false`, revoke with a note,
      re-approve — seven assertions, run against the packaged build on two boxes. The helpers at
      `f8ccb54` were the right shape; they were rewritten inline against `ms_docker_curl`, with
      the poll handling the ticket described.

      **The mutation that mattered: `withdraw` replaced by a bare `disconnect`, which is exactly
      the pre-`P-196` defect. The first version of step 2 passed.** Both of its assertions —
      `stopped scanning` and the operator's sentence — are true on the old path too: a bare close
      makes the probe reconnect, and the handshake it comes back on is refused with the same code
      and the same sentence, so the probe stops either way. On a real network that refusal is
      hours away, which is the whole bug; in a container it is one second away, which is why
      asserting the outcome proved nothing.

      What tells them apart is **whether the probe had to reconnect to find out**. Step 2 now
      takes a journal cursor before revoking, reads only the slice after it, and asserts that
      `stopped scanning` appears *before* `link to core closed` — true when the reject lands on
      the live connection, false when the link drops first. Re-measured: the mutation now fails
      on that assertion and on nothing else. A second mutation — `approve` no longer closing the
      session, which is `P-189`'s defect — fails step 1 and nothing else.

      **What step 3 could not assert, and why.** `hasOwnKey` on the API is
      `access_key_hash AND access_key_confirmed_at`, and confirmation is written when the probe
      *presents* the key, at the handshake after the one that issued it — so it is false here by
      design, on a link that is up and working. The first run failed on it. The assertion reads
      the registration row instead: revoking cleared the hash, and re-approval put one back.

      `NRestarts` is checked at each step and stayed `0` throughout, which is half of every
      assertion above: bouncing the service would prove the handshake works, which was never in
      doubt, and would hide whether the decision reached a live connection.

- [x] **P-203 — a report is one query per sensor, and nobody has measured what that costs** · S ·
      E-04 · `ReportRenderer` calls `HistoryService.forSensor` once per subject, sequentially, and
      that was the right call for `E-04`: a batched query would be a second implementation of
      `segmentsFor` — stitching a rollup tier together with everything newer than its watermark —
      and the first sign of a disagreement would be a report and the sensor page showing different
      numbers for the same hour. Correct beats fast for the ticket that establishes the rule.

      **But nobody knows what it costs, and `MAX_CELLS` is not the bound that matters.** A cell
      limit bounds the document; it does not bound the round trips. A report over 500 sensors is
      500 calls, each of which is several statements, and `E-08` will run those on a schedule
      against the same database serving live checks — which is the one competitor that certainly
      reaches everything else (`P-192`).

      The ticket is a measurement first: render a report over 1, 10, 100 and 500 sensors at a
      month and at a year, with the conditions printed the way `test:perf` prints them, and put the
      numbers in `docs/findings/`. Then decide.

      **`E-06` added a second thing to measure while you are there: the formatting, which is CPU on
      the event loop rather than round trips.** At the cell limit, HTML and CSV take about a second
      each; a PDF at its 400-page bound takes about three. `ReportRunner` bounds concurrency at
      two, so the worst case is two renders competing with every request the core is serving. That
      may be fine — a scheduled report runs at 03:00 — but it is a number this ticket should take
      rather than a thing to find out from a latency graph. Batching is one answer; a concurrency limit is
      another and is much cheaper; and it may turn out that 500 sequential reads of a rollup tier
      are fine and the honest outcome is a finding saying so. **No change without the number** —
      `CLAUDE.md` does not allow a performance claim without a measurement committed to the repo,
      and that cuts both ways.

      **Done 2026-09-13** — `docs/findings/2026-09-13-report-render-cost.md`, measured over 500
      two-channel sensors against 17.5 million real rollup rows. **About 20 ms a sensor, linear**,
      from either tier, and nearly all of it is the series query aggregating its buckets: the round
      trips a batch would save are 1.5 ms a sensor, so **batching is not worth a second
      implementation of `segmentsFor`**, and the ticket's own condition — no change without the
      number — is what says not to build it.

      **The number that did change something was the 500-sensor row.** A default report over 500
      sensors is five times `MAX_CELLS`, and the renderer read every sensor's history — 10.4 s and
      1,500 transactions against the live database — before counting the document and refusing it,
      on every scheduled run. Both terms of the count are known before any read, so
      `ReportRenderer.build` now asks `HistoryService.channelCounts` first: refused in 7 ms and one
      transaction, with the same error and the same advice, and a test that the estimate equals
      what the finished document counts.

      **And `E-06`'s worry was right.** Every format holds the event loop for its whole duration —
      HTML 0.8–0.95 s, XML 0.73 s, CSV 0.45 s, a `graph_only` PDF 0.63 s, and a PDF that will be
      refused for its page count 1.4–1.6 s before it says so. Two reports rendering at once made a
      concurrent sensor-page read wait **1.27 s at p95 and 2.6 s at worst**, against 11 ms idle. That
      is `P-204`. Two harness bugs were found on the way and are written up in the finding: an
      event-loop histogram that cannot see the first interval after it is enabled, and a latency
      sampler frozen by the very stall it was measuring — coordinated omission, which hid a
      2.8-second wait behind a 30 ms worst case on the second run.

- [x] **P-204 — a report's formatting holds the core's event loop** · M · P-203 · Measured in
      `docs/findings/2026-09-13-report-render-cost.md`: every format is synchronous for its whole
      duration, up to about a second for an HTML document near the value limit and a second and a
      half for a PDF refused for its page count, and two reports rendering at once made a concurrent
      request wait 1.27 s at p95 and 2.6 s at worst. Everything on that loop waits the same — the
      API, the probes' results, the state machine, the WebSocket. A report at 03:00 costs nobody
      anything; "Run now" on a large report at 14:00 freezes the core for everybody.

      **The shape of the fix is the one `CLAUDE.md` uses for checks**: formatting in a
      `worker_threads` worker, the document passed in by structured clone and the bytes passed back,
      at most `ReportRunner`'s two at a time. What makes it an `M` rather than an afternoon: the
      document holds `Date`s and a 14 MiB string on the way back, which is worth measuring rather
      than assuming cheap; `pdfkit`'s font has to load in the worker; an error has to come back as
      the same `ReportError` with the same code, or a refusal becomes a 500; a worker that dies must
      fail one run and not the runner; and a pool is exactly the kind of subsystem `CLAUDE.md` says
      adds a metric to Core Health. **Done when** `report-render-performance.test.ts`'s two-reports
      case holds a concurrent request's p95 near its idle value, and its guard assertion is
      replaced with a budget.

      **Worth doing alongside, and cheaper**: the PDF's page refusal happens after every cell has
      been measured. A lower bound on the page count — rows divided by the most rows a page can
      hold — would refuse most of those before the second and a half, the way `P-203` moved the
      value refusal before the reads.

      **Done 2026-09-13** — `docs/findings/2026-09-13-report-formatter.md`. Formatting runs in
      `ReportFormatter`: two workers started on first use and given back after a minute idle, eight
      jobs queued and the ninth refused with `409 REPORT_BUSY`, a two-minute timeout that ends the
      worker, a crash that fails one job, and a `ReportError` rebuilt on the core's side so a
      refusal stays a 422. Core Health gains **Report formats waiting** and **Report formats
      refused**. With two 100-sensor reports formatting, a concurrent request measured **p95
      10.8 ms against 12.3 ms idle** (worst 95 ms, the document's copy into the worker), where the
      same run on the loop measured 1,777 ms; the guard is now a budget of idle p95 + 50 ms. The
      PDF lower bound refuses the 1,838-page document in under a millisecond, where it held the
      loop 1.5 s. **The sampler had a second omission**, at the end of the last stall, which made
      `P-203`'s 1,268.6 ms too low — corrected in both findings files.

- [x] **P-205 — a probe's graceful shutdown closes the spool first and loses what its workers
      deliver** · S · P-80 · `docker stop ms-server` on 2026-09-13, at the 5,000-sensor dev load,
      logged "the result spool is closed and cannot accept results" 45 times in the second before
      "shutdown complete", exit code 0. `Lifecycle` runs hooks in reverse registration order, and
      `main.ts` closed the spool inside `spool-drain`, the last hook registered — so it ran *first*,
      with the scheduler still dispatching and every worker still delivering. `P-80` had noticed
      the reachability and made the refusal honest (`unwritten`); the order itself stayed, each
      refusal was its own error line, and the readings were gone.

      **P-205 outcome.** The spool closes in its own `result-spool` hook, registered before any
      runner so it runs last; `spool-drain` stops the drain only, and what lands afterwards is on
      disk for the next start. `CheckPool.stop({ drainMs })` answers queued checks at once and
      gives running ones a bounded window — 5 s in `main.ts` — before abandoning the rest, and a
      worker that dies inside the window settles its check rather than making the drain wait out
      the bound. `resultSink` gains `close()`: after it, and on any `SpoolClosedError`, results are
      counted and logged **once**, and `main.ts` logs the totals in one `result spool closed` line.
      **`pool-stopped` results are counted as `abandoned` and not spooled** — "probe is stopping"
      is not a reading of the device, and fixing the order would otherwise have handed the core a
      failed scan for every hung check on every restart. They had never reached the core before
      either: the closed spool refused them. `ProcessRunner.stop` answered nothing it had queued —
      it truncated the array, leaving accepted checks unsettled and uncounted — and now settles
      them as `pool-stopped` too. `shutdown-order.test.ts` wires the real `Lifecycle`, pool, sink
      and spool with three checks running when shutdown starts: the old order counts all three
      under one warning, the new one reads all three back from disk. Disabling the drain window
      fails both.

      **Confirmed live, 2026-09-13**, at the dev load: 5,001 sensors, the pool grown to 64. The
      probe ran from this commit's build against the dev database, with the main checkout's
      `dev/data` and `dev/tls` mounted in, for three minutes (15,405 checks dispatched), and was
      stopped with `docker stop`. The hooks ran in the new order — drain, scheduler, pool (5 s
      window, `finishedWhileDraining: 0`, `abandoned: 0`), `result spool closed` last — and the
      spool went from **95 pending when the drain stopped to 167 when it closed**: 72 results
      settled after the drain stopped, each of which the old order would have refused with its own
      error line. `results: { abandoned: 0, unspooled: 0 }`, spool `unwritten: 0`, no refusal
      logged, "shutdown complete" exit 0, about a second from SIGTERM. The old build, stopped the
      same way a minute earlier, happened to log no refusals — whether it does depends on checks
      settling between the two hooks — so the 45 from 16:27 is the comparison. The first run of the
      new build never reached its shutdown — the kernel killed the probe first — and is `P-206`.

      kill in six seconds, and the runs it survived bottomed out at 9.9–23.4% with swap gone.

      core — the first health field since `P-178`, so the first the heartbeat has had to gate.
      Also exported to Prometheus as `ms_{probe,core}_machine_memory_available_{ratio,bytes}`.

- [x] **P-210 — a probe near its own cgroup ceiling is killed with memory to spare** · S · P-208 ·

      ceiling it is measured against, and resident memory is not what the cgroup counts (page cache
      charged to it is). **Done when** Probe Health reports headroom to the probe's own cgroup limit
      where there is one (`memory.max` and `memory.current` under cgroup v2 — the limit is what

      enough. Core Health's `ms-core.service` has the same pair (`6G`/`8G`).

      Health. `readLimitMemory` in `@ms/shared` walks the process's cgroup v2 path from
      `/proc/self/cgroup` up to the root: at each level the ceiling is the **lower of `memory.high`
      and `memory.max`**, because the lower acts first — on the stock units that is `MemoryHigh`,
      which throttles rather than kills — the usage is the **working set**, `memory.current` less
      `inactive_file`, because page cache fills a cgroup to its ceiling on purpose, and the tightest
      level wins. **Not `process.availableMemory()`**, which this ticket proposed: it counts page
      cache, and with 180 MB of it in a 200 MiB `memory.high` it said 2 MiB were left of a ceiling
      the working set used 18 MiB of. (`process.constrainedMemory()` does find `MemoryHigh` on
      libuv 1.52; the reader walks the tree itself so that each ceiling is measured against the
      usage at its own level.) A **gap** with no limit anywhere up the tree, on cgroup v1 and on a
      hybrid host, and off Linux — WinSW sets none. The highest of the last thirty seconds, through
      the same watch `P-208`'s channel uses, renamed `AvailableMemoryWatch` now that it watches two
      things. **Default limits: warning above 80%, error above 100%** — the error where the kernel
      acts, the warning because `P-206`'s start-up surge was 21% of the stock 4 GiB. Protocol 18,
      capability `memoryLimit`; `healthForPeer` strips only what the core's version lacks, so a
      core at 17 still gets 17's pair. Prometheus: `ms_{probe,core}_memory_limit_usage_ratio` and
      `ms_{probe,core}_memory_limit_bytes`. `smoke-install.sh` gains `MS_SMOKE_KEEP=1`, which leaves
      its box running for a measurement like this one.

      **Measured** (`findings/2026-09-27-memory-limit.md`), under the shipped unit in the smoke
      test's systemd box: the core's route matched the kernel's own files at every heartbeat; a
      ceiling moved to put the probe at 85% was a **Warning** 27 s later and in `sample`; and the
      channel was a gap in `sample`, not a zero, while the probe was down. **Past the ceiling**:
      with swap the kernel held the probe at 93% of it, stalled at most 2.4% of the time and
      working — a Warning, correctly. Without swap it was stalled 73% of the time within 17 s, and
      **systemd's watchdog killed it** — the kernel never did — and restarted it into the same
      ceiling, where start-up alone stalled it again (`P-213`). A probe that far gone rarely gets
      out the heartbeat that would report it; what the core sees is the link drop, which makes the
      80% warning the limit that does the work. **Not measured**: cgroup v1 and a parent slice's

- [x] **P-211 — the report formatter's timeout test fails under a full `npm test`** · S · P-204 ·
      Seen 2026-09-27: "ends a job that runs out of time, with its worker, and carries on" in
      `packages/core/test/report-formatter.test.ts` failed once in a full `npm test --workspace
      @ms/core` (2,634 tests; the test took 3,048 ms), then passed 3/3 alone. Its limit had already
      gone from 300 ms to 1.5 s for the same reason: the pool's clock started when a job was handed
      to a worker, and the healthy job after the hung one runs on a new worker, which loads `pdfkit`
      and the rest of the renderer before it can begin.

      **It was the formatter, and no number would have fixed the test**: the limit was measuring the
      machine's load, not the report. In the dev toolchain container (eight CPUs) a format worker is
      ready **0.44 s** after it is started at p50 with no load added, 0.77 s worst of 30; with
      sixteen busy loops running, **3–5 s at p50 and 11.3 s worst** of 130 — and the old test failed
      **10 runs in 10** under that load. The healthy job's real work, two rows of CSV, took **167 ms
      at worst** under the same load. Production's limit is two minutes, so no report failed there
      for this; but a limit that counts start-up means less the busier the core is.

      **Fixed.** A format worker says `ready` once its imports have loaded, and the job's clock
      (`timeoutMs`) starts then — the rule the check workers' pool already follows. Start-up gets a
      clock of its own, `startTimeoutMs`, default two minutes (what a stuck start-up had before,
      inside the job's two), so a worker that never finishes starting is still ended with the job it
      was started for, and the queue behind it gets a new worker. The test's limit is now 1 s, six
      times the worst CSV, and it **passed 10 runs in 10** under the load that failed the old one 10
      in 10. In three full `npm test --workspace @ms/core` runs it passed taking 3.8, 5.7 and 3.5 s,
      against the 3.0 s of the run that failed. **Two new tests, deterministic whatever the load**: `gated-format-worker.ts` stays in
      start-up until the test opens a `BroadcastChannel` gate, so one holds a worker there past the
      job's limit and sees the job succeed, and the other never opens it and sees both jobs ended by
      the start-up clock. Each fails against the mutation it guards: the old clock, and no start-up
      clock.

      search box's placeholder is "Search names and hosts", `TreeView`'s comment and

      with one escaped pattern. The listing already LEFT JOINs `device_config`, so on every row
      that is not a device `dc.host` is null, the host arm is null, and the row is decided by its
      name alone: groups, probes and sensors are found by name as before, and a sensor is **not**
      found by its device's host — the device is the match. The parentheses matter: without them
      the OR binds below the AND and the host arm escapes every other filter, which the new test
      of `q` beside `kind` and `tag` catches. `host` stays the exact, case-folded lookup on the
      `lower(host)` index. No new index: the name match was already an unindexed scan, and neither
      column has a trigram index. The OpenAPI document describes `q` and `host`, and the route's
      description says the same so `api-reference.md` does. The map designer's object picker
      (`G-03`) sends the same `q`, so a sensor-list widget can now be pointed at a device by
      address too. Search results show a device's host, or a match by address would not say why
      it matched.

      `q` with a host fragment still ANDs with `kind` and `tag`; `host` does not accept a
      fragment. `api-routes.test.ts`: the tree's own request (`?q=…&limit=200`) finds a device by
      a hostname fragment in the other case and by an address fragment, still by name, and `host`
      stays exact. Mutated in `dist`: name-only fails three of them, an unparenthesised OR fails
      the AND test.

      `web-ui.md` said search results "come back flat, with the path written out", and so did

      like every other walk. Attached by the service after the keyset query, the way `effective`
      is, so the listing's own query is untouched; `ObjectService.list` now takes its expansions as
      one object (`{ effective, path }`) rather than a positional key list. An id deleted between
      the two reads gets **no** `path` rather than an empty one, which would say "the root". Opt-in,
      because it is a second statement and the tree's own levels already know where they are. The
      token list is the listing's own: `?include=ancestors`, the detail route's word, is a 400
      rather than a second name for the same thing. `path` is declared on `ms:objectSummary`,
      without which `additionalProperties: false` drops it with a 200; the route's description and
      `api-reference.md` say what it is.

- [x] **M-19 — A template's user and group recipients have never been delivered to** · M · A-01,
      A-12, N-07 · Found 2026-09-28 by bc8184 while scoping `V2-05`. `CAPABILITIES.MD` marks
      "recipients as users, user groups, or raw addresses" `[V1]`, and the template API has
      accepted all three kinds since `N-05`; `EmailTransport` resolved only `address`. A template
      naming only people failed every send as "cannot be resolved until accounts exist" — accounts
      have had an `email` since `A-01` — and one naming people *and* an address sent to the
      address and **dropped the people silently**. Email is the only method with
      `usesRecipients`, so the fix is email's alone.

      **Done when:**

      1. **Resolved at send time**, not when the template is saved: a user to their account's
         address, a group to its members', deduplicated, so a change of membership applies to the
         next send. Disabled accounts and accounts with no address are skipped and **named in the
         delivery result**; the send fails only when nobody resolves, and permanently then.
      2. **One question decided and documented: does a recipient who cannot read the sensor get
         the message?** `A-12` makes an object somebody cannot see absent; an email naming a
         device in a carved-out branch would be the way round that. Argued in the ticket, the
         rule kept in one place, and tested whichever way it goes.
      3. **One resolver, exported**, which `K-05`'s ticket emails reuse rather than rewrite.
      4. *(Moved to `M-20`: the web editor offering users and groups.)*
      5. A table over user, group, mixed, disabled, no address and not permitted; a regression
         test that the mixed case no longer drops anybody silently; a MailHog delivery test.
      6. The stale comment in `email.ts` goes.

      **M-19 outcome.** `RecipientResolver` (`notifications/recipients.ts`) is the one resolver,
      exported for `K-05`. `EmailTransport` requires one and calls it at send time. Both the
      dispatcher and the test send reach it through `send`, so they cannot resolve differently.

      - **A user or group recipient's value is its id**, as a decimal string. Nothing had ever
        read that value, so there was no convention to keep, and the template API now refuses
        any other value for those two kinds. A group is sent to at its members' own addresses,
        deduplicated together with the raw addresses and read at send time.
      - **Skipped recipients are named.** A recipient is skipped when the account or group does
        not exist, the group has no members, the account is disabled, it has no address, or it
        may not read the sensor. Each is named in the delivery result and in the notification
        log's new `skippedRecipients` (migration 056), which the Logs view shows as "Not sent
        to …". A send that reaches nobody fails permanently and names them all. "Cannot be
        resolved until accounts exist" is gone.
      - **Decided: a recipient who cannot read the sensor is not sent the message.** `A-12`
        makes an object somebody cannot see absent, and an email naming it would be the way
        round that: the device's name, its host and its message, in their inbox. The rule is one
        call to `AccessService.resolveManyFor`, asked about every sensor the message names. For
        a digest that is every sensor in it, so one hidden sensor withholds the whole digest
        from that person rather than sending it with a line missing. Administrators are sent
        everything. A deleted sensor's message goes to administrators only, as its log does. A
        raw address is not an account and is always sent to.
      - The editor offering users and groups is `M-20`.

      `recipients.test.ts` is a table of 12 cases, plus a group read at send time rather than
      when the template was saved. `email-delivery.test.ts` adds the refusal sentences, the
      mixed regression, and a MailHog send to a group's members that records who it missed.
      The migrator test takes 055 and 056 up and back down. The summarisation test asserts that
      a digest asks about every sensor it lists. A vitest covers the Logs row. Mutation 3/3: the
      rights check skipped (5 cases fail), the skipped names dropped from a partial send (2 fail),
      and a digest asking only about its lead sensor (1 fails).

      the login stored instead of the id, the no-address badge dropped, the box left undescribed,

- [x] **P-236 — under checks that hang to their timeout, the pool grows past the memory it has and
      the probe is OOM-killed** · M · P-34, P-210 · Found by `P-216b`
      (`docs/findings/2026-09-29-probe-starvation-b.md`). The pool sizer (`P-34`) derives its
      ceiling from Little's law on measured durations and knows nothing about memory: with 5,000
      `port.tcp` checks each waiting out a 5 s timeout it wants about 540 workers and is clamped to
      `autoPoolCeilingMax()`, 256, and `#grow()` goes there in one step while the queue is non-empty.
      At 35–40 MiB a worker that is about 9.5 GiB, past the shipped `MemoryMax=6G`. In a 4 GiB box
      the probe died at 98–110 workers, six times, and the start limit left it failed. **Probe
      Health read 95% of its memory limit (`P-210`) and nothing acted on it.**

      - **A memory cap on the ceiling.** `memoryCap = held + floor((available − reserve) /
        perWorker)`. `available` is `readLimitMemory()`, the tightest cgroup level against its
        working set. `reserve` is the larger of 256 MiB and 10% of the limit, for the main thread,
        the spool, the log's backlog and workers' heaps growing after they start. `perWorker` is a
        measured constant in `measured.ts`, 40 MiB, citing the finding. It corrects itself,
        because `available` is read again at every step.
      - **Where there is no cgroup limit** (cgroup v1, Windows under WinSW), `available` is the
        machine's (`P-208`). The probe then competes with whatever else runs there and `reserve` is
        its only protection, so `administration.md` recommends `MemoryMax` for exactly that case.
      - **Applied twice.** The sizer takes `min(derived, memoryCap)` every 30 s, and `#grow()` clamps
        each step to the live headroom, since growth is immediate and the sizer is not. Below the
        reserve, spare idle workers are retired down to `minSize` through the over-ceiling path,
        never one in the middle of a check (`P-26`). An explicit `workerPoolSize` is the operator's
        word and is honoured, with a warning when it exceeds the cap.
      - **Past the cap, nothing new.** Checks wait in the bounded queue and are refused and counted
        as now, and scheduler lag and `checkWait` rise: saturation that shows, not a death.
      - **When the cap binds, one log line per episode**, with derived, cap, available and
        perWorker, not one per sizer pass.
      - **On Probe Health**: `poolCeiling`, `poolMemoryCap`, and `poolHeldBack` (derived less
        effective). Probe protocol **19**, allocated 2026-09-29.

      **Done when** table tests cover the cap's arithmetic (a limit, a gap, the no-limit fallback,
      under the reserve), a pool test drops the headroom mid-growth, and a scenario test with a
      sensor type that only ends on abort shows the pool stopping at the cap, refusals counted,
      `poolHeldBack` above zero, and no worker retired mid-check. Acceptance is `P-216c`: the same
      4 GiB box, and the probe stays up with `NRestarts` 0.

      **Landed** (2026-09-29). `runner/memory-cap.ts` holds the arithmetic and a reading of memory
      that is kept for a second, because the pool asks on every growth attempt and a saturated
      probe attempts on every submit. **Enforced in the pool rather than in the sizer**, which is
      one change from the design above: growth and every ceiling the sizer sets both pass through
      the pool, so one place bounds both, and the sizer's ceiling stays the workload's number so
      `poolHeldBack` can say how far apart the two are. Two things the design did not foresee:
      - **A saturated pool never has a spare worker**, so the over-ceiling sweep could not give
        memory back while the probe was busy, which is when it is short. A worker that comes free
        while the pool is over what memory allows is now given up instead of handed the next
        check, and never one in the middle of a check.
      - **Workers that have been given up are still resident until their threads exit.** Counting
        them against shrinking would give up more to free memory already on its way back, and a
        mutation that did so took eight workers told to shed to three down to the floor. Counting
        them against growing is right, and that is what the pool does.

      21 tests in `pool-memory-cap.test.ts`, the scenario included, each mutation-checked: growth
      that ignores memory, no giving back while saturated, exiting workers counted against
      shrinking, and a log line per attempt all fail them. `P-216c` is the acceptance.

      **Accepted by `P-216c`** (2026-09-29, `docs/findings/2026-09-29-probe-starvation-c.md`): the
      same 4 GiB box and workload as `P-216b`, and no OOM kill in any stage. The pool stayed at
      79–131 workers, up to 207 held back, and resident at or below 3.2 GiB.

      refusals (a newer schema, an edited migration) exit 78. `down` follows `applied_at`, and `up`

      `installation.md` and `troubleshooting.md` now `reset-failed` before starting.
