      30 s budget, was a path no production request takes.

      The harness now builds the same 5,000 objects three ways: an administrator's API token, a
      non-administrator's token holding `write` at the root (the longest rights walk the tree has),
      and no authentication, kept so the difference is authentication and nothing else. The
      callers are interleaved within each sample. The rate limit is raised for the authenticated
      callers in the fixture only (`ApiServerOptions.rateLimit`, which `A-39` replaces with a
      setting). Measured in a booked window, 2026-09-29, 3 samples each into its own empty
      database:

      | | no auth | admin token | non-admin token |
      | --- | --- | --- | --- |
      | one request (`P-19`) | 2.8 s | 2.6 s | 3.5 s |
      | serial, one object per request | 27.1 s | 35.7 s | 44.7 s |
      | 8 in flight | 8.9 s | 11.5 s | 12.1 s |

      **The criterion holds for every caller through the bulk route, 88% spare or more.** It never
      held as a real caller on the serial path: authentication costs 1.7 ms per create for an
      administrator and 3.5 ms for anyone else, and every sample of each caller is clear of every
      sample of the one before it. At the default rate limit no account can build that way anyway:
      five windows, at least four minutes (`A-39`). The per-create cost was profiled statement by
      statement; the most expensive part is the writer's sight, which nearly every write resolves
      and never reads (`P-235`). `docs/findings/2026-09-29-tree-build-with-authentication.md`.

- [x] **P-235 — `writerFor` resolves the writer's sight on every write; only sensor types that
      read other objects need it (A-29)** · S · A-29, P-225 · Found 2026-09-29 profiling
      `P-225`'s per-create cost. Authentication adds three queries to a create for an administrator
      and four for anyone else. The most expensive of them is `visibilityFor`, the writer's sight:
      the administrator check, the access epoch and every grant, in one query. `writerFor`
      resolves it eagerly for every write, so `A-29` can check what a sensor's parameters name.
      Its only consumer is `assertMayName` (`sensor-reads.ts`), which runs only for types in
      `readingTypes()`. A group, device or Ping create pays for it and never reads it.

      Per sensor create, 1,000 serial creates per caller, pg driver wrapped. The times were taken
      under load (1.06 per CPU, another client on the database), so the counts are exact and the
      times indicative:

      | Statement | admin | non-admin |
      | --- | --- | --- |
      | token lookup | 1 / 1.3 ms | 1 / 1.3 ms |
      | permission check, administrator `EXISTS` (`AccessService.resolve`) | 1 / 0.9 ms | 1 / 0.9 ms |
      | permission check, rights walk | — | 1 / 1.9 ms |
      | **writer's sight (`visibilityFor`)** | **1 / 3.2 ms** | **1 / 3.3 ms** |

      Make `Writer.voucher.sees` lazy, resolved on first use and memoised per request. **Resolve it
      through the write's own transaction, never a separate query on the pool:** a voucher computed
      against a different snapshot from the write it vouches for would reopen the race `A-29`
      closed. Note that today's eager sight is not resolved that way. `writerFor` reads it on the
      pool before the transaction opens, so this is a change to make, not one to preserve. Not in
      scope: the administrator fact is asked twice per request, once by the permission check and
      once inside the sight.

      **Done when** authentication adds three queries to a non-administrator's `POST /objects`
      where it added four, and two to an administrator's where it added three; a sensor type that
      reads other objects still has its writer's sight checked, inside the write's transaction,
      with `A-29`'s tests unchanged and passing; and the next quiet `P-225` run records the
      difference.

      **P-235 outcome.** `Voucher.sees` is a `Sees`: either a `Visibility`, as before, or a
      function of a `Queryable` that resolves one. `writerFor` hands over the function, and
      `assertMayName` calls it with the write's own transaction, only after it has found
      something named.
      - Behind the function is the request's own memo: a `within(q)` beside `once()` in the
        per-request sight, sharing its `resolved`. A request that resolved its sight for another
        reason does not resolve it twice. One that resolves it here does so on the connection the
        transaction holds, against the same snapshot as the write.
      - A group, device or Ping create never resolves it.
      - A `PUBLIC` route's sight refuses when asked, as before. No `PUBLIC` route writes objects,
        so nothing there ever asks.
      - `A-29`'s tests build vouchers from a resolved `Visibility`, which is still a `Sees`, so
        none changed.

      **Tests.**
      - `object-visibility.test.ts` 1, through the API with authentication wired, spying on the
        server's `AccessService.visibilityFor`. An operator's group, device and Ping creates never
        call it. A factory naming a readable sensor calls it once, and not on the pool.
      - `sensor-reads.test.ts` 1, through the service: a deferred sight is not asked for a Ping.
        It is asked once each for a factory that is allowed and one that is refused, and neither
        time on the pool.

      The statement counts in the done-when are this removal exactly: the one statement gone is
      `visibilityFor`. They are left to `P-225`'s next quiet run, which wraps the driver. The
      affected suites pass, 255 tests across `sensor-reads`, `object-visibility`,
      `sensor-vouching`, `objects-service`, `api-routes`, `access-matrix`, `factory-service`,
      `audit-sweep`, `auth-api` and `discovery-scope`.

      Mutation 2/2, against the API test:
      - `writerFor` resolving eagerly again;
      - `within` resolving on the pool instead of the connection it is given.

- [x] **P-237 — the batch-size sweep's relative check is narrower than the case's run-to-run
      spread** · S · S-07, P-233 · Found in `P-233`'s window. `ingestion-performance.test.ts`
      asserts that the shipped 1,000-row batch writes with a lower p99 than the 5,000-row one, in
      the same run. Five sweeps of one commit, within four minutes, measured the shipped size's p99
      at 22.9, 285.6, 73.8, 24.2 and 38.2 ms, and one of them failed that check by 0.3 ms: 73.8
      against 73.5 (`findings/2026-09-29-probe-gate-ingestion.md`). A check that loses by 0.3 ms
      against a spread of 23 to 286 ms fails at random, and a `test:perf` that fails at random
      teaches people to stop reading it.

      **Done when** the comparison is robust, for example the median of several sweeps, or a
      margin taken from the measured spread and stated in the test, or it is dropped because the
      absolute budgets already carry the claim. The entry says which, and why.

      **Done: made robust, by comparing medians.** The check now asserts
      `shipped.p50 < largest.p50`, and the test states the measured margin beside it.
      - **Why the old one failed at random.** The sweep makes 100 writes at 1,000 rows and 20
        at 5,000. `stats()` takes index `floor(0.99 × n)`, which is the last index at both
        sizes, so each p99 was the single slowest write. The check compared two stalls.
      - **Why medians.** A median is taken over half the writes, which one stall does not move,
        and it is the latency a larger batch actually adds. That cost is the decision the check
        exists to guard.
      - **Why not drop it.** The absolute budgets do not carry that claim. They say the shipped
        size is fast enough, not that the default is not simply as large as it will go.

      **Measured deliberately under load**: five sweeps back to back, at 0.61 per CPU, with
      `ms-core` on the database. `perf-conditions` is recorded in
      `findings/2026-09-29-batch-sweep-median-under-load.md`.
      - **The medians separate.** The shipped size's median ran from 18.4 to 39.7 ms, the
        5,000-row size's from 102.1 to 160.5 ms, and the narrowest gap was 2.8×.
      - **The maxima do not.** In one sweep the 2,000-row size beat the shipped one at p99.
      - **The absolute budget failed three times and is not moved.** The shipped size's p99,
        the slowest of its 100 writes, went over 100 ms in three of the five sweeps (113.3 to
        135.8 ms). That is the phase criterion, which is measured on a quiet machine, and it
        held three of three in `P-233`'s quiet reruns. So a busy machine breaks a budget taken
        on a maximum. It is not a regression.

      **The same shape elsewhere**, as asked: every percentile in `packages/*/test/perf` taken
      over too few samples to be anything but the maximum. The full table is in the findings
      file.
      - **Absolute budgets on a maximum, noted.**
        - The sweep's own p99 budget.
        - The state machine's steady and flapping p99s: at most about 100 writes, and about 20.
        - The gate's worst batch, which already says it is a maximum.
      - **The replay soak: relative, compares maxima, left as it is.** Its quiet arm is 40
        batches, and a default run's replay arm is 15. But every live batch sits on the flush
        timer's ~263 ms floor, and failing its 3× budget needs a ~560 ms stall. That margin is
        fifty times the arm's measured spread, where this check had 0.3 ms, and a stall that
        large is what the case is for.
      - **The soak's quiet maximum does loosen the check.** Moving that arm to its median would
        change `R-08`'s recorded statistic. Decided: it stays as it is, because the check exists
        to catch the stall a maximum catches (WatchDog, 2026-09-29).
      - **Real percentiles.** `P-204`'s report-render p95 (184 and 161 samples) and the
        scheduler's p95 jitter (every dispatch) are genuine percentiles.

      `cloned` and `deleted`.

        and the dependency recompute.

        probe's clock, which only its sweep has.

        caught error aborted resolves with tag `ROLLBACK` and no error. `ReachabilitySync`'s catch
        can therefore answer success for a mutation that wrote nothing. Filed as `P-249`.

        still holds stays frozen and is not thawed. It is carried by that probe, and when two
        sets hold it, by whichever froze it last.

- [x] **P-240 — the ownership cache can keep a moved sensor's old probe** · S · P-228 · Found in
      review round four (`findings/2026-09-29-review-round-4.md`, `P-240`). Medium.
      `ResultCacheInvalidator.record` clears the ownership cache at once and again on a
      250 ms timer (`invalidation.ts:66`). The timer is not tied to the move's commit. If a
      move's sinks and commit take longer than 250 ms, an admit from the old probe in between
      re-reads the pre-move owner and caches it after the second clear. The old probe's results
      are then accepted, and the new probe's are refused as foreign, until something else
      clears the cache. At 5,000 sensors, with ScheduleSync's recompute in the sink chain, that
      is plausible but was not measured. `#forgetSensor` and `#forgetEverything` clear the
      channel and policy caches on the same timer.

      **Done when** all three clears also run after commit, through `q.afterCommit` as
      `probes/notifier.ts` does, and the timer is kept only for a `Queryable` without it. Test
      with a stub `afterCommit` and fake timers: an admit between the move and its commit
      caches the old owner, and the post-commit clear takes it out. Mutants as usual.

      **Done.** `ResultCacheInvalidator` still clears inside the mutation's transaction, and now
      clears a second time from `q.afterCommit`, as `probes/notifier.ts` does:
      - **All three clears.** That covers the owners on a move, the policies on a setting change
        or a move, and a sensor's channels, and everything on a delete.
      - **The 250 ms timer remains only for a `Queryable` without `afterCommit`**, which is a
        caller outside a transaction.
      - **Rollback.** A transaction that rolls back runs no second pass, which is `tx`'s contract,
        and changes nothing a cache could hold.

      **One step further than the ticket: a read in flight across the second clear.** The
      ownership cache already had the guard, and the channel and policy caches did not.
      - **The race.** A channel or policy read that began before the commit, and finished after
        the post-commit clear, put the old value back. That is the same silent failure, in a
        narrower window. The timer had it too.
      - **The fix.** `ChannelResolver` and `SensorStateService` now count their clears, and keep a
        read only if none happened while it ran.
      - **Returned even when not cached.** A policy read a clear overtook is still returned to
        the batch that asked for it. Falling back to the default policy there would be `P-86`'s
        false transition.

      **Tests.**
      - `cache-invalidation.test.ts` needs no database: a stub `Queryable` collects the commit
        hooks, and `node:test`'s fake timers stand in for the clock. It covers:
        - each cache cleared at the commit, and not by a timer, with a second of sinks between;
        - nothing a second time for a rollback;
        - the timer for a caller with no transaction;
        - no second pass after `stop()`;
        - the finding's own sequence against a real `SensorOwnership`: A's batch between the old
          timer and the commit caches A, and after the commit B is admitted, where it used to be
          refused as `moved`;
        - a channel read overtaken by a forget, and by a clear: used for its batch, and not
          cached.
      - `state-ingestion.test.ts`: a policy resolve overtaken by `forgetPolicies` and by `clear`
        is used for its batch (Down at the first failure under `retryWarnings = 0`), and not
        cached.

      **Mutations caught: 15 of 15.** Each was applied alone, built, and run against its own tests.
      - Four take out a part of the invalidator: the commit hook, the hook's body, `stop()`
        and the timer fallback.
      - Four take out a second pass, one each: channels, policies, owners, everything.
      - Seven take out a part of the new guards: the channel cache's count on a clear and on a
        forget, and its check before caching; the policy cache's count on a forget and on a
        clear, and its check before caching; and the batch using what it resolved.

      The first version of "always the timer" did not compile, because removing the check also
      removed TypeScript's narrowing, so it was rewritten to fall through to the timer.

        admitted for B, and a sensor that was in the group when it moved still reads as

        lock, and `created_at` is the database's at the start of the create's transaction. On

- [x] **P-242 — an on-demand check runs process-isolated types in the query pool** · S · P-236,
      S-19 · Found in review round four (`findings/2026-09-29-review-round-4.md`, `P-242`).
      - **Medium.** `QueryRunner.run` sends every type to the query worker pool
        (`queries/runner.ts:89`), including the types the dispatch tables run in a child
        process. So "check now" on `exe.script` runs in a worker without the script directory,
        and always answers a false "no script directory configured".
      - **Low, from the critic's spot check.** The query pool is built without `memoryCap` or
        `abortGraceMs` (`probe/src/main.ts:375-381`, compared with `:187-199`), outside
        `P-236`'s budget.

      **Done when:**
      - isolated types go to a query `ProcessRunner`: the same memory limit, uid, gid and child
        environment, one at a time, a bounded queue, and `busy` when it is full. If that is
        deferred, the query answers `unsupported` with the reason, and never runs them in a
        worker.
      - the query pool gets `memoryCap` and `abortGraceMs`.
      Test with a configured script directory: the answer carries the script's reading.
      Mutants as usual.

      **Outcome.** The isolated types run in a process on demand, and the second finding was
      verified first and holds only in half.
      - **A process runner of the query runner's own.** `QueryRunner` takes the isolated set
        from `dispatchTables()` and the scheduled process runner's isolation: memory limit, uid,
        gid and child environment, now one object in `main.ts` that both runners are built from.
        It runs one at a time behind the pool's queue bound, and a full queue is `busy` with the
        pool's words. It stops with no drain, as the pool does: the process runner would
        otherwise wait for a hung script inside a ten-second shutdown hook, `P-227` over again.
      - **`abortGraceMs`: real.** The query pool used the pool's own two seconds whatever
        `checkAbortGraceMs` said. The two agree at the default, so only a changed setting showed
        it. It is passed now.
      - **`memoryCap`: not passed, and why.** A pool of one never holds fewer than one worker,
        because the floor is at least one (`pool.ts`, `#ceiling`), so a cap cannot bind it. And
        that worker is already inside the check pool's budget: `MemoryCap` reads what memory is
        available from the cgroup, not what the pools add up to, so the query worker's resident
        memory is counted as used. Passing one would change nothing a test can see.

      **Tests** (`query-runner.test.ts`, with a real script directory and the real catalogue in
      the child):
      - the answer carries the script's reading, with nothing in this process's environment to
        lend it a script directory;
      - one at a time, and `busy` when the queue is full;
      - a stop answers a running script at once, `offline`;
      - a worker whose check ignores its abort is held for the configured grace, five seconds
        against the pool's own two, asserted as a wait not yet over so load cannot fail it.
      The `main.ts` wiring is covered by no unit test, as before.

      Mutation 6/6: isolated types sent to the pool; several scripts at once; an unbounded
      process queue; a stop that waits the script out; the pool keeping its own grace; the
      child given none of the isolation settings.

- [x] **P-243 — under CPU starvation at the memory limit, a 15 s ping misses a 30 s watchdog** ·
      M · P-220, P-215 · Found by `P-216c` (`docs/findings/2026-09-29-probe-starvation-c.md`).
      With load 72 on 8 CPUs and the box at 4,096 of 4,096 MiB, both services' main threads were
      held for 7–15 s at a time: sampler gaps up to 15.0 s, single blocks of 7.4 s, and GC up to
      3.7 s on a 30 MiB heap. The probe's interval timer then fired 30.4 s after its last ping,
      against `WatchdogSec=30`, and systemd killed it. The core, whose stdout was never stalled,
      reached 25.6 s in the same stage. Every ping that did start reached PID 1 in 48–700 ms, so
      the loss is in the timer, not in `systemd-notify`. A 15 s ping against 30 s leaves room for
      one late ping, and blocks that long use it up.

      Three answers, and the entry has to choose one and say why:
      - **The ping moves off the main thread.** Nearly free, and wrong on its face: a worker thread
        that pings while the main loop is hung is a watchdog that cannot see what it exists for.
        It would need the worker to ping only on proof of main-loop progress, which is the main
        thread again.
      - **The margin changes.** Ping at `WatchdogSec`/6, every 5 s, and the longest gap becomes the
        longest block plus 5 s: 20 s against these blocks. That keeps `WatchdogSec=30`, and so how
        soon a hung service is caught, and costs four more `systemd-notify` spawns a minute.
      - **Starvation that deep is correctly a kill.** Seven-to-fifteen-second stalls are a
        service not serving, but the restart lands on the same host, under the same load, and
        counts toward `P-215`'s start limit (`H-23`). So this answer needs showing that the
        restart helps.

      **Done when** the choice is made and measured in the `P-216` harness's starvation stages,
      under the same conditions: no watchdog kill of either service across three runs, and the
      pings sent against those received in the findings. If the answer is the kill, the findings
      show the restart helped. The core's 25.6 s is part of the acceptance, not only the probe's.

      **Done: the margin.** Both services ping every `WatchdogSec`/6, which is 5 s against the
      shipped 30, still from the main thread. The longest gap becomes the longest block plus
      5 s, rather than plus 15.
      - **Not off the main thread:** a watchdog that pings through a hung loop cannot see what
        it exists for.
      - **Not the kill:** the restart relieved nothing, and it counts toward `P-215`'s limit.

      Three runs of the `P-216` harness from one `d247b02` tarball: 0 kills. PID 1 received
      688 of 688 core pings and 689 of 689 probe pings, with no gap past 6.2 s against 30.

      **Milder than `P-216c`:** blocks up to 5.0 s against 7–15, and memory `some` up to 2.80%
      against 3.37%. So this shows the cadence holds under that stress, not under `P-216c`'s.
      The harness was not made harsher to force a kill.

      The stalled-log stage no longer stresses the log now that `P-216` part 3 summarises
      refusals. The runs predate `P-244`'s reserve.
      (`findings/2026-09-29-watchdog-cadence.md`)

- [x] **P-244 — the memory cap holds a saturated probe over `memoryLimitUsage`'s warning** · S ·
      P-236, M-21 · Found by `P-216c`. The cap keeps back 10% of the limit, so a saturated probe
      settles at about 90% of it: 89.9–94.7% in every stage of that run, the baseline included.
      Probe Health warns on `memoryLimitUsage` above 80%. Whether that is a problem depends on
      what it looks like to an operator:
      - **One warning per saturation episode**, beside `poolUsage`'s, clearing when the pool
        does, is one condition read two ways. It may be acceptable if the two are the same
        episode and one is suppressed.
      - **A standing warning** for as long as the workload keeps the pool saturated, which on a
        probe whose targets are down can be days, is an alarm-volume problem. It is also a
        warning that has stopped meaning "about to be killed", which is the only thing it was
        for.

      Candidate fixes: a reserve of the larger of 256 MiB and 25% of the limit, so the cap stops
      under the warning; or the limit channel's warning set relative to the cap. **Done when** a
      scenario test drives a saturated, capped probe through Probe Health's sweep and ingestion,
      the entry says which of the two it is and which fix, and the test shows one alarm for one
      saturation.

      **Done: the second, a standing warning, and it was true.** The workers stay until the pool
      shrinks, so the warning outlived the saturation, and `poolUsage` was already Down for the
      saturation itself. The warning was also right: its limit is where `P-206`'s surge (14% of
      the ceiling in five seconds) stops fitting, and the cap was parking the probe past it.
      **Fixed with the reserve**, now the larger of 256 MiB and 25%, moved to `@ms/shared` as
      `memoryReserveBytes` so the core's test uses the real arithmetic. A saturated probe now
      settles at or under 75% of its ceiling, clear of the 80% warning. On the machine path it
      stays above `memoryAvailable`'s 20% warning, where at a tenth it sat on the 10% error.
      Not the other fix: the declared limits are static per channel, and a warning that moves
      with the cap would stop warning at 90%, where the surge kills. The cost is workers while
      memory binds: at 6 GiB, about 107 rather than 130.

      **Uncapped, because the limits are fractions too.** Assuming 40 MiB a worker, 300 MiB
      besides and the 256-worker ceiling, a saturated pool settles at:
      - **1 GiB:** 256 MiB kept back (the floor), 11 workers, 72.3%.
      - **4 GiB:** 1 GiB kept back, 69 workers, 74.7%.
      - **16 GiB:** 4 GiB kept back, and never reached. Memory would hold 299 workers, so the
        ceiling binds first at 256, which is 64.3%.

      `max(256 MiB, min(25%, 1 GiB))` gives the same three numbers. It differs only between
      them, and there it is wrong: the stock 6 GiB settles at 83.0% with 120 workers, and
      8 GiB at 87.2%. Every ceiling above 5 GiB would be back over the warning. On a probe
      with no ceiling of its own, it would let a 16 GiB machine fall to 6% available, under
      `memoryAvailable`'s 10% error. The test is
      `saturated-memory-cap-scenario.test.ts`, which runs Probe Health through ingestion and the
      state machine for a probe on a ceiling and one on the machine: calm, two saturations, and
      the full idle pool between them. Each history reads up, down, up, down, up, with nothing
      about memory in a Down. With a tenth, the probe on a ceiling reads up, down, warning, down, warning, at 89.5% of its limit: the standing warning `P-216c` saw.

- [x] **P-245 — `P-219`'s memory fold outlives its record window, and is folded twice** · S ·
      P-219 · Found in review round 4b (`findings/2026-09-29-review-round-4b.md`, `P-245`).
      - **Medium** (`probe-endpoint.ts:1567`), found by two areas. `#foldMemory` keeps a running
        minimum per probe, and only a Probe Health record takes it. A probe with no Probe Health,
        a withheld one, or one created days later therefore records a low from days before as
        its first reading, which is a fresh Down.
      - **Low** (`probe/src/health/report.ts:333`). A low the core already folded is folded
        again when its ack has not reached the probe (a lost ack, or a stalled loop), so one
        squeeze lands in two records.

      **Done when** every sweep drains every fold, so a fold only ever holds the lows since the
      last sweep, including on the no-sensor early return. The double count is either made
      idempotent per heartbeat seq, on protocol 23 (allocated if you take it), or accepted as
      at-least-once with the reason in the entry and administration.md. Tests for each of the
      four ways into the stale fold. Mutants as usual.

      **P-245 outcome.**
      - **The endpoint's `drainMemory()` replaces `takeMemory(probe)`.** It takes every probe's
        fold at once and empties them all. Probe Health's sweep calls it first, before anything
        that can skip a record, and shares the result among the sensors on each probe.
      - **So a fold holds only the lows since the last sweep.** A low no record takes is let go,
        and is a gap. That covers every way the sweep can pass a probe by: no sensor on it, no
        sensors at all, a withheld sensor, one naming no probe, `M-22`'s boot grace, and a sweep
        that failed, which the findings did not list.
      - **The double count is accepted as at-least-once, and protocol 23 is not taken.** A low is
        folded twice only when the probe never read the ack for its heartbeat. The next record
        then repeats a low that did happen, so a Warning or Down lasts one record longer, or
        comes back for one record.
        - Exactly once would need each unacknowledged low on the wire with its seq. The core
          would keep the highest seq it folded, and would need a probe process identity to reset
          that after a restart, because the seq starts again. The protocol has no such identity.
        - That is two protocol changes to save one record, in a case that needs a lost or unread
          ack to meet a low near a limit.
        - `administration.md` says it, and says what a heartbeat no record takes becomes.
          `P-219`'s outcome is amended where it claimed exactly once.

      **Tests.**
      - `probe-health.test.ts` 7, in a table: a fold of 4% and a sweep that records nothing of
        the probe, then a report of 60% and an ordinary sweep, which records 60 and not 4. There
        is one row for each way in above, and each asserts the skipping sweep drained. The
        control: 4 then 60 with no sweep between records 4.
      - The 6 `P-219` fold tests are moved to the drain. They take a map, and "taken once for its
        two sensors" is "drained once in the sweep".

      - **A name that resolves to nothing fails the check** with "did not resolve", naming the

        `::ffff:10.1.1.1`, and that is unwrapped in any spelling, hex included. Before this, such
        a sender missed even a device whose host was the literal `10.1.1.1`.
      - **IPv6.** Other IPv6 addresses take the URL standard's form: lower case, zeros
        compressed. An operator's `2001:DB8:0::1` matches a socket's `2001:db8::1`.
      - **Zones.** A zone is kept, because it names the link.

      `10.1.` rule is matched against the unwrapped sender too. It had the same defect: nothing
      from a dual-stack listener starts with `10.1.`.

        `throw`s.
      - The three "only this device" descriptions say a name is looked up on the probe, and that
        one resolving to nothing fails the check. `sensor-reference.md` is regenerated.
      - The simulators' `sendUdp` and `exportNetflowV5` send from `udp6` for an IPv6 target.
      - The flow half lands here, so `B-07` need not carry it, as the finding suggested.

        - eleven spellings;
        - literals of both families asking nothing;
        - one lookup per name per TTL, in either case, and the renumbered answer after it;
        - failures and empty answers asked again;
        - a blank host;
        - the "did not resolve" refusal;
        - a sender compared in canonical form.

        syslog over UDP and TCP from `@ms/simulators`, traps from `net-snmp`, and NetFlow v5 from
        the simulator's exporter. Each suite covers:
        - senders from `127.0.0.1` and `::1`, with the wrapped IPv4 source asserted as the
          premise;
        - the device by name (`localhost`), for an IPv4 sender and an IPv6 one;
        - the device by address in four spellings, asserting which sender counted;
        - `no-such-device.invalid` failing, flow's "silence is idle" included, where it used to
          read zero for ever;
        - no lookup at all with "only this device" off.

        produces. That is why it passed for the wrong reason. Its helpers now default to an

        - `::ffff:` never unwrapped;
        - the pattern unanchored, so `1::ffff:…` is taken for IPv4;
        - the octets swapped within each word;
        - IPv6 left as typed;
        - the zone dropped;
        - the sender not trimmed.

        - a literal sent to the lookup;
        - a literal left uncanonical;
        - the answers left uncanonical;
        - no cache;
        - `<=` at the TTL;
        - a case-sensitive key;
        - a failure cached;
        - an empty answer cached;
        - `ttlMs` ignored;
        - a blank host looked up;
        - the untrimmed name looked up.

      - **In the types, 6:**

        - each of the three types resolving with "only this device" off;
        - the trap rules shown the raw sender.

      - **Medium** (`ingestion/service.ts:703`). A core whose clock is more than 15 minutes slow

        `shares.ts:73`), and the probe's discovery token bucket (`discovery/sweep.ts:247`). A
        clock step reads as a stalled sweep, locks clients out, or freezes a discovery run.
      - **Critic, unverified.** The login throttle's persisted timestamps keep an address blocked
        across a backward step. Clamp future-dated values to now. Also check the four sites the
        findings doc lists.

        more), and the Probe Health clock warnings stand down while it does, as `M-21` does for

      - unparseable timestamps are counted on Core Health;

      **Done.**
      - **The core names its own clock.** `health/core-clock.ts` judges it once, for both
        sweeps, from the live links. If two or more connected remote probes all read ahead by
        more than a minute, the fault is the core's. The local probe reads the core's clock, so
        it is left out. With fewer than two remote probes the reading gaps.
      - **Core Health's `clockBehind`** gives the smallest lead among the remote probes. It warns
        at 60 s, where Probe Health's `clockOffset` warns, and errors at 900 s, where ingestion
        refuses everything. A test pins both limits to those two sources.
      - **Each Probe Health stands down while Core Health owns it.** Its `clockOffset` and
        `resultsFutureDated` gap, and its sentence gives the offset in words, as `M-21` does for
        memory.
      - **Scenario test** (`core-clock-scenario.test.ts`, with a local probe and three remote
        probes, through both sweeps, ingestion and the state machine):
        - every probe 20 min ahead: one alarm, Core Health Down;
        - every probe 2 min ahead: Core Health Warning alone;
        - one probe ahead: that probe's Probe Health alone;
        - one remote probe connected: Core Health stays Up;
        - two remote probes and the local one: Core Health's again.
      - **Unparseable timestamps** are counted as results before the error branch, in
        `discardedUnreadableTime`, and logged once a batch. They show on Core Health's
        `resultsUnreadableTime`, which warns above 0.
      - **Monotonic now, each with a clock-step test:**
        - the alarm scheduler's `overdueMs`, which Core Health takes as it is;
        - both rate limiters, where `x-ratelimit-reset` stays a Unix time;
        - the discovery sweep's bucket and progress;
        - the identify runner, the replay pacer and the HTTP delivery deadline, three of the
          critic's four.
      - **The fourth, `schedules/sweep.ts`, stays on the wall clock.** It aligns to the minute
        of a schedule's wall-clock boundaries and costs at most one late minute.
      - **The critic's login throttle finding was real.** Failures stamped before a backward step
        stayed in the window. The check now rewrites future-dated rows to now, in the same
        round trip, and reads them as now.
      - **Mutants:** 14, one per change, each killed by its test. Five first survived: their
        tests replaced `Date.now` after the code had captured it. They now replace it before.
      - **With fewer than two connected remote probes, a slow core still reads as the probe's
        fault.** One probe ahead cannot be told apart from one probe whose own clock is ahead.
        So `clockBehind` gaps and the operator sees that probe's Probe Health warn on
        `clockOffset` and, past 15 minutes, `resultsFutureDated`, naming the probe. The fix
        the operator reaches for, the probe host's time sync, does not clear it. The
        administration guide says to check the core's clock when that happens.
      - **While `clockBehind` stands, results are still refused as future-dated**, so every
        sensor on a remote probe holds its last state. The core cannot know which clock is
        right, so it keeps refusing. The freeze adds no alarm of its own: the sensors are not
        Unknown, `delivering` stays 1 because results still arrive, and `ClockFreeze` needs a
        probe behind, not ahead. So Core Health's one alarm is the whole of it, and its error
        message says that no sensor on a remote probe is being updated.
      - **Heavy run: one load failure.** Core 3855 of 3856, probe 390 of 390. The one failure was
        alarm-scheduler's "waits out a latency and then fires" (33 s against its 20 s wait). This
        change does not touch that path, and the file alone passed three times of three.

- [ ] **P-251 — the batch-size sweep's p99 budget is its slowest write** · S · P-237, S-07 ·
      Found by `P-237` (`findings/2026-09-29-batch-sweep-median-under-load.md`). Low.
      - **The p99 is the last index.** The sweep writes 100,000 readings at each size, which is
        100 writes at the shipped 1,000 rows. `Ingestor.stats()` takes the p99 at index
        `floor(0.99 × n)`, the last of the 100. So the phase's "p99 write inside 100 ms" is a
        budget on the maximum.
      - **Under load it failed three of five.** At 0.61 per CPU, with `ms-core` connected, the
        sweep went over at 121.4, 135.8 and 113.3 ms. The median never went above 39.7 ms, and
        `P-233`'s quiet reruns held three of three.

      **Done when** the budget is one of two things, whichever costs the default `test:perf`
      less wall time:
      - a real percentile, with at least 200 writes per size so the p99 is not the last index;
      - reported as "max" and budgeted as a maximum.
      The entry says which, and why.

      **Measured 2026-10-17 in a quiet window** (`findings/2026-10-17-batch-sweep-quiet-window.md`).
      Even quiet, the shipped size's "p99", its slowest write, went over 100 ms in two sweeps of
      five (102.3 and 200.7 ms), while its median stayed at 14 to 20 ms. Over 300 writes at the
      shipped size, a real p99 held three of three, at 35.6 to 49.4 ms. A maximum costs no wall
      time but cannot keep the 100 ms number. A real percentile at the shipped size alone costs
      about 2 to 4 s. The findings recommend the second.

- [x] **P-252 — `notification-timers` reads an idle sample the database pool can spoil** ·
      S · P-229 · Found 2026-10-04 by `P-229`. Its "2 timers with 2000 pending, 1 idle" case
      failed twice under load and passed on `main` and on `P-229` alike with nothing else
      running: whether it passes depends on whether the pool's idle-client timers are still
      pending when the idle sample is taken. **Done when** the sample counts only the
      notifier's own timers, or waits for the pool to be idle, and passes ten runs in a row
      beside one other container.

      **P-252 outcome.** Worse than the ticket said: **the count never saw the notifier's timer at
      all.** `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` names only the handles keeping the process alive,
      and the scheduler `unref`s its timer, so every sample counted the database pool's idle
      clients, each of which holds a 10 s idle timer in `pg-pool`, and nothing else. The arming
      wakes the scheduler, whose sweep takes a second client while the scan holds one, so the
      pool sometimes held one more client at the armed sample than at the idle one: the
      failure. A design with an `unref`'d timer per notification would have passed. The same
      count was in `alarm-scheduler.test.ts`.
      - **Fix**: `test/support/notifier-timers.ts`. `watchNotifierTimers` wraps `setTimeout`
        and `clearTimeout` for the test and counts the live timers started from
        `src/notifications/`, `unref`'d included; `otherTimers` keeps the old process-wide
        count, less the pool's idle clients read in the same turn. Both tests use them and wait
        to see the scheduler's timer before relying on the count. The perf test grows the pool
        to four clients before the armed sample, so the old spoil happens on every run.
      - **Measured**: twelve runs in a row beside another toolchain container, load 4–8: notifier
        timers 1, 1 (0 once, between cycles), 1; other timers 0, 0, 0. With an `unref`'d timer
        per sensor in the engine it reads 10,001 and fails, where the old count read 0. The old
        count fails every run once the pool is grown (5 against 2).
        `docs/findings/2026-08-26-notification-timers.md` carries a correction: its "2 idle, 2
        pending" were pool timers.

- [x] **P-249 — a mutation that failed inside its transaction is answered as committed** · M ·
      P-103, P-111 · Found 2026-09-29 while designing `P-239`'s failure path, and measured.
      **High**: a silent loss behind a success answer.
      - **Measured** with node-pg against the test database. The sequence was `BEGIN`, an
        `INSERT`, a `SELECT 1/0` whose error is caught, then `COMMIT`. The `COMMIT` resolves with
        no error and command tag `ROLLBACK`, and the row is not there. PostgreSQL rolls back a
        transaction an error has aborted, and says so only in the tag.
      - **`Database.transaction()` never reads the tag** (`db/pool.ts:179`). It returns the
        callback's result as if it had committed. `tx()` then runs every `afterCommit` hook for a
        transaction that wrote nothing.
      - **So a catch inside someone else's transaction is a silent loss.** `ReachabilitySync`
        catches any error from `resync`, so as not to fail the mutation
        (`reachability-sync.ts:54`). A failed statement in there leaves the mutation's
        transaction aborted. If nothing after it queries, the object service answers success, and
        the move, its audit row and every other sink's write are gone. The after-commit hooks
        announce a commit that did not happen. No other sink or catch site has been audited.

      **Done when:**
      - `transaction()` throws a `DatabaseError` when `COMMIT`'s command is `ROLLBACK`, and no
        `afterCommit` hook runs for it;
      - a `savepoint(fn)` helper exists for code that must catch a database error inside
        someone else's transaction;
      - every audit sink, and every other catch inside a transaction, is listed, and each one
        either moves into a savepoint or rethrows;
      - there is a test for each half. With a savepoint, a sink that fails a statement and catches
        leaves the mutation committing. Without one, the API answers an error, not success.

      Owner: after `P-229`, which is changing `db/pool.ts` now. `P-239`'s `ClockFreezeSync`
      rethrows already.

      **Decided 2026-10-04 by WatchDog**, on Roman's "you decide".
      **`P-229` is finished first**: its
      session asked only for leave to start its full run while at most one other run is on the
      VM, and that is given. Its branch `p229-wip` (35 files, uncommitted, in the
      `elastic-shannon-539fbe` worktree) is rebased on `main`, run whole, landed, and then this
      ticket is taken. **And `v1.0.0-rc.1` is not cut until both have landed:** a candidate
      that can answer a lost write as committed would spend `H-09`'s week finding it.

      **P-249 outcome.** `Database.tx` and `transaction()` read the `COMMIT`'s command tag, and a
      `ROLLBACK` throws a `DatabaseError` with SQLSTATE `25P02` (`SQLSTATE.inFailedTransaction`,
      `phase: commit`, `abortedBy`/`abortedBySqlstate` naming the first failure no savepoint
      undid); no `afterCommit` hook runs, and the API answers it as a masked 500. `savepoint(q, fn)`

      there is none): a throw rolls back to it and is rethrown, an `fn` that caught its own failure

      inside are kept only if it is released. Nested savepoints are named apart.

      hook, a savepoint rolled back or released with its hooks, one whose work caught its own
      failure, nesting, the pool; and through the API, a sink catching without a savepoint is a 500

      - *Medium.* `resync` changed `#byProbe`, `#unreachable` and `#carrier` inside the mutation's
        transaction, and nothing undid it when a later sink (`ClockFreezeSync`, `TriggerSync`) or
        the `COMMIT` rolled the mutation back. A sensor left under its live probe was then held

        or its `COMMIT` answers `ROLLBACK`. A savepoint runs its own when it is rolled back to, and
        hands them to the enclosing transaction when it is released. `resync` registers one that

        being owed only once the transaction that re-decided them commits.

        until its next result. A result decided while the move was open misses the cache
        (`reevaluate` dropped the moved sensor's entry), reads the committed row on its own
        connection, and lays the moved overlay over it. The state service then caches that, and
        `decide` folds the cached facts and never re-reads the overlay. So a sensor still under
        its live probe was decided Unknown from that cache for every result the probe sent.
        It stayed so until a transition or an eviction dropped the entry, and a sensor behind a
        lost probe sends no result at all. `resync`'s undo now drops what it re-decided from
        the state service's cache (`forgetSensors`, on a `ReachabilityStates` that only the
        reachability asks for). It also owes those sensors a re-decision, which the delivery
        sweep's `retryGivenUp` makes against the overlay as it is again.
      - **A read that straddles the rollback, and a sweep already in flight** (both found by
        the review). A cold read whose rows arrived before the undo and whose policy read
        finished after it caches the moved overlay, and the undo had nothing to forget. A
        re-decision that moves nothing would leave that entry deciding the sensor Unknown for
        every result. So a settlement, the sweep's or a resync's, now drops what it settles from
        the cache. And a sweep that read what was owed before a rollback owed it again cleared
        the new owing when it committed a decision made against the rolled-back overlay. Each
        owing is now numbered, and a settlement clears only the owings it read.
      - **`claim`: under a savepoint.** Handed a transaction, the unique violation that means
        "already running" aborted it: the caller answered busy and then lost its other writes to
        a `25P02` at commit. It costs nothing on the pool, which is every caller today.
      - **`publish` and `publishProbe`: the pool, by type.** A savepoint would hide the abort but
        still read what has not committed, which `afterCommit` exists to prevent (`U-02`). Both
        now take `StreamPool` (`Pick<Database, 'query' | 'tx'>`). A transaction's executor has
        no `tx`, so the compiler refuses one. The test fakes gained a `tx`.
      - **Tests.**
        - `probe-offline.test.ts`: a result is decided while the move is open and comes out
          Unknown. After the rollback it is forgotten and owed, the live probe's next result is
          Up, and the sweep settles it and drops it from the cache. A second case holds a sweep
          after it has read what is owed, rolls a second move back, and the second owing
          outlasts that sweep.
        - `report-runs.test.ts`: a claim inside `db.tx` answers busy, and the transaction still
          commits its other write.
        - `state-stream.test.ts`: at the type level, `Queryable` is refused and `Database` is
          taken, for both methods.
      - **Mutants 9/9:** the undo forgets nothing, or owes nothing; a give-up owes nothing (the
        `#owe` refactor); an owing already held is not renewed; a settlement clears any owing,
        or forgets nothing; `claim` without the savepoint; `publish` or `publishProbe` back on
        `Queryable`.
      - **Left to new tickets:** the Core Health reading (`P-400`) and the build-hygiene guard
        (`P-401`). The line numbers `P-249` cites for `stream.ts` and `main.ts` had gone stale;
        the methods are named above.

- [ ] **P-401 — nothing stops a `catch` inside a transaction that swallows without a savepoint**
      · M · P-253 · Found 2026-10-04 by `P-249`'s review, left by `P-253`. A failed statement
      aborts a PostgreSQL transaction, so a `catch` that does not rethrow leaves its caller's
      transaction unusable and every write in it lost at commit. `P-253` fixed the three sites
      in `src`. The durable guard is a build-hygiene check, and it needs the TypeScript
      syntax tree, not a regex. It looks at a `try` that uses a parameter of an enclosing
      function typed `Queryable` or `PoolClient`, or the first parameter of a callback passed to
      `tx`, `transaction`, `withClient`, `savepoint` or `#txOrPreview`. It flags a `catch` that
      can finish without a `throw`, unless every use of that parameter inside the `try` is
      within a `savepoint(…)` call. Two known false positives, each an allow-list entry with
      its reason, keyed by file and function:
      - `probes/clock-freeze.ts` `ClockFreeze.#settle`: `if (caller !== undefined) throw error;
        return 0;`, where the `return` runs only after its own `tx` rolled back.
      - `probes/reachability.ts` `resync`: its re-decision `try` passes `q` to `#settled`, which
        only registers `afterCommit` and runs no statement.

      **Done when** the check runs in `build-hygiene.test.ts` with a floor and planted cases,
      and it reports only the allow-listed sites on the current tree.

- [x] **P-403 — `exe.script.advanced`'s primary never takes the program's name** · XS · P-402 ·
      Found 2026-10-17 by `P-402`. `primaryName` says "Empty uses whatever the program calls
      it". The channel is created with its sensor, before any program has run, so it is named by
      its key (`createChannels` writes the declaration, whose name is the key when `primaryName`
      is empty). Ingestion never renames an existing row. So only a primary whose row a reading
      creates — after an edit that changes `primaryChannel` — ever takes the program's name.
      **Done when** decided: let the first reading that names an existing primary still named by
      its key rename it (a write on the ingestion path, audited), or change the description to
      say the key is used.

      **Decided 2026-10-17 by the user:** the first reading that names an existing primary still
      named by its key renames it, a write on the ingestion path, audited. **Done when** that
      rename is in place, with a test, rather than a change to the description.

      **P-403 outcome. The first reading that names a primary still named by its key renames it,
      once, in the batch's own transaction.**
      - **The rule** (`nameFromReading`, `ingestion/channels.ts`). The row is its sensor's
        primary and named by its key. The sensor's own stored parameters make that key primary
        and name it by its key or not at all. A reading names it something other than its key.
        Then the name is the reading's, and so is the unit where neither the row nor the
        declaration has one: what a reading that created the row would have written
        (`channelLabel`), so a primary a create made and one a reading made end the same.
        - **Once.** Afterwards the row is not named by its key, so a later name, warm or cold,
          is not taken. Emptying `primaryName` names it by its key again (the edit), and the next
          reading that names it renames it, which is what "Empty uses whatever the program calls
          it" says.
        - **Never a person's name.** No route writes a channel's name; a person names one
          through a parameter, which is the declaration. A `primaryName` makes the declared name
          something of its own, and the row holds it. A row an older build named by its key while
          a name of its own is declared is left for the start-up pass (`P-404`), which writes the
          declared one.
        - **Never on a fallback's word**, nor an unregistered type's: neither says anything.
        - **Only the primary**, as decided. A declared non-primary channel named by its key
          stays so.
      - **The cost, at 5,000 sensors a minute.** A cached reading pays `reading.name !==
        undefined`, and only a reading that names something pays two more comparisons against
        the cached row. `is_primary` rides in the query that already reads the row. No query is
        issued unless a reading names a primary still named by its key. One left as it is (a
        name of its own, a fallback, already renamed) is held in memory (`#nameSettled`) until
        the sensor is forgotten or the core restarts. So the common case adds no statement, which
        a statement count in `declared-labels.test.ts` pins with a declaring resolver (see
        Review).
      - **An edit of a sensor's parameters now forgets the sensor** (`ResultCacheInvalidator`),
        as a channel's entry already did. Without it, a refusal outlived the edit that undid its
        reason (an emptied `primaryName`, parameters the type can answer for again) whenever the
        edit rewrote no channel, until a restart. An edit that changes no parameter, such as a
        rename of the sensor, forgets nothing. It costs one query on the next batch, per edit,
        and one pass over the cache per audit call (see Review).
      - **The write.** In the batch's own transaction: the `object` rows `FOR NO KEY UPDATE SKIP
        LOCKED`, then `sensor_config`, then the channel rows, the edit's order. `SKIP LOCKED`
        because the batch may already hold other sensors from `#create`, and a second wait in its
        own order could cross another batch's. A held sensor is not settled; the next reading that
        names it tries again. Everything is decided again under the lock, so two batches never
        both rename it. The version moves by trigger, and this batch's readings carry the new
        name.
      - **The actor is `ingestion`** (`{ kind: 'system', component: 'ingestion' }`), the one that
        moves a primary a reading created (`P-314`): a reading did it, and no person. Each rename
        is a `channel.redeclared` entry through `ingestionAuditSinks`, as the start-up passes'
        are (`P-323` by `declared-primary-startup-repair`, `P-402` by
        `declared-label-startup-repair`). `S-18`'s limits pass writes no entry at all. The
        sinks' invalidator forgets the sensor, so the next batch reads the name once.
      - **No migration.** "Named by its key" is the whole mark.
      - **Tests.** `declared-labels.test.ts`, 18 cases.
        - 13 table cases of `nameFromReading`.
        - 5 against the database:
          - through a warm cache, once, audited by `ingestion`, the version moved, and the batch
            and the next one carrying the new name;
          - on a cold read after a restart, keeping a unit the row has;
          - a person's `primaryName`, a row an older build named by its key under a declared
            name, and a declared non-primary channel are all kept, and emptying `primaryName`
            lets the next reading name it;
          - a fallback and an unregistered type are left; afterwards a settled primary, a
            renamed one, a named channel that is not primary and a reading that names the
            primary by its key cost no statement warm, and only the read of the rows cold;
          - a held sensor is skipped without waiting, and renamed at the next reading;
          - once a forget follows parameters the type can answer for, the next reading renames
            a primary that had been left.
        - `cache-invalidation.test.ts`: an edit that changed a parameter forgets the sensor, now
          and at the commit, and one that changed none forgets nothing; 5,001 sensors of one call
          are forgotten in one pass with one hook; `forgetMany` drops only the sensors it names.
      - **Review.** Three findings, all fixed.
        - **A forget a sensor was a scan of the cache a sensor.** A move or a clone that clears
          thousands of sensors' own secrets records an `object.updated` for each in one audit
          call (`#clearSecretsSentElsewhere`), and the new branch forgot each in turn, inside the
          mover's transaction and again after it: seconds of blocked event loop, twice. The
          invalidator now gathers the sensors of a call and forgets them once, with one hook for
          the commit, through `ChannelResolver.forgetMany`, which walks the cache, the settled
          set and `#outsideLater` once each. `forget` is `forgetMany` of one. The channel
          entries' forgets go the same way.
        - **The unit rule's declared half was untested**: the table case named for it gave the
          row the declared unit already. A case with a row with no unit under a declared one now
          expects none.
        - **The cost claim was pinned less than said.** `ingestion.test.ts`'s cache test builds
          its resolver without a declaration, so `#nameFromReadings` issues nothing there
          whatever the filters do. The statement count now sends, warm and cold, a name on a
          channel that is not primary and a reading that names the primary by its key.
      - **Mutants 29/29:**
        - The rule: `is_primary`, the name being the key, a reading naming it by its key, a
          fallback, the declared primary's key, or a declared name of its own ignored; the unit
          always the reading's.
        - The resolver: a cached reading or a cold row never wanting a name; `is_primary` not
          carried in the cache; the lock waiting instead of `SKIP LOCKED`; the settled set not
          consulted, not added to, or kept by `forget`; no forget after a rename; the renaming
          batch keeping the key; no audit entry; the UPDATE writing only the unit.
        - The invalidator: an edit of parameters forgetting nothing.
        - Review: the invalidator forgetting a sensor at a time; `forgetMany` dropping every
          sensor, matching ids by their first digits, or keeping a settled refusal; no forget
          after a rename; the unit rule without its declared half; the cached path or the cold
          path without `isPrimary`; `#wantName` without its by-key return.
      - **Docs.** `adding-a-sensor-type.md`, and `channel.redeclared`'s comment lists its system
        writers. `primaryName`'s description needed no change: it is true now.

- [x] **P-405 — a declared channel name over 200 characters, or empty, refuses the sensor** · S ·
      P-402 · Found 2026-10-17 by `P-402`'s review. `channel.name` holds 1 to 200 characters
      (its CHECK), and nothing checks a type's declaration against that. `P-402` fits a declared
      name and unit where ingestion creates the row (`channelLabel`, `fitLabel`). Every other
      writer passes the declaration as it is.
      - `createChannels` and `createChannelsFor` (`objects/repository.ts`): a create and a
        tree create (`createTree`).
      - The edit's re-declaration (`planRedeclaration`), which writes `after.name`.
      So an `http.transaction` step with no name, which is named by its path (up to 2,048
      characters), fails the create with a CHECK violation rather than a 400 that says why, and
      an edit that moves a step to such a path fails the same way. A type that declares an empty
      name fails it too. A unit has no CHECK, so a unit refuses nothing. They already differ in
      one case. `fitLabel` counts UTF-16 units, as `clip` does for the wire. The CHECK counts
      code points. So a declared name over 200 UTF-16 units that fits in 200 code points — one
      character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is enough (an `ssh.script` name allows 200
      code points) — is written whole by a create and clipped by ingestion. **Done when** every writer of a declared name or unit fits it as
      `channelLabel` does (an empty one standing aside for the key), counting as the column
      does, the ingestion path and the create path cannot drift (one function), and a test
      creates and edits an `http.transaction` sensor whose unnamed step has a 2,048-character
      path.

      **P-405 outcome. One rule for every writer, counted as the column counts.**
      - **The rule.** `declaredLabel(key, name, unit)` in `state/declared-limits.ts` fits the
        name to 200 and the unit to 50 (`fitLabel`), and makes an empty name the key.
        - `draftsOf` (`objects/sensor-type-gate.ts`) calls it. That covers a create, a tree
          create and an edit's re-declaration, which all write from those drafts.
        - `channelLabel` calls it too. That covers ingestion and `P-402`'s repair.
        - So one function names a channel whichever of them writes it.
        - The catalogue still returns exactly what a type declared. Fitting is the core's
          concern, for its column.
      - **Code points.** `fitLabel` now counts as the column's `length()` and the wire's
        `maxLength` do, and never cuts a pair. `clip` still counts UTF-16 units for the wire,

- [x] **P-254 — a trap or syslog message before a sensor's first scan is counted by nobody** ·
      S · T-06, T-20 · Found 2026-10-04 by `H-15`
      (`findings/2026-10-04-field-test-dress-rehearsal.md`). After a probe restart, the
      listener starts receiving at once. Each sensor's cursor is registered only at its first
      scan, and `Ring.drain` registers it at the *current* sequence, so everything already in the
      ring is skipped.
      - Observed: three traps sent 41 s after the restart were counted in Probe Health's
        `trapReceived`, and in neither trap sensor's `count` or `dropped`.
      - Three sent once the cursors existed were counted.
      - That is up to one scan interval of traps or syslog per sensor per restart, lost without
        a count. A device rebooting alongside the probe sends exactly then. The comment in
        `ring.ts` says a first scan "has genuinely received nothing", and the listener had.

      **Done when** a sensor's first drain after a listener starts reads from the listener's
      start (or a message received before the first scan is counted as `dropped`), with a test
      that sends before the first drain and asserts the count.

      **P-254 outcome (2026-10-07).** `NotificationRing` (`listeners/ring.ts`, shared by the trap,
      syslog and flow listeners) now tells apart the three reasons a sensor has no cursor:
      - **A probe restart.** The sensor is in the first set the probe hands `retain`, or it
        drains before any set was handed. Its first drain reads from sequence 0, with `since` set
        to the listener's start. Whatever the ring overwrote before then is that sensor's
        `dropped`.
      - **A sensor new to a running probe** (in a later set, not the first). It starts at its
        first drain with nothing and nothing dropped, as before.
      - **A cursor `retain` removed** (deleted, paused, moved). It leaves the restart set too, so
        it returns as new, whether or not it had scanned before it left.

      `retain` is handed every held sensor of every type, so the first set is kept as candidates,
      not cursors. A ping sensor in it costs one number and claims nothing.

      **Probe Health stays once a record.** An overwrite with no cursor behind it goes to an
      unclaimed count rather than `unread`. The first restart sensor that drains moves it into
      `unread`, so `trapOverwritten`/`syslogOverwritten` still equal what the slowest sensor
      reports `dropped`, and that loss is added at the scan rather than as it happened. No new
      channel and no message shape change, so no protocol bump. `docs/administration.md`'s row
      says so.

      Tests:
      - **`ring.test.ts` (new).** Restart before the first set and after it (`H-15`'s two
        sensors 9 s apart), a reconnect's re-push, overflow counted once across two sensors,
        what one sensor read and the other had not, no double count after a sensor was behind;
        new sensor before and after the sweep names it, with no loss claimed; a removed sensor
        returning, having scanned or not.
      - **The listener tests.** Trap, syslog and flow each send before the first drain and
        assert the count. The older cases that meant "new sensor" now say so with `retain`.
      - **`probe-listeners.test.ts`.** A case starts `ms-probe`, has `FakeCore` hold the config
        (`holdConfig`/`sendConfig`), sends three traps and three syslog messages, then sends the
        config. Each sensor's first scan reads 3.

      **Mutations 10/10**, run against the six listener unit files, and the first one also
      against the probe case: restart reads from now; every sensor new after the first set; no
      sensor a restart one before it; the claim not moved into `unread`; moved twice; unclaimed
      never kept; kept for counted records too; `since` now; every set treated as the first; a
      sensor that left stays a restart candidate.

      **Review, 2026-10-07: two defects and a test gap, fixed in a second commit.**
      - **A restart reads one interval back, not to the listener's start.** Read to the start,
        a probe that waited two hours for its core handed every sensor's first scan two hours
        as one reading. Trap `count` and syslog `messages` are per-scan counts, and their limits
        are set per interval, so every limited sensor would alarm on the reconnect: many alarms
        for one outage. Calling the excess `dropped` instead would fail every sensor that does
        not tolerate a loss, which is the same storm. Normalising to a rate, as flow does, would
        need the interval inside the check, and that crosses `pool.ts`.

        So `due-dispatch` hands the interval to `drain`. The first scan reads from
        max(listener start, now − interval), and `since` says so. What the ring overwrote
        inside that window is `dropped`. Exactness comes from the arrival times of the last
        `bufferSize` overwritten records, kept beside the ring with a counted flag, so Probe
        Health stays once a record.

        only. It is neither read nor lost. The trap, syslog and flow types name it in the
        message, and it moves no channel. A flood of more than twice the buffer within one
        interval starts the window at the oldest arrival known. That scan still fails on its
        dropped, and the rest is `earlier`.
      - **The restart set is the first *complete* push.** `onConfig` now carries `final`, true
        when absent. `core-handlers` sweeps cursors only once a push completes. Before, a link
        cut after chunk one settled anyway, the sweep made chunk one the restart set, and later
        chunks returned as new. The same rule also stops a cut push deleting cursors (`P-42`'s
        shape). The pool is still sized on every settle.
      - **The process-level test takes the swept-set branch.** Sensors have 60 s intervals and
        phases of 35–45 s. The first push is cut after the syslog sensor's chunk, the link
        drops, and the whole push follows on reconnect. Each first scan is asserted to come more
        than 4 s after that push applied, and each reads 3. The older case now shows the window:
        1 s sensors scanning 2.5 s after the early messages read 0, fail nothing, and name the
        three in their message.
      - **The alarm volume** is covered by `listener-restart-scenario.test.ts`. 20 trap and 20
        syslog sensors with a limit of 5 a minute sit through a two-hour wait for the core at
        three a minute, with buffers of 100 overrun. Their first scans give 0 failures and 0
        limit breaches, and read + earlier + dropped equals each listener's received count. The
        same traffic read back to the listener's start alarms on all 20 trap sensors.

      restart's first scan), `core-handlers.test.ts` (5 cases of a cut push), `due-dispatch`
      (the interval as the window), and a flow sensor case for the message. **Mutations 14/14**:
      window ignored; search inverted; overwritten arrivals unused; or not kept; push-time count
      forgotten; window loss not counted; or counted twice; `earlier` zero; `since` the listener
      start; a cut push swept; `final` ignored in the handlers; or in the client (process case);
      dispatch with no window; the note never said. No protocol change.

      **Re-review, 2026-10-07: three more, fixed in a third commit.**
      - **A flood the ring cannot date is `dropped`, not `earlier`.** The search over the
        last 2 × `bufferSize` arrivals clamped at its lower end. When every known arrival was
        inside the window, it called everything older `earlier`, though it may have arrived
        inside it too. The note then said "before" a `since` that was the listener's start.
        - Now, when the oldest arrival the ring can date is inside the window, the read starts
          where the sensor resumes, and the whole loss is `dropped`. That also covers a window
          reaching past the listener's start.
        - Probe Health takes what a resume lost from a running total of overwrites not counted
          at push time. The flags count the dated part; the total counts the rest. So it no
          longer depends on the side array.
        - Tests: 1,000 in a buffer of 100 inside the window gives `dropped` 900 and `unread`
          900, once across two sensors. A window reaching the listener's start counts all six
          lost as dropped, with `earlier` 0.
      - **The window is measured on a monotonic clock.** Arrivals, the listener's start and
        each cursor's last drain are stamped with `performance.now` (injectable as `monotonic`
        on each listener). The wall clock is read only for `at`, `since` and `until`, and
        `since` is now less monotonic elapsed time, so it never falls after `until`. The test
        steps the wall clock back an hour between arrivals; the scan reads the three in the
        interval, names the two before, and covers exactly one monotonic minute.
      - **A cut push parks, rather than keeps, the cursors it leaves off the wheel.**
        `retain(ids, complete)` is now required on `CursorSweeper`, and `core-handlers` sweeps
        every settle and says which kind it was. A complete push sweeps as before. A cut one
        parks each absent sensor's cursor with where it stood and when it last scanned, and
        those parked sensors stop counting what they miss. When the whole push brings a sensor
        back, it reads one interval back from its own position, and what came before since its
        last scan is `earlier`. A whole push that leaves it out makes it new.
