          the message, a name and a unit, a pair kept; the property now asserts every string is
          well formed by Node's own `isWellFormed`. `spool-drain.test.ts`: a record appended as
          an earlier build wrote it is sent fitted, and the core's parser takes it; 2,000
          results with 2,000-character messages go in more than one batch, each of which
          `encodeFrame` takes as a whole `results` message, all in order, none `oversized`; a
          1,500-byte result under a 1,000-byte bound is discarded and counted and the next one
          sent.
        - **Mutation 7/7:** the key's surrogate check, the text's replacement, the drain not
          fitting, `peek`'s byte bound and its byte count, the oversized result sent, and not
          counted.
        - **Runs:** shared `result-fit`, `messages`, `run-program`, 126/126; sensors `ping`,
          `icmp-ping`, 36/36; probe `process-runner`, `check-pool`, `script-groups`,
          `query-runner`, `result-sink`, `spool`, `spool-drain`, `core-client`,
          `probe-health-report`, 246/246; core `program-delivery`, `email-delivery`, 61/61. None
          skipped.

- [x] **P-278 — a script leader that exits before the runner reads its line is never recorded**
      · S · P-266 · Found 2026-10-07 in `P-266`. A script whose leader exits before the runner
      reads its `started` line cannot be told from someone else's process once the leader is
      reaped, so it is not recorded. If the check process then dies outright, what the script
      left in its group keeps running. **Done when** the check process holds the leader unreaped
      (or passes a pidfd) until the runner has acknowledged the group, or the gap is measured and
      documented as accepted, with a test either way.

      **P-278 outcome. The gap is closed in the runner. A group whose leader has gone by the time
      its line is read is judged by its members, as the end already judged one.**
      - **Neither of the first two ways.** Node reaps every child it spawns as soon as the child
        exits, and it exposes no `pidfd_open`. So the check process can neither hold its script
        unreaped nor pass a pidfd without a native module, which `P-266` turned down for the same
        reason.
      - **What still names the script's group.** `N` stays allocated while any process has it as
        its group or session id. A script that exits at once leaves its helpers in group and
        session `N`, and nothing outside the script can join that session.
      - **The new rule.** In `ScriptGroups.#startedWithoutLeader`, a `started N` whose `/proc/N` is
        gone has its members read from all of `/proc`. The group is recorded when every member:
        - is in session `N`;
        - has the runner's uid, when one is set;
        - started no earlier than the check process, whose `starttime` the runner reads at its own
          spawn of it (`onSpawn`).

        A member that fails any of these makes the line a refusal, counted, as a forgery is. No
        members means the script and all it started have gone, and nothing is recorded. A check
        process whose own start could not be read records nothing, as before.
      - **What a forged line can now buy.** Only a kill of processes started during this check,
        of the uid the check's script already runs as, which that uid could kill itself.
        Without a uid, the probe runs scripts as itself, and a root probe does not start that way
        without `allowScriptsAsRoot` (`P-276`).
      - **At the end.** A group recorded this way holds `LEADER_GONE`, which no real `starttime`
        equals, so any process at `N` then is a reuse and is left alone (`scriptGroupsRecycled`).
        `/proc/N` gone takes the members branch `P-266` already had.
      - **Still open.** A group whose id was reused, inside the runner's lag, by a new session
        leader that exits leaving members passes the same test. That is `P-266`'s 250 ms window,
        from the other side. The orphan case, a check process killed between its script's spawn
        and the line being read, is unchanged: still a refusal.
      - **Tests.** `script-groups.test.ts` gains 9 tests on an injected `/proc`. They cover
        recording and killing, a member started before the check, of another uid and in another

- [x] **P-282 — ping counts duplicate replies as replies** · S · P-277 · Found 2026-10-07 in
      `P-277`. `(DUP!)` lines from the system `ping` are counted as replies, which hides packet
      loss and skews jitter. **Done when** duplicates are left out of the reply count and the
      timing figures (and counted on their own if useful), with parser tests for Linux and
      macOS `ping` output.

      **P-282 outcome. A second answer to the same request is a duplicate, not a reply.**
      - **One parser, so one fix.** `parsePingOutput` in `packages/sensors/src/support/ping.ts` is
        what `icmp.ping`, `icmp.jitter`, the discovery sweep's `pingOnce` and the `P-07` perf
        test all read ping through. There is no raw-socket path to check: `P-07`'s fast path was
        never built, and every ICMP check runs the system binary.
      - **It reads line by line now**, where it used to take every `time=` in the output. A timed
        line is a duplicate if ping marks it `(DUP!)` (iputils, BSD and BusyBox all do), or if
        its `icmp_seq` has already been answered. The second rule catches the same fact with no
        marker, which is what the last line of a flood looks like when `P-277`'s 64 KiB bound
        cuts it short. Duplicates go into `outcome.duplicates` and nowhere else: not `times`, so
        not the loss, the averages, min/max or the jitter. Windows prints neither a sequence nor
        a marker, and nothing changes there.
      - **Counted where a count already goes: the message.** Both sensors append *N duplicates
        not counted* to the message when there were any (`duplicatesNote`). A device that answers
        twice is worth knowing about (a loop or a shared address), but it is not a channel: no
        limit on it would mean anything. There is no new heartbeat field and no protocol change.
      - **Tests** (`ping.test.ts`): iputils output (two of four answered, each twice) parses to
        two replies, 50% loss and an average of 0.405 ms, not 0% and 2.9 ms. macOS output parses
        the same, with its 24.95 ms copy not taken as the slowest reply. The jitter equals the
        jitter of the first answers alone. BusyBox (`seq=`, so the marker is all there is) parses
        to one duplicate. A cut-off unmarked copy is caught by its sequence number. Distinct
        sequences are never merged, and Windows has no duplicates.
      - **Mutations** (each restored byte for byte, `dist` rebuilt): with no duplicate check at
        all, the iputils, macOS, jitter and cut-line tests fail. With no sequence rule, the cut-line
        test fails. With no marker rule, the BusyBox test fails. A `duplicatesNote` that never
        speaks fails its own test.

      Found 2026-10-07 in `P-275`. The refused-group warning is a rate limit, so a refusal in the
      first record after a probe restart or a long link gap has no rate: it is counted and logged

      - **How.** `scriptGroupsRefused` stays a counter, now with **no limit**; a new core-computed
        channel `scriptGroupsRefusedRecently` (*Script groups refused (5 min)*) **warns above 0.5**.
        Each sweep, for every connected probe, `ProbeHealthService` feeds the growth of the running
        total into a `RecentCount` through a `DeltaMeter`: a total that fell or an uptime that fell
        is a restart and all of it is new; growth across a link gap is growth (the baseline
        outlives the session, unlike `logDropped`'s, because a refusal made while the link was down
        is still one). `RECENT_TOTALS` holds both such counts (`P-283`'s `resultsDiscarded` is the
        other), on an injectable monotonic clock. No protocol change: the total is 31's.

        counter shape is stored on its row, and a channel is not removed.
      - **What it does not see** (corrected on review): when this core meets a probe for the
        first time and the probe was already running, what it counted before the first heartbeat
        of that connection is a baseline, and that record gaps rather than reading 0. So a refusal
        or discard made while the probe was cut off from a core that restarted meanwhile is
        missed. Once the core knows a probe, growth across any link gap counts, a restart at 32 is
        told by `instanceId`, and from a probe at 31 a restart inside a gap longer than the old
        process's uptime, with a total no lower, is not seen.

        again between refusals a minute apart); the warning clears five minutes after the last.
      - **Tests (core `probe-health`):** across a counter reset (4 to 1 after a restart counts 1,
        and a restart whose total does not fall, by its uptime); a refusal during a 2- and a
        10-minute link gap counted on the first record back; the window kept at 270 s and gone at
        300 s; a probe started after the core counted in full, one already running not at all;
        gaps for no total and no link; and the whole path — sweep, ingestion, limit, state — Warning
        on a restarted probe's first record, held through a burst, Up five minutes after the last.
        `health-types` pins the declaration and position.
      - **Known leftover:** an install that already ran protocol 31 keeps the declared rate limit
        on its existing `scriptGroupsRefused` channels: `applyDeclaredLimits` writes declared
        limits but never takes one away that a type stopped declaring. Harmless (it warns in a
        record the window also warns in); listed as a follow-up.
      - **Amended on review** (a second commit). Two defects in the baseline.
        - *The first sight of a probe absorbed what this core should have counted.* The baseline
          was the total at the first sweep that read the probe, so a probe cut off across a core
          restart that refused or discarded while cut off — or a drain that discarded in the
          seconds after `welcome`, before the first heartbeat a heartbeat interval later — read 0
          and stayed Up. Now the baseline sweep **gaps** unless it counted something; the endpoint
          keeps each session's **first report** (`ProbeLink.firstHealth`) and a probe met first is
          baselined from it, not from the latest; and the probe **sends a heartbeat on `welcome`,
          before `setState('connected')`**, so before the drain can send. Its cost: one heartbeat
          more per connection, and the CPU channel's first reading a heartbeat sooner. Still
          missed: what the probe counted before that first report, as above.
        - *A restart inside a link gap longer than the old process's uptime was growth.* Total and
          uptime both rose (2 at 100 s, then 2 at 3,000 s after a restart counted 0). Chosen over
          inferring from the implied start time (now less uptime, with slack for heartbeat age and
          sweep interval): **`instanceId`**, a UUID the probe process picks at start
          (`PROCESS_INSTANCE`), on every heartbeat at protocol 32 under `unsendableReadings`,
          schema-bounded to a UUID. Exact where the inference needs a slack that misses short-lived
          processes, and simpler; `DeltaMeter.take` takes it as an optional fourth argument and
          falls back to the inference where either reading lacks one (a probe at 31).

          3, 0) and, as the control, without it (0, 1, 1, 3, 0); a reading without an instance
          infers. Core `probe-health`: the same table through the sweep; a discard already in the
          first report after a core restart gaps; one made after the first report is counted on
          the first sweep; every baseline that read 0 now reads a gap and then 0.

          client was not yet `connected`. `capabilities.test.ts`: `instanceId` stripped below 32,

      - **Decisions, taken by the orchestrator** and named in the push question:
        1. **An open, bounded word, not an enum.** `failure.phase` is a lower-case letter, then
           letters, digits and hyphens, 32 at most (`FAILURE_PHASE`). A new transport's phase
           needs no protocol bump; a closed list would have made each one a bump, as
           `RejectCode` did for `P-326`.
        2. **The check's own phase first.** The error's `phase` when it names one, else the
           runner's when that is not `execute`, else no `failure`: `execute` says only that the
           check threw. A check process that runs out of time throws from where it was (`walk`,
           `exec`), and that is sent, with its message saying the time ran out. The pool's own
           timeout settles the check before its error arrives, so there it is `timeout`.
        3. **A plain host or nothing.** `target` is taken from the error's `target` or `host`
           and kept only when it is letters, digits and `. _ - : % [ ]`, up to 255
           (`FAILURE_TARGET`): a name, an address (IPv6 bracketed or not, with a zone), or
           either with a port. Listed, not filtered, so `@`, `/`, `?`, `#`, `=` and spaces cannot
           pass, and a host built from a URL cannot carry a user, a password or a token to a
           reader of the sensor. A name outside ASCII is left off; the device's host says it.
        4. **Both tables.** `failure_phase` and `failure_target` on `sensor_runtime` and on
           `sensor_state`, nullable, a target never without its phase (a CHECK on each).
        5. **The error code stays in the message.** `ECONNRESET` is in the prose, and the
           ticket's Done-when names the phase and the target.
        6. **Beside the message, by its rule** (`state-machine.md` §2.2). The scan's own when
           the scan failed and its words explain the state; what is stored when a person or a
           hold decided the state; nothing once a pause, an acknowledgement, a hold or a release
           writes words of its own (`writeStateChanges` clears both); held with the message by a
           pause that committed while the result was in flight (`P-147`). **Never a cause**: a
           phase that moves while the state and the cause stand records no transition.
      - **Protocol 35.** `CheckResult.failure?: { phase, target? }`, under `failurePhase`, only
        beside `outcome: 'error'` (an `allOf` rule). It may stand beside `withheld` or
        `notStarted`. `resultForPeer` takes it out for a core below 35, which also covers a
        spooled result replayed to an older core. `fitFailure` bounds it; `fitResult` keeps it
        on a failed check only. **The core mends, never refuses, for it**: a phase that is not
        a word drops the failure and a target that is not plain drops the target (`fittable`
        takes `/failure`), since the field decides nothing and refusing would lose a failed
        check.

        refusal names `check`, `resolve` or `connect` with the device's host; a check that could
        not start names `startup` or `pool-disabled` and no host.

        1. **Only a probe's held result stores a failure**: a refusal (owner
           `credentials-probe:<id>`) and a check it could not start. A sentence the core writes
           itself (`A-29`, `A-41`, a factory's voucher, the health sensors) stores none, since no
           probe named anything; inventing `{phase:'check'}` for `A-41`'s own refusal would claim
           a check that never ran.

           `SensorVouching` holds per owner, so the words and the place always come from the same
           owner. `settleOrThrow` takes it; a sweep's `settle` keeps its strings and holds none.
        3. **A sibling accessor.** `heldWords()` beside `withheld()`, which keeps its strings for
           its 66 test readers and `FactoryVouching`. `withheldSensors` now returns `HeldWords`,
           so `main.ts` does not compile until it is rewired.

           change, or from a probe that moved to 35, gets its place.

      - `#run` settles a run whose start-up bound fired as `startup` before it reads the answer,

        `timedOut` and read "Stopped at its timeout"; an `ok` one was a reading from a check the
        runner had given up before it saw it begin. Now each is counted in `startupFailed` and

        has not seen the check begin, and the stop it sends goes out in that turn: a reading
        after it is from a check the runner has said it gave up. The run's outcome is no longer

      · P-265 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-407`'s review. `NotStarted.release` lets a sensor go

      - `NotStarted.release` calls `forgetSensors` for every sensor it lets go, as

           transition into Down (Acknowledged), which review showed is not the acknowledgement's

        returns at once while nothing is held, the normal state of an installation, and is a

        inputs, a withholding): a load held open across a release, released only once everything
        chained on the load has run under the hold, is decided and cached under the facts as

- [x] **P-414 — a rewrite decided from an unlocked read can overwrite a pause committed
      meanwhile** · S · P-147 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-410`'s design. `reevaluate` reads its
      rows with no lock (`loadRuntimes`) and `writeStateChanges` sets the state and cause
      unconditionally, so a reword or a hold decided from a read taken before a pause committed
      can write Unknown over a row whose pause flags say paused, while `sensor_state` says
      paused. `writeRuntimes` has `P-147`'s guard; this path has none. `P-410` makes it likelier
      by rewording on every round of a starved probe. Same family as `P-412`. **Done when**
      `writeStateChanges` cannot overwrite a state its read did not see (a guard on the row it
      read, as `writeRuntimes`'), with a test that commits a pause between the read and the
      write.

      **P-414 outcome. A re-decision locks the rows it will write and decides them again from
      that read.**
      - **Decisions, taken by the orchestrator** and named in the push question:
        1. **Decided again, not guarded.** A guard that skips a row that moved since the read
           (a row version, or the state compared) would leave a lost probe's sensor at the
           state of its last batch when that batch landed between the read and the write, where
           today it is written Unknown. So `reevaluate` decides from its unlocked read, takes the
           rows it will write — rewrites and the acknowledgements a recovery clears — with
           `lockRuntimes` (`FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, in id order), and decides them again from that;
           only the second answer is written. A writer still open is waited for and read as it
           committed. Not a pause guard as `writeRuntimes`' either: a result or a simulated error
           committed meanwhile is the same overwrite.
        2. **No more rows locked than before.** Every row it locks it already locked, by
           `writeStateHistory` (`P-394`) or by the write itself; now earlier, and all in id
           order, which the rewrite-only rows were not. The rows it decides nothing for stay
           unlocked, such as a lost probe's paused and simulated sensors and the probe-alarm
           sensors re-decided beside them. A row decided unchanged from a stale read is not
           re-checked (`P-416`).
      - **Cost.** A second read and decision of the rows it writes, only when it writes any.
      - **Code.** `reevaluate`'s decision is `#redecide`, run once or twice; its cause is a named
        `ReevaluationCause`. `lockRuntimes` sits beside `loadRuntimes`.
      - **Docs.** `state-machine.md`, a note beside `P-108`'s; `writeStateChanges`' header.
      - **Tests.** `reevaluate-race.test.ts`, against PostgreSQL, a lost probe's re-decision with
        something committed on another connection between its read and its write: a pause, left
        as it is and recorded over by nothing; a pause still open when the re-decision locks,
        waited for and left; a simulated error, which outranks the lost probe; two results
        reaching Down, the transition written from Down and not from the Up it first read; a
        not-started round's new words, a reword with no transition, under a pause, locked and
        left; and of three sensors, the two it writes locked in id order and the one it leaves
        not.
      - **Review.** Ten findings over six things, fixed: `ReevaluationCause` had taken
        `PolicySource`'s doc comment; the note, the comment and the test's header gave the old
        failure the wrong signature (a lost probe's overwrite recorded Unknown after the pause;

- [x] **P-415 — a result decided before a hold and stored after the hold's re-decision overwrites
      it** · S · P-147 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-414`'s review. Ingestion decides a batch, with

      `batchMaxDelayMs` later. A probe lost in between — `#handleClose` calls
      `reachability.lost` without waiting for the session's pending batch — re-decides its
      sensors Unknown/probe and commits first; the batch's `writeRuntimes`, which guards only a
      pause (`P-147`), then writes its Up or Down over that. The history's newest row stays
      Unknown (the batch's transitions are stamped as measured, before it), nothing re-decides
      the sensor while its probe is held, and `found()` then decides it unchanged: the row says
      Up across the outage and the history says Unknown, in the table uptime is computed from,
      until the sensor next changes state. The same for a frozen clock, a factory's unreached
      inputs, a check its probe could not start and a withholding, and in mirror for a batch
      decided during a silence hold and stored after `resumed()`. **Done when** a result stored
      after a hold's re-decision cannot leave the row disagreeing with the hold (for instance,
      the written sensors a live hold covers are re-decided in the ingest transaction, whose
      rows are locked by then), with a test that decides a batch, commits a lost probe's
      re-decision and then flushes the batch.

      to the hold.**
      - **Decisions, taken by the orchestrator** and named in the push question:
        1. **Asked of the row, locked, not of the decision.** Inside the write's transaction and
           before its history, `SensorStateService.overtaken` takes the writes a probe's hold
           holds now (a lost probe, a frozen clock, a check its probe could not start, a
           factory's unreached inputs) that say other than Unknown/probe, reads their rows
           locked in id order (`lockRuntimeStates`), and names those whose row already says
           Unknown/probe (`leftToHold`). A hold whose re-decision has committed is on the row;
           one laid but not committed waits on the lock and decides from what the write leaves
           (`P-414`). The first version answered from the decision alone (`standsUnder`); its
           review confirmed 17 findings, among them that it was neither safe (an
           acknowledgement's lapse) nor complete (a release committed first).
        2. **Only those rows locked, and after the rows the write moves.** Locking every row a
           write touches before its history closed a cycle with a release (`found()` locks a
           master, then its dependency recompute pauses dependents whose steady results ride in
           the same write), and so did locking a held dependent ahead of a master a release has
           let go of, whose transition the write carries. Taking every moved row first instead
           crossed the hold itself, which locks its rows in id order, when a moved row of its
           probe came ahead of a steady one. So the unheld rows the transitions move are taken
           first, in id order, as the history took them before anything was asked, and then
           the held rows asked about, together in id order. A held steady dependent
           ahead of a steady master still can cross (`P-422`). With nothing held, the normal
           state, the write takes its rows as it did before.
        3. **Kept, not re-decided.** `writeRuntimes` keeps those rows' state, cause, words,
           place and `since`, beside `P-147`'s pause guard, and writes the scan facts, the
           failure count and the verdict. The row already says what the hold decides, so
           nothing is decided in the ingest transaction: no hold's words to find (`P-413`), no
           alarm reaction outside the ingestor's per-source gating (`P-146`).
        4. **The history and the stream follow the row; the reactions follow what was
           measured.** An overtaken sensor's transitions measured before its newest stored row
           stay as history (`P-145`). Any at or after it (a probe's clock ahead, a hold that
           decided the row unchanged and wrote nothing) are left out (`beforeTheNewest`), and
           none is announced, since the stream shows the last frame it got (`U-02`). Every one
           is reacted to as measured, whatever the probe's clock stamped it, as it would have
           been had the write gone first: a master's recovery starts its dependents' delay, and
           a Down ends one (`M-11`). Leaving a recovery stamped after the hold's row out of the
           reaction left the dependents the hold let go to page.
        5. **Probe holds only, and the hold's direction only.** A second design, which also
           compared the row with what each result was decided from and re-decided every row
           that had moved, had 16 defects confirmed against it before it was written: holds'
           words, holds that roll back, acknowledgements, stale sources and the alarm gating.

        carries one of them takes up to two statements locking rows its history and its `UPDATE`

      - **Logged** at info, with the sensors, when a write is overtaken.
      - **Code.** The five holds' facts are read in one place, `#heldFacts`, which

      - **Docs.** `state-machine.md`, a note after `P-414`'s.
      - **Tests.**
        - `state-machine.test.ts`: `leftToHold`, ten rows. It is asked only of a sensor a

        - `overtaken-results.test.ts`, against PostgreSQL through the `Ingestor`: a lost

- [x] **P-416 — a probe lost while its `found()` is still writing leaves its sensors at their last
      reading** · S · P-414 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-414`'s review. `#online` clears the overlay
      before its transaction, which re-decides each sensor from Unknown/probe to what it last
      read. A `lost()` that arrives before that commits sets the overlay again; its unlocked
      read sees the committed Unknown/probe and decides nothing, so `P-414` locks nothing and
      decides nothing again; `found()` then commits Up. Nothing re-decides the sensor while the
      probe stays away, and the history records Up across the outage. A flapping link or a
      probe in a crash loop fits the window, which is every round trip of a large probe's
      re-decision. **Done when** `lost()` and `found()`/`resumed()` for one probe cannot
      interleave their re-decisions (one at a time per probe, or `found()` re-deciding, or
      owing, what was lost again since it began), with a test that holds `found()`'s
      transaction open across a `lost()`.

      **P-416 outcome. A probe's loss and its return run one at a time.**
      - **Decisions, taken by the orchestrator:**
        1. **Each call whole, in turn per probe.** `ProbeReachability` keeps a chain per probe
           (`#inTurn`). Each `lost`, `found` and `resumed` runs only once the one called before
           it has settled, and it runs whole: its overlay change, its tree read and its
           re-decision. Each then reads what the one before it committed, and decides under the
           overlay it laid itself. This fixes three orders:
           - a loss during a return's write, the ticket's case;
           - a return during a loss's write, which left a connected probe's sensors Unknown;
           - a return during a loss's read of the tree, which found no hold to let go of.
        2. **Not just the transactions.** A first version kept the overlay change at call time
           and let only the transactions wait. Its review confirmed four defects. A newer
           call's overlay change reached a re-decision still in flight, which then decided
           under it in the other call's words. The guards that tried to make up for this (a
           return stepping aside for a newer loss, a failed return restoring its hold only if
           none was there) left a connected probe held after a failed return followed by a
           loss and a return.
           Taking whole calls in turn makes every guard unnecessary. The cost is that a newer
           call's overlay change waits for the one before it, a few milliseconds at most, and a
           result decided meanwhile sees the overlay as it was (`P-418`).
        3. **A failed loss lets go of what it holds now.** It releases the sensors as a resync
           has left them, rather than the list it read, since a resync can re-read the probe's
           sensors while the loss is writing. Before, a sensor that arrived meanwhile stayed held
           behind a hold that was never written.
      - **Not changed, and filed.**
        - A resync (a tree change) and the delivery sweep's `retryGivenUp` do not take turns.
          They re-decide what a tree change moved across the overlay, or what a failure owed.
        - A superseded session's close still calls `lost`, after the newer session's `found` if
          the close is handled late (`P-427`).
        - The review's run of the full suite failed one timing test, which compares one login
          with one other (`P-428`).
      - **Docs.** `state-machine.md`, a note after `P-415`'s, which is rewrapped.
      - **Tests.** `probe-reachability-turns.test.ts`, against PostgreSQL. Each case holds one call
        open, inside its write or its tree read, across the others:
        - a loss during a return's write, and a return during a loss's write;
        - a resumption during a silence's write;
        - a return during a loss's tree read;
        - loss, return, loss, return, taken in that order, each in its own words;
        - a failed loss, a return and a newer loss;
        - a failed return, with a loss called after it;
        - a failed loss whose sensors a resync re-read meanwhile.
      - **Review.** Two lenses and a verifier on the first version: 4 confirmed, 1 refuted. The
        version that landed answers all four.
      - **Mutants.** 5 of 5 killed: `found`, `lost` or `resumed` outside its turn, a turn that does
        not wait, and a failed loss letting go of the list it read.

- [ ] **P-417 — a hold that a result write in flight does not wait for** · S · P-415, P-416 ·
      Found 2026-10-17 in `P-415`'s reviews. A write locks only the rows a probe's hold holds
      when it asks (`P-415`), so a hold laid after the question, whose re-decision commits
      before the write's `UPDATE` reaches the row, is written over. And `reevaluate` locks only
      the rows it will rewrite (`P-414`): a row at Unknown/probe that nothing holds (a
      not-started sensor let go by the batch's own started result, which `NotStarted.release`
      does not re-decide, or a hold forgotten by a core restart) is decided unchanged by a probe
      lost while the batch's write is open, so nothing waits for the write, which then commits
      the batch's Up for a probe that is gone, and `found()` later decides it unchanged:
      `P-416`'s mechanism, from an ingest write. **Done when** neither can leave a write over a
      hold: a hold's re-decision also locks, and decides again, the rows it decides unchanged on
      a hold fact (cause probe or access), and one laid after the write asked is re-checked
      before its `UPDATE` or waits for it, with a test for each that holds an ingest write open
      across a `lost()`.

- [ ] **P-418 — a result decided from a row re-decided since is written as decided** · M · P-415
      · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-415`'s design review. The write compares nothing it was decided
      from. A batch decided under a hold let go since writes Unknown/probe over the release's
      state (a silence hold's last batch over `resumed()`), and the release decided without it.
      A hold and its release both committed between decide and write (a link flap) leave the row
      as the batch found it, so the batch's Down goes in while the history ends on `found()`'s Up;
      a release that has cleared its overlay but not committed when the write asks waits on the
      write or reads after it and decides the row unchanged, so the batch's Down goes in while
      the history ends on the hold's Unknown.
      An acknowledgement extended between the two is wiped by the lapse the write carries.
      **Done when** a write decided from a row that has moved since (state, cause, `since`,
      acknowledgement) leaves it and is re-decided in the ingest transaction from what it
      stores, in the result's own words for a state its readings decide, with a test for each.
      The design review found what that has to get right: `P-413`'s words first; no alarm
      reaction of its own, outside the ingestor's per-source gating (`P-146`, `P-169`); a write
      the floors refuse not re-decided; an acknowledgement its result expired cleared; a stale
      source's batch not re-decided on the core's clock ahead of the replay behind it.

- [ ] **P-419 — a hold or a release whose transaction fails owes no re-decision** · S · P-249 ·
      Found 2026-10-17 in `P-415`'s design review. `ProbeReachability.lost`'s catch releases the
      overlay and returns 0, and `ClockFreeze`'s `restore()` and `SensorVouching`'s put-back do
      the same. A batch decided under the overlay before it rolled back is written as decided,
      Unknown/probe for a probe that is connected, and if the probe reconnects before the
      delivery sweep retries, `found()` finds no entry and nothing re-decides the sensor until
      its next result. `P-415` adds a case: a write it kept on a row already at Unknown/probe
      (a not-started sensor let go by its own result) for a hold laid but not committed is left
      Unknown if that hold rolls back, with nothing holding it. **Done when** each such failure
      drops the cache and owes its sensors a re-decision, as `#undoOnRollback` and
      `retryGivenUp` do, with a test per holder and one for the kept write.

- [ ] **P-420 — a result decided before a withholding and stored after it writes over it** · S ·
      P-415, M-23 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-415`'s reviews. `P-415` leaves withholdings out.
      Keeping a write behind a committed withholding the way it keeps one behind a probe's hold
      would page each dependent: the kept Down still reaches the dependency reaction, but
      `applyPauses` holds dependents from the master's row, which the keep leaves at
      Unknown/access; `M-23`'s until-evaluated mark was decided on the Warning the withholding
      saw; and the reaction's Down clears any `dependency_clear_at`, that mark included
      (`markRecoveries`). Today the Down is written over Unknown/access, which holds the
      dependents and leaves the row Down while withheld. And `holdUntilEvaluated`
      reads its `state IN (...)` against the committed row, so a withholding that runs while the
      Down is being written sets no mark either. **Done when** a write behind a withholding keeps
      Unknown/access and a master's measured Down still holds its dependents until it is
      evaluated, with an `M-17` scenario test of a master and its dependents in both orders.

- [ ] **P-421 — a result written behind a pause committed since is still announced** · S ·
      P-147, P-415 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-415`'s review. `writeRuntimes` keeps a paused row's
      state when a pause committed between a batch's decision and its write (`P-147`), but the
      batch's transitions are written and announced as decided: an operator pauses a sensor as
      its Down is in flight, the pause's frame goes out, then the Down's, and every open tree
      shows Down while the row says Paused. A paused sensor is not scanned, so nothing corrects
      it until a resubscribe. `P-415` keeps a probe hold's rows out of the announcement and ends
      their history on the hold's row; a pause's are not. **Done when** a write the pause guard
      holds announces nothing of the state it did not write, and its history does not end
      after the pause's row, with a test through the `Ingestor`.

- [ ] **P-422 — a result write and a release's dependency recompute can lock rows crosswise** ·
      S · P-415, P-394 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-415`'s fourth review. A release (`found()`,
      `resumed()`, a thaw, a not-started resync) locks a master's runtime row, re-decides it,
      and its dependency recompute then writes the dependents' rows (`applyPauses`). A result
      write takes rows in id order and then in its `UPDATE`'s scan order, neither of which
      follows master before dependent. `P-415` takes the unheld rows its transitions move
      first and then the held rows it asks about, but a write that asks about a held dependent
      with a steady result and carries its master's steady result still holds the dependent
      while its `UPDATE` waits on the master; a hold whose recompute lets go of a dependent the
      same write moves finds the write holding the dependent and waiting on the held master;
      and on `main` already, the `UPDATE` can reach a dependent before its master. PostgreSQL then
      aborts one of the two. A write aborted is nacked and offered again, which costs a retry;
      a release aborted puts its hold back (`#online`'s catch) with nothing to retry it while
      the probe stays connected, so a connected probe's sensors stay Unknown until it next
      reconnects. **Done when** a deadlock between the two costs a retry and never a held
      probe: the release paths retry on `deadlock_detected` (`40P01`), as
      `credential-vouching.ts` counts a write that gave way, with a scenario test of a master
      on one probe and a held dependent on another, a write holding the dependent open across
      the release.

- [ ] **P-423 — the web has no words for the phases `P-406` added** · XS · P-406 · Found
      2026-10-17 in `P-406`. Five phases are new: `handshake` (TLS, mail, HTTP, databases),
      `send` (SMTP), `request` (HTTP), `echo` (ping) and `output` (scripts). `failure-words.ts`
      knows none of them, so the web says "Failed in “handshake” on 192.0.2.7". That is honest
      but not words. **Done when** each of the five has a lead with a host and without one, in
      `failure-words.ts`'s table, with its test.

- [ ] **P-424 — a sensor's verdict on what the device answered names no phase** · S · P-406 ·
      Found 2026-10-17 in `P-406`. The transports now say where they failed, but the sensor
      types judge what came back with plain `Error`s, so nothing is stored beside the words:
      - an HTTP status, body, pattern or header the sensor does not accept (`http-shared.ts`,
        `http-content.ts`, `http-advanced.ts`, a transaction step's check);
      - a query that returned the wrong number of rows (`db-shared.ts`);
      - a round-trip message the relay took and the mailbox never got;
      - a TLS handshake with no certificate;
      - a Windows query with no rows (`windows-memory.ts`, `windows-cpu.ts`);
      - the types' own cancels between two transport calls (`tls.security` between versions,
        the round trip while it polls, a database check before it connects).

      A missing credential or host is configuration, and stays without one. **Done when** each
      verdict names the phase it judged (`request` for HTTP, `query` for a database or Windows,
      `handshake` for TLS, a phase for delivery) with the host, and each cancel the phase it
      was in, with a test per type.

- [x] **P-426 — a probe runs two name lookups at a time** · M · A-66 · Found 2026-10-17 by

      or a resolver off the pool for names the hosts file does not have), with the arms run
      again showing what it bought, or the decision not to is written down with the numbers.

      **Read 2026-10-17** (`docs/findings/2026-10-17-name-lookups-a-scan.md`).
      - **The slow arm.** At 100 ms a lookup, half the scans were given up and half were refused.
      - **The one-zone arm.** One silent zone in ten left 6 of the other zones' 2,287 lookups
        answered.
      - **What would fix it.** A larger pool alone moves the slow threshold, not the zone
        failure. Answers kept for a TTL, or a resolver off the pool with a timeout per query,
        removes both.

      **Decided 2026-10-17 by the user**, on the design (`p426-design.md`) and its review:
      1. **Build the `getaddrinfo` slice now: this ticket and `P-425`.** The c-ares resolver is
         decided only after the re-measure (`P-432`). No c-ares, no `probe.nameResolver`, no
         protocol 37 and no `lookupsAnsweredStale`.
      2. **A stale answer may be used for at most 5 minutes past its expiry.**

      **P-426 outcome. One resolver in the probe, which keeps answers and decides what runs.**
      - **What it is.** `NameResolver` (`probe/src/resolver/name-resolver.ts`), in the probe's
        main thread. Scan workers and the query runner's worker ask it over their port to the
        pool (`resolve` / `resolve-ack` / `resolved`, `resolver/protocol.ts`; the worker's side
        is `runner/resolve-client.ts`); discovery's identification asks it directly. Process
        children and fixture pools resolve for themselves.
        - **The answers are `getaddrinfo`'s**, keyed by the lower-cased name and the family
          asked, and asked for exactly that family: family 0 is one lookup, never two merged.
        - **Kept**: an answer 30 s, a denial 30 s (`ENOTFOUND`, `ENODATA`, or more than 64
          addresses, which fails naming the count), one lookup in flight a key, 10,000 names least
          recently asked first, on a monotonic clock. Any other failure is passed to the checks
          waiting and nothing is kept.
        - **Stale**: an expired answer is served at once while one refresh runs, and for at most
          5 minutes past its expiry while the refresh is not answered. A denial drops it.
        - **Holds**: `EAI_AGAIN`, or a lookup past 1 s, holds the name 5 s, doubling to 60 s,
          ±20%, reset by any answer. New checks fail at once, naming the resolver; one already
          waiting for the lookup keeps its own bound. A retry runs only when a check asks.
          Background work never moves a name in the LRU order.
        - **Lanes**: at most 6 lookups at once: one a held name's retry, five shared by first
          lookups and refreshes, at most four each, so one is always kept for each.
          `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16`
          (8 lanes) is exported by `bin/ms-probe` unless set, and set by `ms-probe.service` and
          the WinSW configuration; the probe logs it at start and warns below 16.
        - **Fail-fast**: a check fails at once, given up, when its name is held or every lane its
          lookup's class could take is held by one past 1 s; the lookup stays queued.
        - **Worker side**: the client ends its own wait at its bound and 500 ms, and drops a late
          reply by id. The main thread acknowledges a miss when it reads it; no acknowledgement
          by the end of the bound fails as "the probe’s main thread did not take the lookup
          within N ms (the probe is overloaded)", not given up. The resolver's handler and the
          pool's both turn a throw into a failed lookup naming it.
        - **Check now** asks fresh, single-flighted, ahead of every queued lookup, and uses the
          kept answer only when the resolver does not answer in time, adding that to the
          check's message.
        - **`/etc/hosts` and `/etc/resolv.conf`** are compared by their contents every 5 s: a
          hosts edit drops the names it moves, and a resolv.conf change makes every kept answer
          due and lets holds and denials go; a lookup asked under the old configuration answers
          its own checks, and is kept, as due, only for a name the new one has said nothing of.
        - **A lane's next lookup**: "Check now"'s, then the name whose domain has the smallest
          share of its names failing, the name's own failure left out, then among retries the
          fewest failures in a row and the most recent answer, then the oldest. A failing name
          no check has asked about for 6½ minutes stops counting against its domain.
        - **Probe Health, no protocol change**: `lookupsInFlight` adds the resolver's running and
          queued lookups (`lookupsBesideThePool`); `lookupsGivenUp` counts checks failed for want
          of an answer: the bound, a cancel, a hold, fail-fast, a full queue or `EAI_AGAIN`.
          Protocol 36's two counters are redefined in place, as it is unreleased.
      - **Decisions beyond the review**, taken here:
        1. **"Check now" asks a held name again**, where a scan fails at once: it is how an
           operator sees a DNS fix take. A lookup already stuck still answers it from the kept
           answer. (On the retry lane until the review; ahead of every queued lookup since.)
        2. **The resolver's lanes follow the thread pool**: libuv's lanes less two, between 3
           and 6, so a probe started without the launcher queues less inside libuv; it warns.
        3. **The WinSW configuration sets `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16` too**, as the unit does.
        4. **A queue of at most 10,000 lookups**; a check refused by a full one is given up.
        5. **The probe's own failures are worded as the probe's** (`probeFailed`): a main
           thread too busy to take the lookup, a fault in the resolver, a wait the probe ended.
           None is "no address", and none is given up.
        6. **A `getaddrinfo` that throws is a fault**, and nothing of it is kept.
        7. **A hold is logged at warn at most once a minute**, with how many more were held.
        8. **A check worker runs only `run` messages**: its port now carries the resolver's.
        9. **The perf case's lanes model is the resolver's `getaddrinfo`**, in its own thread,
           at 8 lanes; the model's answering control arm is gone (`system` is the real one),
           and `MS_DNS_WARM_MINUTES` sets how long the warm zone arm runs once its zone is
           silent.

      - **Review.** The review confirmed three major findings and the minor ones below

        1. **A hosts or resolv.conf change was a cold start** (major): every answer, hold and
           failure count was dropped, so a silent zone's names took the first lanes again and
           the answering zones failed behind them, after the edit the docs called the usual
           fix; and the files were compared by `stat`, so a rewrite with the same contents did
           it too. Now the contents are compared (a SHA-256 a file). A hosts edit drops only
           the names whose lines it changed (`hostsNames`). A resolv.conf change makes every
           kept answer due now, within the same grace, lets holds and denials go, and detaches
           lookups still running under the old configuration, whose answer is kept only when
           nothing is (and then as due). **Failures in a row are kept** across it, decided here:
           a name that was not answering is asked again as a retry, on the one retry lane, so a
           zone still silent cannot take the first and shared lanes the answering zones are
           asked on; a name the edit fixed answers its retry at once. Scenario test added: ten
           silent names, more than the four first lanes, a hosts edit giving one of them an
           address and then a resolv.conf rewrite, both mid-outage; zone A never changes
           state, the fixed device never does either, and the other nine go Down once after
           the grace.
        2. **One first-in first-out retry lane for every held name** (major): a name of an
           answering zone held once waited behind every silent name's retry, about 25 minutes
           at 50 names and 30 s, and "Check now" joined the same queue. **Decided here: a lane
           takes the name whose domain (the name less its first label) has the smallest share
           of its names failing** (failing over kept + 1, so a lone device's one failure is
           not a whole zone's), then among retries the fewest failures in a row, then the
           oldest. Why the domain over the other options: a zone that stops answering is a
           domain, so this separates it from the answering zones from its first failure,
           including the first cycle, when every silent name has failed once just as the
           answering name has, which ordering by failures alone cannot; a cap per name or a
           second retry lane for one failure fills with the silent zone's first retries just
           the same. It only reorders a queue, so it never holds a lookup back when nothing
           else waits, and with every name in one domain it is the old order. It applies to
           every queue, so a silent zone's first refreshes and first lookups also go behind
           an answering zone's (the warm zone arm, and a cold restart once a silent name has
           failed). **"Check now" is no longer a retry**: it starts its lookup on a first
           lookup's lane, ahead of every queued one, and moves a queued lookup it joins there.

           answering in 1–10 s failed checks that used to pass. The hold is for new checks

           an answer ("Check now" and a kept answer). The queued fail-fast behind lanes all
           stuck stays, as the synthesis decided it. The outage scenario's first scan after the
           restart now takes the bound, as its checks are each waiting for a lookup.

- [ ] **P-427 — a superseded session's close marks its probe lost after the newer one found it**
      · S · P-416, R-05 · Found 2026-10-17 in `P-416`'s review. When a probe reconnects while its
      old connection is still open, the endpoint destroys the old connection. Its `#handleClose`
      then calls `reachability.lost` for that session's probe without asking whether a newer
      session has replaced it, unlike the `#sessions` and `#pending` cleanup just above, which
      goes by identity. If that close is handled after the new session's `#lookUp` has called
      `found`, the turns `P-416` added run `lost` last. A connected probe is then held, with
      every result decided Unknown/probe, until it next reconnects: the delivery sweep clears
      only a silence. **Done when** a close of a session that a live newer session for the same
      probe has replaced does not call `lost`, with a test that closes the old connection after
      the new one's `found`.

- [ ] **P-428 — the login timing test compares one login with one other** · XS · A-47 · Found
      2026-10-17 in `P-416`'s full suite. `accounts.test.ts`, "spends comparable time on an account
      that does not exist", times one wrong password for a real account and one for an absent
      account, and asserts the absent one took more than a quarter as long. One stall on the
      real account broke it: 111 ms against 600 ms, on a VM another run was sharing. It passed
      three times out of three when rerun alone. **Done when** each side is the median of
      several logins, so that one stall cannot decide it, and the claim (the decoy verification
      happens at all) stands.

- [ ] **P-429 — re-wording an acknowledgement does not reword the sensor** · XS · M-02, P-411 ·
      Found 2026-10-17 in `P-411`. `canAcknowledge` lets an operator acknowledge a sensor that is
      already Down (Acknowledged), and the columns take the new deadline and actor, but the
      re-decision it runs decides the same state and cause, and the same-state branch rewords
      only a hold's words (`#heldWords`), so the sensor keeps the first acknowledgement's message
      until a hold lets it go, when it says the new one: `P-411` keeps the words in force in
      `sensor_runtime.acknowledged_message` (migration 084), which the re-wording writes.
      **Done when** an acknowledgement over an acknowledged sensor says its own words on the
      sensor at once, with a test that acknowledges again in new words.

            named, tested rule (`NARROWINGS`, named on `CheckOff.narrowing`). A narrowing is a
            shape that every glibc from 2.28 to 2.42 reads alike, in a way the check could
            follow, which the check is off for all the same:
            - `no-server`: resolv.conf is absent or names no server, and glibc asks 127.0.0.1;
            - `blank-search`: a `search` or `domain` line names no domain, and glibc skips it;
            - `domain-words`: a `domain` line names more than one, and glibc takes the first;
            - `search-shape`: a search domain, or the hostname's domain when it is searched, is
              not a lower-case name, and glibc takes it as written;
            - `ndots-over-15`: glibc takes 15;
            - `unreadable-as-absent`: the hosts file, gai.conf or /etc/ld.so.preload cannot be
              read, and glibc reads it as a file that is not there.

            Each has its rows, and a mutant that drops its name fails them.
        - **Round 3** (an independent review of `04fd3c5e` found four false vouches and two
          lower defects, and S6 one more). Decided 2026-10-19 by Claude, under the user's
          delegation:
          - **An action group on any other nsswitch.conf line turns the check off.** From 2.33
            glibc reads the file as a whole (nss/nss_database.c `process_line`), and a line it
            cannot parse, for any database it knows, fails the read. Then `getaddrinfo` asks
            nothing at all. Only `[…]` can fail to parse (nss/nss_action_parse.c). The rule
            takes every line with a `[`, comments included, which costs nothing on stock Rocky 9
            or Debian 12: neither has one. Rows at 2.32 and 2.36.
          - **A `::1` or `::ffff:a.b.c.d` hosts line gives the name for family 4.** Asked for
            AF_INET, files-hosts.c's `LINE_PARSER` maps them to 127.0.0.1 or a.b.c.d. So family
            4 for `ip6-localhost` or `ip6-loopback` on Debian's stock `::1` line is now
            `local:hosts`, where it was walked. Rows at families 0, 4 and 6, and pins that
            `::2`, `1::1`, an IPv4-compatible address and the near-misses of `::ffff:` are not
            mapped.
          - **A reading the watch tells during load is kept, not dropped.** The resolver sets
            what it told before it tells, so it never sends a reading again. Before, a look that
            came during load was lost, and the policy vouched on stale servers until restart.
          - **`LD_PRELOAD` or `LD_AUDIT` non-empty, or /etc/ld.so.preload non-empty, turns the
            check off.** An interposed `getaddrinfo` replaces glibc's. The file is read at load
            and watched as a read-once file. A file that cannot be read is off too, as the
            `unreadable-as-absent` narrowing, since ld.so preloads nothing it cannot `access`.
          - **The reasons say what happened.** An unreadable file is named with its error code,
            for example `(EACCES)`. A move says what the file was and what it is now: `absent`,
            `unreadable (<code>)` or `contents sha256:<12 hex>`. A module's move says its states.
          - **A load or look is bounded by `POLICY_LOOK_MS`, 2 s**, since no resolver constant
            fits a file look. On expiry the check goes off with `fault` until restart, and the
            watch is let go. The re-check below changed this to 10 s, off for now. The bound
            covers load as well as onLook: the same file and module reads with no bound would
            hold up the start S3 awaits. After a fault, a look returns at once rather than
            piling up behind one that hangs, and a look that ends late changes nothing.
          - **`timeout:0` is held as 1**, as send_dg floors every try at 1 s
            (resolv/res_send.c).
        - **Re-check of `508f3fcc`** (fixes 1 to 4 and 7, and the `::ffff:` mapping, held
          against glibc). Decided 2026-10-19 by Claude, under the user's delegation:
          - **The bound is a hang detector, not a budget.** At 2 s it could fire on a healthy
            host and leave the check off until restart. One event-loop stall of 2 s trips it,
            because libuv runs timers before the poll that would deliver reads already done.
            And at load 20, a module look's dozen or so file operations can add up to 2 s.
            `POLICY_LOOK_MS` is now 10 s, and load has its own `POLICY_LOAD_MS`, 30 s.
          - **A look past its bound turns the check off for now** (`slow`), and the watch is
            let go. Its file moves were taken before its first await, so nothing is lost. At
            the next look, a look still not ended is a hang, and the check is off until
            restart (`fault`). A look that has ended has what it found dropped (a generation
            count), and the next look looks again, which can turn the check back on.
          - **A load past its bound** is off for now too. If it ends, it builds its view. If
            the first look after its bound finds it still reading, that is a `fault`.
          - **While `slow`, what load read stands:** the snapshot for the helper's `ready`
            does not change. A move already named stays named.
          - **`#fail` holds for one episode.** The first reason stands, logged once. A hung
            load that fails after its hang is named does not overwrite the reason, and a look
            let go that fails later is dropped, like any other way it can end.

          - **Isolation always ends, and a lookup that never returns freezes nothing (D27).**

              is still unsaid stuck, as §1.11 designs. It ends in any case 8 s
              (`HELPER_ISOLATION_MAX_MS`) after the crash that began it, or after the last crash
              during it, whether or not a suspect is in flight. Before, a suspect sent alone held
              every other helper lookup with no bound, so a `getaddrinfo` that never returned
              froze the helper.
            - The resolver keeps its suspects as a set, held ones included, and calls
              `endIsolation()` only once that set is empty (S2's contract, the header of
              `lookup-helper.ts`). Before, a suspect held at the second crash was forgotten when
              the queue emptied, and isolation ended with it still owed. Now a held suspect is
              asked again alone once its hold ends, with nobody waiting for it.
            - The poison ask never holds new starts back. It is sent at the first moment nothing
              is in flight and isolation is off, and what is asked meanwhile starts beside it.
              One that finds no such moment for a whole period waits for its next
              (`poisonDue`).

              only waits left are for lookups in flight that the child has not said are stuck:
              a suspect sent alone, or what was in flight when the next suspect is due. Each
              lasts at most the child's stuck clock (1 s), and the lapse ends them anyway. A
              fail-fast branch for them could never fire before the child speaks, so none was
              written: no test could reach it, and no mutant could judge it.

              stuck was not charged once isolation had ended. The re-check below found that this
              broke D27, and it is fixed there.

      - **S6 built** 2026-10-19, on `feat/p432-s6-check` (on S3's branch), for the coordinator to
        land: **the name check.** `DnsCheck` (`dns-check.ts`) asks a name's servers what glibc
        would ask, with c-ares (`caresAsker`: one fresh channel per candidate and server, one
        try), and its replies decide only where `getaddrinfo` runs: heard within the routing wait
        (250 ms, or a quarter of the check's bound if less) on the probe's lanes; silent in the
        helper, and only there; unvouched (off, cannot vouch, unproven, stood down, skipped,
        unsafe, deferred) in the helper as S3 routes it. `NAME_CHECK_BUILT` is true, so the check
        is on for every shape S4's allowlist takes.
        - **What S6 carries**, as the design's S6 row lists it, less the cuts below: the walk
          (`__res_context_search` and `res_send`: candidates, fast failures, `rotate`, the name
          as it is asked last); keys and their derived phases (D18: heard, silent, mixed,
          unknown), two scouts, the walk again at 5 s doubling to 60 s; the ledger's three pools
          (heard 8, discovery 4, urgent 2) and each server's bucket (D19: 10 a second, 20 at
          once, 5 kept for key walks) in `ForwardBudget`; sampling (D20); the canary, misses,
          skips and the stand-down (N8: an hour, doubling to 8 h within a day); D25's marks
          (unsafe keys, a stuck local name walked for an hour, a stuck sample NotHeard, a
          never-walked helper lookup said stuck NotHeard); a verdict whose timer fired late
          dropped (D31). In the resolver: a lookup being walked is `scouting`, counted as
          queued; a silent name's check fails at once while the helper is down, and the name
          stays queued for it; a zone going silent moves its queued samples to the helper; a
          watched-file change resets the check.
        - **Protocol 39**: one capability, `nameCheck`, strips eight fields together:
          `lookupHelperState`, `lookupHelperLosses`, `lookupHelperMemory` (bytes on the wire,
          MB on the channel), `nameCheckState`, `nameLookupsHeard`, `nameLookupsToHelper`,
          `nameCheckMisses`, `nameWalksDeferred`. The core: lookups `ms.probe.lookup-helper-state`
          and `ms.probe.name-check`, every entry Up (the latch stays the helper's one alarm), eight
          Probe Health channels and eight `/metrics` series. `ms-probe config check`'s gate note
          now says where names are asked.
        - **Decided 2026-10-19 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
          - **Cut, by the design's cut order**: overflow (1), the pressure detector (3:
            `nameCheckState` never reads 5), per-name walks of a key's queued helper lookups when
            it is heard again (4), and Check now's walk path (5: Check now goes to the helper on
            an urgent token, as with the check off). Each cut sends names to the helper, the safe
            side, and S6 was already past its size.
          - A silent key's walk again walks the name that asked, not a stored one: the zone is
            judged by a name someone wants.
          - The routing wait is fixed by the lookup's first waiting check's bound; a later,
            shorter check waits on the same walk rather than starting another.
          - A server's rate refused routes `rate` at once, as D19 says; only pool room is waited
            for, to the step's deadline.
          - A step sent as its lookup was asked takes its key's verdict at the lookup's deadline
            (`SAME_DEADLINE_MS`, 2 ms), so the two never disagree about the same silence; a scout
            wait whose timer fired late routes `stall`, as D31 drops a late verdict.
          - A name error for one type with fast failures for the rest moves to the next
            candidate, as glibc keeps the name error's buffer; under `rotate` every server is
            asked at once and each must reply.
          - The canary is a key walk's question: discovery pool, the key side of the bucket.
          - `lookupHelperState` reads a helper not started yet (`idle`) as 2, starting.
          - The end-to-end test sets `RES_OPTIONS=ndots:1` for its probe, so the check is off
            for the environment (`nameCheckState` 2) and no test sends DNS off the machine.
            The S3 scenarios run with `checkBuilt: false`, so they keep measuring what S3
            measured; SC1 builds the check with an asker that answers as the zones do.
          - **SC1 runs 30 silent names, not 10.** At 10, six scans give up 50 checks in five
            minutes, under `P-441`'s limit of 100, so "one Warning in both modes" would assert
            0 = 0. At 30 both modes give exactly one.

          under `options edns0`; a server that answers the two differently would make the
          check's verdict differ from `getaddrinfo`'s. The policy does not turn the check off
          for `edns0` today; the differential decides.

          stub is played through it. glibc's questions to the stub are read off `lo` (tcpdump);
          resolved's own upstream questions are kept with the run, never judged. The run fails if
          resolved is not active before and after. A row was added to S4's table for the stub file
          as Ubuntu writes it for a link with a search domain (`search corp.example`), beside the
          `search .` one: 267 rows.
        - **What a row is held to** (`test/differential/names-differential.ts`, pure, and run
          unchanged in the boxes):
          1. The policy, loaded in the box against the row's real files, that glibc, the modules
             installed and the lookup's environment, classifies the question as the row says:
             class, `via`, candidates, types, servers and `rotate`. A row is judged by what the
             policy reads there, not only by the export.
          2. For each plan, glibc's questions are the plan's wire exactly, as
             `[server, name, type, try]` in the order the servers saw them: none for a `local`
             name, and under `rotate` one of `wireByOffset`, whose offset is kept.
          - Every server the row's resolv.conf names is a simulator, the ones past the third
            included, and so are 127.0.0.1 and ::1 when no row server is, so a question sent
            anywhere unnamed is in the wire.
          - Each plan's `getaddrinfo` runs in a process of its own through `systemLookup`, the call
            behind `systemResolve` and the helper. So nsswitch.conf and gai.conf are read afresh,
            as glibc reads them once per process below 2.33, and `rotate` starts at random. Every
            cache is cold: no nscd, a simulator with no cache, and resolved with `Cache=no`.

            glibc, Node, whether resolved served the stub).
          - **Every plan of every row must be recorded in every image that replays it**
            (`system-names.test`, D30's "an unverified row fails the run"). A row exported anew,
            or a new image, fails the suite until the differential has recorded it, so a change
            to the policy's tables needs a differential run before it lands.
          - **Boxes of the base images, not the smoke images.** The glibc and the NSS modules
            are the distribution's either way, and the smoke images' PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB,
            which the differential never touches, take minutes to build. Debian 11 takes its
            packages from the snapshot its base image was built from, because its security pool
            on deb.debian.org no longer has the arm64 packages its index lists.
          - **resolved is told three things beyond the cold cache**, each so that the stub
            answers as the plan says and nothing else asks: `ResolveUnicastSingleLabel=yes`,
            since otherwise resolved answers a single-label name SERVFAIL itself and glibc asks
            it again (a wire, but of resolved's making, not the plan's); LLMNR and mDNS off; and a
            dummy link with an address in 198.18.0.0/15 and the default route, because resolved
            asks its global servers only while a link has a routable address, and with no
            network it answers SERVFAIL at once.

            earlier run before it starts, and hands the verdict only the runs this invocation

            claim only the policy's reading: no plan waits out a 30 s try.
          - **Found on the way: a silent plan held the next plan's questions.** The S5 simulator
            models a forwarder, and an unanswered question holds its slot for 10 s and takes in
            every identical question meanwhile. In the first attempt at run 3, the plan after
            `all-silent` found its questions held: `answer` went unanswered and glibc asked
            every try again (10 questions for 2). Run 2 could not show it, because its one
            silent plan came last in each row. Every replay server now holds a slot for 1 ms
            (`NAMESERVER`), and `names-differential.test` asks one question silent and then
            answered.
          - **The stub beside another server is not played** (7). Through resolved, the stub's
            questions come from a capture and every other server's from the simulator. With no
            clock shared between them, the order across them is not seen, so the replay records
            such a row as a setup problem. No committed row is one, and
            `names-differential.test` asserts that.
          - **A replay that stops leaves no run** (8). Each image's run is written to
            `<image>.json.partial` and moved into place only once complete. `names-verify` reads
            each file on its own, names one that is not a run, and judges the rest.
          - **The verdict runs in a box this invocation built** (10), not always `debian12`.
          - **Each base is the digest the recordings were made on** (12), read from

          - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
            - **For 7, a setup problem, not a merge by time.** The simulator's log carries no
              timestamps, and a pcap's are the kernel's wall clock. A merge would rest on two
              clocks agreeing to the millisecond. No row needs the stub beside another server
              yet, and the suggested fallback is exact.
            - **For 4, the export skips literals, and the replay refuses one.** Changing
              `names-lookup` to refuse would have stopped the whole image's run on the first
              literal. The replay's refusal fails that row alone.
            - **For 6, the silent plan only where waiting it out takes at most 6 s.** That is
              4 rows and about 16 s an image. The defaults wait 10 s to 28 s a row, and a
              30 s `timeout` 150 s, past the lookup's own 120 s bound. The plan has one candidate
              only, as whether a search walk goes on after a timeout is another question
              (`__res_context_search` stops on anything but NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL).
            - **For 12, the digests come from the recordings, not a second table in the

      - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation**, landing S3, S6 and S8
        together on `integ/r5-1019`:
        - **SC12 claims what K4 promises.** With four silent labels on a cold scan, an
          answering label whose lookup reaches the helper after the fourth waits behind the
          helper's 4 first lanes and fails at the 1 s stuck bound, as K4 decided. The old script
          passed only while the fourth silent label happened to arrive last. S3's fix narrows
          the scenario to three silent labels and asserts their overlap, not the code. K4 stands:
          SC12 runs with the check off, and with the check on, an answering name its servers are
          heard for goes to the probe's lanes and never queues behind the helper's.
        - **The check's missing EDNS record is a known limit in 1.0, bounded by D25.** Measured
          2026-10-20 in the toolchain: Node 24.19.0's c-ares 1.34.6 sends a question with
          ARCOUNT 0, while glibc sends an OPT record under `options edns0`, which
          systemd-resolved's stub `resolv.conf` sets. Only a server that answers the two
          differently can make the check disagree with `getaddrinfo`. The side that matters, a
          server that answers plain questions and drops EDNS ones, puts a name on the probe's
          lanes that then sticks there, and D25 marks its zone at the first such lookup, so later
          ones go to the helper. The other side sends names to the helper, which is safe.
          Building our own asker would replace the design's c-ares. Node exposes no EDNS flag.
          `P-454` holds the fix, and the release notes list the limit.
        - **`P-453`, `P-460` and `P-461` are in 1.0, before the rc.3 cut.** The field test runs
          the gate (the user's decision of 2026-10-19), so a working name poisoned for an hour by
          an outside kill would be a false alarm there (`P-453`). The design gives S8 two
          recordings before the cut, and `P-460` is the second. `P-461` is the one place the
          policy is not shown off in a real box.

          never-cut list: an avoided name started from the probe's queues (`#pumpProbe`), and an
          avoided name settled after `stop()` with the probe's pool.

        - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
          - **One check, at the point of start, rather than one at each path that queues on the
            probe's lanes.**
            - A name becomes avoided while its lookup waits: a crash of its other family, a
              poison mark, a suspect.
            - Many paths queue a lookup there: the route at the ask, a walk's verdict, a sample,
              the fall-back when the helper goes down or rests, Check now's promotion.
            - Only the start is the moment `getaddrinfo` is asked, which is the moment D27 is
              about. One check there covers every path, including any added later.
            - The cost is one set lookup per start in gate mode.
          - **A moved lookup goes to the helper as unvouched, even when its walk was heard.**
            The walk vouched for the probe's lanes, which the name may no longer use. As
            unvouched it falls back as any avoided name does when the helper goes down.
            `#fallBack` moves only unvouched lookups, and `#gateRefusal` then fails it. Left as
            heard, it waited out its check's bound in a queue nothing serves: the route mutant.
          - **The D27 rows route at the probe's own 250 ms, not the file's 60 ms.** At 60 ms the
            `verdict` row with the helper rejoining then down was routed silent in four of eight
            mutant runs while another session's suite shared the VM. When that happens it tests
            nothing.
      - **The gate track's fix round 1 built** 2026-10-20, on `feat/p432-gate-r2`, for the
        coordinator to land: six review items on the second round and `P-453`.
        - **A check whose own ask starts a refused lookup is told at once** (items 1, 2 and 5,
          one defect, which the second round's `#offProbe` brought in).
          - `#offProbe` settles a refused lookup inside `#run`. When the pump that runs it is
            the asking check's own, in `#ask`, the lookup was settled before that check had
            joined it. Two pumps do that: Check now's `#promote`, which exempts a lookup from
            `P-438`'s rule or moves a held name's retry to a free first lane, and the pump that
            lets a lookup held back only by `P-438`'s window go.
          - The check then waited its whole bound on a settled lookup and failed
            `RESOLVER_LATE`, naming a slow resolver. On a worker's port it got no reply at all.

        - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
          - **The check is answered in `#ask`, with the words `#offProbe` kept, rather than the
            settle deferred** (the review's option 1).
            - A deferred settle leaves a lookup `queued` in no queue until it runs. Each of
              `#lanesStuck`, `#silentRefusal`, `#queuedCount`, `#fallBack` and `#rejoin` would
              then have to skip it, and one that did not would tell the check the wrong cause.
            - The words are kept rather than judged again, so the check is told exactly what
              the lookup's other checks were. Nothing between the refusal and the read can
              change them.
            - `#ask` is not entered again: once stopped, `#start`, `#run` and `#offProbe` would
              settle the new lookup in the same way, and it would loop.
            - Not counted again in `routed.faulted`: one lookup refused is one fault, as
              `#fallBack` and `#scouted` count it, however many checks wait for it.
          - **The slow first read: the code, not the docs.**
            - The bound is a hang detector, not a budget (`POLICY_LOOK_MS`'s comment): one stall
              can pass it. That is why every later read gets a look to end in.
            - The read at start needs that grace most. A probe starting on a starved host is
              the one likeliest to read slowly, and losing the check until restart there costs
              it for the whole run.
            - The cost: a first read that really hangs is named a hang one look later, at least
              5 s after the 30 s. The check is off for the whole time either way.
          - **The poison re-ask: the docs, not the code.**
            - D27's re-ask holds nothing back (`#poisonAsk`). The moment with nothing in flight is
              its start only. A new child's first pump is such a moment, so the re-ask asked
              again there gets the same start as an hourly one.
            - Sending it truly alone would hold back every lookup queued during the rejoin
              window, which D27 rejected. Dropping it for its next due re-ask would put it off an
              hour, since the helper moves `nextAskAt` as it asks.
            - What the review names, every name in flight avoided at a crash then, is the same
              as for any re-ask with lookups started beside it. Isolation begins at the second
              loss.
          - **The failed send: the docs.** The code is right: an ask the child never saw is
            never charged.

          for a name avoided since it queued, while the helper is down or resting, waits until
          that lookup starts (and is refused), or until its lanes are stuck (`RESOLVER_STUCK`),
          rather than failing at once as a new ask for the name would. D27 holds. A ticket
          number is owed by the coordinator.
