              sees takes the window that read closed as well as the one it opens
              (`PeakWindows.lossSeen`). The poll is `stoppedLook`, run in the third block on a
              clock the test moves.
            - **The windows must reach the arm's end, and a failed read fails the arm.**
              `PeakWindows.finish` records where it cut the last window, `peakFacts` carries it
              and any failure into the facts, and the judge fails a last window short of the end,
              an end not measured, and any read that failed.
          - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
            - **N1 by reading before each look, not by a window from the SIGSTOP**: that would
              allow the transient through the seconds before the detach, while the stopped
              child's tokens are still held and nothing can pass 18; nor by a hook on the helper's
              route, which is production code. The loss came after the look before, so after every
              read but the last: the transient is allowed from at most one poll and a read's round
              trip before the loss was seen. P1's losses are its own kills, cut at once as before:
              the read is posted in the kill's own turn, before the helper can see the exit, fork,
              and have the next child ask again. The printed windows merge runs of one kind.
            - **A failed read fails the arm**, not only a print: the stretch it ends was held to
              no bound, as an unread stretch is, which round 1 already fails.
            - **P3's answer after the stall has no upper bound**: after a 15 s stall the timers
              run first, a quarter of the sensors due at once, so the read of the waiting reply
              can come late without being another reply's. The three facts together say it was
              the waiting one; the time is printed. `repliesDuring` stays a print: it counts every
              client's replies, so it cannot say the stall's own was among them.
            - **The lookup's state is read off the probe's lanes, not the model**: a lookup
              settles in the turn its reply is read (the model's promise and the lanes'
              continuation run before the next I/O callback), so one whose reply was read before
              the send's callback is not open there.
          - **Tests**, each run after the last change: `name-lookups.test.ts`'s third block, 85 of
            85 in about three seconds (74 before: six judge cases, three for P3's setup and three
            for the windows' end and a failed read; and five on their own: a loss a poll sees on
            a clock the test moves, with the window judged both ways; P2's look through its
            detach, `hung` loss and next child; a last read that fails, through `peakFacts`;
            P3's setup from flights and a simulator log; the probe lanes' open lookups at the
            simulator, answered and failed). P1, P2 and P3 scaled down again, all held (276 s).
            Prettier and eslint on the changed files.
          - **Mutants: 24, on the toolchain**, each restored with `shutil.copy` and `os.utime`,
            checked with `filecmp`, its marker seen in `dist` before its run and none left after
            the last rebuild, `dist` read back against the source:
            - the judge, 7, each killed by the case made to break it: P3's lookup settled, never
              answered, answered during the stall, reply not sent; a failed read; a last window
              short of the end; an end not measured;
            - the windows, 9: `lossSeen` not taking the last window, or not the open one; a cut
              that opens the transient again after a loss's window ended; the timer's next
              window decided once its read is in (an overlapping loss then reached back); no
              `endMs`; P2's look not reading first, or cutting a loss rather than taking the
              window read; `peakFacts` without the failure, or without the end;
            - P3's setup and the lanes, 7: the lookup always open; a failed lookup counted as
              answered; no bound on the reply's time, or on the question's; a settled lookup
              left open; an answer, or a failure, not recorded;
            - through its arm, 1: P3's stall begun only once its lookup had settled, the item's
              own case. The arm failed with the lookup settled before the stall and never
              answered after it, while its reply read as sent before the stall ended, which is
              all round 1's judge asked.
          - **Shown to run, scaled down**: P2 read its peak 401 times, its detach's window from
            the read before that look 10.6 s long, the peak at most 3 in and out of its windows;
            P1's as before; both reached their end. P3's stall held its own lookup's reply
            unread: open as the stall began, its reply sent before it ended, answered 66 ms after.
        - **S7 review round 3, fixed** 2026-10-20, on `feat/p432-s7-perf` (one finding, N3: since
          round 2's 50 ms windows the judge's bound on the transient's length could not fire), in
          commits after round 2's: test code and docs only, no production code.
          - **What changed.** The judge reads the transient a run at a time. The windows that meet
            with it are merged (`stretches`, which the print used, is now the judge's), and each run
            must lie inside the stretch its losses allow: from the loss, or a second before a poll
            saw it, to 10.5 s and a late timer's second after it, the stretches of losses that meet
            taken together. The judge fails a run past that stretch, a run with no loss to open it,
            and windows with no loss times (`lossesAt`). The times are the arm's stamps, not
            `PeakWindows`': P1 stamps each kill before its cut (`killedAt`), P2's are its look's
            `downAt` and `hungAt` (`lossTimes`), and `peakFacts` carries them onto the windows'
            clock (`PeakWindows.since`). The per-window length check is gone, since the run's
            covers one window or many. The printed windows name the losses.
          - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
            - **N3 by the losses' times, not a fixed length per run.** A run bounded by a length
              alone (10.5 s, the late timer's second, and a poll and a read's round trip) would
              fail two losses whose windows meet, which D16 allows (10 s after each loss, at most 5
              losses in 10 minutes), and would pass a transient of the right length where no loss
              was. The times are the arm's own, so a fault in what cuts the windows (the finding's:
              `lossSeen` at every look) is judged against something the windows did not say.
            - **A loss a poll saw may open its transient a second early; one the arm made, not at
              all.** P2's look stamps a loss after the read before it. The window that read closed
              began a poll's 50 ms and two reads' round trips before the stamp: a second, behind a
              busy event loop, as the late timer's. P1's kill is stamped before its cut, so its
              transient starts at the kill.
          - **Tests**, each run after the last change: `name-lookups.test.ts`'s third block, 91 of
            91 in about three seconds (85 before). Four judge cases: the finding's own (the
            transient kept on from the detach through the `hung` loss's window in 50 ms windows),
            one where no loss was, one from before its kill, and the losses' times not measured.
            Two cases on their own: P2's 50 ms windows judged clean inside their losses' stretches,
            the kept-on run named once as a run, and a seen loss's second tried either side of the
            bound; and the losses on the windows' clock through `lossTimes` and `peakFacts`.
            `PeakWindows`' overlapping losses are judged clean too, and fail without the later
            loss. P1 and P2 scaled down again, both held (202 s). Prettier and eslint on the
            changed files.
          - **Mutants: 14, on the toolchain**, each restored with `shutil.copy` and `os.utime`,
            checked with `filecmp`, its marker seen in `dist` before its run and none left after
            the last rebuild:
            - the judge, 8, each killed: the runs not merged; a run's end not bounded; a run with
              no loss passed; a made loss given a seen one's second; a seen loss given none; the
              stretches of losses that meet not merged; the losses' times not required; a seen
              loss's second widened to 1.2 s;
            - the losses' plumbing, 4, each killed: `since` without the windows' origin; the kills
              as seen; the `hung` loss dropped; `peakFacts` without the losses;
            - through their arms, 2, in one build since each changes only its own arm: P2's look
              taking every look as the detach's loss, the finding's own fault, failed P2 with the
              transient at 18.0–45.6 s, past 10.5 s after a loss, across 736 windows each too short
              for round 1's check; P1's kill stamped after its cut's read failed both its runs with
              no loss to open them.

- [ ] **P-433 — a device under `targetPolicy: none` resolves outside the probe's resolver** · S ·
      P-426, A-57 · Filed 2026-10-17 by `P-426`. Under `probe.targetPolicy: none`,
      `checkedTarget` returns before resolving, and the transport's socket resolves the name
      itself: a `getaddrinfo` on every connection, outside `P-426`'s cache, its lanes and its
      holds, and outside Probe Health's counts. A probe set to `none` with a silent zone has
      `A-66`'s collapse back for exactly the names it serves. **Done when** a device by name
      under `none` is resolved by the probe's resolver and connected to at an address it
      answered, as under the other policies but without the policy's check, counted on Probe
      Health, with a test per transport family (socket `lookup`, SNMP, SSH, HTTP).

- [ ] **P-434 — a channel name or unit a build takes away stays on existing sensors** · XS ·
      P-404 · Found 2026-10-17 by `P-404`. The start-up pass writes a declared name and unit only
      where they say something of their own (`channelLabel`): a name more than the key, a unit
      that is not empty. A build that stops naming a channel, declaring it by its key so that
      readings may name it, or that drops its unit, leaves the old words on every existing
      sensor. New sensors get the key or no unit, side by side with them: `P-404`'s problem in
      the other direction, as `P-291` was `S-18`'s. Nothing on the row says whether its words
      came from an older declaration or from a reading, which is why the pass cannot take them
      away. **Done when** decided: record where each channel's name and unit came from (a
      migration, as `limits_source` did for limits), so that a withdrawn declaration is taken
      back without touching a reading's words; or the type guide says a build cannot take a name
      or a unit away from existing sensors, and why.

- [x] **P-441 — Probe Health does not flag a resolver that is not keeping up** · S · P-426, A-66 ·
      Found 2026-10-18 in `P-426`'s quiet window
      (`docs/findings/2026-10-18-name-lookups-through-the-resolver.md`).
      - **What Probe Health showed.** `lookupsInFlight` reached 449 to 483 in both zone arms, and `lookupsGivenUp` counted every check that failed for want of an answer. Neither channel has a limit, so Probe Health stayed Up through a restart that put about 2,250 sensors on healthy devices into Warning. The resolver was named only in those sensors' messages and in the probe's log.
      - **The counter can hide the burst.** `lookupsGivenUp` is stored as a rate and a counter that falls reads as a reset, so the burst after a restart can hide behind the first record.
      - **Done when** Probe Health goes Warning while the resolver is giving checks up, and says so in a message that names the resolver and the domains not answering. Judge the defaults against this finding's arms: Warning in the cold zone arm and the every-name-silent arm, not in the warm zone arm's answering zone, and not on the slow arm's first scan.
      - **Done when, also:** a restart's given-up checks are not lost to the counter reset, with a test for each.

      **P-441 outcome** (with `P-432` S3's protocol 38, 2026-10-19). Probe Health gains
      `lookupsGivenUpRecently`, **Warning from 100**: the checks given up in the last five
      minutes, which the core counts from `lookupsGivenUp`'s running total as it counts
      `scriptGroupsRefusedRecently`, so a restart's burst is counted whole and the Warning clears
      five minutes after the last. The sensor's message names the resolver and up to three
      domains not answering, from the probe's `lookupsNotAnswering` (`names of a single label`
      for those), at protocol 38. The limit against the finding's arms: the slow arm gives up 0
      and does not warn; the warm arm's answering zone gives up 0, and its silent zone 738 once
      its grace is over, which warns, as that zone's outage; the cold arm 5,751 and every name
      silent 5,000, which warn. The same signal in both modes of `probe.nameResolver`
      (`P-432`'s SC10 holds them to one Warning each). Tests: `probe-health.test.ts` in the
      core (the count across a restart's reset, the domains, and nothing said while nothing is
      given up), `health-types.test.ts` (the limit), `probe-health-report.test.ts` (the domains
      in both modes) and the capabilities' strip below 38.
- [x] **P-442 — a TLS identity test reads no server name under load and says nothing about why** · XS ·
      A-71 · Found 2026-10-18 in `S4`'s second full suite, on a host at a load near 270. In
      `packages/sensors/test/tls-address-identity.test.ts`, 'tls.security on a device given by
      name still asks for it by name' failed at `assert.deepEqual(certificate.named,
      ['localhost'])` with `[]`: the `tls.certificate` run reached no handshake. The `tls.security`
      half before it passed. The test passed 8 of 8 alone and in the next full suite, and the
      branch changed nothing in `packages/sensors`. The assertion does not print the
      execution's message, so the run cannot say whether the check timed out (5 s), was refused
      or never resolved `localhost`. **Done when** the test asserts the execution's outcome with
      `execution.message` before it reads `named`, so the next failure names its cause, and that
      cause is either fixed or filed.

      **P-442 outcome.** Not load but a port: `localhost` answers `::1` first, neither TLS sensor
      asks for the device's `v4`, and `127.0.0.1:0` can be handed a port this file still holds on
      `::1`, so the handshake went to another TLS server (a decoy there gives the `[]` found); the
      case answers its own lookup with `127.0.0.1` and asserts each outcome, with its message,
      before the names.
- [x] **P-443 — the resolver client's late-answer test gives the ack 40 ms and reads busy under load** · XS ·
      P-426 · Found 2026-10-18 in `S4`'s fourth full suite, run beside an rpm smoke. In
      `packages/probe/test/resolve-client.test.ts`, 'ends its own wait at its bound and a little
      slack, and drops the late answer by its id' asks with `waitMs: 60`, so the ack bound
      (`waitMs - ACK_LEAD_MS`) is 40 ms. The test's own `await next()` and `postMessage` took
      longer than that, and the client rejected with `ERESOLVERBUSY` instead of
      `ERESOLVERLATE`. The probe package passed 756 of 756 alone straight after, and the branch
      changed no probe code. **Done when** the test sets its ack bound apart from its wait (the
      client takes `ackWithinMs`), so it tests the late path and not the scheduler, with a mutant
      showing it still fails when the late timer is removed.

      **P-443 outcome.** The late case's ack bound is 10 s, past its wait and slack, so only the
      late timer can end it (a mutant without that timer fails it); the ack-50 ms case had the
      same race and now answers on a port with no channel between.
- [x] **A-85 — HTTP, TLS, SSH and database checks ignore the device's IP version** · S · A-57 ·
      Found 2026-10-18 while fixing `P-442`, then audited type by type against `04411fff`
      (every claim re-checked by a second reader, none refuted).
      - **Honoured** on the lookup and the connect: `port.*`, `mail.*`, `snmp.*` (`auto` is IPv4 by design), and `icmp.*`, which passes `-4`/`-6` to the ping binary. A credential set that pins a device to one address is also honoured, since `pinTarget` takes the family.
      - **Not honoured:**
        - `tls.certificate` and `tls.security`: `guardOf` (`checked-target.ts:116`) carries no family, and `handshake()` gives `tls.connect` none.
        - The five HTTP types: `readCommon` (`http/request.ts:641`) never reads `ipVersion`, and `checkedForRequest` asks for family 0.
        - The four `ssh.*` types: `ssh/check.ts:62` and `ssh/session.ts:553`. ssh2 is not given `forceIPv4`/`forceIPv6` under policy `none`.
        - The three `db.*` types: family 0 on purpose (`db-shared.ts:318`), "as the drivers always connected", which the device's setting contradicts.
      - **What it does to a `v4` device** whose name has an A and an AAAA:
        - The guard judges the AAAA too, so a link-local AAAA (or a ULA under `private`) refuses the check, and the device reads Down over an address it would never use.
        - Otherwise Node's address selection tries the resolver's first family. On a host with global IPv6 that is IPv6, with IPv4 only as a fallback after 250 ms. The check then measures the path the operator ruled out.
        - A `v6` device is the mirror image: a name with only an A record connects over IPv4 rather than failing as `port.*` and `mail.*` do.
      - **Harmless:** the listener types (`snmp.trap`, `syslog.receiver`, `flow.netflow`) resolve with family 0 only to recognise a sender. `windows.*` is withheld from v1.
      - **Side finding, dev only:** on darwin `icmp.*` passes `-4`/`-6`, which macOS `ping` does not take.
      **Done when** each of the eleven types (and `db.*`, or a stated reason it stays family 0) asks the guard for the device's family and connects only over it, under every policy including `none`. Proof is a test per transport against a simulator listening on `127.0.0.1` and `::1` at once, for a `v4`, a `v6` and an `auto` device; and `CAPABILITIES.MD`/the type guide say what `ipVersion` does.

      **A-85 outcome.** All eleven types and `db.*` ask the guard for the device's family and
      connect only over it, under every policy; `auto` is family 0 as before, and nothing stays
      family 0 on purpose. `port.*` and `mail.*` keep the family and now walk it too.
      `checked-target.ts` has `familyOf`, `anAddressOf`, `noAddressSaid`, `socketUnresolved`,
      `familyLookup`, `familyOfAnswer`, `connectFailure` and `resolvedUnchecked`, and `lookupFor`
      takes the family.
      - **No socket is told the family.** One told `family: 4|6` asks its lookup for one
        address and connects to that alone, so a name whose first address of the family is dead
        fails. Under the guarded policies the socket gets `checkedLookup`, as before. Under
        `none` it gets `familyLookup`, which is `dns.lookup` forced to the family, keeping
        `all: true`, so Node still walks every address of it (`autoSelectFamily`).
      - **TLS:** both types pass the family to the guard and to `lookupFor`. `handshake()` reads
        it only for its wording. `tls.security` rethrows the name's failure when every handshake
        failed to resolve, in place of "accepted no TLS version".
      - **HTTP:** `readCommon` reads `ipVersion`, `checkedForRequest` asks for it, and a request
        with no checked address (`none`) gets `familyLookup`. `resolveRedirect` strips a URL's
        IPv6 brackets and compares addresses as a `BlockList` matches them. Before this, a
        same-host redirect on a device given as an IPv6 address was never followed.
      - **SSH:** the guard asks for the family. Under `none` a `v4`/`v6` name is connected on the
        session's own socket through `familyLookup`, not by `ssh2`, whose `forceIPv4`/`forceIPv6`
        would be a second lookup path. A pinned target still wins and resolves nothing.
        `SshPhase` gains `resolve`: a socket's `ENOTFOUND`/`EAI_AGAIN` fails there, in the guard's
        words. `SshTarget.ipVersion` is in the pool key.
      - **Databases:** the device's guard and SQL Server's redirect guard ask for the family.
        Under `none`, a named `v4`/`v6` device's driver is handed a socket through
        `familyLookup` (`pg` and `mysql2` a `stream`, `tedious` a `connector`). A device given as
        an address keeps the family for its routed server, which `tedious`'s connector resolves
        over it when nothing checks it. A routed name with no address of the family says so
        (`DbRoutedUnresolvedError` takes the family and the device's host).
      - **`port.tcp`, `port.range`, `mail.*`:** they passed `family` beside the checked lookup,
        so they tried the first address alone under every policy. They now pass it to
        `lookupFor`. `port.tcp` drops its own `unresolved` and says the guard's sentence, phase
        `resolve`, and so does its socket under `none`. The mail sensors name the family too.
        `port.range` under `none` resolves the name once for the scan (`resolvedUnchecked`) and
        fails one that does not resolve, phase `resolve`, where it read every port closed.
      - **Wording, every transport, every policy:** a name with no address of the family fails
        `did not resolve to an IPv6 address` (or IPv4), phase `resolve`, in the guard's words.
        `EAI_AGAIN` says the probe's resolver is not answering, never that a record is missing.
      - **Review** (18 confirmed, all minor or nit): fixed in the same commit. The walk under
        `none` (A85-1, DRV-1, ERR-5, T1), the walk for `port.*`/`mail.*`, SSH's resolve phase
        (A85-3, DRV-2, ERR-1, T3), `EAI_AGAIN` (ERR-2), the routed family (A85-2, A85-4, DRV-3,
        ERR-3, T4), IPv6 redirect brackets (A85-5), `port.tcp`/mail wording (ERR-4),
        `tls.security`'s diagnosis (ERR-6), the SSH pin (T2). A literal of the other family is
        `A-87`.
      - **Second check** (three minor, two small), fixed in the same commit. **A85-B1:** an
        IPv4-mapped answer (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`) is IPv4 (`familyOfAnswer`, with `unmapped`) in the
        guard's filter, `pinTarget`'s candidates, `familyLookup` (which now filters, and answers
        `ENOTFOUND` when nothing of the family is left) and `resolvedUnchecked`. macOS answers an
        IPv6 lookup with them for a name with only A records, and a `v6` device on a macOS probe was
        reached over IPv4. The answer keeps its spelling, which the policy's refusal names and the

      - **Third check** (one minor regression, four small), fixed in the same commit. **R3-1:**

      - **Tests:** `packages/sensors/test/ip-version.test.ts`, 260 cases. Every server is two

        - a link-local AAAA and A, and a ULA and an RFC 1918 address, beside loopback;

        - an IPv4-mapped answer for a `v6` device, under both, and for an `auto` one;

        - every address refusing, the message naming a cause and both addresses, phase `connect`;
        - `EAI_AGAIN` under `none`, for `v6` and `auto`.
        Also covered: every HTTP type under `none`; `port.range` under both policies, and under

        answer not pinned; the SSH pool key; what a driver and a redirect are handed; and
        `tedious`'s connector for a routed server under `none`. `db-checked-target.test.ts` adds a

      - **Mutants:** 34 for the first round, each failing the cases of its own rule. The old
        sixteen, on the code as it now is, the TLS connect now two: the family taken from each guard

- [x] **P-453 — a lookup helper child killed from outside while isolating poisons a working name** · XS ·
      P-432 · Found 2026-10-19 by `P-432` S3, writing its scenarios. While the helper isolates
      (D27), a suspect is sent alone, and any `exit` loss with it alone in flight charges it
      (`lookup-helper.ts`, `#lose`), as it charges a poison name's hourly re-ask: the name is
      marked poison, its checks fail at once for an hour, and it is never asked on the probe's
      own lanes. The loss's signal is not looked at. An exit says nothing of the name when the
      child was ended by SIGKILL, SIGTERM or SIGINT from outside (an operator, the kernel's OOM
      killer, a cgroup kill), or exited with a code: `getaddrinfo` crashing raises a signal of
      its own. A channel that closes before the exit is read says neither, so the charge waits
      for the exit. The scenarios kill the child only between scans, so none ran into it. **Done when** only a signal a crash raises (SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGABRT, SIGILL,
      SIGFPE, SIGTRAP, SIGSYS) charges a suspect or a re-ask, and any other end is an `exit` loss
      charged to no one, its suspects asked again alone, with a test for each and a mutant.

      **P-453 outcome. Only a crash is charged, and every name in flight at any end stays off the
      probe's lanes.** Built 2026-10-20 on `feat/p432-gate-r2`, in
      `packages/probe/src/resolver/lookup-helper.ts`. No protocol change and no migration.
      - **The signal decides.** `CRASH_SIGNALS` holds the seven, and `crashedBy` reads the
        child's end. An `exit` loss charges its lookup only when the child ended by one of them.
        S3's rule stands: only a lookup alone in flight is charged, a suspect or a poison name's
        re-ask. SIGKILL, SIGTERM, SIGINT and any exit code charge no one. A suspect is asked
        again alone. A poison mark keeps its retry, not doubled, and its name is asked again.
      - **A channel that closes before the exit is read waits for the exit** (`#awaitExit`). This
        happens only when a chargeable lookup is alone in flight and the channel closed, or the
        child broke the protocol, first. A loss taken on an ask that could not be written never
        waits: that ask stays in flight and is never charged, so no lookup in flight is
        chargeable, and the loss is taken at once (corrected in the gate track's fix round 1,
        under `P-432`). The child is sent SIGKILL at once. A process
        already dead is not changed by it, and its exit still says how it died. While the helper
        waits, nothing is sent to the child, nothing it says is read, and it is not judged. An
        exit not read within `exitWaitMs` (1 s), counted after the polls, is taken as no crash.
        The loss keeps the cause it was first taken on, with the exit's status added.
      - **An ask that could not be written is never charged** (`unsent`): the child never saw
        the name.
      - **Tests.** `lookup-helper.test.ts` has 11 tests under 'the lookup helper: only a crash is
        charged':
        - a table of 12 ends: each crash signal charges and is the mark's signal; each other end
          charges no one, asks again alone, keeps the helper isolating, and keeps the name off
          the probe's lanes;
        - three suspects ended by SIGKILL rest the helper on the fifth loss, with nothing poison;
        - a poison re-ask ended by SIGKILL is not charged again, then one ended by SIGSEGV is;
        - a channel closed before the exit is read: nothing is sent, read or judged until the
          exit, and then a crash is charged;
        - the same, with SIGTERM: not charged;
        - a live child whose channel closed is killed, and its exit by that SIGKILL is not
          charged;
        - a protocol fault: nothing is sent to the child during the wait, and nothing it sends
          is taken;
        - an error the child reports during the wait takes no loss of its own;
        - an exit not read within the wait: charged to no one, after the polls; a stop during
          the wait ends it;
        - an ask that could not be written is not charged;
        - a memory loss keeps its names off the probe's lanes.
      - **Mutants: 19, all killed.** Any signal taken as a crash. SIGSYS dropped from the set.
        The signal ignored in the charge. The exit's signal not recorded. No wait for the exit.
        Asks sent during the wait. Messages read during the wait. The child judged during the
        wait. The wait's timer left after a stop. The timer left after the loss. The cause it
        was first lost on dropped. The guard against other losses during the wait removed.
        `over` never set. No polls before the timer's loss. Unsent asks charged. No avoidance on
        a memory loss. No kill when the wait starts. Lookups charged when not alone in flight.
        Lookups charged when neither suspect nor re-ask.
      - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
        - **An end that is not a crash still keeps every name in flight off the probe's lanes**
          (the avoidance entry), and **so does a `memory` loss**, which kept none before.
          - D27 says a name that may have ended the child never reaches the probe's own
            `getaddrinfo`.
          - A name whose lookup grows the child's memory is caught in one of two ways. The
            helper's 256 MiB cap, read every 500 ms, catches it as a `memory` loss. If it grows
            past the cap between reads, the kernel's or the cgroup's OOM killer catches it, as an
            uncharged SIGKILL. Neither can be told apart from a leak or a kill from outside.
          - So such an end is never charged, which would make a working name poison on a guess.
            It is always avoided: asked on the probe's own lanes, the same name could grow the
            probe, whose cgroup (`MemoryMax=6G`) holds every check.
          - Repeated losses rest the helper as before, so a name that ends every child costs the
            same rest a crash would.
          - What is left: a cgroup-wide OOM kill takes the probe with the helper, and no routing
            prevents it.
        - **The exit wait is 1 s, and only for a lone chargeable lookup.** Node's `disconnect`
          and `exit` come in either order. Without the wait, a crash first seen as a closed
          channel would never be charged. The exit of a process sent SIGKILL is read within
          milliseconds, and the bound covers one that never exits. The helper stays up
          meanwhile, and its asks are refused as unavailable, which the resolver routes as it
          routes any refused ask.
        - **A Windows crash is not read** (`P-464`). On Windows a crash ends with an NTSTATUS
          exit code, not a signal, so no end is charged there: names are still avoided and
          losses still rest the helper. Release 1.1 is the Windows release.
        - **Names in flight when the helper goes quiet, or is lost `hung`, are not avoided**
          (`P-463`). Neither is a crash or a memory loss, and `P-453` is about how an `exit` is
          read. A lookup that hangs on the probe's lanes holds a lane and nothing more, and
          D25's stuck marks bound that. Whether a name can wedge the child itself, and so the
          probe, is that ticket's to settle.

- [x] **P-460 — the name gate's differential has glibc's wire and not yet the walk's** · S ·
      P-432 · Filed 2026-10-20 by `P-432` S8. S8 records what glibc sends for each of S4's rows
      in seven images and holds the policy to it. D30's second recording, the walk's wire from
      `DnsCheck.route` alone (no lanes, no helper), needs S6. **Done when**, with S6 landed,
      `name-gate-differential.sh` records the walk for every row and plan beside glibc's and

      heard if and only if glibc returned within 1 s; plus §7.5's regression assertions (gate
      answers against `system`'s, the helper's against the lanes'), its budget rows (dnsmasq at
      `dns-forward-max=30` with a 150-name silent zone in both modes, the same after a helper
      SIGKILL, resolved's distinct upstream questions), and its answer rows (TC with TCP dropped,
      with and without `edns0`; FORMERR; A answered and AAAA SERVFAIL from server 1 with server 2
      silent).

      **P-460 outcome.** `name-gate-differential.sh` plays each plan twice, in separate runs:
      glibc's wire (A), and then the walk's alone (B). The walk is `DnsCheck.route` in a
      `names-modes` process of the row's own, with a `ForwardBudget` and c-ares of its own, no
      lanes and no helper, proven by its canary. In run 4 the canary was asked with the plan's
      answers already set, and was answered only because the S5 simulator answers `localhost`
      itself; since fix round 1 every server answers NXDOMAIN until the checks are proven. The
      same process then makes §7.5's regression lookups. **Run 4 passed in all seven images on
      this build**: 260 rows in each image (251 on Rocky 8) and 2,966 plans, every walk agreeing
      with glibc's (2,128 heard, 70 silent and 768 local), every regression holding, the 6 answer
      rows in every image, both budget boxes and the five boxes with the check off. Each image's
      box took 303–494 s from its start, and the whole run about 50 minutes
      (`docs/findings/2026-10-20-name-gate-differential.md`, run 4). Those per-image times are
      the script's lines, which counted the answer rows as rows (266, and 257 on Rocky 8) and, for
      Ubuntu 24.04, held about 72 s of the resolved budget box: its replay took about 317 s.
      - **The walk is held to glibc's first asks** (`walkProblems`): each (server, name, type)
        once, at its first question, the transport and the try aside, the name in lower case.
        - A heard walk asked exactly glibc's first asks, in order. A silent one asked a
          non-empty prefix of them.
        - Heard if and only if glibc returned within 1 s (`WITHIN_MS`).
        - No question is asked twice over UDP, and a walked row is routed by its walk.
        - A `local` row is routed `local` with nothing asked.
        - Under `rotate` the walk asks every server at once while glibc starts at one: the
          names are glibc's in order, each asked of every server, and heard means glibc was
          quick, but not the other way round. Fix round 1 holds the types too, and has the plan
          decide where the one-way rule applies (below).
      - **The OPT record is asserted as it is** (`optProblems`, `P-454`): glibc's questions carry
        one under `options edns0` and none without, and the check's never do. No row fails on
        the difference alone, so the run says if either side moves.
      - **The regressions** (`modesProblems`), labelled as such: gate mode answered as `system`
        mode, the helper's child as the probe's lanes (`systemLookup`), and gate mode ran the name
        where its walk said (heard or local on the lanes, silent in the helper, from
        `lookupsToHelper`).
      - **Six answer rows** (`ANSWER_ROWS`), each one plan in every image, with a simulator of
        its own, so a server's TCP/53 can be closed. Each wire below was predicted, then seen in a
        narrowed box run before the full one:
        - **TC with TCP/53 refused**, without and with `edns0`. glibc asks server 1 A and AAAA
          over UDP, is refused over TCP, and asks server 2 both over TCP. The walk asks both
          servers over UDP and is heard.
        - **FORMERR** from server 1: glibc takes it as the answer and returns `ENOTFOUND` without
          asking server 2, and the walk is heard at server 1.
        - **A answered and AAAA SERVFAIL** from server 1, server 2 silent: glibc returns the A in
          about 10 ms and never asks server 2.
        - **FORMERR to a question with OPT**, under `edns0`: glibc's questions carry OPT, it

        - **dnsmasq 2.90 at `dns-forward-max=30`** (Debian 12): `system` held at most 6 distinct

        - `system`'s 6 is the zone's 3 lanes in an outage (`P-438`'s "unacked: 3"), A and AAAA

      - **The committed recordings are schema 3**: each recording keeps glibc's OPT flags, and

      - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
        - **The walk is compared with glibc's first asks, not its wire.** The walk asks each
          question once (§1.4), and glibc asks again on each try and over TCP after TC, so
          "in order, up to where each stops" can only mean first asks.
        - **Under `rotate`, heard-if-and-only-if holds one way.** glibc may start at the one
          server that answers while the walk, asking every server, waits on a silent one: a
          silent walk and a quick glibc agree there. A heard walk with a slow glibc still fails.

        - **The EDNS-deaf row is P-454's listed divergence**, asserted exactly: heard, and

        - **"TCP dropped" is TCP/53 refused.** The boxes have no network and no firewall to drop

        - **"Distinct forwards" is the upstream's peak of distinct questions held at once**

          whole window says nothing of the table's size at any instant.
        - **The answer rows live in the differential**, not in S4's export. S4's plans answer only

          reading. The answer rows claim what servers do.
        - **The walk is judged only against a glibc wire that verified.** A row whose world was
          not set up, or which the policy misread, is already a problem, and holding its walk to a
          wire in question would add noise to it.
        - **A process per row for the walk and the regressions**, with every resolver new for each

        - The toolchain's: first asks (dedupe, TCP, case); the heard and silent orders; rotate's

          ways; a local row's route and wire; a walk routed otherwise or not recorded; each OPT
          rule, `then-none` both halves, the lengths and the walk's; each regression, a silent
          walk on the lanes, and the lookups not recorded; each answer-row check, its
          divergence, its walk, OPT and regression; the verdict's answer rows not replayed,
          strays and recorded when failing, S4's plans not held to each of the three, `edns0`

      - **Fix round 1** (the review of `c87aa235`, ten items). Run 5 failed on one stalled walk,
        and run 6 passed after it (below).
        - **Under `rotate`, the plan decides whether the walk is heard** (`walkProblems` takes
          the plan, `silentServer`). Where one of the row's servers is silent to a type glibc
          asks, the walk must be silent, whatever glibc's time. Where none is, heard if and only
          if glibc returned within 1 s, as without `rotate`. Before, the one-way rule covered
          every rotating plan, so a walk wrongly silent on the 6 all-answering plans of the two
          rotating rows passed in every image.
        - **Under `rotate`, the walk's types are glibc's** (`rotateDiffers`). It asks no type of
          a name glibc did not ask of it. Each name it went past, or was heard at, it asked of
          every server with every type glibc asked of that name. The name a silent walk stopped

          latest digest is not the one at load, in the order it reads them), and the resolver
          marks exactly those after every look.

          ended, before the next one, and both read-once cases edited the first file read once at
          their glibc. The box now counts the looks the policy is told of, waits after its hold for
          a look after the edit's to end, and reads the lines again (`killed.restartSaid`,
          `looksAfterEdit`); the verdict holds both readings to D28. A fourth case, `gai-not-first`
          (gai.conf at Debian 11, behind nsswitch.conf), can fail it, and each case now names every
          file read once at its glibc, so that the case goes on editing a file that is not first.

          `["/etc/gai.conf","/etc/nsswitch.conf"]` by the run's end, as the review said.

          IPv4 or IPv6 address"). Against a policy that maps `10.1` to 10.0.0.1, the box fails:
          the check is on, and its canary asks.

          server's cache held and their TTL were a constant and a literal in the replay. The row

          the row (`setSequencePlan`), and the digest moves with any of them. The committed
          recordings are run 9's, under the new digest.
        - **`respawned` was false whenever the helper rested** (low), so "no new child" was never
          observed. The box records the helper's child (`pid`, `killedPid`, `inFlight`). Any child
          but the one killed is a new one, whatever the state says, and a rest until restart must
          hold no child at all.

          first narrowed run showed broken, and the header said every `P-462` case writes a hosts:
          line with no action group. Both now say what the box does.

        - **The resolver asks the policy which files are skewed, by name, at every look.** The
          other way was to mark the look's moves and skip the fallback once the helper was
          marked. But only the policy knows which read-once files differ from what this process's
          glibc read, and a move found during load reaches no look's moves; one question covers
          both paths. The helper says each file once, so asking at every look logs nothing more.
        - **`nameserver 10.1` is a box, not a recorded reason**, as `LOCALDOMAIN=""` was (decision
          7 above). The user's allowlist takes a nameserver line only as a literal, which the
          policy reads as a dotted quad or an IPv6 address, so the check is off for `10.1`. The
          box shows that in situ, and fails if a policy change starts taking the form. It claims
          no wire: what glibc asks of 10.0.0.1 is not measured, since the check claims nothing for
          it.
        - **The cache's contents are in the row**, not in a constant the digest names beside it.
          Then what the replay plays a row with is in the row or the world and nowhere else, so a

        - **The skew box counts looks by wrapping the policy's `looked`**, in the box only, and

- [x] **P-463 — names in flight when the lookup helper goes quiet are not kept off the probe's
      lanes** · XS · P-432, P-453 · Filed 2026-10-20 by `P-453`. D27 keeps every name in flight
      at an `exit` or `memory` loss off the probe's own `getaddrinfo` until ten minutes after
      the helper is next up. Two kinds of name get no such entry. The first is the lookups
      detached when the child goes quiet (`unresponsive`, D26). The second is those in flight
      at a `hung` loss. While the helper is down, the next lookup of one of them runs on the
      probe's lanes by its `P-426` class. The child's event loop does not run `getaddrinfo`,
      which runs on libuv's threads. A name could wedge the child only through the process: an
      NSS module holding a lock the main thread needs, or a lookup that grows the child until
      it swaps. If it does, the same lookup on the probe's lanes could wedge the probe. **Done
      when** the names detached at `unresponsive` and those in flight at a `hung` loss get the
      avoidance entry, with a test and a mutant each. The alternative is a decision recorded
      against a measured cost: how many names a starved host's quiet child keeps off the
      probe's lanes, and for how long.

      **P-463 outcome. Every name in flight when the child goes quiet is kept off the probe's
      lanes, and so every name in flight at a `hung` loss.** Built 2026-10-20 on
      `feat/p432-helper-r3`, in `packages/probe/src/resolver/lookup-helper.ts`. No protocol
      change and no migration.
      - **At the quiet** (`#notAnswering`, the third quiet tick), every lookup in flight gets the
        entry an `exit` or `memory` loss gives (`#keepOff`): kept off from then until ten minutes
        after the helper is next up. That is each lookup detached at this quiet, and each one let
        go at an earlier quiet and still running, whose ten minutes began when the child answered
        again and begin again from the next time it does.
      - **A `hung` loss adds no entry of its own.** A child is killed as hung only after it went
        quiet (20 quiet ticks counted through the third), and nothing is asked of it until it
        answers again: `ask` refuses unless the route is `up`, which a quiet child's is not. So
        every lookup in flight at a `hung` loss was in flight at that quiet, with no `up` between
        to start its ten minutes. A second write at the loss could not be told from none by any
        test, an equivalent mutant, so none was added. The hung test proves the names are kept
        off through the loss, the backoff or rest after it, and ten minutes of the next child.
      - **The resolver is unchanged.** It asks `avoidsSystem` on every path to the probe's lanes
        (`#start`, `#offProbe` and `#gateRefusal`). While the helper is down, such a name's check
        fails at once with `RESOLVER_FAULT`, saying the probe does not ask its own `getaddrinfo`
        for it. Once the child answers again it is asked in the helper, unvouched. This departs
        from the design's §1.11 row for `up` to `unresponsive`, where a new check of a detached
        name starts a lookup on the probe's lanes while the helper is down. It now fails at once
        there, as a name of an `exit` loss does.
      - **The warning says it.** `the lookup helper is not answering` now says the names are kept
        off the probe's lanes, with `keptOff` (every lookup in flight) beside `detached` (those
        let go at this quiet).
      - **The doubles keep names off as the helper does.** `FakeHelper.goQuiet` adds the names in
        flight to `avoided`. LR7's model also keeps a `hung` loss's names off, since the model can
        lose a child as hung without its going quiet first.
      - **Docs.** `administration.md`, in the helper's failures, and the release notes. The
        runbook makes each `not answering` line a finding, recorded with its `keptOff`, so the
        field test measures what this costs (fix round 1, below, moved the measure to the hourly
        summary).
      - **Tests.**
        - `lookup-helper.test.ts`, 'names in flight when the child goes quiet are kept off the
          probe's lanes (P-463)', 3 tests:
          - a name in flight at the quiet, in each family a lookup of it asks for, kept off while
            the child is quiet for an hour and for ten minutes after it answers again, with the
            warning's `keptOff`;
          - a name let go at an earlier quiet and still in flight at the next, its ten minutes
            already run, kept off again until ten minutes after the next answer;
          - a name in flight at a `hung` loss, as a first loss (a backoff) and as the fifth in ten
            minutes (a rest), kept off through an hour with no child up and for ten minutes after
            the next is up.
        - `name-resolver-gate.test.ts`, N10 rewritten. A quiet child's lookup is detached, and a
          new check of its name fails at once while the helper is down, never on the probe's own
          `getaddrinfo`, while a name not in flight goes to its `P-426` class there. Once the
          child answers, the name is asked in the helper, and the detached `EAI_AGAIN` holds
          nothing.
      - **Mutants: 3, all killed.**
        - No entry at the quiet: all 3 fail, the hung test among them.
        - An entry only for the lookups newly detached: the earlier-quiet test fails.
        - The entry's ten minutes run from the quiet, not from the next `up`: all 3 fail.
      - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
        - **Kept off, without measuring the cost first.** The ticket allows a decision recorded
          against a measured cost instead. Measuring would not change it.
          - **The cost is not bounded by the code** (corrected in fix round 1, below; this said
            the code bounds it at 8 names per quiet). At most 8 lookups are in flight at one
            quiet (6 lanes and 2 for Check now; a detached lookup keeps its token until it
            settles). But each name stays off until ten minutes after the helper is next up, and
            a quiet the child comes back from is not a loss, so it never rests the helper. The
            names kept off at a moment are those of every quiet and loss whose ten minutes have
            not run, and they grow with how often the child goes quiet, which the host decides.
            In `SC18`, three quiets a few seconds apart keep 9 names off, where each quiet's
            line said 3 at most.
          - Each fails its check at once only while the helper is not answering or rests, and
            only when no answer is kept for it (30 s, and five minutes' grace past that): a name
            checked within that passes on its kept answer. For ten minutes after it answers,
            each is asked in the helper rather than walked.
          - What it costs is how often a starved host's child goes quiet, and which of the names
            kept off are then checked with no answer kept. Only the field test shows that, and
            the hourly summary measures it there: `checksFaulted` (fix round 2; fix round 1 named
            `routed.faulted`, which counts lookups), `helper.quiets` and `helper.keptOffPeak`
            (fix round 1). Each `not answering` line says the names kept off then
            (`keptOffNow`).
          - Against that cost: a name that quiets the child through its process would quiet the
            probe if asked on the probe's lanes. D27 is on the design's never-cut list. An
            `exit` loss's names already cost the same (`P-453`'s decision).
        - **Every name in flight at the quiet, not only those detached at it.** A lookup let go at
          an earlier quiet and still running when the child goes quiet again is as likely as any
          to be what quieted it. Leaving its first entry would let its ten minutes run out while
          the child is quiet, and its next check would then go to the probe's lanes. Measured
          against the alternative by the second test's mutant.
        - **The same ten minutes, from the next `up`, as an `exit` loss's.** A quiet child that
          answers again has run the name, and a name that quiets it again is kept off again.
      - **Fix round 1** (the review of `8c9cb5ca`, five items, one of them medium; built

        - **The hourly summary carries the cost.** `helper.quiets`, every quiet since the start,

            path but a counter.
        - **Mutants: 13, all killed.** Each had its marker found in `dist`, was restored by copy
          and compared byte for byte, and the final build was checked against the source with no
          marker left. Each was run on `name-resolver-gate` and `name-resolver-check`:
          - no check counted at the settle: the `#offProbe` summary test, the extended D27 test
            and the two-checks test;
          - a check counted at the settle though served its kept answer: the rejoin-window test;
          - checks counted per lookup refused, the counter as the review found it: the
            two-checks, refresh and rejoin-window tests;
          - a check counted at the ask though served its kept answer: the as-it-asks test;
          - no check counted at the ask: the extended D27 test, the as-it-asks test and the stop
            test;
          - the check that joins a refused lookup not counted: the extended D27 test;
          - `checksFaulted` not reset at a summary: the stop test;
          - no summary at the stop: 7 tests;
          - a summary at every stop, the tick running or not: the stop test and the
            throwing-summary test;
          - the stop's summary without `stopping`: the two-checks and stop tests;
          - no guard around the stop's summary: the throwing-summary test;
          - the summary without `checksFaulted`: 7 tests;
          - `#refuse` not counting `routed.faulted`: 5 tests.
      - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation** (fix round 2):
        - **A count of checks beside `routed.faulted`, not either of the review's fixes alone.**
          - Calling `routed.faulted` a proxy would leave the field test without the measure
            `P-463`'s decision rests on: how many checks failed for names kept off. Only the
            field test can show that.
          - Counting waiters into `routed.faulted` would mix units in `routed`, whose other
            fields, like the design's §5 "routes by kind", count lookups. It would also reverse
            the D27 round's recorded rule for the joining check.
          - It would still miscount. A "Check now" served its kept answer is a waiter that did
            not fail, and the check that joins a lookup refused in its own pump is not a waiter.
          - So `routed.faulted` keeps its unit and is described as lookups, and `checksFaulted`
            counts each check told the failure. That is at the one place a waiter is told
            (`#settle`) and the one place an ask is (`#refusedNow`).
          - Not counted in it: checks failed at a loss, which the loss line counts, and those
            failed for a name DNS did not answer while the helper is down. Neither is the cost of
            keeping a name off.
        - **The stop says a last summary; the runbook also says what an unplanned end drops.**
          The review offered either. A periodic count said at shutdown is the usual practice.
          Saying in the runbook only that each stop drops up to an hour would lose that hour at
          every planned restart of the field week, and the sums could not get it back. A probe
          killed outright still says nothing, so the runbook tells such an end by its last
          summary and takes the counts that run since start per start.
        - **Said from `NameResolver.stop`, before the helper's stop.**
          - The stop's own refusals ("the probe is stopping") are not a cost of keeping names
            off, and they come once the pool has drained. Saying the summary first keeps them out
            without a filter.
          - A quiet after it is still said, on a `not answering` line or the helper's stopping
            line (fix round 1).
        - **The same message, with `stopping: true`.** A reader of the log, and the runbook, finds
          every summary under one message, and the field says that this one covers part of an
          hour.
      - **Fix round 3** (the review of `b509bc17`, item 8; built 2026-10-20 on
        `feat/p432-helper-r3`). The runbook only: no code, no protocol change and no migration.
        - **An end that said nothing is told by its start line** (item 8). Fix round 2 keyed the
          rule on a start's last summary. A start killed or crashed before its first hourly
          summary has its `probe.nameResolver is gate` line and no summary, so the rule never
          fired for it: an `ms-probe` OOM-killed 40 minutes after a start, or crash-looping
          under systemd, dropped its checks failed at once and its quiets from the week without
          being named.
          - A start is now its start line, and each summary the start's above it. A start whose
            summaries do not end with a `stopping` one, none at all included, ended without
            stopping. What it counted since its last summary, or since its start line if it said
            none, was never said.
          - The write-up names each such end by its start line's time, with the time it leaves
            uncounted, the `the lookup helper is not answering` lines in that time and the
            sensors whose checks failed at once in it.
          - The start still running at the end reading is not an end. Its counts are its
            summaries before the end reading, and the `stopping` one the drill's stop says after
            it is not the week's. The sums run to the end reading.
          - A command lists every start and summary in order, across reboots
            (`journalctl -u ms-probe --since <day> -o short-iso`, `grep -F` on the two
            messages). The list holds an earlier boot only where the journal is kept on disk, and
            a boot of the week missing from `journalctl --list-boots` is a time left uncounted.
        - **Tests.**
          - `name-resolution.test.ts`, a new describe, 'the field-test runbook’s ends that said
            nothing (P-463 fix round 3)', 1 test. It reads step 4's criterion for the gate's
            summary: a start is its `probe.nameResolver is gate` line; the rule covers a start
            with no summary and says what it leaves unsaid; the start running at the end reading
            is not an end; fix round 2's rule is gone. It then runs `buildNameResolution` in gate
            mode four times on one journal, as journald holds it: stopped after an hour, killed
            before its first summary, killed after it, and running at the end reading. The
            runbook's own `grep -F` patterns list 4 start lines and summaries of 2, 0, 1 and 1,
            step 1 quotes the start line the probe logs, and the rule names the two killed starts
            and no other.
          - Run on the final build, on the shared VM and not in a quiet window:
            `name-resolution` 6 of 6, `name-resolver-gate` 69 of 69 and `name-resolution-process`
            4 of 4, and the core's `build-hygiene` and `candidate-surface`, which read the
            runbook, 48 of 48. `tsc` is clean, and prettier and eslint are clean on the changed
            files.
          - **Quiet window:** none owed. Nothing here is measured.
        - **Mutants: 7, all killed**, each by the new test. Each was restored by copy and
          compared byte for byte; the two in code had their markers found in `dist`, and the
          final build was checked for none left:
          - the rule keyed on the last summary, as fix round 2 had it;
          - the command without the start line's pattern;
          - no exception for the start running at the end reading;
          - no definition of a start;
          - step 1 quoting another start line;
          - the probe logging another start line (code);
          - the stop's summary without `stopping` (code).
      - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation** (fix round 3):
        - **Keyed on the start line, as the review suggested.** The start line is the one line
          every start says, before the helper or the gate's clock starts, so a start that said
          no summary is still in the list.
        - **The start running at the end reading is excepted, and the sums stop at the end
          reading.** Fix round 2's rule, and the review's wording alone, would also name the
          start still running at the end reading, which has said no `stopping` summary only
          because it has not stopped. The drill stops that probe after the end reading, and its
          `stopping` summary then holds time that is not the week's, the drill's refusals among
          it.
        - **The write-up names what the log still shows of an unsaid time, not only the time.**
          The quiets are on the `not answering` lines, rate-limited, so they are a floor. The
          checks failed at once are in the sensors' own messages, which the probe sends as each
          check ends rather than at a summary. Naming the end without them would leave the 12
          checks and 3 quiets of the review's case unnamed.
        - **The test is in the probe's `name-resolution.test.ts`, not the core's
          `build-hygiene.test.ts`.** The rule rests on what the probe logs, the start line and
          the stop's `stopping` summary, and only the probe's tests can produce those lines. The
          core's tests that read the runbook still pass on it.
        - **Not changed: the probe does not keep its counts where a kill survives them.** A
          SIGKILL or a power loss ends a process before it can say anything, and the counts are
          a field-test measure, which the runbook can bound; keeping them on disk would add a
          write on the gate's path for the one week that reads them.
- [ ] **P-464 — a lookup helper crash on Windows is charged to no one** · XS · P-453, Release
      1.1 · Filed 2026-10-20 by `P-453`. Only a crash signal charges a name. On Windows a
      process that crashes reports no signal: it exits with an NTSTATUS code, which Node
      reports unsigned, for example 3221225477 for `0xC0000005`. The codes that matter:
      - `0xC0000005` access violation;
      - `0xC0000409` fail-fast, including the stack-buffer-overrun check;
      - `0xC00000FD` stack overflow;
      - `0xC000001D` illegal instruction;
      - `0xC0000094` integer divide by zero;
      - `0x80000003` breakpoint.

      So no name is ever poison there. While the helper isolates, a name that crashes it is
      asked again alone at every loss until five losses rest the helper. Its names are still
      kept off the probe's lanes. **Done when** `crashedBy` also reads those exit codes on
      `win32`, with a table test of codes and platforms and a mutant. Release 1.1's Windows
      field run must confirm the code of a real crash of the child before the release.

- [x] **P-467 — Probe Health carries fourteen name fields, and the user decided six** · S ·
      P-432 · Filed 2026-10-20 by the coordinator's decision on `integ/r6-1020` (under `P-432`).
      The user decided on 2026-10-18 (OPEN-5) that Probe Health has six name fields at protocol
      38: `nameResolverMode`, `lookupHelperTrouble`, `nameCheckOnSeconds`, `namePassedStuck`,
      `nameHelperStuck` and `nameQuestionsOpen`, with what the other eight would carry logged at
      the design's levels and the helper's memory in the log and the hourly summary. S6 built the
      eight anyway (`lookupHelperState`, `lookupHelperLosses`, `lookupHelperMemory`,
      `nameCheckState`, `nameLookupsHeard`, `nameLookupsToHelper`, `nameCheckMisses`,
      `nameWalksDeferred`) under a `nameCheck` capability at protocol 39. **Done when** they are
      gone from the probe's report, the protocol, `healthForPeer`, the sensor type's channels, the
      core's lookups, `/metrics`, the generated references and every document; what they carried
      is in the log at the design's levels and in the hourly summary; and the runbook's step 4
      reads the six and the summary, with the commands.

      **P-467 outcome.**
      - **The eight are gone, and 38 is the newest protocol again.** `nameCheck` and its strip in
        `healthForPeer`, the eight fields and their schema entries, `PROTOCOL_VERSION` 39, the
        eight Probe Health channels, the lookups `ms.probe.lookup-helper-state` and
        `ms.probe.name-check`, the eight `/metrics` series, and the probe's report of them.
        `NameResolutionHealth.gate` is the latch and three counts again, and `helperStateValue`

- [x] **P-469 — the lookup helper's loss line does not say who sent a SIGKILL** · XS · P-432,
      P-453 · Filed 2026-10-20 by the coordinator's decision under `P-432`, that a SIGKILL the
      probe sent is told apart from one from outside. The helper sends SIGKILL itself whenever it
      loses a child that lives: a protocol break ('it sent a message the probe cannot read', 'it
      sent N addresses for …', 'it said it was ready twice'), a quiet child (`hung`), its memory,
      a start that did not come. It also sends one after an ask that could not be written, after
      the channel closed first, and in `#awaitExit`. The child sends one to itself after its
      `fatal`. So `signal` `SIGKILL` on `the lookup helper was lost` does not say whether the
      kernel's OOM killer or a cgroup kill ended the child, and the runbook sent the operator to
      `journalctl -k` for every `SIGKILL` with `reason` `exit`. **Done when** the loss and its
      line say who sent it, the runbook sends the operator to `journalctl -k` only for one from
      outside, and `P-453`'s rule holds: a SIGKILL is never charged, whoever sent it.

      **P-469 outcome. The loss says who sent the SIGKILL its child ended by.** Built 2026-10-20 on
      `feat/p432-helper-r3`, in `packages/probe/src/resolver/lookup-helper.ts`. No protocol
      change and no migration. The fields track's Probe Health and hourly summary are not
      touched.
      - **`killedBy`** is on `HelperLoss` and on the loss's line, only when the exit says SIGKILL:
        - `probe`: the helper sent it while the child still talked to it, for the line's `why`;
        - `itself`: the child said why it ends itself (`fatal`), as it then does with SIGKILL;
        - `outside`: neither, the kernel's OOM killer, a cgroup kill or a person.
      - **How it is told.** `#killProcess` counts a kill as the probe's only when `kill()` says it
        was sent and the child still talked to the probe: its channel open, no send to it failed
        (`sendFailed`), no `fatal` read. The loss fills `killedBy` when the exit is read, and
        again when its line is said, since a `fatal` can be read after the exit.
      - **`P-453`'s rule is untouched.** Only a crash signal charges a name. `killedBy` changes no
        charge.
      - **The runbook** (the helper-loss reading under the gate's channels) sends the operator to
        `journalctl -k` only for `outside`, and reads `probe` from the line's `why` and `itself`
        from its `fatal`. `administration.md` names the field in the helper's failures, and the
        release notes say it.
      - **Tests.** `lookup-helper.test.ts`, 'who sent a SIGKILL (P-469)':
        - a table of 14 ends. The probe at a message it cannot read, at more addresses than it
          may send, at a second ready, past its memory, quiet for 20 ticks, and at no ready by the
          start bound. Outside with its exit read first, with its channel read closed first, and
          with an ask then not written (the probe's kill in both of the last coming after the
          child was ending). The child itself with its `fatal` read before and after its exit.
          And three ends that are not SIGKILL (SIGTERM, SIGSEGV, an exit code), which name no
          sender. Each checks the loss and the line;
        - a SIGKILL never charged: a suspect alone, its child killed by the probe (after waiting
          for the exit), by itself, or from outside (after waiting), each asked again alone and
          kept off the probe's lanes;
        - a kill the probe sent to a child that does not go at once: the line said before the exit
          names no sender, and the loss names the probe once the exit is read;
        - with real children: one killed from outside by SIGKILL is `outside` (new); U8's hung
          child is `probe`; U18's child killed from outside and then sent an ask that could not
          be written is `outside`. U18 is the case a rule of "the probe sent a SIGKILL first"
          would get wrong.
      - **Mutants: 9, all killed.**
        - Any kill the probe sent counted as its own: U18, the real outside kill, the table and
          the never-charged table fail. The real child fails because in that run the probe read
          its channel's end before its exit and killed a dead process, as at an OOM kill.
        - The probe's kill never counted: U8, the table, the never-charged table and the late
          exit fail.
        - No `itself`: the table and the never-charged table.
        - Not filled again as the line is said: the table, the row whose `fatal` comes after the
          exit.
        - Not filled at the exit: the late exit.
        - A sender named for any end: the table's three ends that are not SIGKILL.
        - A failed send not marked: U18 and the table.
        - The line naming no sender: the table and the real outside kill.
        - A closed channel not read as ending: the real outside kill (the same order again), the
          table and the never-charged table.
      - **Decided 2026-10-20 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
        - **A kill the probe sends once the child is ending is not counted as the probe's.**
          - Neither side closes the channel while the child lives. The production child has no
            call that closes it, and it SIGKILLs itself on its own `disconnect`. The probe never
            disconnects it. So a channel the probe reads as closed, or a send to it that fails,
            means the child is already exiting. Its exit status is already set, and the probe's
            SIGKILL cannot change it.
          - An OOM kill is exactly this case. The kernel ends the child, Node hands the probe
            the channel's end and the exit in either order, and when the end comes first the
            probe kills a process already dead.
          - The costs are not even. Counting such a kill as the probe's would hide an OOM kill
            from the operator, while counting it as from outside costs at most a look at
            `journalctl -k` that finds nothing.
          - The coordinator's brief listed these two among the kills the probe sends. It does send
            them, but they are not the SIGKILL the exit reports.
        - **A third value, `itself`.** The child ends itself with SIGKILL after its `fatal`. Read
          as `outside`, that would send the operator to the kernel's log for a fault the line
          already names.
        - **The cause is the line's `why`, not a second field.** Every kill the probe counts is sent
          by the loss it takes, so the cause is that loss's `why` on every path, `#awaitExit`'s
          included.
        - **A loss said before its exit is read names no sender.** That is a child that did not go
          at the kill, such as one in D state. The loss itself is filled when the exit comes, as
          its `signal` is.
