- [x] **P-437 — a probe's pool fills free memory to the reserve and then churns at it** · S ·
      P-426, P-271 · Found 2026-10-17 on `ms-server`. The dev probe grows its pool whenever a check
      is queued, until the machine's available memory reaches `reserveMb`, and then the memory
      gate holds and releases it every second or two with no hysteresis.
      - **On `a2852ea3`**, after 54 minutes: probe RSS 2.27 GB, 42–46 workers, 1,183 "growing the
        check pool" in an hour, and the gate's warning about once a second.
      - **On `5b6bbd2a`**, after a Docker restart left more memory free: 61–63 workers (about
        50 MB each), RSS 3.3 GB after 10 minutes. In those 10 minutes: 244 grows, 256 shrinks,
        311 holds and 311 releases, with `availableMb` 1,992 against `reserveMb` 1,984.
      - **The cost.** Each grow is a worker start, so the churn costs CPU and floods the log.
        Holding the machine at its reserve squeezes everything else on it: here, two test suites
        and the VM, which went down at a host load near 270. This was not proven to be the cause.
      - **Not `P-426`'s.** It does not size the pool, but measure per-worker memory before and
        after it.

      **Done when:**
      - the gate has hysteresis (hold below the reserve, release only some way above it), and
        its warning is said once a hold, not once a toggle;
      - growth is bounded by demand that lasts, not by one queued check;
      - a test drives available memory around the reserve and asserts at most one hold and one
        release, and a bounded number of grows;
      - `pool-memory-cap.test.ts`'s line count is extended to the toggle case.

      **P-437 outcome. The pool holds at the reserve, with a margin either side, and a straggler
      waits 200 ms before the pool grows for it.** In `packages/probe/src/runner/pool.ts`.
      No protocol change and no migration. Revised after four reviews; what changed is listed
      under "The review", "The second review", "The third review" and "The fourth review".
      `P-439`, a loading worker counted twice, is fixed here as well.
      - **The design: hysteresis, and the pool holds its size inside the band.**
        - The memory gate is a state, `MemoryGate`, either `open` or `holding`. `holding` carries
          `heldAt`, the size the pool held at once memory refused.
        - A hold starts when memory refuses a growth that checks were waiting for.
        - It ends only when a reading has room for one worker past
          `MEMORY_RELEASE_MARGIN_WORKERS` (1) beyond `heldAt`, or beyond the pool now where that
          is more: room for two workers above the reserve at the size it held at. A reading taken
          below `heldAt` needs a worker more for each it was taken short of it, and no reading
          taken while a worker loads ends a hold (the third review). It does not end when the
          queue empties: that was the toggle, once a second, because the wheel hands over a
          second's checks at once.
        - With an explicit `workerPoolSize`, it ends on room past the pool now only. That pool's
          `heldAt` is the size it grew to past memory, which memory by definition did not have:
          measured against it the hold never ended, and the next burst past memory said nothing.
        - `heldAt` is never past `maxSize`: a ceiling lowered under it brings it down too (the
          fourth review).
        - It is looked at on every pump, in `stats()`, and when a retired worker's thread exits,
          so a pool with nothing to pump still ends it.
        - While it holds, the pool may grow back to `heldAt`, as far as memory has room, and no
          further. Workers given back as idle or for a fall are bought again with no line. Past
          the size a shed for memory left it at, each worker needs room for itself and the shed
          margin (`shedTo`, the fourth review); idle give-backs are bought back as before.
        - Workers go back only once memory is `MEMORY_SHED_MARGIN_WORKERS` (1) worker's worth
          below the reserve, not at the line growth stops at.
        - So from giving a worker back at `heldAt` to growing past it, both read at that size, is
          a band three workers wide: 120 MiB at 40 MiB a worker. Between a shed and growing a
          worker back below `heldAt` it was not: 2e − a, where e is the estimate and a what a
          worker really holds, 30 MiB at 40 against 50, and since the fourth review 3e − a,
          70 MiB. This said three workers for both.
      - **The margins are in workers, because a worker is the gate's unit, and in the estimate's
        units**: a worker is counted at `WORKER_RESIDENT_MIB`'s 40 MiB, so what the margins are in
        real memory depends on that figure (`P-440`).
        - The ±10 MiB of noise this was tested at is a quarter of one worker.
        - So is the estimate's error per worker, about 10 MiB: 50 measured against 40.
        - One worker given back as idle does not end a hold, because the release is measured
          against `heldAt` and not the smaller pool. **Measured against `heldAt` alone, several
          did.** Each frees what it really held and is counted at the estimate, so with s spare
          above the reserve at the size the hold started at, k give-backs ended it once
          s + (actual − estimate) × k ≥ 2 × estimate: eight at `ms-server`'s 8 MiB, twelve from
          the bottom of the band. Where the next burst wanted no more than two past `heldAt`,
          the cycle after it came again every quiet stretch (the third review). **Now none
          does** while a worker costs less than twice the estimate: a reading taken below
          `heldAt` counts each worker it was taken short of it as one more. The scenario's idle
          arm, below.
        - The shed margin lets the probe into its reserve by at most one worker: 79% of a 1 GiB
          ceiling, under `memoryLimitUsage`'s 80%, and less of any larger one. `P-244`'s eight
          rows now compute the settle point with the margin, and still hold.
      - **Why one queued check grew the pool to 61 and more.** Three causes:
        - **The ceiling.** The derived ceiling never goes below 64 (`P-34`'s `min`), so a probe
          whose wheel hands over 61 checks in a second may hold 61 workers whatever the checks
          cost. That is `P-34`'s, and it stays.
        - **The instant queue.** Growth answered it, so the pool followed the largest burst.
          Since this, a shortfall under a tenth of the pool (`BURST_FRACTION`) is stragglers. The
          pool grows for them only once the oldest has waited `GROW_AFTER_MS`, 200 ms, and then
          for the whole queue in one step. A larger shortfall is a burst and grows the pool at
          once, as before; one check is a burst for a pool of ten or fewer.
        - **The gate.** At the reserve, each worker shed for noise was bought back by the next
          queued check: *from N to N + 1, queued 1*. Gone.
      - **`GROW_AFTER_MS` is 200 ms, a judgement: a worker's load already fills the dispatch
        budget, so no wait fits inside it.** The wait adds to a lasting straggler's load; it does
        not replace it.
        One worker loading the real catalogue, spawn to ready, twenty spawns a run in the
        toolchain container (`test/perf/pool-stragglers.test.ts`), on 8 cores with `ms-server`
        and other suites on the host each time:

        | Run | Load | p50 | p95 |
        | --- | --- | --- | --- |
        | 1 | not recorded | — | about 3,700 ms |
        | 2 | 11.4 | 615 ms | 977 ms |
        | 3 | 9.9 | 643 ms | 1,303 ms |
        | 4 | 16.1 | 974 ms | 2,055 ms |
        | 5, second review | 7.8 | 745 ms | 3,194 ms |
        | 6, second review | 5.4 | 468 ms | 940 ms |
        | 7, third review | 19–20 | 3,169 ms | 13,471 ms |
        | 8, the close | 3.1 | 540 ms | 743 ms |

        500 ms plus any of those p95s is past the 1,000 ms budget, and so is 200 ms: the budget
        less the p95 leaves 60 ms or less, 23 ms or less in the first four, which is growing on
        sight. The first review's rule was
        the budget less the p95, floored at 200 ms, and on these numbers the floor is all of it.
        So 200 ms is a judgement, not derived from them: longer than most checks, so that a busy
        worker usually takes a straggler first, and short enough to add little to one that
        lasts. A straggler that lasts starts at most 200 ms later than it did. The perf test
        prints the wait plus the p95 against the budget and asserts nothing: its bound was the
        wait against the budget less the load, floored at the wait itself, which nothing it
        measured could fail. The unit suite's constant test is what stops the wait being raised,
        and a test of a pool built with no `growAfterMs` is what makes the probe's pool use it.
      - **The logs.**
        - *memory is holding the check pool back* is a warning once per hold, now with `heldAt`,
          `growsAgainAboveMb` and `givesBackBelowMb`: the first line applies with the pool at
          `heldAt`, the second at any size (the third review).
        - *memory has room for more workers again; the check pool may grow* is at info, once per
          release, with `heldForMs`.
        - *nothing is waiting for a worker; memory is no longer holding the check pool back* is
          gone, for both kinds of pool, which the release notes say.
        - With an explicit `workerPoolSize`, *workerPoolSize allows more workers than memory
          holds* is once per hold, and once at start where the floor it starts is already past
          memory, as a fixed size's is (the third review), without the two MB fields: such a
          pool never stops growing or gives a worker back for memory. Its release line is
          *memory has room for the workers the check pool holds again*, with `cap` and
          `maxSize`. That is what is measured, and it can be well under what the setting allows.
        - *growing the check pool* gains `waitedMs`.
      - **Probe Health and `/metrics`** have no hold or release count, and none is added.
        - While the gate holds, `poolCeiling` is `heldAt` as far as memory has room, or the
          workers held where memory keeps more. With the pool at `heldAt`, it and
          `poolHeldBack` are steady, and move when memory crosses a margin, not with each
          reading. Below `heldAt`, after idle give-backs or a fall, they follow what memory
          allows from reading to reading, since that is what the pool may grow back to.
        - `poolMemoryCap` stays each reading's own number. It can read at least one under
          `poolSize` while the pool holds: one inside the shed margin, more while it sheds.
        - Probe Health's sentence, *memory holds the pool at N workers*, is about the ceiling
          memory sets, not the gate. It can outlast the release line wherever memory allows
          fewer than `maxSize`, and appear with no hold at all. `troubleshooting.md` says so.
      - **The scenario** (`pool-at-the-reserve-scenario.test.ts`) measures the gate, at twelve
        workers, and nothing else:
        - The real pool reads the real `MemoryCap`, and memory is a closed loop: 50 MiB a worker,
          against the 40 MiB the cap assumes.
        - A 4 GiB ceiling, so a 1,024 MiB reserve.
        - ±10 MiB of noise, new each simulated second, at 30 ms a second.
        - Sixteen checks a second, against memory for twelve workers: a burst every second.
        - Only the memory source's clock is simulated. 200 ms is about seven simulated seconds,
          and the idle window half an hour. So the straggler rule is kept out, with a wait of a
          minute, and idle shrink is off, which could not fire inside the run anyway. In the first
          mutant run, with the shipped wait, the no-straggler mutant failed the ample phase on a
          loaded host: checks kept past a 30 ms tick left stragglers behind sixteen workers, and
          growing for them reached the memory line. That was the host's load, not the gate.
        - Phases: settling; 4 MiB above the reserve; at it; 4 MiB below it; a fall of 200 MiB;
          recovered; then, past the ten minutes, a fall of 125 MiB with ±20 MiB of noise for 300 s
          (the fourth review), and 800 MiB more for 90 s. It was 400 MiB until the
          second review's runs: on a loaded host, checks kept past a tick grew the pool from 16
          to 20, which at 400 MiB was the memory line, and it held there once. That was the
          host's load, not the gate's; at 800 MiB the line is about 28. Since the third review
          the pool's ceiling is 24, under that line: at 64, a loaded host's checks grew it to 28
          and it held there, twice at a load of 30–40, under mutants that cannot reach it.

        | Ten minutes | Grows | Shrinks | Holds | Releases | Warnings |
        | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
        | `ms-server` on `5b6bbd2a` (the ticket) | 244 | 256 | 311 | 311 | 311 |
        | The scenario, on `da857d19`'s pool | 144 | 135 | 565 | 565 | 565 |
        | The scenario, first round | 18 | 8 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
        | The scenario, after review | 17 | 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
        | The scenario, after the second review | 17 | 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
        | The scenario, after the third review | 17 | 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
        | The scenario, after the fourth review | 17 | 7 | 1 | 0 | 1 |

        By phase, after review:
        - **Settling**: 12 grows, 2 shrinks (the estimate's overshoot given back), 1 hold.
        - **The three stretches at the reserve, 390 s**: nothing at all.
        - **The fall**: 5 shrinks, 12 workers to 7, and 1 grow back to 8 inside the hold.
        - **The recovery**: 4 grows back to 12 inside the hold, with no release and no hold. In

        - **Waits**: the pool's `waitMs` p95, Probe Health's `queueWaitMs`, was 9.1 and 11.2 ms
          at the reserve on two runs, a third short of the burst, and 0.0 ms with memory ample.

        The same counts on both runs of each round, but for the ample phase's above.

        After the fourth review, on four runs, the same counts every time:
        - **Settling**, **the three stretches** and **the ten minutes**: as above.
        - **The fall**: 5 shrinks, 12 workers to 7, and none grown back.

        - **Waits**: p95 8.6–9.5 ms at the reserve, 9.6–10.4 ms in the fall of 125 MiB, 7.4–7.9 ms

        Asserted:
        - nothing moves at the reserve;
        - the fall sheds at least four, grows back at most one, with no hold or release;
        - the recovery grows back from where the fall left it, to within a shed margin of 12, with
          no hold or release (it was at least four grows, back to 12, before the fourth review);
        - the fall of 125 MiB with ±20 MiB sheds at least one and moves the pool at most four
          times, with no hold or release (the fourth review);
        - ample memory brings one release, no hold and at least 15 workers, the burst less its
          straggler (16 before the fourth review, when the pool came to it from 12);

        - 1 hold in the ten minutes, 1 release after them, and a warning only for each hold;
        - at most 30 grows and 15 shrinks in the ten minutes;
        - every accepted check is answered.

        The refusal assertion is gone: it compared a counter with itself, and the scenario
        never refuses.
      - **The idle arm** (`P-437`'s second and third reviews), in the same file: a hold formed
        near the line, with the ceiling two workers past it, then quiet and busy in turn, with a
        real idle window of a second.
        - Memory for eight workers with 15 MiB spare above the reserve at eight, ±5 MiB of noise

        - **Busy again**: bursts of ten grow the pool back to 8 inside the hold, with no line.

        | Run | Ramp | Quiet | Busy again | Quiet again | Busy a third time |
        | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
        | 1, third review | 7 grows, a hold at 8 | 7 given back, no release | 7 grows back to 8, nothing said | 7 given back, no release | 7 grows back to 8, nothing said |

      - **The review** (17 confirmed findings and 1 disputed, several the same; each fixed once):
        - A hold could end only in `#pump`, so a pool with nothing to pump kept reporting it, and
          idle shrinking made the reported shortfall grow. `stats()` and a retired worker's exit
          now look as well.
        - One idle give-back could end a hold. The release is measured against `heldAt`, and
          the pool may grow back to it inside the hold.
        - The explicit-size release line said more than was measured. It is reworded, with
          `cap` and `maxSize`, and the explicit warning lost two fields that did not apply. The
          release notes name both new lines.
        - `GROW_AFTER_MS` was justified as staying inside the dispatch budget, which held only
          for stragglers a worker takes. It is 200 ms, from the measurement above.
        - `P-244`'s rows ignored the shed margin.
        - The `poolUsage` comparison raced its period in the unit suite, and moved to
          `test:perf`. The straggler test needed a 100 ms check to finish in 400 ms; it has 2 s.
        - The release-with-nothing-waiting test released with a check still queued. It now
          releases on a result's pump.
        - The scenario's refusal assertion compared a counter with itself. Waits are asserted
          instead.
        - No test covered a straggler at the memory line, or two stragglers.
        - The disputed one, upheld: the pump's comment, a test message and this outcome
          conflated the gate with Probe Health's sentence. Corrected, and `poolMemoryCap` reads
          at least one under.
      - **The second review** (10 confirmed, 2 disputed, 1 refuted; no major):
        - An explicit size's hold never ended on its own: its release was measured against the
          size it grew to past memory. Now against the pool now, with a test.
        - `heldAt` kept the loading workers counted twice (`P-439`), so a hold started during a
          ramp needed room for as many more again. Fixed here, with a test and a mutant.
        - The claims that a give-back is not a release held only for one. Corrected here, in the
          code and in `administration.md`; the scenario has an idle arm that shows the release
          after several, and the one bounded cycle after it. `P-440` says the margins are in its
          units.
        - The ceiling was said to be steady through idle give-backs; it is steady only at
          `heldAt`, and follows the reading below it. Corrected in the same three places.
        - The perf guard passed by construction. It prints and asserts nothing, and the claims
          that it bounded the wait are gone. 200 ms is called a judgement, here, in `pool.ts` and
          in the constant test; `sizing.md` gives the p95 range and says a straggler that lasts
          can start outside the budget.
        - No test used the default wait, which is the probe's. One does now.
        - The scenario compared waits across two phases: a floor in one phase now. The one-look
          bound allowed no early timer: 10 now. The hold-once test never pumped with growth
          refused: it does now. A comment still said half a second.
        - Refuted: `BURST_FRACTION`'s doc, read as claiming a lasting straggler waits at most
          `GROW_AFTER_MS` in all.
      - **The third review** (three minor and four nits, on `2cb60730`; F1 was found major and
        confirmed minor):
        - **A thread Node cannot make shut the probe down** (B, from before `P-437`). `new Worker`
          throws `ERR_WORKER_INIT_FAILED` where the thread cannot be created, under a systemd
          `TasksMax` or `threads-max`, and the rejection escaped every `void` chain that spawns
          to the probe's `unhandledRejection` handler. `#spawn` now counts it as a start that
          died, with that line, the growing delay, and the latch where nothing loads. Tested with
          a worker factory that throws (`createWorker`, an option for tests); two mutants.
        - **F1: a reading taken while workers load ended a hold.** A slot is in
          `#slots`, and so in the reading, from when its thread starts, before most of its memory
          is in use, so room read high by about the workers loading. No release while any slot
          loads, or on a reading that says some did: `MemoryCapReading` gains `loading`, and
          `MemoryCap` keeps the count with the reading it keeps for a second. A test drives each
          guard alone. The size a new hold starts at leaves the loading workers out of the room it
          reads, as the finding asked. That guard binds only where growth comes more than a
          worker at once, past a pool of ten: a straggler under a tenth waits, and the check that
          makes it a burst grows the pool for both. No test reached it in the third round, and
          its mutant survived; at the close it has one (decided below).
        - **F2: the cycle after a release by give-backs was a loop** wherever the next burst
          wanted no more than `heldAt` + 2, as at `ms-server`'s 64 against 62: a release and a
          warning every quiet stretch. **Chosen: bound it in code**, not correct the claim. A
          reading taken below `heldAt` counts each worker it was taken short of it as one more
          (`MemoryCapReading` gains `held`, the workers it counted), so no number of idle
          give-backs ends a hold while a worker costs less than twice the estimate. Counted from
          the reading, not the pool: from the pool, the burst after a quiet stretch still released
          (the idle arm, above). The cost: a quiet pool keeps its hold until demand brings it back
          to `heldAt` and memory has room past it, or memory read at its size has room for twice
          its shortfall and two more, and Probe Health says memory holds it meanwhile. The idle
          arm shows one hold and one warning over two cycles. Kept, with a test for each way it
          ends (decided below).

      - **Decided 2026-10-19 by Claude, under the user's delegation:**
        - **F1's guard on the size a hold starts at is kept, with a test.** It is reachable:
          past a pool of ten, a straggler under a tenth waits, the check that makes it a burst
          grows the pool for both, and a reading taken while a worker loads counts it as
          resident. 'starts a hold at the room its loaded workers leave, not counting those still
          loading' has eleven workers, the eleventh loading, two checks behind them and memory
          that reads room for twelve: the hold starts at eleven and the pool stays there. Its
          mutant, the room taken as read, now fails it: the hold starts at twelve.
        - **F2's trade-off is kept: stability over responsiveness**, provided a hold always ends,
          so that no check waits on one for ever. It ends on either of two things, each with a
          test and a mutant that fails it:
          - **demand that brings the pool back to `heldAt`**, where a reading needs only the
            release margin past it. 'ends a quiet hold once demand brings the pool back to the
            size it held at, with room past it': held at three and given back to one, memory
            with room for five is no release while it is quiet, and Probe Health's ceiling stays
            3; a burst of five grows it back to three inside the hold, the release comes there,
            and the pool grows to five, every check with a worker. Mutant: the shortfall counted
            from the floor rather than the reading, so a pool back at `heldAt` still reads short;
            the burst's last two never get a worker.

- [x] **P-439 — a loading worker is counted twice in what the pool holds** · XS · P-437, P-271 ·
      Found 2026-10-18 by `P-437`, by reading the code; not measured. `#grow`'s `held` is
      `#slots.length + #growing`. A spawn is in both from the moment `#start` pushes its slot until
      the worker says ready, which `P-271` already says of `start`'s own. Growth near memory compares
      `held + unmet` with what memory allows. So a pool growing fast near its reserve can be refused
      while its loading workers are counted twice, and since `P-437` that starts a hold: one
      warning, and one release once they have loaded, that memory did not cause. **Done when** a
      loading worker is counted once, with `P-271`'s tests kept meaningful, a test of a hold during
      a ramp, and a mutant.

      **P-439 outcome. Each loading worker is counted once, in `P-437`'s commit.** `P-437`'s
      second review found the double count worse than this ticket said: since `P-437` a hold
      records what the pool holds as `heldAt`, so one started during a ramp kept the loading
      workers counted twice for its whole life, and needed room for as many more again before it
      ended, up to `SPAWN_CONCURRENCY` workers past the line its warning gave.
      - A slot is marked `onItsWay` from when its thread starts until its spawn settles, and
        `#held` is `#slots` and `#growing` less those. `#spawn` takes the spawn off `#growing`
        and clears the mark in one `finally`, so no pump sees a worker counted twice or not at
        all while the slot is in `#slots`; the callers' own decrements are gone. `#grow`,
        `#ceiling` and `#considerRelease` use `#held`. `#pump`'s over-memory retire loop skips a
        slot still on its way (`P-437`'s third review): retired out of `#slots` before its spawn
        settled, it would be counted on its way with nothing to take it off.
      - Test: `pool-memory-cap.test.ts`, a hold started with four workers loading a registry
        that takes 400 ms. Its warning says it held five, and it releases at the true `heldAt`
        and the margin, not past it. `P-271`'s tests are unchanged and pass.
      - Mutant: `#held` without the subtraction. It fails the ramp hold, whose warning says 9 held,
        and, in the second review's idle arm, the ramp, which then held where no quiet stretch ended
        it. At the close it fails the ramp hold, the loading-release test and the hold-start test;
        the idle arm, now ramping from one, passes it.

- [x] **P-438 — a probe restarted during an outage starts with nothing kept** · M · P-426, A-66 ·
      Filed 2026-10-18 by the user's decision, for 1.0 ahead of rc.3. The third quiet window ran
      `test:perf`'s name lookups at full size on `5b6bbd2a`: slow 5,000 of 5,000, the warm zone's
      answering 36,000 of 36,000, everything silent with nothing refused and jitter p95 28 ms. The
      one case left is the cold one, a probe restarted in the middle of a one-zone outage: 29,249
      of the answering zone's 31,500 checks answered and 2,251 given up, the last of its 450 names
      kept 31 s from the wheel's start. The probe's resolver keeps answers in memory only, so a
      restart is a cold start: the silent zone's first lookups take the lanes, and the answering
      zone's queue behind them until `getaddrinfo` gives up on each.

      **Done when:**
      - the probe writes the answers its resolver keeps to a file in its own state directory at
        stop and periodically: bounded in size, mode 0600, written to a temporary file and renamed,
        and never holding the event loop the scheduler runs on;
      - at start it loads that file before the first scan, each answer served as P-426 serves an
        expired one (while a refresh asks again) and never past its grace, with the file's
        wall-clock times turned to the monotonic clock and a time in the future or past the grace
        not used;
      - a missing, corrupt, truncated, oversized, wrong-version or foreign file is ignored with one
        log line, never a refusal to start, each with a test;
      - whether holds, denials and failures in a row survive a restart is decided and argued;
      - Probe Health shows how many answers were loaded at start;
      - a scenario: a probe runs warm, stops during a one-zone outage, and a second starts from its
        file and answers the answering zone from its first scan;
      - `test:perf` has the restart-during-outage arm with the file loaded, and the command for a
        quiet window to read it against the third window's 2,251 and 31 s.

      **P-438 outcome. The resolver's answers are kept across a restart; a domain not known to
      answer leaves a lane to the others.**
      - **The file.** `probe/src/resolver/answer-file.ts` keeps `name-answers.json` in the probe's
        spool directory (`probe.spoolDir`, `/var/lib/ms-probe/spool` on Linux), beside
        `identity.json` and the spool's cursor; the spool reads only its `.ndjson` files and its
        cursor.
        - **Format 1**: `format`, `version`, `writtenAt`, on Linux `bootId` and `monotonicAt`
          (the review's AF-3), and the answers, each its name, family, addresses, and when it was
          answered and expires on the wall clock, most recently asked first.
        - **Written** every 60 s and at stop, never two at once, 500 answers a slice with a turn of
          the event loop between, at most 4 MiB (the least recently asked left out). To a new
          temporary file at 0600, the mode set again whatever the umask, synced and renamed over
          the last: a write that fails keeps the file before it and logs one warning.
        - **Read** before the first scan: `main.ts` loads it, then starts the resolver and the
          timer. The `name-resolver` shutdown hook (now 2 s) stops the resolver and writes,
          after the check pool's hook and well inside the ten seconds the spool is left.
      - **What is loaded** (`NameResolver.restore`): each answer as expired, its expiry the
        earlier of its own and now, so the first check of its name is served it while a refresh
        asks again, and never past its own expiry and 5 minutes. The file's wall-clock times
        become ages at the load, from how long ago it was written as well as that can be known:
        since this boot, by the monotonic clock, or the wall clock's when it says longer; before
        it, by the wall clock, and nothing loaded when that says less than the uptime (the clock
        was put back at the boot); with no boot known, by the wall clock, and nothing loaded from
        a file written in the future. Not loaded either: an answer past its grace, a name the
        hosts file gives now for its family, when nsswitch.conf reads the file first, a name
        given twice or kept already, any over 10,000, and an entry this build could not have
        written (no name, an address for a name, no address or more than 64, an address of
        another family, times out of order or kept longer than 30 s).
      - **A file it cannot use is a cold start, never a refusal to start**, in one line naming
        why: none (info), a symbolic link, not a regular file (from the `lstat`, before any open,
        so a FIFO is never opened; opened `O_NONBLOCK` on POSIX for one put there since), larger
        than 4 MiB, owned by another user or with any group or other mode bit (POSIX), a path it
        cannot look at, cut short or not JSON, another format, a version but 1 (said in at most
        40 characters), no `writtenAt`, boot fields the probe does not write, a time it cannot
        tell the age of, or no list. An unexpected error is a cold start too.
      - **Decided: answers only.** Holds, denials and failures in a row are not kept. A restart is
        what an operator does after fixing DNS, and a kept "not answering" or "no such name"
        would hide the fix for up to a minute (the longest hold) or 30 s (a denial), failing
        scans that would pass; answers alone remove the measured failure. A name the hosts file
        gives is neither written nor loaded: the file is read again at start, and may have
        changed.
      - **No config key**: the path follows `probe.spoolDir`, and nothing in it needs tuning.
      - **Protocol 37**, a message change, so not 36 in place (36 builds run on `ms-server` and in
        development, and the heartbeat's schema is closed): capability `answerFile` and the
        heartbeat's `answersLoaded`, stripped for a core below 37. Core Probe Health reads it (a
        gap when absent), the Probe Health type has a channel "Name answers loaded at start" with
        no limits, and `/metrics` has `ms_probe_name_answers_loaded`. `api-reference.md` and
        `sensor-reference.md` regenerated.
      - **Deploy, checked, nothing changed.** On Linux `setup.sh` makes `/var/lib/ms-<svc>` 0750,
        owned by the service user, for `--components probe` too, which the packages and
        `install-probe.sh` run; the unit runs as `ms-probe` with `StateDirectory=ms-probe` and
        `ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/ms-probe`, and the probe makes its spool directory itself. On
        Windows the mode bits and the owner check do not apply, and the spool directory inherits
        `ProgramData`'s access list: filed as `P-444`.
      - **The cap** (decided 2026-10-18 in three rounds; `P-432`'s second design round reached the
        same rule and calls it "unacked: 3"; tightened by the review below). A domain
        (`domainOf`, so a sub-zone is its own) may hold all 4 first-lookup lanes only while both
        hold (`#heldBack`, `#answering`, `#stuckLately`):
        - (a) one of its names got an answer from DNS under the current configuration within the
          last `ANSWER_MS` (30 s), an answer for a name the hosts file lists for the family not
          counting, whatever nsswitch.conf says; an answer the answer file gave counts until a
          lookup for its name settles, and never past its own grace, and not for a name the hosts
          file lists;
        - (b) it has had no lookup stuck lately: none in flight, a first lookup, a refresh or a
          retry, has run past `STUCK_MS` with no lookup of the domain that ran as long answering
          since it started (`silentSoFar`), and none ended so, stuck without an answer, within
          the last `STUCK_MS` or since the last of its names answered from DNS.

        Otherwise it may hold 3. So a never-answered domain gets 3 on the first tick, before any
        of its lookups is stuck, and the answering domains keep the fourth; a healthy domain is
        held to 3 only until its first answer; a zone answering in part is held while one name
        hangs, and through the `STUCK_MS` after its hanging lookups end together, by when those
        asked as they ended are stuck in turn. The rounds before: capping only while a lookup is
        stuck could not reach a cold first tick, where about 8 silent names of the 80 a tick asks
        fill the 4 lanes within a millisecond; capping only what had not answered missed a zone
        answering in part.
        - **A resolv.conf or nsswitch.conf change** resets both: every domain's last answer, its
          loaded answers and its stuck history. An answer from a lookup the change cut loose
          does not count.
        - **The last shared lane** is not taken by a first lookup of a domain with a lookup stuck
          lately, (b)'s, counting as taken every lane the refreshes running and queued may hold
          (`first + 1 + min(4, refreshes running + queued) >= 5`): a lane freed goes to a first
          lookup before a refresh (`#next`), so judged by what was running, each stuck refresh of
          a warm zone gone silent that ended let its first lookup take the fourth shared lane and
          its queued refresh the fifth.
        - **A name the hosts file gives is never held back**, by either, where `getaddrinfo`
          answers it from the file: nsswitch.conf's `hosts` line reads the file before DNS (with
          no nsswitch.conf watched, Windows alone), and the file gives the name, as written,
          trailing dot and all, an address of the family asked, or any for family 0. The line is
          read as glibc reads it: the last `hosts` line, its name ended at a blank or a colon, a
          list starting with an action read as none; the file is first when `files` comes before
          any source that asks DNS with only `myhostname` or `mymachines` ahead, or when
          `resolve` does (`hostsFileFirst`). `/etc/nsswitch.conf` is now watched beside the
          hosts file and resolv.conf, and a change to it is a configuration change; a missing one
          is glibc's default, DNS first. `answersToSave` and `restore` leave out the same names
          by the same rule. Not in the decision; found by the hosts-edit scenario, where the
          operator's fix for one silent device was held off the last shared lane and its sensor
          went Warning for a scan. Said here so it can be undone.
        - A lookup held back stays queued and waits for one of its own domain's first lookups to
          end, or, held off the last shared lane, for any shared lane (`#blockers`), or for the
          `STUCK_MS` after a stuck end to pass, which a timer marks (`#endedStuck`); `#ask` and a
          configuration change look at the queue again too. Its check
          fails at once when each of those is stuck, as it is asked (`#ask`) or when the last of
          them becomes stuck (`#onStuck`). The FIFO and the ranked picks skip it, and a lane
          every queued first lookup is held back from goes to a queued refresh (`#next`).
          "Check now" is held to neither. With 3 lanes the cap is 1, and a domain whose refresh
          is stuck takes no first lane.
        - **Left as it is**: two domains held to 3 at once can take the 4 between them; `P-432`'s
          helper bounds that, and a restart from the file keeps the answering zones answered
          then (the two-zone scenario below).
        - Lane tests that put every name in one domain or asked before any answer: "fails a check
          at once when every lane … is stuck" has its stuck names in two domains, "fails a check
          at once behind every refresh lane stuck" has its first lookup in another domain, and
          "keeps what the new configuration said" runs with 7 lanes, since the old
          configuration's three lookups fill the 3 a domain not yet answering under the new one
          may hold.
      - **The review** (2026-10-18, on `4febccd2`): 16 confirmed (2 major), 1 disputed, 1
        refuted. Every one fixed:

        - **L3, F3, AF-2**: one grace end per domain, the latest of any loaded and never lowered.

        - **L2-slow-answering** (major): a lookup in flight past `STUCK_MS` counted as stuck when

- [ ] **P-444 — a Windows probe's data directory inherits `ProgramData`'s access list** · S ·
      H-06, P-438 · Found 2026-10-18 by `P-438`. `install-probe.ps1` makes
      `%ProgramData%\MonitoringSystem\probe\spool` and leaves its access list to inheritance; it
      locks down `tls\probe.key` alone, to SYSTEM and Administrators with inheritance broken. The
      spool directory holds `identity.json`, which carries the key the core issued to this probe
      once approved, the spooled results, and since `P-438` `name-answers.json`, the names of the
      probe's devices and their addresses. Inherited from a default `ProgramData`, every local user
      can read them, and can create a file in the directory. The probe makes no owner or mode check
      on Windows, as it does on POSIX, so a local user could put an answer file in place before the
      probe's first write, and the probe would serve its addresses for up to five minutes: the
      target policy and a credential's pinned address still judge each, but a check with a
      credential and no pin would send it to whatever address the policy allows. **Done when** the
      installer, and `ms-setup.ps1` on an upgrade, give the probe's data directory to SYSTEM and
      Administrators only, inheritance broken, as they do the key; the probe refuses an answer
      file on Windows whose owner is not the service's account or whose list grants anyone else,
      with a test where one can run; and the Windows smoke (`S-11`) reads the list.
- [x] **P-286 — two small pool and test leftovers from `P-271`** · S · P-271 · Found 2026-10-07 in
      `P-271`. `#recycle` does not count its worker in `#terminating` while the thread exits, as
      `#retire` and `#startTimedOut` do, so a memory reading during a slow terminate treats that
      worker's memory as someone else's. And `windows-transport.test.ts` "kills a PowerShell that
      ignores SIGTERM" asserts `tookMs < 2_000`, a wall-clock upper bound. **Done when** both are
      fixed, with a test for the first.

      **P-286 outcome. A recycled worker is resident until it exits, and the test waits.**
      - **`#recycle`** now adds its worker to `#terminating` for the length of the terminate and
        takes it off in a `finally`, as `#retire` and `#startTimedOut` do. A memory reading taken
        in that window is asked with the held workers plus this one, so it no longer reads the
        exiting worker's memory as taken by something else. The replacement is still counted in
        `#growing`, as `P-271` left it.
      - **The test** (`pool-memory-cap.test.ts`, "a worker recycled for ignoring its abort") uses
        `test.block`, `P-271`'s fixture, which holds the thread in native code for 5 s. With a
        pool of two, it waits (bounded) for the worker to leave `#slots`, takes a reading, then
        checks the thread was still blocked. The reading is asked with 2 (one held, one exiting).
        Once the replacement is in, the reading is asked with 2 again, not 3.
      - **The PowerShell test** waits for the fake with `until` and for the kill with `within`
        (15 s), not a hand-rolled deadline loop and `tookMs < 2_000`. That the kill lands inside
        the pool's grace is a structural fact: `POWERSHELL_GRACE_MS` is under the probe's floor,
        which the next test (`P-267`) holds. The asserted message, *killed with SIGKILL, having
        ignored SIGTERM for 1000 ms*, says the kill came from that timer. The lower bound
        (`tookMs >= POWERSHELL_GRACE_MS - 5`) stays, because load can only make it easier to
        meet.
      - **Mutations** (each restored byte for byte, `dist` rebuilt): with no count in
        `#recycle`, the reading inside the terminate is asked with 1, not 2. With a count that is
        never taken off, the reading after the replacement is asked with 3.
      - **Not done:** two other tests in `windows-transport.test.ts` ("kills a script that will
        not finish", "ends PowerShell on the check's cancel") still assert `< 15_000` on the wall
        clock. That bound is generous, but it is the same kind of assert.

- [x] **P-287 — two Windows transport tests still bound a wall clock** · XS · P-286 · Found
      2026-10-07 in `P-286`. "kills a script that will not finish" and "ends PowerShell on the
      check's cancel" in `windows-transport.test.ts` assert `< 15_000` on the wall clock, the kind
      of assert a loaded VM breaks. **Done when** each waits through `within` and asserts what
      happened, not how long it took.

      **P-287 outcome.** Neither test reads the clock now. Each waits for the run's rejection
      through the sensors package's `within`, and then asserts the whole anchored message.
      - **The script that will not finish** must have been "still running after 700 ms and was
        stopped with SIGTERM", ending there. This is what the old bound stood for: it was ended
        at its own timeout, and was never killed after a grace.
      - **The cancel** must name the end of the check and its reason. The run's own one-minute
        timeout would not say either.
      - **The bounds.** `within` gives up at 15 s for the first test and at 30 s for the cancel.
        The 30 s is well inside that one minute, so an abort that reached nothing is reported as a
        wait that gave up, naming what it waited for.
      - **Mutations, each failing the tests.** With the check's signal not passed to PowerShell,
        the cancel test fails at `within`'s 30 s and names the wait. With every timeout ending
        by SIGKILL, both tests fail on the message.

- [x] **P-288 — a stored batch sent again counts its refused results again** · S · P-281 · Found
      2026-10-07 in `P-281`'s review. The core counts what it refused from a batch when it acks
      it. A batch whose ack was lost is sent again, stored idempotently (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`)
      and acked again, so its refusals are counted twice on Reports refused; the core keeps no
      record of batch ids. **Done when** decided: remember recent batch ids per probe and count a
      batch once, or accept the rare double count and say so, with a test that loses the first
      ack either way.

      **P-288 outcome. Counted once, by the result rather than the batch.** In
      `IngestionService.unfitResults` (`packages/core/src/ingestion/service.ts`). No protocol
      change and no migration.
      - **What decided it: a batch id cannot say the batch was seen.** The probe names a batch
        `<gid>-<seq>` and numbers every send (`CoreClient.sendResults`), so a batch sent again
        after a lost ack arrives under a new id; the drain peeks the spool again, so it may also
        carry results queued since; and `seq` starts at 0 with the process, so a remembered id
        would one day name a different batch and suppress a real count. Remembering batch ids
        would have counted nothing once.
      - **The store's own identity instead**: the same sensor at the same time is the same
        result (it is what `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` goes by). The parser's report now carries a
        refused result's `at` (a string of the schema's 1-64 characters, else null) and a fitted
        one's, and ingestion remembers each counted one by probe GID, sensor and time in one
        insertion-ordered `Set` across all probes, the oldest forgotten past

- [x] **P-291 — a limit a sensor type stops declaring stays on its channels** · S · P-284 · Found
      2026-10-07 in `P-284`. `applyDeclaredLimits` (`packages/core/src/state/declared-limits.ts`)
      writes declared limits but never removes one the type no longer declares. An install that
      ran protocol 31 keeps `scriptGroupsRefused`'s old 0.00001 rate warning although the docs say
      it has none. **Done when** a `declared` limit for a key the type no longer declares is
      cleared at start-up, an operator-set one is left, with a test.

      **P-291 outcome.** The start-up pass now also clears: a channel whose `limits_source` is
      `declared`, on a sensor whose type declares no `limits` for that key any more, goes back to
      `limits = '{}'` and `limits_source = 'unset'` — what a channel created by this build holds,
      and what lets a later build declare a limit for it again. `operator` rows are never read or
      written, whatever they hold. It runs before the pass's early return, so a type that dropped
      its last declaration is cleared too. The report gains `cleared`, logged at info when
      non-zero; a second start clears nothing, so no ETag churns.
      - **Per channel, not per bound, and no migration.** `limits_source` is one column per
        channel; there is no per-field source. A type that still declares a channel but dropped
        one bound needed nothing new: the existing pass writes the whole declaration over the
        whole column, so the dropped bound goes with it (now pinned by a test). Limits are not
        inherited — they live on the channel row and the resolver never sees them — so nothing
        there moves.
      - **Only where the type's answer covers the key.** A row is cleared when (a) `channels({})`
        names the key and declares no limits on it, or (b) the type's `paramsSchema` admits no
        parameter at all (`additionalProperties: false`, no `properties`, no
        `patternProperties`), so `{}` is every sensor's read and a key it does not name is gone.
        A sensor whose type this build does not register is left alone.
        `adding-a-sensor-type.md` no longer says declarations are "never re-applied", which had
        been untrue since the start-up pass, and says what a start does now.
      - **Amended on review** (a second commit). The first commit cleared any undeclared key of a
        type whose `channels({})` did not throw, on the theory that a parameter-dependent type
        would throw. None does: the catalogue calls `channels({})` at registration, and
        `ssh-script`, `snmp-table`, `port-tcp` and the rest answer with a placeholder set on
        purpose. So a limit declared at creation on a channel only real parameters produce (a
        banner channel, a table column) would have been reset at the next start, ending its
        alarm silently. Latent — only the two health types declare limits — but the guide
        promised the opposite. Rule (b) is decided from the schema rather than from a new
        `SensorType` flag: it is provable from what a type already says, and it errs towards
        leaving a limit. The cost is that Probe Health, which has a `probeId` parameter, is not
        (b): a key it drops outright keeps a stale declared limit, which nothing evaluates unless
        something still reports that key. The concrete case is (a) and still clears.

        channel's outcome can only get less severe: the next reading turns a stale Warning to Up,

        the same one the condition clearing would have made, so nothing can multiply. The
        concrete case barely moves state at all: the total's old rate warning fired only when a

- [x] **P-293 — the start-up limits pass cannot tell a type's fixed channels from its
      parameter-made ones** · S · P-291 · Found 2026-10-08 in `P-291`'s review. The pass reads
      `channels({})`, and every shipped type answers it with a placeholder, so it treats `{}` as
      the authority for each key `{}` names: a limit a type declares on such a key only for some
      parameters would be overwritten or cleared at the next start. A key `{}` does not name is
      cleared only for a type whose `paramsSchema` admits no parameter, so Probe Health (which
      takes `probeId`) keeps the declared limit of a key it drops outright, and sensors of an
      unregistered type keep theirs. Latent: only the two health types declare limits.

      parameters (the catalogue refusing `limits` on a parameter-made channel otherwise), or
      per-sensor evaluation from stored parameters, with tests.

      **P-293 outcome. An explicit flag, `SensorType.fixedChannels`, and only a type with it may
      declare `limits`.** It says `channels({})` is every sensor's answer, declarations included.
      Core Health and Probe Health set it (Probe Health's `probeId` chooses the probe, never the
      channels); no other shipped type declares limits, so no other needs it.
      - **The catalogue holds it** (`catalogue.ts`). At registration: a type without the flag that
        declares `limits` on a channel `{}` names is refused; a type with it must answer `{}` (not
        throw), and answer the same with its schema's defaults filled in. At `channelsFor`, which
        is how every sensor gets its channels and the one place a channel only real parameters
        produce is ever seen: a fixed type answering anything but its `{}` answer throws, and so
        does a type without the flag answering a channel with `limits`. Both throw
        `BAD_SENSOR_TYPE` rather than repair, since either is a type saying one thing and doing
        another. Usable-limits checks now cover every declared limit, since all of them are in a
        fixed `{}` answer.
      - **The pass gets simpler, not cleverer** (`declared-limits.ts`). Declarations are read from
        fixed types only, and a `declared` row is cleared on any registered type whose key no fixed
        answer declares. For a fixed type `{}` speaks for every sensor; any other type declares
        nothing, so a declared row on it can only be an earlier build's. `bare`, `fixed` and
        `admitsNoParameters` are gone. Probe Health's dropped keys are now cleared. A type this
        build does not register is still left alone: a build profile that leaves a type out is not
        withdrawing its declarations, and a cleared row would be put back the next time it was
        registered anyway.
      - **Why not per-sensor evaluation.** It would let limits depend on parameters, which nothing
        needs (`S-18` limits are for channels about this system, which do not vary per sensor). It
        would also need every sensor's stored parameters read and evaluated at each start, and a
        rule for what an edit that changes a sensor's channels does to their limits. The flag makes
        the case the pass cannot answer impossible to write, at registration where the catalogue can see it.
      - **Docs.** `adding-a-sensor-type.md`: a `fixedChannels` section, the `limits` bullet says only
        such a type may declare them, and the registration table has the row. The `ChannelDef.limits`
        and `ChannelLimitDefaults` comments no longer say "never re-applied".
      - **No scenario test.** Clearing a limit can only make a channel's outcome less severe, as in
        `P-291`, and no shipped type's limits change.
      - **Tests.** `catalogue.test.ts` (sensors), 16 new: a table of 10 registrations (limits without
        the flag, with and without a parameter; the flag with `{}` throwing; the flag with defaults
        that change the channels; four accepted shapes; the two cases only `channelsFor` can see)
        and a table of 5 `channelsFor` lookups (limits on a parameter-made channel refused; the
        same type with parameters that make none; a parameter-made channel without limits; a fixed
        type whose real parameters change its channels refused, and one whose do not). Plus the
        shipped catalogue: exactly the two health types declare limits, both flagged, and Probe
        Health with a `probeId` answers as `{}` does. `declared-limits.test.ts` (core): a table of
        11 rows across a fixed type with no parameter, a fixed type with one, a parameter-made type,
        an unregistered type and an operator-owned row, for a key the type declares, names bare,
        dropped, or only real parameters produce, each checking a second start does nothing; and
        the real Probe Health type clearing a declared limit on a key it no longer has while its
        own declared channels stay as they were; and a start with a registered type whose
        `channels({})` throws, which the pass no longer asks. The P-291 `shaped` tests that relied on a
        parameter-made channel declaring a limit were replaced by the table, since the catalogue
        now refuses that type.

        its length; `unfit-results`' bound cases use the new option and stat names.

        every refusal.** One key out for every key in walked a full set's keys from the start,
        past the holes V8 leaves until it rebuilds the table: a million keys took 8.7 s, 43.5 ms
        a batch of 5,000 and 82 ms at worst, synchronously in `acceptProbeResults`, on the core's
        event loop. Before `P-295` only rare unfit results paid it; a spool draining after a
        delete or a move pays it on every result. Now the memory is its own class,
        `ResultMemory` (`packages/core/src/ingestion/result-memory.ts`, the constants with it):
        a probe's set grows past `RESULTS_REMEMBERED` by `RESULTS_REMEMBERED_SLACK` (a tenth, at
        least one) and is trimmed back to the bound in one pass, oldest first. A key seen again
        is still deleted and added, so a trim reaches it last; the probe-level LRU is unchanged.
        At least the last 10,000 of a probe are remembered, at most 11,000; worst case about
        75 MB (was 70), and `administration.md` says so.
        - **Measured** (`test/perf/result-memory-performance.test.ts`, run alone in the
          toolchain; the full `test:perf` was not run, since it needs a quiet machine and
          `ms-server` stopped): a million refused results through `unfitResults` with the set
          full, 0.50 s in all, a batch of 5,000 mean 2.5 ms, median 2.2 ms, worst 35.9 ms; a
          second run 0.63 s, mean 3.1, median 2.7, worst 43.2. The worst is one batch in 200
          and its cause was not looked into (a collection or a table rebuild would look like
          it); the median is what a drain pays. Budget: a mean under 15 ms a batch. With the
          per-key eviction put back it read 8.70 s, mean 43.5, median 43.4, worst 81.7, and
          failed the budget.
        - **Tests.** `result-memory.test.ts` (no database): 110 keys under a bound of 100 are all
          kept and the 111th trims to 100, the eleven oldest gone; 10,000 keys never take it past
          110 nor below 100 once full, and the last 100 always stay; a key seen again survives the
          trim the next key starts while the two oldest go; the probe heard from least recently
          is forgotten; the defaults are 10,000, 32 and a tenth, trimmed once at 11,001.
          `unfit-results.test.ts`'s bound cases, at a bound of 2 and so a slack of 1, now step
          past the slack to see the trim. Mutation: the slack set to nothing (per-key eviction)
          fails the perf budget and two of the five memory tests.

      - **Amended on review** (a second commit). **The fallback was silent.** A bare `catch`

        - **Test** (`channel-provisioning.test.ts`, real database): four sensors of a test type

- [x] **P-299 — late and dropped-withheld results are counted again when a batch is sent again**
      · S · P-295 · Found 2026-10-08 in `P-295`. `A-53`'s `late` and `A-72`'s `withheldDropped`
      count on every arrival, so a resend after a lost ack counts them twice; `reported()` returns
      them as counts, so they cannot be named by sensor and time. **Done when** they go through the
      result memory as `unearned` now does, with a lost-ack test.

      **P-299 outcome. Lists, through the same memory, under the same key.** No protocol change, no
      migration, the bound unchanged.
      - **`CredentialVouching.reported`** returns `late` and `withheldDropped` as the results as
        sent (`ReportedBatch`), as `unearned` has been since `P-295`. `IngestionService` counts
        each list through one helper, `#countedOnce`, which `unearned` now uses too:
        `#firstCount('refused', gid, sensorId, at)` in `ResultMemory`. Probe Health's
        `lateRefusals` and `resultsWithheld` (`ProbeRefusals.late` / `.withheld`) count a result
        once however often it is sent; `resultsReceived` still counts every arrival.
      - **One key for every result that is refused or dropped, not a kind each.** One arrival meets
        at most one of unfit, unknown, moved, foreign, unearned, late or withheld. Across arrivals
        the judgement can change, since the grace runs out between them: a late refusal whose ack
        was lost, sent again past the ten minutes, is judged an unearned mark then. It is still
        the refusal the probe made under the configuration before, counted already, and counting
        it again on `reportsRefused` would call an honest probe one that marks what it should not.
      - **Windows: none of these two feeds one, so nothing had to keep counting arrivals.**
        `lateRefusals` and `resultsWithheld` are plain 64-bit counters with no limit, no lookup and
        no state. The five-minute windows that exist: `ProbeRefusals`' `reportsForeign`
        (`FOREIGN_WINDOW_MS`, warns; still counts every arrival, as `P-295` left it), ingestion's
        `timeRefusals` past/future (`TIME_REFUSAL_WINDOW_MS`, results refused for their clock; not
        routed through the memory, untouched), and Probe Health's `#recentCount` windows
        (`scriptGroupsRefusedRecently`, `resultsDiscarded`), which take the probe's own counters
        and never see a resend. Alarm volume unchanged, so no scenario test.
      - **Memory.** Late and withheld results now take places in a probe's set, so a probe's
        spool draining after a downgrade or a change to what it is left fills it too, to the same
        bound (10,000 a probe and a tenth, 32 probes, about 75 MB worst case); `result-memory.ts`
        says so. The log lines say what arrived, with `countedBefore` when some was counted.
      - **Tests.** `credential-pinning.test.ts`, on the database with one ingestion service: a
        probe left two named sensors comes back too old to pin, so one's refusal is late and the
        other's reading withheld; acked (`lateRefusals` 1, `resultsWithheld` 1); the ack lost, the
        same two again under a new batch id with one more of each queued since: 2 and 2, not 3
        and 3, `reportsRefused` 0, `resultsReceived` 6, `resultsRemembered` 4. The unit cases on
        `reported` read `.late.length` / `.withheldDropped.length`.

- [x] **P-300 — an unfit query answer is counted only when on time, and never on Core Health** ·
      S · P-289 · Found 2026-10-08 in `P-289`. A query answer that arrives after its deadline with
      an unfit result is only debug-logged; refused query answers are on Probe Health's Reports

      - **A late unfit answer** (`ProbeQueryService.deliver`, nobody awaiting the id) is refused
        as an on-time one is: `unfit` +1, `reportsRefused` +1 on the probe that sent it (the
        totals only, from a GID that owns no probe object), and warned with the sensor id and
        reason, *answered a query nobody awaits with a result that cannot be made to fit*. There
        is no caller to answer `too-old`, but the probe still needs upgrading. A late answer that
        fits, or was only fitted, is the debug line it was. Counted once: a query's answer is not
        spooled, so nothing sends it again, and no memory is needed.
      - **Core Health's `resultsRefusedUnfit` is now batches plus query answers**
        (`ingestionDiscards().refusedUnfit + queries().unfit`; the `queries` source gains
        `unfit`), and so is `ms_core_results_refused_unfit_total` (help text says so). One
        counter, not a second channel: the same older build met through **Check now**, and the
        channel is already the fleet's total of what `reportsRefused` counts for not fitting,
        which counted query answers since `P-289`. Both terms run from the process's start, so the
        sum is a counter. No limit, as before; alarm volume unchanged, so no scenario test.
      - **Docs.** `administration.md`'s Core Health row and refusal table (the line that said
        query answers are not in `resultsRefusedUnfit` now says they are, late ones too); the
        channel's comment in `packages/sensors`.
      - **Tests.** `probe-queries.test.ts`: an unfit answer after the deadline counts `unfit` and
        `reportsRefused`, settles nobody, and is warned naming the sensor; a late fitted or fitting
        one counts and warns nothing; one from a null probe counts the totals only.
        `unfit-results.test.ts` (real TLS endpoint): after the on-time refused and fitted answers,
        a query left to expire (100 ms, the protocol's least) is answered with `outcome: 'maybe'`;
        once the next answer on the link is taken, `unfit` is 2, `reportsRefused` +2, the link up,
        the warn line there. `core-health.test.ts`: 4 from batches and 3 from answers read 7;
        answers alone read. `metrics.test.ts`: the exported counter is the sum (3 + 2). The
        `queries` stubs in three scenario tests and `support/health.ts` carry `unfit`.
      - **Amended on review** (a second commit). **A late unfit answer was counted as it
        arrived, against a probe the session might not know yet, and from any peer.** The
        endpoint hands a `query-result` straight to the query service, not behind `pending`, and
        a session's probe object is resolved after the welcome (`#queueConfig`); late answers
        come exactly then, since a probe's query runner goes on across a disconnect and answers
        on the new connection. So Core Health's total rose and the probe's `reportsRefused` did
        not, and a peer nobody approved could move `ms_core_results_refused_unfit_total`. Now
        `deliver` counts nothing for a late answer and hands its refused result back; the
        endpoint (`#countLateUnfit`) chains the count behind `session.pending`, as `#queueResults`
        does a batch's, and calls the new `ProbeQuerySink.refusedLate` with the resolved probe
        object, or logs and counts nothing for a session that was not approved. An answer
        someone awaits is still delivered and counted at once. Tests: `unfit-results.test.ts`, a
        late unfit answer sent after the welcome while `probeObjectFor` is held is not counted;
        once the lookup is let go and a batch sent after it is acked, the probe's
        `reportsRefused` and the totals are +1, `unfit` 1 and ingestion's `refusedUnfit`
        unchanged, so Core Health's sum moves with the probe's count; from an unapproved session
        (its batch nacked behind the same admission) nothing is counted. `probe-queries.test.ts`:
        `deliver` hands the late refused result back uncounted, `refusedLate` counts it (and the
        totals only for a null probe), an awaited answer hands back nothing. The endpoint test
        sinks gain `refusedLate`.

- [x] **P-302 — a cloned sensor's channels lose their lookup, counter width and limit source** ·
      S · P-297 · Found 2026-10-08 in `P-297`. The clone path in `repository.ts` (about line 1812)
      copies channels without `lookup_id`, `counter_bits` and `limits_source`. A cloned
      `snmp.traffic` sensor stores cumulative octets as values on `in`/`out`/`total` and judges
      `status` by nothing; the channels already exist, so ingestion never declares them again and
      nothing repairs them. **Done when** a clone copies every declared property of a channel (or
      re-declares from the type), existing broken clones are repaired or said, with a test over the
      shipped types that declare lookups or counters.

      **P-302 outcome. A clone copies every column of its source's channels, from one list a test
      holds against the table; migration 073 repairs the rows the old clone wrote.**
      - **Copied, not declared again.** A clone stores its source's `params` as they are, so its
        type declares for it exactly what the source's create declared: for the declared columns
        the two choices give the same row. They differ on everything else, which is an operator's
        and which a declaration would lose: thresholds and `limits_source` (`S-18`), a lookup set or
        cleared (`M-06`), scaling, decimals and the spike filter (`M-07`), the display flags. A
        clone is its source. And the drift that caused this was a hand-written column list missing
        the three columns added after it (009, 023, 038), so the fix is aimed at that:
        `CLONED_CHANNEL_COLUMNS` builds the statement, and a test reads `channel`'s columns from
        `information_schema` and requires each to be in it or in `CHANNEL_COLUMNS_A_CLONE_OWNS`. A
        column added later fails that test until somebody decides.
      - **Every column, and what a clone does with it.** Copied: `key`, `name`, `unit`,
        `is_primary`, `lookup_id`, `counter_bits` (declared; no API sets the last one), `limits`
        and `limits_source`, `scale_mul`, `scale_div`, `decimals`, `spike_min`, `spike_max`,
        `show_in_graph`, `show_in_table`. Its own: `id` and `sensor_id` (new, so no history),
        `created_at` and `updated_at`. Not copied, being keyed by the channel id:
        `channel_counter`, so a clone's first counter reading is a `first`, as a new sensor's is,
        and the samples. `limits_source` was the quiet one: written as `unset`, an operator's
        threshold on a fixed type is replaced by the declared default at the next start.
      - **Migration 073 (`channel-declared-shape`) repairs what it safely can, with an `N-28` data
        step** that builds the core's catalogue (`standardCatalogue(sensorTypesFor(BUILD.profile))`,
        not through `profile.ts`, which would pull the v2 modules into the migrations' graph) and
        asks each sensor's type with its stored parameters, in windows of sensor ids.
        - **`counter_bits` is written** where the type declares a counter and the row has none. No
          API sets the column, so an empty one is never a decision. It turns stored totals into
          rates from the next readings on, and the only states it can move are the ones totals
          latched: a rate threshold a climbing total held in Down or Warning clears.
        - **`lookup_id` is not written, only said.** An empty one may be an operator's `M-06`
          clear, and on an old clone that clear was made on the *source*, which the old clone did
          not copy, `object.cloned` (root ids only) cannot reliably name, and audit retention
          erases anyway. Filling it would turn every shut port on every clone Down at the first
          scan; not filling it leaves the channel judged by nothing, as it is today. So 073 logs
          one warning: per type, the channels whose type declares a lookup their row lacks, and
          the first 50 sensors holding them. `installation.md` gives the query to list them all
          and the `PATCH /api/v1/objects/:id/channels/:key` call to set one. A narrowly provable
          safe case exists (a channel on a sensor whose `object.cloned` root is the sensor itself,
          whose source still exists with the same type and parameters and holds the lookup on
          that key: copy the source's) but is not implemented.
        - **`limits_source`, on a row holding thresholds as `unset`** (only the old clone wrote
          that): `declared` on a `fixedChannels` type, so the start-up pass brings it to this
          build's declaration or clears it where there is none (`P-291`), as it already did to
          every such clone that lived through a start; a clone made since the last start carries
          the declaration of the build it was made under, and labelled `operator` it would keep
          that for good across a skipped release. `operator` on any other type, which cannot
          declare limits (`P-293`), so its thresholds were a person's on the source; and on a type
          this build does not register, which the start-up pass leaves alone anyway.
        - A set width is never changed. A type that throws for the stored parameters, or that this
          build does not register, is left alone and counted (no `{}` guess written for good).
          `up` adds a note to `channel.counter_bits`'s comment; the rollback puts back 023's
          comment and keeps the rows, which the build before reads correctly.
      - **It reads the shape, not only clones.** The row cannot say how it was made, and the same
        rows came from ingestion before `P-80` (a key a later build declared) and from `P-297`'s
        `{}` era; they get the same width and the same warning. It also fills one direction of
        `P-303` once: a sensor edited from gauge to counter mode becomes a counter.
      - **What an operator sees.** Stored totals stay: a total cannot become a rate after the fact,
        and nothing rewrites history. The first reading after the upgrade has no baseline and
        stores nothing; from the second, rates. A graph across it shows the climbing totals, a
        one-scan gap, then rates far below. A rate threshold the totals held in Down or Warning
        clears once rates arrive; nothing else changes state. A status channel without its lookup
