      `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, and PostgreSQL's defaults for all three are off. No
      installer set them either. `pool-starvation.test.ts` reproduced it: an outside session holds
      one row, five core updates of that row take a pool of five, `pg_stat_activity` shows each
      waiting on the lock, and a read of an unlocked table fails with "timeout exceeded when trying
      to connect" after `connectTimeoutMs`. The five end only when the holder rolls back. Realistic
      holders: an operator's `psql` left in a transaction; a backup's `ACCESS SHARE` on an old
      chunk with housekeeping's `drop_chunks` queued behind it and every later reader queued
      behind the drop; a long-range query nothing cancels.

      startup options, from `database.statementTimeoutMs` (60 s), `database.lockTimeoutMs` (5 s)
      and `database.idleInTransactionTimeoutMs` (60 s), each 0 for off. The defaults rest on
      `docs/findings/2026-09-28-object-visibility.md` (the slowest read path's budget, a stream
      snapshot, is 2 s) and `docs/findings/2026-09-29-tree-build-with-authentication.md` (a
      5,000-object tree in one request, 3.5 s at most). Longer or shorter limits per path, as
      `SET LOCAL` inside that path's one transaction: rollups 10 minutes; `compress_chunk` 30
      minutes and a 2 s lock; `drop_chunks` a 2 s lock, the chunk skipped and counted and retried
      next pass; the tree lock 30 s; report rendering 10 minutes. TCP keepalive on the pool, since
      a statement timeout cannot fire on a server that has gone.

         statement) answers 503 with no `Retry-After` and a message naming
         `database.statementTimeoutMs`: the same query times out again, so a client must not
         retry it by itself. 57014 also comes from a hand's `pg_cancel_backend`, so the log carries
         the server's own message, which tells the two apart.
      2. Every waiter on the tree lock that is not a request has a defined 55P03 behaviour.
         Provisioning under the 30 s lock stops that run with a reason and never takes the pump
         with it. The outcome lists every caller that is not a request and what each does.
      3. No override reaches the pool: `SET LOCAL` only where the work is one transaction. Work
         that spans transactions or holds a session gets its own client, or its own pool, built
         with the timeouts off, and nothing ever `SET`s or `RESET`s a pooled client, since a
         `RESET` that throws hands the pool a client at 0. The test and perf harnesses (5,000-object
         builds, `MS_BENCH_FILL`, the replay soak) are not cut by the 60 s default.
      4. 25P03 ends the backend. The client that sees it is released with the error, so the pool
         discards it; a test shows the next checkout gets a live client and the process survives,
         with the client in use when it happens, not only idle.

         `application_name = 'ms-core'`, not this one's own backend. A statement blocked on a lock
         is active, and shows.

         raises nothing on Probe Health; it is a Core Health count. A scenario test holds a lock
         for 30 s on the table ingestion writes: exactly one Core Health warning, no Probe Health
         warning, and the probe's re-offer leaves no gap once it is released.
      7. The entry cites the findings the defaults rest on (above).
      8. `pool-starvation.test.ts` is the acceptance test. Mutants as usual, the 57014/55P03 split
         and the discard among them.

      outside the core", with the query that finds the holder.

- [x] **P-238 — a start refused on migration drift does not say which migration** · S · P-222,
      H-03 · Found 2026-09-29, when the development `ms-server` had restarted about 470 times
      with "an already-applied migration has been edited; the database and this build disagree
      about the schema". Nothing more: a refused start prints its message and exits 78 (`P-222`),
      and the ids and names were in the error's context, which never reaches the line. Finding
      the migration took `ms-core migrate status`, which named it and gave neither checksum. It
      was 059, applied from a draft that was edited before it landed (`H-24` is that cause). The
      same held for the refusal of a database newer than the build. With `autoMigrate` off,
      `refuseSchema` named the drifted migrations but gave no checksums, and named the newest
      unknown one.

      **Done when** a start refused on drift names each migration with the checksum it was applied
      under and this build's, in the line it prints and in a log line, whether `autoMigrate` is on
      or off, and a refusal of a newer database names its newest migration.

      **P-238 outcome.** `describeDrift` is the one wording: each drifted migration's id, name and
      both checksums in full. The full value is what tells one version of a migration from another,
      and what a record can be put right with. It names five and counts the rest, because a build
      that changed every migration's text needs no list of sixty.
      - **The migrator's refusal** puts it in the message. A refused start prints that message and
        `ms-core migrate up` or `down` prints it too. The refusal also logs it at error with every
        drifted migration as structured fields, and adds both checksums to the error's context.
      - **`refuseSchema`**, the check with `autoMigrate` off, uses the same wording.
      - **The newer-database refusal** says how many migrations the build does not define, and
        the newest, as `refuseSchema` already did.
      - **`ms-core migrate status`** prints both checksums under each drifted migration.
      - `troubleshooting.md` gives both wordings of each refusal and says what the checksums are.
      - `runMigrateCommand` takes only the database section of the config, which is all it reads,
        so a test can call it without a whole core's.

      **Tests.**
      - `migrator.test.ts` 2 and one assertion:
        - an edited migration named with both checksums, in `up`'s and `down`'s refusals and in
          one error line each, with the structured list;
        - `migrate status` against a migrated scratch database with a record edited, listing
          both checksums under it;
        - the newer-database refusal naming its newest migration.
      - `schema-gate.test.ts` 1 and one assertion: the checksums in the drift refusal, and five
        named of seven with the rest counted.

      Mutation 6/6, each alone against its own file:
      - the migrator's message without the list;
      - no log line;
      - the list unbounded;
      - `migrate status` without the applied checksum;
      - the newer refusal without its newest;
      - `refuseSchema` with names only (2 tests).

- [x] **P-209 — ms-server stayed Up for ten hours with no core in it** · S · — · On 2026-09-15
      the UI on :5173 answered `502 Bad Gateway`. The dev PostgreSQL had stopped cleanly the day
      before and has no restart policy, so it stayed down when Docker restarted at 01:02 UTC;
      `ms-server` came back, and its core died with `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND postgres` 1.3 s in —
      inside the supervisor's three-second pause, before `wait -n $core $probe` was reached. Bash
      had already disposed of the core's job, printed `wait: 9: no such job`, and waited on the
      probe alone: the container reported Up while the probe dialled a core that was not there
      15,500 times. **It only happens under `bash -c`**, which is how `dev-services.sh` ran the
      supervisor; the same lines run as a file returned from `wait -n` at once.

      **Fixed.** The supervisor is its own file, `scripts/lib/ms-server-supervisor.sh`, run with
      `exec`; it starts the probe only if the core is still alive after the pause, and polls both
      with `kill -0` instead of `wait -n`, taking the status from `wait <pid>`.
      `scripts/test-ms-server-supervisor.sh` runs it against a fake `node` — the core dying during
      the pause, the core dying later, the probe exiting cleanly, and `docker stop` — each **both
      as a file and as `bash -c`**, because a test run one way passed against the broken version;
      it does fail against it, on the first case under `bash -c`, and CI now runs it beside
      shellcheck. Live: with PostgreSQL stopped the container restarted 8 times in 45 s instead of
      staying Up, and with PostgreSQL back it served the API again 21 s later without anybody
      touching it; `docker stop` still shuts both down cleanly in about a second.

- [x] **P-202 — a third of the shell scripts are shellchecked by nothing** · S · P-198 · The CI
      step spells its inputs out — `scripts/*.sh scripts/sizing/*.sh deploy/*.sh` — and that list
      reaches 24 of the repository's 36 shell scripts. The twelve it misses are not the harmless
      ones:

      - **`scripts/lib/api-auth.sh` and `scripts/lib/smoke-names.sh`**, which every smoke harness
        and the soak harness *source*. A parse error in either breaks all of them at once, and
        `P-200` added one of those files without the glob noticing.
      - **`scripts/smoke/provision-postgres.sh`, `configure-core.sh`, `api-token.sh`**, which run
        *inside* the smoke boxes. A defect there fails every smoke test from the inside, where the
        symptom is a box that will not provision rather than a script that will not parse.
      - `scripts/spike/run.sh` and the five `dev/**` scripts.

      **Enumerated rather than derived, which is the failure this repository already has a rule
      about.** `H-07`'s API-reference completeness guard is derived from the live route set for
      exactly this reason: a list maintained by hand covers what somebody remembered. A directory
      added later — `scripts/lib` was — is invisible to it, silently, for ever.

      All twelve are clean today, so this is a guard to widen and not a pile of warnings to fix.
      `git ls-files '*.sh'` is the derived list, and it cannot miss a directory nobody thought of.

      **P-202 outcome.** The step is `git ls-files '*.sh' | xargs shellcheck -S warning`, and it
      covers all 36. Proved by mutation rather than by reading: an `SC2164` planted in
      `scripts/lib/smoke-names.sh` is **invisible to the old glob and caught by the new one**.

      **The first mutation was the wrong one and nearly produced a wrong conclusion.** `SC2086`,
      an unquoted expansion, is *info* severity — correctly filtered by `-S warning` — so the new
      command passed and the obvious reading was "the guard does not work". The other reading was
      worse and had to be ruled out: `git ls-files` failing inside the container would leave
      `xargs` with nothing and shellcheck exiting 0 over no files at all, which is a guard that
      silently checks nothing. It returns 36 in there, so that was not it. **A mutation that a
      filter discards proves nothing about the filter** — pick one that clears the threshold being
      tested.

- [x] **P-201 — the runner pool shares one workspace, and the script that builds it recommends
      two** · S · P-198, P-200 · `scripts/dev-runner.sh` passes the same `--work` to every runner
      it registers, so a pool of two agents derives the same checkout path —
      `<work>/watchdog/watchdog` — for both. Its own header calls two "the useful number".

      **Following that advice breaks CI in the way that is hardest to read.** `install-smoke` and
      `enrol-smoke` both `needs: build`, so they become runnable at the same moment; with two
      runners they start together, in one directory. The second job's checkout cleans the tree
      under the first, `package.sh` stages both into `build/<name>-<version>` and opens with
      `rm -rf`, and `release/` holds one set of tarballs for two jobs that may not even be at the
      same commit. What either job reports afterwards is a packaging or install failure, which is
      exactly what these jobs are for — so the false one looks like the real thing.

      Nothing has hit it because the pool has only ever been one runner, which serialises
      everything. That is luck, not design, and it is one environment variable from ending.

      **Two fixes, and the first is the load-bearing one.** Give each runner its own work
      directory — `${WORK}-${i}`, bind-mounted at the same path inside and out as now, since that
      trick is what makes compose's `.:/workspace` resolve. Then two jobs have two checkouts and
      the rest of the collision goes with it.

      **The second closes a hole in `P-200`.** The smoke suffix is
      `GITHUB_RUN_ID`-`GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT`, which is per *run*, not per *job* — two jobs in one
      run share it. It does not bite today only because the harnesses that run in CI use different
      base names (`ms-smoke-install-<distro>` against `ms-smoke-core`), so a matrix over distros,
      or any second job running the same harness, would collide. `GITHUB_JOB` belongs in the
      suffix.

      **P-201 outcome.** Each runner gets `${WORK}-${i}`, created and bind-mounted at that path
      inside and out. Verified by registering a pool of two: they report
      `/Users/admin/watchdog-runner-work-1` and `-2`. The smoke suffix gained `GITHUB_JOB`, so two
      jobs of one run no longer share it — `…-555-1-install-smoke` against `…-555-1-enrol-smoke`,
      and a second attempt differs again.

      **A third defect fell out of testing it, in this script since it was written.** Re-running
      it failed on a name conflict rather than replacing the pool: the stale-container filter was
      `name=^watchdog-runner-[0-9]\+$`, and Docker's name filter is a Go RE2 pattern where `\+`
      is an escaped literal plus, not "one or more". It matched nothing, always. Measured on the
      live daemon before and after: `0` containers against `1`. Every earlier re-registration in
      this session worked only because the container had been removed by hand first — which is
      why nobody noticed.

- [x] **P-200 — the smoke tests take fixed container names, and CI is on the developer's Docker
      now** · S · P-198 · Every smoke harness names its boxes the same way on every run —
      `ms-smoke-core` and `ms-smoke-probe` on a network called `ms-smoke-net`
      (`smoke-enrol.sh`), `ms-smoke-install-<distro>` (`smoke-install.sh`),
      `ms-smoke-backup-origin` / `-target` (`smoke-restore.sh`) — and each starts by removing
      those names, then removes them again from an `EXIT` trap.

      **That was free on a hosted runner and is not free now.** Since `P-198` the same machine
      runs CI and is the machine somebody develops on, so a push and a hand-run of the same script
      overlap whenever the two happen within a few minutes of each other. They do not collide over
      a port or fail to start: the second run's `cleanup()` **deletes the first run's boxes
      mid-test**, and what the first run then reports is a probe that stopped answering — which
      reads exactly like the defect these tests exist to find.

      It nearly happened while `P-199` was being written: a local `smoke-enrol.sh` and CI's
      `enrol-smoke` were minutes apart on 2026-09-09, and only the order they reached their
      container stages kept them apart.

      **The fix is a suffix, not a lock.** A run id in the names — `${MS_SMOKE_RUN:-$$}` or
      `GITHUB_RUN_ID` when there is one — makes concurrent runs independent rather than serialised,
      which matters because `enrol-smoke` takes minutes and a lock would make a push wait for
      whatever somebody is doing by hand. The `EXIT` trap then removes only what that run created,
      which is the same rule `P-198` applied to compose with `-p watchdog-ci`.

      Worth doing with it: the image tag `ms-smoke:bookworm` is shared and should stay shared —
      two runs building the same content under one tag is fine and the rebuild is most of the
      runtime. Only the *containers* and the *network* need to be per-run.

      **P-200 outcome.** `scripts/lib/smoke-names.sh` beside `api-auth.sh`, sourced by all four
      harnesses: `ms_smoke_name core` gives `ms-smoke-core-<run>`, where the run is
      `MS_SMOKE_RUN`, else `GITHUB_RUN_ID`-`GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT`, else the PID. The attempt is in
      there because a re-run of a CI run repeats its id; the PID is enough for anything local,
      since two concurrent runs on one machine cannot share one.

      **Per-run names cost the one virtue fixed names had** — the next run tidied up after a
      killed one — so the containers carry an `ms-smoke` label and the epoch second they started,
      and every harness reaps labelled containers older than an hour before it begins. **The age
      is a label rather than a parsed timestamp** because the two places this runs, a Mac and the
      Linux runner image, disagree about parsing an ISO date; an integer comparison behaves the
      same in both. An hour, because the longest harness here is minutes.

      Proved rather than argued. A bystander container wearing the **old fixed name** was left
      running while a full `smoke-enrol.sh` went by: it survived both the startup cleanup and the
      `EXIT` trap, which the previous code would have deleted twice over, and the run's own box
      was gone afterwards. The reaper was checked from both sides — it removes a two-hour-old
      orphan and leaves a fresh one alone.

      **What this does not fix, and it surfaced while testing.** Two runs *in the same checkout*
      still collide, one level below the containers: `package.sh` stages into
      `build/<name>-<version>` and starts with `rm -rf`, so the second run deletes the first's
      staging mid-copy — `cp: cannot create regular file …/build/ms-0.1.0/etc/core.json`. That is
      **not** the case this ticket was written for: CI checks out into the runner's own workspace,
      so its `build/` and `release/` are not the developer's. Making two runs share one checkout
      safely means threading a run id through `package.sh` and the `newest()` lookup the harnesses
      use to find what it produced, which is a larger change than this one and wants its own
      ticket if anybody needs it.

- [x] **P-199 — two of the four withdrawal doors are proved by unit tests only** · S · P-197,
      P-198 · `P-196` closed four doors: `revoke`, `remove`, a narrowed `allow-from`, and the
      approval that reopens one. `P-197` put the first through a smoke test on two boxes. The
      other two still reach a live connection only in unit tests, and `P-197` named the specific
      thing that leaves uncovered: **`remoteAddressOf` is reached by nothing that runs the real
      services.**

      **It is the input to the `allow-from` decision, and returning `null` makes the whole
      withdrawal a silent no-op** — the probe carries on scanning from an address the operator has
      just excluded, the registration reads as narrowed, and nothing anywhere says otherwise. That
      is the same shape as the defects `P-189` and `P-196` were: a decision that wrote its rows
      and never reached the machine.

      **Two boxes are what make it testable.** On one host the probe's address is loopback, which
      proves nothing about an address filter; the smoke harness already has a probe on its own box
      with an address of its own, so the assertion is available for the cost of writing it.

      Both halves are worth asserting, and the first is the one a naive implementation fails:
      narrowing a filter that **still covers** the probe must cost nothing, and one that excludes
      it must stop it — on the live connection, not at the next handshake. The refusal carries the
      address (`this probe is not accepted from …`), so the probe's own address arriving in its
      own journal is the end-to-end proof that the lookup answered.

      `remove` is deliberately not covered: it is the same `withdraw` with a different code and no
      `remoteAddressOf`, and it would have to run after this one, by which point the probe is
      already stopped and the assertion would be hollow — `P-197`'s ordering rule.

      **P-199 outcome.** Four assertions at the end of `smoke-enrol.sh`, after the re-approval so
      they cannot hollow out what came before: the core recorded an address at all, a filter that
      still covers the probe costs it nothing, a filter that excludes it stops it on the live
      connection rather than at the next handshake, and the probe is told *which* address was
      refused. Measured on 2026-09-09 against a probe at `172.23.0.3` — a real address on the
      second box, which is the whole reason this cannot be done on one host.

      **Two mutations, both caught, each by the assertion meant for it and by no other.** Making
      `remoteAddressOf` return `null` — the silent no-op this ticket exists for — fails "a filter
      that excludes it stops it": the probe carries on scanning from an address its operator has
      just excluded. Dropping the `!addressAllowedFor(...)` half of the guard, so every edit
      withdraws, fails "a filter that still covers it costs nothing" while the exclusion case
      stays green. That is the pair: one mutation proves the filter bites, the other proves it
      does not bite when it should not.

      **A methodology defect worth recording, because it cost two days.** The first mutation run
      was killed part-way and the restore was sequenced *after* the wait, so it never ran: the
      mutated `remoteAddressOf` sat in the working tree until 2026-09-11. Nothing was committed
      with it and CI stayed green throughout — the mutation never left the machine — but the rule
      is now the stronger one. **The restore belongs in a `trap … EXIT INT TERM`, not after the
      command**, so a run that dies half way still puts the file back. The second mutation was run
      that way and restored itself.

      switched off in August when the account's Actions spending limit went unpaid, and hosted
      jobs since then fail in two seconds with zero steps. Six jobs, several written after that
      date, had therefore never executed anywhere. A job that has never run is not coverage; it
      is a paragraph of YAML that says what somebody expected.

      **The fix was a runner, not a payment.** `AlphaMerge/sociall-media-chatbot` had already hit
      this and answered it: self-hosted runners on the machines that are already here, selected by
      repository variable so a hosted one can come back without a code change. Same shape here —
      `dev/runner/Dockerfile` and `scripts/dev-runner.sh` build and register a runner labelled
      `watchdog-linux`, and the four Linux jobs target it through `CI_RUNNER_LINUX`.

      **The runner needs the host's Docker, which is what makes two details load-bearing.** Every
      job here shells out — the toolchain runs through compose, both smoke tests boot privileged
      systemd boxes — so the image carries the Docker CLI and the socket is bind-mounted. And the
      work directory is mounted at the *same path* inside and out, because `docker-compose.dev.yml`
      mounts `.:/workspace` and the host daemon resolves that path itself; with the usual
      `/home/runner/_work` it mounts an empty directory and the toolchain comes up with no source
      in it.

      findable while CI could not start:

      - **`down -v` in the teardown job would have deleted the developer's database.** On a
        throwaway hosted VM the flag costs nothing; on a runner sharing this machine's Docker the
        default project name is the one their stack is already running under. Fixed before the
        first run, not by it — `-p watchdog-ci` scopes what `-v` removes.
      - **Two port collisions with the dev stack.** The `build` job's `services:` block wanted
        5432 and could not have been reached anyway: a service container is published to the host
        and this runner is itself a container, so `localhost` in the job is not where the service
        is. It was also a second, drifting PostgreSQL — no `shm_size`, no pinned licence. It now
        starts the repository's own compose postgres on `MS_DEV_PG_PORT`.
      - **No `ping` in the runner image**, and seven `icmp.*` tests said so. `CLAUDE.md` names the
        system binary as the default ICMP path; hosted images happen to carry it, so the
        dependency had never had to be stated. `shellcheck` was in the same position.
      - **`latest-pg17` is a moving tag, and it moved.** The developer's container was 2.29.2 and
        CI pulled 2.30.0 the day it was released, from the same line of the same file — so a
        query-plan test passed for one and failed for the other. 2.30.0 wraps the plan in
        `Custom Scan (DeferredChunkAppend)`, which prints no children under a plain `EXPLAIN`.
        Measured with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE …)`: the `Index Scan` is still there and there is still no
        `Sort`, so the property held and the string moved. The test runs the plan now and passes
        on both versions — both checked, because a fix verified only against the new one would
        have moved the breakage. The image is pinned.
      - **A high-severity advisory in a production dependency** (`A-09`). `npm audit
        --omit=dev --audit-level=high` had been a build step for weeks and had never executed;
        its first run reported nodemailer ≤9.1.0 with four advisories, two of them
        recipient-domain validation bypasses that deliver mail to an attacker-controlled domain.
        In a product whose whole notification path is operator-authored templates sent to
        operator-supplied addresses. Bumped to 10.0.1.
      - **Artifact storage is billed separately from minutes**, so local runners did nothing about
        it and the upload failed an otherwise green run — with this repository storing no
        artifacts at all, the quota being consumed elsewhere in the account. `windows-install` is
        the only consumer and it is skipped until there is a Windows machine, so the upload now
        carries the same condition as the job that downloads it.

      **The two Windows jobs are skipped, not deleted** — `if: vars.CI_RUNNER_WINDOWS != ''`,
      which is the chatbot project's pattern verbatim. There is no Windows box here, so they wait
      for one rather than failing red every run. Setting that variable brings back the MSI install
      (`H-06`), the TimescaleDB provisioning (`S-11`) and the artifact they need, together.

      Green on 2026-09-09: build, tests, dev-compose, install smoke and enrolment smoke. The
      enrolment run is also the first execution of `P-197`'s approve/revoke assertions anywhere
      but by hand.

- [x] **P-196 — a probe the core has stopped trusting keeps scanning until it happens to
      reconnect** · M · R-01, P-189 · `P-189` closed one of four doors. `approve` reaches a
      connected probe now; `revoke`, `remove` and a narrowed `allow-from` still write their rows
      and tell the live connection nothing, so the refusal only bites at a handshake that may be
      hours away.

      **It is worse than the approval case it mirrors, and `disconnect` alone would not fix it.**
      A probe that merely loses the core is built to carry on: it keeps checking and spools to
      disk (`R-02`), so an outage costs no data. `ProbeConnections.disconnect` is a bare
      `connection.destroy(reason)` — exactly what a blip looks like — which is right for approval,
      where the reconnect *is* the mechanism, and silently wrong here. A machine somebody had just
      revoked would go on probing devices on their network for as long as its process happened to
      live, which is precisely what revoking it was meant to stop.

      **P-196 outcome. The close carries a reason, and the probe acts on the code.**
      `ProbeConnections` gains `withdraw(gid, code, detail)` beside `disconnect`, and the two stay
      separate on purpose: one is for a decision the probe should come *back* from, the other for
      one it should not. `rejectionStopsMonitoring` in `@ms/shared` is where the split lives,
      beside the union rather than inside the probe, for the reason `capabilities.ts` exists — a
      meaning scattered across call sites is a meaning that drifts.

      Trust withdrawn — `revoked`, `not-approved`, `source-not-allowed` — drops the assignments
      and scans nothing. Cannot agree or cannot ask — `protocol-version`, `bad-access-key`,
      `internal-error` — keeps scanning and spooling, because nobody has said the machine must
      stop and an operator fixes one end: there the spool is exactly right, and clearing would
      turn a mistyped key into a hole in the graphs rather than a gap of minutes. A `switch` with
      no `default`, so a new code is a type error.

      **The fingerprint is cleared with the assignments, and that is the subtle half.** It is what
      the next `hello` presents, so a probe that dropped its configuration and still claimed to
      hold it would be answered `config-unchanged` on re-approval — connected, approved and
      scanning nothing, which is `P-189`'s failure reached from the other end.

      **The operator's own sentence travels with it.** "revoked" tells whoever reads the probe's
      journal nothing they did not know; "decommissioned, replaced by web-dc4" tells them
      everything. `refusedFrom` and the revoke note are the same strings `admit` sends at a
      refused handshake, so a probe refused live and one refused on reconnect read identically.

      `remove` withdraws with `not-approved` rather than `revoked` — a forgotten probe that comes
      back enrols as a stranger and waits in the queue, so both stop it and only one is true.
      Deleting the row while a probe is still connected would otherwise leave the least
      accountable state here: a machine checking devices under assignments the core no longer has
      any record of giving it.

      **`allow-from` needed the decision kept in the registry.** The rule is not "is this address
      in the list": an empty per-probe filter defers to the installation's `enrolFrom`, so
      clearing one does not mean "anywhere" everywhere. That rule already existed inside `admit`;
      it is now `#addressAllowedFor`, used by both, because two copies would disagree the first
      time somebody changed one. The transport answers `remoteAddressOf` and nothing else.
      Narrowing a filter that still covers the probe costs nothing, which is the case that had to
      be got right — tightening a range around the machines already inside it must not be an
      outage.

      `packages/probe/test/core-client.test.ts` is new. The endpoint's tests drive a hand-written
      probe stub, which agrees with whatever the core does by construction, and `core-handlers.ts`
      does not carry `reject`; nothing covered the client's own reading of one. That is exactly
      where "the probe kept scanning after it was refused" lives — nothing fails, nothing logs an
      error. Mutations 2/2 on the probe side and 4/4 on the registry: the two stop-scanning tests
      and the four withdrawal tests fail against the old code, while the three that assert
      *absence* pass either way, which is the point of having them.

      Found on the way: `smoke-enrol.sh` still had the `grep -q` under `pipefail` defect that
      `smoke-install.sh` grew its `matches` helper for. It matters more there — one of the two
      uses is a **negative** assertion, so a spurious SIGPIPE would not flake, it would quietly
      pass and stop catching the regression it exists to catch. Same helper, carried across.

      **Not covered by a smoke test**, which is `P-197`. `smoke-install.sh` deliberately stops at
      "pending approval" and `smoke-enrol.sh` never approves, so there is no packaged flow to
      extend without building an approve-and-revoke sequence across two boxes with
      authentication — its own ticket rather than a rider on this one. What that leaves untested
      is the `attach` wiring in `main.ts`: both halves have unit tests and the line joining them
      does not, which is the shape of the defect this ticket and `P-189` both were.

- [x] **P-195 — the one test that turned CI red, and could only fail where it mattered** · S ·
      A-09, H-06 · `refuses nothing at all under \`none\`` in `http-ssrf.test.ts` is the **sole**
      failure in every CI run before the workflow was disabled — three checked, same single test
      each time, and it takes the whole pipeline down with it because `install smoke test` and
      `remote probe enrolment` both depend on the build job.

      `AssertionError: Missing expected rejection`, in 5.5 ms. **GitHub's runners are Azure VMs,
      where 169.254.169.254 is the live instance-metadata service and answers immediately.** The
      test asked for a request to it under policy `none` and required a rejection, so a request
      that succeeded read as a broken guard — when the guard had done exactly the right thing by
      standing aside.

      **The shape was the defect, and three tests shared it.** Each checks that the guard did
      *not* fire, and each did so by requiring the request to fail for some unrelated reason —
      holding a negative hostage to a positive. Everywhere the address is unreachable that works
      by accident; on the one class of machine where it answers, it inverts. Replaced with a
      `refusalFrom` helper that returns the refusal message or `undefined`, and says nothing about
      whether the request then succeeded, which is the thing these cases were never about.

      **And the test was making the request it exists to prevent.** Under `none` the guard steps
      aside by design, so naming 169.254.169.254 there meant every cloud machine that ran this
      file really did query its own metadata service — on purpose, in a file whose entire subject
      is not doing that. It uses 169.254.1.1 now: link-local too, so it makes the same point
      (refused by default, reached under `none`), and it is nobody's credential endpoint. The
      cases that assert *refusal* keep the famous address, because those never send anything.

      **Catalogued as entry 37** in `docs/findings/2026-09-04-tests-that-passed-for-the-wrong-reason.md`,
      with the audit that followed it: all 966 `assert.rejects`/`assert.throws` predicates in the
      workspace were scanned for one asserting only a negative about the error, and after this fix
      there are none. The other tests holding hardcoded addresses hold them as data rather than as
      connection targets. **And the same policy is tested correctly ten metres away** —
      `webhook-delivery.test.ts` covers it through the pure predicate with injected resolution, no
      socket, and has never been red. Two tests of one rule; only the one that reached the network
      could be wrong about the network.

      **Mutation 1/1, and it says why this survived.** A new case points the guard at a local
      server that answers 200; restoring the old "a call that succeeds is a refusal" behaviour
      reddens that case **and only that case**. The other seven cannot see the bug, because every
      one of them reaches something unreachable — which is why it passed on every developer
      machine for as long as the file existed and failed on every run of the only environment
      that disagreed.

      **What this unblocks is `H-06` — but something else blocks it now, and it is not ours.**
      On the operator's instruction the workflow was enabled again and given `workflow_dispatch`,
      so it can be run on demand rather than only on a push. The first dispatch failed in four
      seconds with no steps at all, and the check-run annotation says why:

      > The job was not started because recent account payments have failed or your spending limit
      > needs to be increased.

      **The workflow is disabled again**, at the operator's word, once that came back — an
      enabled workflow that cannot start a job only turns every push red. `workflow_dispatch`
      stays in the file, so re-enabling is one command the moment the account is settled.

      **So `H-06` is blocked on GitHub billing, not on hardware and no longer on a red test.**
      That is very likely why the workflow was disabled in the first place — the last runs before
      it went quiet are failures followed by cancellations, which is what running out of minutes
      looks like from the inside. Worth knowing before anybody plans around `windows-latest`: it
      bills at twice the Linux rate. Until the account is settled, the `windows-install` job it
      gates is the half of `H-06` that has never run: install the MSI with `msiexec /qn`,
      assert both services registered, both firewall rules exist, an upgrade keeps an edited
      configuration, and an uninstall leaves ProgramData alone.

- [x] **P-194 — creating objects does not get slower as the installation fills up** · S · P-193, P-19 · Left behind by `P-193`, which found it by accident while
      removing it as a confound. The same 5,000-object serial build costs

      | into a database holding | serial | 8 in flight |
      | --- | --- | --- |
      | nothing | 20.9 s | 6.5 s |
      | 5,000 objects | 27.9 s | — |
      | 10,000 objects | — | 8.5 s |

      about a third more the second time. **Two points, taken from two different runs**, so the
      shape of the curve is unknown — whether it is linear in row count, a step where a plan
      flips, or something that flattens. Nothing here should be read as a measured law.

      **The decisive experiment is cheap and comes first: build the BULK tree into a populated
      database.** Every bulk number ever taken started from empty, so the one comparison that
      separates the two candidate explanations has never been made. Bulk writes the same 5,000
      rows in one request; serial writes them in 5,000. If bulk into a populated database also
      costs a third more, the cost is per-row — indexes, audit rows, dead tuples, the planner —
      and the request path is innocent. If bulk stays flat, it is per-request, and the suspects
      are the things every create pays and a tree insert pays once: `lockTreeShared`, the
      `anyActive` probe, the parent `SELECT`, and `M-08`'s ancestor walk. That is 2.2 s per
      sample against 20.9 s for the serial equivalent, so measure it before measuring anything
      else.

      **Why this is not urgent.** The headroom on the budgeted case is 30%, not the 7% it looked
      like before `P-193`; the v1 target is 5,000 sensors and the first 5,000 are the ones the
      criterion is about; and `P-19`'s bulk path does the same work in 2.2 s, so anyone who meets
      this at scale has a fix already shipped. It matters for the operator who grows past the v1
      target one device at a time, and it is the sort of thing `H-09`'s field test would surface
      as "provisioning got slow" without anyone knowing why.

      **What must not happen is a budget moved to accommodate it.** The tree build measures a
      first install into an empty database, which is what `PLAN.md`'s criterion describes. If the
      curve turns out to matter, it wants its own measurement at a stated fill level — not a
      wider budget on the existing one, which would hide both.

      **P-194 outcome: there is no effect, and the question was smaller than the noise.**
      `docs/findings/2026-09-08-tree-build-fill-and-noise.txt`. The sweep is committed behind
      `MS_BENCH_FILL=1` — off by default, three minutes, and the answer only moves when the write
      path does.

      | already there | bulk up | bulk down | serial up | serial down |
      | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
      | 0 | 2.3 s | 2.1 s | 21.9 s | 22.0 s |
      | 5,000 | 6.5 s | 6.2 s | 27.0 s | 22.7 s |
      | 10,000 | 2.7 s | 6.1 s | 25.0 s | 21.4 s |
      | 20,000 | 1.6 s | 1.6 s | 20.9 s | 20.6 s |

      A fill effect is a trend both directions agree on. There is none: the **fastest** point for
      both paths is 20,000 objects already present, and the two directions disagree outright at
      10,000. **The first attempt swept ascending only and produced a tidy curve going the wrong
      way**, because the prefill that creates the fill also warms the process — more fill meant
      more warm-up immediately before the measurement. Sweeping both directions is what caught it.

      **And the premise could not have been tested the way it was stated.** Four runs the same
      day, quiet machine, conditions recorded, one commit:

      | | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 | run 4 |
      | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
      | serial, 3-sample median | 20.9 s | 22.0 s | 23.2 s | 25.7 s |
      | within-run spread | 0.6 s | 1.1 s | 3.3 s | 0.8 s |
      | bulk | 2.2 s | 2.2 s | 2.3 s | 2.2 s |
      | 8 in flight | 6.5 s | 7.2 s | 6.7 s | 7.1 s |

      The serial median moves 4.8 s across runs — a fifth of it — while bulk moves 0.1 s. **The
      noise is proportional to the round-trips**: 5,000 sequential requests accumulate scheduling
      jitter that one request does not. "About a third more" is inside the scatter of the same
      build measured four times.

      **This retracts a number from `P-193`.** That ticket read serial-into-empty (20.9 s) against
      serial-after-bulk (27.9 s) as "the seven seconds were 5,000 rows". The direction may hold —
      the populated readings do sit high — but a single 20.9 against a single 27.9, when the same
      measurement spans 20.9 to 25.7 unaided, establishes no magnitude. The structural finding
      behind it stands, because that was a fact about the code rather than a measurement: the
      variants really did share one database and really were not comparable.

      **The lasting fix is the one that costs nothing.** A within-run spread of 0.6 s on a number
      whose real range is 4.8 s is precise about the wrong thing, and it is what invited two
      over-readings in one day. The test now prints the across-run range in its own output, so the
      next reader meets the uncertainty where the numbers are rather than in a findings file they
      would have to know to look for.

      **P-193 outcome, and the ticket's own premise was wrong.** There is no per-request
      regression. All three variants ran in **one** scratch database in declaration order, so bulk
      built into an empty one, serial into a database already holding bulk's 5,000 objects, and
      the concurrent pass into 10,000. Give each its own empty database and the numbers are:

      | | median | samples | spread | against the 30 s budget |
      | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
      | serial | **20.9 s** | 21.5, 20.8, 20.9 | 0.6 s | **30% spare** |
      | 8 in flight | 6.5 s | 6.7, 6.5, 6.4 | 0.3 s | 78% spare |
      | bulk | 2.2 s | 2.3, 2.2, 2.2 | 0.1 s | 93% spare |

      Measured on a machine whose quietness the run recorded rather than asserted (`P-192`):
      `docs/findings/2026-09-08-tree-build-was-two-measurements.txt`.

      Against 27.9 s, 8.5 s and 2.3 s in the same morning's run. Bulk is unchanged because bulk
      always did start from empty; the other two moved because they no longer carry a previous
      test's rows. ~~**The seven seconds were 5,000 rows, not the per-request path.**~~

      **Corrected the same day by `P-194`: the seven seconds are not established.** The same
      measurement, repeated four times on a quiet machine, spans 20.9 to 25.7 s on its own, so a
      single 20.9 against a single 27.9 does not size the effect — and `P-194`'s fill sweep finds
      no effect of database size at all up to 20,000 objects. What survives is the structural
      half, which was never a measurement: the three variants shared one database and were not
      comparable with each other.

      **So the reasoning in `2026-09-08-perf-budgets-clean-run.txt` is withdrawn**, and the file
      says so above the section rather than quietly losing it. "Both variants that pay 5,000
      requests got slower, the one that pays one got faster, therefore the per-request path is
      drifting" compared variants differing in two ways and blamed one of them. The caveat was
      written down and then not applied.

      **The sampling this ticket asked for was still worth adding, and it also proves the
      opposite of what the ticket assumed.** The spread over three samples is 0.6 s. These were
      never noisy measurements — a median would not have found this, and would have made a
      confounded number look more trustworthy. The samples earn their 55 seconds by bounding the
      variance, not by smoothing it.

      **And it puts `P-19`'s erosion in a different light.** The footnote this test prints says
      the baseline after `S-16` was 21.0 s; measured from empty it is 20.9 s. The step to 28.8 s
      that `P-19` recorded on 2026-08-29 and read as Phase 3 eroding the margin arrived in the
      same change that put the bulk case in front of the serial one. `M-02`'s `sensor_runtime`
      row is genuinely written and genuinely costs something, but most of that step was the test
      changing what it measured. **Nobody was clever enough to notice for ten days**, and the
      thing that surfaced it was giving each sample a clean database — not any of the analysis
      built on top of the confounded numbers, including two of mine today.

      **What is actually left is a scaling question, not a regression.** A second 5,000-object
      tree built into an installation that already holds 5,000 costs about a third more than the
      first. That is worth knowing and it is not urgent: the headroom is 30%, not 7%.

- [x] **P-192 — the perf suite records the wrong machine's conditions** · S · P-21, P-19 · The
      budgets run inside the Docker toolchain container, and the only conditions anybody has ever
      written down are the *host's*: a macOS load average and `docker stats` percentages, read by
      hand and pasted into a findings file afterwards. Those are not the numbers that govern the
      measurement. Measured 2026-09-08, at the same moment: the host reported load **25.50**, the
      VM the tests actually run in reported **1.29** on 8 CPUs.

      So `docs/findings/2026-09-08-perf-budgets-under-contention.txt` documents a busy machine
      without establishing that the busyness ever reached the test, and cannot say what did. Its
      one failure — the serial tree build, 30.7 s against a 30 s budget, 26.0 s on the quiet run
      the day before — is left unexplained rather than explained.

      **This is the third time somebody has re-derived the conditions after the fact.** `P-19`
      did it on 2026-08-28 (four failures at 32-36 s, re-measured at 25.2 s with the stack
      stopped). `P-21` did it for the case it could fix — 1,300 unit tests sharing the database —
      and scoped the rest out in as many words: what contends is the suite, "not whatever else the
      operator has open". This is that remainder, and it has now cost a run.

      **The signal is available from inside the container and needs no Docker socket.** Verified:
      `os.loadavg()` and `os.cpus().length` give the VM's own load, and `pg_stat_activity` on the
      shared database, as the `monitoring` role, names the competitors —

      | datname | application_name | state | n |
      | --- | --- | --- | --- |
      | monitoring | ms-core | idle | 2 |
      | monitoring | ms-core | active | 1 |

      — which is exactly the precondition `CLAUDE.md` states in prose ("stop `ms-server` first")
      and nothing checks. It also catches the case prose cannot: a second developer, or a parallel
      session, on the same database.

      Print those at the top of `npm run test:perf`, so they land in the findings file with the
      numbers instead of being reconstructed from memory beside them. **Warn, never block** — "run
      it anyway" is a legitimate thing to want, and a gate that refuses is a gate people route
      around.

      Not a budget change. The serial tree build's margin is `P-19`'s business and `P-19` has
      already answered it: the fix is the bulk path, which does the same 5,000 objects in 2.4 s
      with 92% spare, and the serial case stays because the criterion should be met without anyone
      having to be clever.

      **P-192 outcome.** `scripts/perf-conditions.mjs`, first thing in the root `test:perf`, so
      the conditions are in the run's own output rather than beside it in somebody's memory. It
      prints the container's load average per CPU and, from `pg_stat_activity`, names every other
      client backend on the shared PostgreSQL — cluster-wide rather than filtered to one database,
      because the suite builds scratch databases and a backend on `monitoring` competes with them
      for the same CPU, I/O and buffers.

      **It warns and never blocks**, and all three branches are verified to exit 0: quiet, busy,
      and no database reachable. A gate that refuses to measure is a gate people route around, and
      "run it anyway" is a legitimate thing to want — the run it produces just needs to say so.

      **The wiring is asserted, because dropping it fails in the worst way available**: the run
      still passes, the numbers still look like numbers, and the one line saying what they were
      measured against is silently gone. `build-hygiene` — which runs on every push — fails if the
      root `test:perf` stops naming the script or the script stops existing. Mutations 2/2 redden
      it.

      **First use, the same day, found something.** `docs/findings/2026-09-08-perf-budgets-clean-run.txt`
      is the first run whose quietness is recorded rather than asserted, and against it the serial
      tree build reads 27.9 s where 2026-09-07 read 26.0 s — on a machine that was *quieter*, with
      eleven of thirteen other cases faster. That is `P-193`.

- [x] **P-191 — an authentication exemption for a route that does not exist** · S · U-17, P-187 ·
      `ALWAYS_PUBLIC` in `authentication.ts` listed `/api/v1/health`. There has never been such a
      route: the health endpoints are `/core-health`, `/probes/:id/health` and
      `/notification-health`, all behind `READS`. The entry exempted nothing, which is why nothing
      ever failed — **and a dead line in the list of paths that skip authentication reads, to the
      next person, as evidence that an unauthenticated liveness endpoint exists.** Whether this
      installation should have one is a real question, and a load balancer or a systemd unit
      generally wants it; leaving the line here implied the decision had already been taken.

      Removed, and the list is exported so a test can assert every entry is a route the server
      actually registered. **This list fails silently in both directions** — an entry matching
      nothing is invisible, and a missing entry is invisible until somebody cannot log in — which
      is exactly the shape that deserves a guard rather than care. Mutation 1/1: putting the dead

      **Found by accident, and it had a second victim.** `scripts/dev-reset.sh` used that path as
      its readiness probe, so `curl -sf` never succeeded, `break` never fired, and every reset sat
      out the full sixty seconds looking like a slow migration — measured: `exit 22` against the
      old path, `exit 0` against `/auth/session`, which is public and answers 200 to anybody.
      Mine, from `P-187`, and it "worked" only because a minute is long enough for the core to
      come up regardless. **A readiness probe that never succeeds is indistinguishable from one
      that is merely patient**, which is why it survived four resets without being noticed.

- [x] **P-188 — `soak.sh --teardown` will now delete the dev stack's working fixture** · S ·
      U-20 · The dev database's 5,000-sensor load *is* a soak tree: `provision.mjs` names its root
      `Soak`, finds an existing one and leaves it alone, and that is what the 5,047 sensors in
      `dev/` have been all along. `--teardown` removes it.

      **Until `U-20` it could not.** It counted `expectedDescendants` from a page of `/tree`,
      which is capped, so it asked to delete 999 of 5,250 and the core refused every time. That
      refusal was the only thing standing between an idle `--teardown` and an afternoon rebuilding
      the fixture — and it was refusing for the wrong reason, so fixing the count removed the
      guard as a side effect. Nobody decided that; it fell out.

      Wants a deliberate answer rather than the accidental one it had. The cheapest is for
      `--teardown` to say what it is about to remove and require a confirmation — the core already
      returns exact counts through `/objects/:id/counts`, so "5,251 objects, 5,000 of them sensors:
      type the number to confirm" costs one call it already makes. Worth considering alongside:
      the dev fixture and a harness's scratch tree sharing a name is the underlying reason this is
      even a question.

      **P-188 outcome.** `--remove` prints what it is about to delete — the object, its name, and
      the breakdown from `/objects/:id/counts`, which it already fetches for `expectedDescendants`
      — and then asks. `--yes` (or `MS_ASSUME_YES=1`) for a script; a typed `y` for a person; and
      a **refusal** when there is no terminal to ask on and no flag, because a non-interactive run
      that nobody has been asked about is exactly the case this exists for. `soak.sh --teardown`
      passes `--yes` through.

      The guard lives in `provision.mjs`, not in the shell wrapper, so calling the script directly
      is protected too — the danger is in the thing that sends the `DELETE`.

      **Two defects found by running it rather than reading it.** `--teardown` `exec`ed *above*
      `ms_api_require`, so the one subcommand that deletes things was also the one that reported a
      missing credential as a `fetch` stack trace; it goes through the gate now, while `--report`
      stays above it because it reads a file and needs nothing. And **Ctrl+D at the prompt threw
      an unhandled `AbortError`** — `readline.question` rejects on EOF rather than returning an
      empty answer — so an operator who hit it got a stack trace instead of a decision. EOF is a
      no, the same as every other answer that is not `y`.

      Verified against a stub core that records whether the `DELETE` ever arrives, in all four
      paths: no terminal and no flag refuses with zero `DELETE`s; `--yes` sends one; a real
      pseudo-terminal answering `n` leaves it alone; answering `y` removes it. The live dev tree
      was never a target — 5,051 sensors and one `Soak` root before and after.

      **Not fixed, and deliberately:** the name collision underneath all this. The dev fixture and
      a harness's scratch tree are the same object because `provision.mjs` finds an existing
      `Soak` and leaves it alone, which is the behaviour that makes the harness idempotent and
      also the behaviour that made a working fixture out of a scratch tree. Renaming would orphan
      the tree every dev stack is carrying. **Also not fixed:** there is no test. `scripts/` has no
      harness and inventing one is bigger than this ticket, so the guard is verified and not
      guarded — a regression here would be silent.

- [x] **U-18 — `.ms-label` silently overrides every colour utility beside it** · S · U-17 ·
      The class sets `color: var(--ms-text-muted)` and is unlayered, so it beats any Tailwind
      text utility on the same element — those live in `@layer utilities`, and unlayered CSS wins.
      `class="ms-label text-accent-contrast"` renders muted grey, and on a filled accent button
      that measures about 1.5:1 against WCAG 1.4.3's 4.5:1. Found by looking at the rendered
      login button, not by any test.

      `U-17`'s own two buttons are fixed — they use the primary-button spelling the other nine
      call sites use, which does not include `ms-label`. **What is still there is the general
      case**: the header's theme toggle carries `aria-pressed:border-accent aria-pressed:text-accent`
      and the ink half of that has never applied, and nothing stops the next one. Either
      `.ms-label` drops its colour and every call site states one, or it moves into
      `@layer components` so utilities win — the second is one line and changes what forty
      existing labels look like, so it wants looking at rather than assuming. Whichever way, the
      thing worth having is that a colour utility written next to it either works or fails to
      compile, rather than being quietly discarded.

      **U-18 outcome.** `.ms-label` moved into `@layer components`. That is the whole fix: a call
      site naming no colour still gets the muted one, because the layer still applies, and a call
      site naming one now gets what it asked for. Eight call sites were asking for something they
      were not getting — the masthead's `text-text`, the error panel's `text-down-fg` on its
      label and its "Try again" button, four `hover:text-text` states that did nothing at all, and
      the theme toggle's `aria-pressed:text-accent`, which is the one this ticket was written
      about.

      **The chart rules stay unlayered, and that is the half worth guarding.** `.ms-chart*`
      overrides `uplot/dist/uPlot.min.css`, which is imported from a component and is itself
      unlayered — layering ours would make it lose, and the chart would quietly take uPlot's
      palette instead of the app's. So the fix is not "move the custom CSS into a layer": it is
      one rule in, and a test that asserts the other rules stay out. Mutations 2/2, one in each
      direction.

      **Measured, and smaller than the ticket claimed.** On the surviving call sites the muted
      colour already met AA in both themes, so this is a correctness fix rather than a contrast
      one — declarations written, accepted and discarded. Against the running app: the error
      panel's label goes 6.15 → 6.61 in dark and 4.80 → 5.53 in light; the masthead 6.37 → 14.86
      and 5.56 → 16.67; the pressed toggle 6.37 → 5.86 and 5.56 → 5.62, which is *lower* in dark
      and still well clear of 4.5. The one genuine failure — about 1.5:1, `ms-label
      text-accent-contrast` on a filled accent button — was fixed in `U-17` by spelling that
      button the way the other nine primary buttons are spelled, and this ticket does not depend
      on it. What is fixed here is the class of bug: the next colour utility written beside
      `ms-label` works, and there is no reason muted would have kept passing on the next

      The container `div` added in `U-17` carried `ms-label` and no label text; removed, because
