- [x] **A-40 — A stored secret follows its endpoint wherever a writer points it** · M · A-05,
      N-05, A-29 · Found 2026-09-29 by `V2-07`'s design review, which found it for a directory's
      bind password and noted that it is not only a directory's problem. A write that leaves out a
      secret keeps it, because the form it came from was rendered without it, and that rule never
      asked whether the write changed where the secret goes. A template editor holds `write`, and
      never sees the secret headers an administrator set on an HTTP action. They could still point
      its URL at a host of their own and press "test", and the headers went with it.

      Decided (WatchDog, 2026-09-29). The inventory found the same shape in three places that share
      one mechanism, and those are this ticket; the device credential case is `A-41`, and
      `http.transaction`'s placeholders are `A-42`.
      1. **Notification methods.** Each method declares which visible settings each of its
         secrets goes to (`secretDestinations`), and the registry refuses a method that does not.
         Changing a webhook's URL clears its `secretHeaders`, and changing a program's path clears
         its `secretArgs`, unless the same request sends them again. The audit entry names what
         went. `/templates/:id/test` sends what is stored, so it never sends a secret to a
         destination changed since the secret was set.
      2. **A rediscovery rule's community.** An edit that changes the rule's range or its probe and
         does not send the community clears it, and the audit entry says so.
      3. **A sensor's own secret parameters.** `SensorType.secretDestinations`, required for every
         `writeOnly` parameter and checked by the catalogue when a type registers. `exe.script` and
         `exe.script.advanced` bind `secret` to the program, its arguments, its environment and
         its working directory. All four, because a script that takes its target as an argument is
         the common case. The SNMP polling types bind their community, `authKey` and `privKey` to
         `port`, since on a shared host anyone can listen on a high UDP port. `[]` says a secret
         goes only to the device the sensor is on, which is `A-41`'s to bind.

      **Done when** a writer who re-points a template and tests it has a receiver that sees no
      secret; a rule moved to another range or probe keeps no community it was not sent; a script
      sensor whose program, arguments, environment or directory changes keeps no secret it was not
      sent; and each clearing is in the audit log by name, never by value.

      **Outcome.** All three, through one rule: a secret carries over an edit that leaves it out
      only while every setting that says where it goes is unchanged. A notification method and a
      sensor type each declare that in `secretDestinations`, and the registry and the catalogue
      refuse one that stores a secret without saying. The catalogue check found what the inventory
      had not: the eight SNMP polling types spread a write-only community, `authKey` and `privKey`
      into their own parameters, and would not register until they declared them. The audit entry
      says which secrets an edit left behind: `secretsCleared` on templates and sensors, and
      `communityLeftBehind` on rediscovery rules. It never records the value.
      - URLs are compared as addresses: `HTTPS://Hooks.Example.test/pager` is where
        `https://hooks.example.test/pager` was. A sensor's parameters are compared after the
        type's own defaults are filled in, so a client that leaves out a field at its default has
        moved nothing. Arrays and objects are compared by their JSON, so a reordered object reads as
        a move. That costs a secret re-entered, and the other mistake would carry it somewhere new.
      - `exe.script`'s `secret` no longer defaults to `""`. The default was stored for every script
        sensor and read back as "set", so a secret this cleared would still have looked present.
        Sensors stored before this keep reading "set" until someone edits them.
      - **Not closed here: the host half.** An SNMP sensor's secrets now stay with its `port`,
        but the device's host they go to is `A-41`'s, and so is every credential set a device
        inherits. Moving, cloning or re-hosting a device still carries them.

      Mutations caught: 25 of 25, each applied alone, built, and run against its own tests. They
      cover a carry that ignores destinations, in both registries; each declared destination
      dropped (webhook URL, program path, the script's four, the SNMP port); URLs compared as
      typed; a patch compared without its defaults; each of the catalogue's five registration
      refusals switched off; the rediscovery range and probe clauses; a community sent again but
      cleared anyway; each of the three audit records; and the script secret's empty default put
      back.

- [x] **A-41 — A device credential goes to whatever host a device writer names** · L · A-05,
      A-29, A-40 · Found 2026-09-29 by `A-40`'s inventory. Credential sets are inherited: an
      administrator sets SNMP, SSH or database credentials on a group, and every device beneath
      uses them. A user with `write` on one of those devices may change its host, and at its next
      connection the probe sends the inherited credentials to the new host. The same happens when a
      writer creates a device under the group, moves one there, or clones one into it. No read
      returns the secret, and none needs to: the new host receives it. Split in two
      (WatchDog, 2026-09-29): this ticket is the voucher; `A-41b` is allowed targets.

      **The inventory, checked mechanically.** Every `writeOnly` sensor parameter, every place a
      sealed credential is opened, and every column that stores a secret maps to a row. It found
      three destinations the first pass had not named. A sensor's `port` chooses the listener an
      inherited set is sent to. `DELETE /objects/:id/credentials/:kind` hands everything beneath to
      the ancestor's set of that kind. And a rediscovery rule records no writer to vouch with.
      A discovery run's community is fixed once it starts, so nothing carries it anywhere.

      Decided (WatchDog, 2026-09-29):
      - **The rule.** A credential set reaches a destination only through a voucher who has
        `write` on the object the set is stored on (its owner). The installation vouches for what
        it does itself, and for everything when authorisation is off.
      - **A destination is the probe, the device's host, and the sensor fields the type names**
        in `secretDestinations` under `kind:<id>` (`'kind:ssh': ['port']`). The catalogue requires
        one for every entry in `credentialKinds`; `[]` means the host alone. The probe is part of
        it because the same private address behind another probe is another machine, so moving a
        device across probes is a new destination and needs no rule of its own.
      - **Checked on every write that brings a set somewhere new**, in the write's transaction:
        a device's host change, create, move or clone; a sensor's create, move or clone, or an
        update to a destination field; a subtree move that changes which ancestor's set applies;
        a set deleted, exposing an ancestor's; and a set written, whose writer vouches for
        everything beneath that resolves to it. The 403 names the kind and the owner, never the
        secret: "bringing the ssh credentials on group 'Datacentre' (#12) to 10.0.0.9:22 needs
        write on that group".
      - **Continuous**, through `A-29`'s withheld path. Each (sensor, kind) records its owner, a
        fingerprint of its destination and its voucher (migration 060). A probe's configuration
        sends a set only while all three still hold and the voucher still has `write` on the
        owner. Otherwise the set is withheld and the sensor held Unknown with the reason — never a
        Down from a failed login. Grant, group and account changes now push configuration, so a
        revoked grant stops the next push.
      - **The upgrade changes nothing.** Migration 060 marks the installation's existing sensors as
        not yet vouched for, and a boot step records the installation as voucher for every
        (sensor, kind) that resolves, before the probe endpoint serves a configuration. It runs in
        one transaction that clears the mark, so a crash halfway runs it again whole.
      - **Secrets in a sensor's own parameters** (SNMP communities and keys, a script's secret)
        follow `A-40`'s rule: a device host change, or a move or clone to another probe, clears
        them unless they are sent again, and the audit lists them. Renumbering a device means
        entering its SNMP communities again; `administration.md` says so as the price.
      - **Discovery.** A run's `created_by` vouches for what it provisions. A rediscovery rule
        records its last writer (migration 061), and its runs vouch as that writer.
      - `administration.md` says that `write` on the object a credential set belongs to is trust
        with that credential, until `A-41b` lets a set name where it may go.

      **Done when** a device writer without `write` on the set's owner cannot bring the set to a
      new destination by any of the writes above, and the probe is never sent it; a grant taken
      away stops the next configuration carrying it; and a **scenario test** shows the upgrade
      (migration, then the boot step, including one aborted halfway and completed on the next
      boot) changes no sensor state and queues no notification.

      **Outcome.** All of it, through one module: `objects/credential-vouching.ts`. A
      (sensor, kind) whose kind resolves to a set records its owner, a fingerprint of where it is
      sent, and who vouched (migration 060). Every write in the list re-reads that in its own
      transaction: the installation's record is kept; a writer with `write` on the owner is
      recorded; an unchanged pair is kept for one without; and a changed pair is refused with
      403, naming the kind, the owner and where it would go. Each probe's configuration asks again
      and leaves out a sensor whose voucher lost `write`, was disabled or deleted, or no longer
      matches. It reads Unknown/`access` through `A-29`'s set, and "check now" answers 409
      `OBJECT_CREDENTIALS_WITHHELD`. Grant and identity changes now push configuration.
      - **The catalogue requires a `kind:<id>` entry for every credential kind a type uses**, and
        refuses one for a kind it does not. Declared on all twenty shipped credentialed types: the
        SNMP port, each HTTP type's port, scheme and TLS check, each mail server's port and
        security, the SSH port, the database port and encryption, and the Windows host override
        and authentication.
      - **Secrets in a sensor's own parameters** are cleared, one audit entry each, when the
        device's host or address family changes, or when a device or sensor moves or is cloned to
        another probe or onto another device.
      - **Discovery.** A run vouches as its `created_by`, and a scheduled one as its rule's last
        writer (`written_by`, migration 061, backfilled from the audit log as 059 was). **A run
        whose rule was deleted creates nothing.** Deleting a rule fails the rule's runs that are
        still going. Each gets "its rule was deleted" on the run and in the audit log
        (`discovery.failed`), and its probe is told to stop. A run that had already finished
        fails the same way when anybody asks to provision it (409 `DISCOVERY_RUN_FAILED`). The
        re-check is `provisionRun`, moved out of `main.ts` so that it is tested.
        `DiscoveryService.fail` is the step `P-241` can reuse for a group that moved. `failed`
        is now terminal: a probe that reports the sweep done afterwards changes nothing, and
        nothing is announced. With authorisation off the installation vouches, as it does for
        every write. A sensor a run cannot vouch for is one of its problems, and the rest of the
        device is made.
      - **The boot step also re-fingerprints, and only what it can show did not move.** It
        stores what every type declares, as written. When a release changes a declaration, a
        record is carried over only if its stored fingerprint equals what the old declaration
        computes from the sensor's values now. A record that matches neither stays withheld. All
        of this happens in the upgrade transaction, and each kind gets one `credential.adopted`
        audit entry counting the pairs recorded as the installation's, carried, and left
        withheld. Without re-fingerprinting, adding a field to `kind:http` would withhold every
        HTTP sensor at once. Without the continuity check, the same release would adopt a record
        somebody had moved.
      - **`SensorVouching.settle` keeps each owner's words.** A sensor moving between probes is
        withheld by one probe's check and released by the other's. In the wrong order, one owner
        released what another still held.
      - `credential-upgrade-scenario.test.ts` migrates an installation with Up sensors and
        triggers on Down and Unknown. It boots once into a failure after the rows are written,
        then boots again, and asserts no state moved and nothing was queued. It also shows that
        without the boot step the same configuration withholds all three sensors and pages three
        times, so the assertions can fail.
      - **Mutants: 69, 68 killed.** The survivor walks up to a sensor's probe farthest-first, which
        changes nothing: a probe's parent is always the root, so every sensor has exactly one
        probe above it. Not mutated: the guard on identification's last batch announcing a run
        that failed meanwhile, which only a race reaches, and `main.ts`'s wiring. For the
        adoption sinks that wiring is pinned by `audit-composition.test.ts`.

- [x] **A-41b — A credential set says where it may go** · M · A-41, P-219, P-216 · Split from
      `A-41` (WatchDog, 2026-09-29). With `A-41` alone, whoever may write the object a set is
      stored on may send it anywhere they can put a device. This lets an administrator bound that,
      and delegate within the bound.
      - **`allowedTargets`**, a declared field in every kind's schema (host names, `*.suffix`
        patterns, addresses, CIDR ranges), and **`hostKeys`** for ssh. Declared rather than a
        column, so `A-43`'s checks, the audit, the reads and the generated form carry them with no
        new route. Each kind's secrets are bound to them through `secretDestinations`, so
        changing the targets clears the secret unless it is sent again (`A-40`'s rule).
      - **A restricted set reaches any destination inside its targets and none outside, whoever
        asks, including the owner's writer.** Widening the targets needs the secret again.
      - **The probe checks too** (protocol 22, after `P-219`'s 20 and `P-216`'s 21 have landed). A
        named host and a CIDR target cannot be decided by the core, which does not resolve names;
        the probe checks the address it resolved, and an ssh host key, before using the set.
        **Until a probe speaks 22, a restricted set it would have to decide is withheld from it,
        not sent.** Fail closed.
      - Core Health counts sets with no targets, and the UI flags them. `administration.md`'s
        sentence becomes: `write` on a set's owner is trust with it unless the set has targets.

      **Done when** a device inside the targets receives the set whoever wrote it, one outside
      does not whoever wrote it, a probe that has not upgraded is not sent a set it cannot check,
      and a probe that has refuses one whose resolved address or host key is outside.

      Decided (WatchDog, 2026-09-29), on a design note:
      - **A name host facing only address or CIDR targets is withheld by the core; the probe
        does not resolve it.** "Resolve, check, connect" is DNS rebinding for exactly the
        attacker this is about: the device writer picks the name and can run its DNS. Pinned
        probe resolution is `A-41c`.
      - **`hostKeys` sits beside the existing `hostKeyFingerprint`, with no migration.** The
        accepted keys are the union, put together in one function (`acceptedHostKeys`).
      - **The one `hostKeyFingerprint` bounds nothing.** Counting it would have handed every
        existing strict SSH set to anyone who can write a device beneath it, on the upgrade.
      - **A widened bound clears the secret; a narrowed one keeps it**, refining `A-40`'s
        any-change rule.
      - **A narrowing write says how many sensors it withholds**, and a scenario test counts the
        alarms that follows.

      **Outcome.** A set with `allowedTargets`, or an SSH set with `hostKeys` and strict checking,
      is *bounded*: its bounds decide where it goes, and nothing else does.
      - **Delivery.** Inside the bounds, every sensor gets the set, whoever wrote it. Outside, or
        undecided, none does, whoever wrote it. `vouch()` skips bounded pairs, so no write is
        refused for them and no voucher is recorded. `CredentialVouching.refusals` asks
        `boundRefusal` instead, at every configuration, and holds the sensor Unknown with one of
        three sentences: outside, undecided, probe too old. "Check now" answers 409 with the same
        words, asking about the probe's version as last registered.
      - **Matching** (`@ms/shared` `allowed-targets.ts`, a table test).
        - Entries are a name, a `*.domain` (strictly below), an address, or a CIDR range, v4 or v6.
          Case, a trailing dot, an IPv6 zone and an IPv4-mapped address are normalised.
        - A host is matched only with entries of its own sort, so an address never matches a name.
        - A name facing only address entries is `undecided`.
        - The vault refuses an entry that parses as none of the four, naming it and its index.
      - **SSH.** `hostKeys` is a list. The transport accepts a key in the list or equal to
        `hostKeyFingerprint` (`acceptedHostKeys`, the one union).
        - The pool key carries the accepted keys, so taking one off opens a new connection.
        - Listing keys while accepting any key is refused at write.
        - Protocol 22's `credentialHostKeys` capability gates it: a set that lists keys is withheld
          from an older probe, which would read the one fingerprint only.
        - **The legacy fingerprint alone is not a bound**, so every set in use before stays under
          `A-41`'s voucher rule, and a test pins that.
      - **Secrets.** Every kind declares `secretDestinations`, and `assertSplittable` refuses a
        kind that leaves a secret unbound to `allowedTargets`.
        - A write that widens a bound clears the secrets bound to it unless the write sends them
          again. Widening means an entry added (even inside an old range), the list emptied, a key
          added, or strict checking turned off.
        - Narrowing keeps them. `secretsCleared` is on the response and the audit entry.
      - **Alarm volume.** The credential write answers `withholds`, the count of sensors beneath
        now outside the bounds, and so does the `credential.set` audit entry.
        - `credential-targets-scenario.test.ts`: narrowing a group's set past 6 devices raised 6
          Unknown pages, the Unknown rules' one per sensor, delivered as 1 digest when the
          window closed, and nothing for the pings beside them.
        - The same narrowing behind a Down master raised 0: the dependents are paused, so they are
          not configured, and the switch's Down stayed the one message.
      - **Core Health** counts sets with no bounds (`credentialsUnbounded`, no limit). **There is
        no credential view in the UI**, so that channel is where they are flagged; `U-21` is the
        view.
      - **Docs:** `administration.md` gets the trust sentence, targets, host keys, delegation,
        the per-probe caveat, and an upgrade note that no upgrade changes who receives a secret.
        `api-reference.md` and `web-ui.md` are updated too.
      - **Tests:** every unit suite on `82e59b1`, in the orchestrator's heavy slot: shared 353,
        simulators 24, sensors 1,065 (10 skipped), core 3,896, probe 387 of 388, web 616.
        - The one was `pool-memory-cap.test.ts` timing out waiting for eight workers at a Mac load
          of 32. The file passed 30/30 whole at a toolchain count of 0.
        - Rebased onto `cd7ab60` (`A-39`, `P-242`): the touched suites and theirs 585/585, tsc,
          prettier and eslint clean, the regenerated references unchanged.
      - **Mutation:** 25 mutants, 25 killed, two of them after a fix.
        - `m3` (`unmapped` made the identity) survived: `BlockList` matches an IPv4-mapped
          address against IPv4 rules either way, so no verdict depended on it. Unmapping range
          networks was wrong besides: `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104` became a refused entry. Ranges now
          stay as written. Addresses are still unmapped, which is what makes `10.0.0.1` and
          `::ffff:10.0.0.1` one entry when a write is compared with the last. Tests pin both,
          and `m25` puts the range unmapping back.
        - `m16` (`unboundedSets` counting the bounded sets) survived a test storing two of
          each. It is now three against two.

- [x] **A-41c — A named device checked against a set's address targets, on the probe** · M ·
      A-41b · Split from `A-41b` (WatchDog, 2026-09-29). A device named by host name, whose
      set's `allowedTargets` name only addresses and ranges, is withheld today. The core does not
      resolve names. The probe cannot simply resolve, check and connect, because the device's
      writer picks the name, can run its DNS, and can answer the check with an inside address
      and the connection with their own. The probe has to connect to the address it checked,
      which is work in each transport:

      | Transport | Pinned how |
      | --- | --- |
      | SNMP (`net-snmp`) | Connect to the checked address. UDP, no name involved. |
      | SSH (`ssh2`) | Connect to the checked address. The host key is the server's identity. |
      | HTTP (`http`/`https`) | A `lookup` answering with the checked address. SNI, `Host` and the certificate stay on the name. |
      | Mail (`net`/`tls`) | A `lookup` on the connect, as for HTTP. |
      | PostgreSQL (`pg`) | Driver work: no `lookup` option. A pre-connected `stream` may do. |
      | MySQL (`mysql2`) | Driver work, likewise (`stream`). |
      | SQL Server (`tedious`) | Driver work: neither option. |
      | Windows (PowerShell/CIM) | Not pinnable from here. Kerberos wants the name. |

      Every address the name resolves to for the device's address family must be inside, as
      `A-09`'s guard reads all of them. A transport that cannot pin stays withheld, as now.

      **Done when** a named device whose every resolved address is inside the targets receives
      the set on the transports above that can pin, the check connects to one of those addresses
      and no other, and a name that resolves outside, or differently between the check and the
      connection, is refused with a sentence saying so.

      **A-41c outcome.** A device named by host name, facing a set whose targets name only
      addresses and ranges, is checked by its probe and connected to at the address that was
      checked, on SNMP, SSH, HTTP and mail. The database drivers and PowerShell stay withheld.
      - **One place resolves and checks**: `pinTarget` (`@ms/sensors`
        `support/pinned-target.ts`), called by `SensorCatalogue.execute` before any type runs, so
        every check on a probe passes through it, in a worker or a child process.
        - It makes no lookup unless a set the check holds has targets the host is `undecided`
          against. An unrestricted set, a device given as an address, and a name a name entry
          covers behave as before.
        - Otherwise it resolves once (`getaddrinfo`, the device's family; both for `auto`), checks
          every address against every set that needs it, and pins one: IPv4 first under `auto`.
        - It refuses, as `CredentialsWithheldError` with the sensor id, target and phase, a host
          outside the targets, a kind the type does not pin, a name that resolves to nothing, and
          a name with any address outside.
      - **Transports take the pin from the check's target** (`CheckTarget.pinned`) and never
        resolve the name. SNMP and SSH connect to the address, and their pool keys carry it. HTTP
        and mail give their socket `pinnedLookup`, so SNI, `Host` and the certificate check stay
        on the name; a lookup for any other name is refused before a byte is sent, and a far end
        that is not the pinned address is refused (`pinnedPeerRefusal`). `A-09`'s metadata guard
        reads the pinned address instead of resolving again. `readCommon` and `readTransport` now
        take the whole target, so no HTTP or mail type can pass the host and forget the pin.
      - **A type says which kinds it pins**: `SensorType.pinnedKinds`, declared on the 19 SNMP,
        SSH, HTTP and mail types, refused at registration when it names a kind the type is not
        sent. The core reads it through `SensorTypeGate.pinsAddress`.
      - **Protocol 24, `credentialAddressPinning`.** `boundRefusal` sends an undecided set only
        when the type pins the kind and the probe speaks 24. Below that the sensor is withheld
        with `probeCannotPin`; a type that cannot pin keeps `undecided`, whose sentence now says
        a driver resolves the name itself. Nothing new is sent towards the probe: it decides from
        the host and the set's own `allowedTargets`, with the same `targetVerdict` the core uses.
        The credential write's `withholds` no longer counts a named device a probe will check.
      - **A refused check reads Unknown, not Down.** The runners mark its result `withheld` (the
        one wire change, stripped for a core below 24 by `resultForPeer`). `CredentialVouching
        .reported`, called by `IngestionService.acceptProbeResults`, takes it out of the batch
        before the state machine sees it and holds the sensor through `A-41`'s set, under
        `credentials-probe:<probe>`, with the probe's sentence. The next result that is not a
        refusal lets it go first, ordered by the probe's clock. A sensor no longer sent to the
        probe is dropped from what the probe refused at the next configuration.
      - **Alarm volume** (`credential-pinning.test.ts`): 6 named devices whose names move outside
        raised 6 Unknown pages, 1 digest, and no Down; the same refusals again raised nothing; the
        names back inside were Up at that scan with no Down in their history.
      - **Docs:** `administration.md` (what the probe does, the per-transport table, the upgrade
        note), `state-machine.md`, `adding-a-sensor-type.md`. The generated references are
        unchanged.
      - **Tests:** shared 62, simulators 24, sensors 64 new (`pinned-target`, `pinned-transports`,
        none skipped) and 640 in the touched suites, probe 126, core 354 and `sensor-vouching` 19,
        all passing on the restored tree. The transport tests name the device `*.invalid`, which
        nothing resolves, and inject a resolver that answers 127.0.0.1 once and an outside
        address ever after: each check reaches its simulator and asks the resolver once. The TLS
        tests trust two generated certificates through `tls.setDefaultCACertificates`.
      - **Mutation:** 34 mutants, 34 killed by a test, none after a fix. Two were first caught by
        the compiler and were run again in a form that compiles.
      - **Not covered by a test:** the calls to `pinnedPeerRefusal` in `fetchHttp` and
        `MailConnection.open` (a real socket given the pinned address cannot arrive anywhere
        else; the function itself is tested), and `resultForPeer` at its two call sites in the
        probe's `CoreClient`, which no probe test drives.
      - **Found, not fixed:** `A-09`'s guard still resolves, checks and then lets the socket
        resolve again for a request that is not pinned. `sensor-vouching.test.ts` failed 2 of 19
        once, at 01:40 UTC, on a hypertable chunk constraint in its own `INSERT ... now()`, and
        passed 19 of 19 forty minutes later.

      **A-41c review.** An independent review confirmed six defects in the above, and each is
      closed. Where a bullet above describes how a refused sensor is let go, this is what is true.
      - **F1, check now sent a restricted set to a probe below 24.** `assignmentFor` read
        `probe_registration.protocol_version`, which `ProbeRegistry.admit` wrote before deciding,
        so a hello refused for its key left 24 in the row while a probe at 23 held the
        connection. Closed three ways. `assignmentFor` takes the version of the live session
        (`ProbeEndpoint.protocolVersionOf`, through `ProbeQueryService.peerVersion`), and nobody on
        the line is version 0. The query carries the version it was decided for, and `sendQuery`
        answers `offline` to a session that speaks another. And the row is written only for a
        hello that was accepted, or refused over the version itself (`R-06`). The same gate
        served `A-41b`'s `hostKeys`, and is closed by the same change.
      - **F2, a settle that failed left the refusal map and the set disagreeing.** `reported`
        wrote its map first and `SensorVouching.settle` swallows a failed write. Now the hold is
        made through `settleOrThrow`, the map is written only after it, and a failure refuses
        the batch back to the probe. A configuration that cannot let a hold go leaves both as
        they were for the next one.
      - **F3, a hold outlived its probe's last sensor.** `assignmentsFor` returned before
        `withhold` for an empty branch. It now settles the empty answer first. A move or a delete
        calls `CredentialVouching.reconcile` once it commits (`ResultCacheInvalidator
        .afterMoveOrDelete`), which drops what a probe refused for sensors no longer under it and
        everything held for a probe that is gone, connected or not. And a result from the probe a
        sensor is under now lets go what another probe refused.
      - **F4, releasing a hold re-decided the sensor before its result.** A sensor Down before
        the refusal went Unknown, Down, Up, with a Down row and an alarm. `SensorVouching.release`
        now drops the hold and the cached runtime and re-decides nothing; the result makes the one
        transition. If the batch is not stored the hold is put back (`stored(false)`), and stored,
        a master among them settles its dependents. A hold is stamped as the probe measured the
        refusal, never ahead of the core's clock: stamped by the core it sorted after the reading
        that let it go, and the history ended on Unknown.
      - **F5, `withheld: true` was believed on any result.** The schema refuses it beside an
        outcome other than `error` or beside readings. `reported` honours it only for a sensor
        that probe's last configuration sent with a set whose targets left the name to it;
        anything else is taken as the result it is and counted with Probe Health's refused
        results.
      - **F6, a resolver that hangs read Down.** `pinTarget` bounds the lookup at half the
        check's timeout, ten seconds at most (`resolveBoundMs`), and refuses in the `resolve`
        phase. The runners hand the check its `timeoutMs` (`CheckContext.timeoutMs`).
      - **Core Health** gains `credentialsWithheld`, Sensors withheld for credentials, read from
        `CredentialVouching.stats()`.
      - **`probe-flow.test.ts`** (`B-07`) named "a core below `flowCounters`" as
        `PROTOCOL_VERSION - 1`, which is 23 now and has them. It asks `versionFor` instead.
      - **Tests:** 783 passing on the restored tree, none skipped: 234 in the shared, sensors and
        probe suites touched, 546 in 19 core suites, and `probe-flow` 3. The alarm-volume
        scenario: a sensor Down before the refusal has one Down row and two pages after it has
        been Unknown and is Up again.
      - **Mutation:** 35 mutants, 35 killed by a test, at least one for each of the six; one was
        first caught by the compiler and run again in a form that compiles.
      - **Not covered by a test:** the wiring in `main.ts` (the invalidator's hook, the sender's
        `protocolVersionOf`, the Core Health source).
      - **Found, not fixed:** a refusal made honestly just before a configuration stops leaving
        the sensor to the probe, and delivered after it, is now a failed scan. With nobody
        connected, "check now" on such a sensor says the probe is too old, where "not connected"
        would be the better sentence.

        counts snapshots, state changes and overflows, and not `subscribe`'s reset. `states`
        changes identity for both, so a view keyed on it cannot tell them apart. The tree, the
        detail page and the map read `states` as before.

        the list's own subscribe. **A first snapshot after a lost connection is not skipped**,

        bound goes from at most 3 fetches to exactly 2. Against the original view all three new
        tests fail, the first with 2 fetches on mount. Four mutations, four killed.

        polite status that is also focused. **The names are `U-90`, fixed 2026-10-20: each now
        carries its field's label; how they read is still the pass's to judge.**

      **Review round 1, 2026-10-20: five medium and two low, all closed** (web only, six
      commits). Six are older than this ticket, found by reading past the tab its walk covered;
      the seventh came with its fourth fix above. Each focus fix asserts `document.activeElement`.
      1. **The rediscovery rules did nothing with focus** (medium, since `D-11`; WCAG 2.4.3). After
         nearly every action it fell to the page: *New rule*, a row's *Delete*, *Keep* and the
         form's buttons were taken away as they were pressed; *Edit*, a switch, the confirmed
         *Delete* and *Save* were disabled as they were; and every accepted change read the list
         again through `useApi`, which goes back to `loading` and took the whole panel down. Now
         the form's heading takes focus as the form opens; *Cancel* and *Show the rule as it is
         now* give it back to *New rule* or that rule's *Edit*; a *Delete* puts it on its question,
         a focusable group named "Confirm deleting Nightly", and *Keep* back on *Delete*; a save
         or a delete puts it on a notice that says what was done ("Saved Nightly.", "Deleted
         Nightly.", "Created Weekly sweep. It is off until it is switched on from its row."), as
         the Credentials tab's does; a refused delete gives it back to the row's *Delete*. A
         switch, the confirmed *Delete*, *Keep*, *Save* and the form's *Cancel* are `aria-disabled`
         while their request is out, with a guard, so the one pressed keeps focus and a second
         press sends nothing. The list as last read stays on screen while it is read again, and
         when that read fails it stays, said to be the old one, with *Try again*. Focus is moved
         only from the page or from inside the panel. The comment that said focus was on the
         row's button when the core refused is true now, and says why.
      2. **Start discovery and a run's Cancel disabled themselves as they were pressed** (medium).
         Both are `aria-disabled` while out, with a guard. A run started from the button puts
         focus on its card's heading (`Card` takes a `headingRef`, which makes its `h2`
         focusable from script); a run that ends with focus on *Cancel* gives it to *Open the
         group*, which takes the button's place. Focus moves from the button or from the page
         only, never from where the operator moved it while the request was out. The two
         comments that said focus was on the button when the core refused are true now.
      3. **A sensor's parameter forms disabled everything while saving** (medium), the defect
         `U-78` fixed for templates. `ParamsForm` and `AddSensor` passed `disabled={saving}` to
         the whole generated form and disabled their buttons, the name and the type. Nothing is
         disabled while out now: *Save parameters*, *Discard changes*, *Create sensor*, *Cancel*
         and the type are `aria-disabled`, with guards, and Enter pressed in a box leaves focus
         in it, through a refusal too. An accepted save, once the form shows what the core holds,
         and a discard move focus from the button pressed, or from the page, to the status line,
         focusable now, which says "Saved." or "Discarded. The form shows the parameters as they
         are stored." `ParamsForm`'s comment that focus was on Save when the core refused is
         corrected.
      4. **A secret that is an object or a list was not drawn as a secret** (medium). The
         webhook's `secretHeaders`, an object marked `writeOnly`, was a password box: what was

         is a JSON box now, inside the keep, replace and clear every secret has, saying "Typed as
         JSON: an object of names and values, such as {"name": "value"}." The program method's
         `secretArgs`, a list marked at the list, was drawn as any list: stored, it read "Nothing
         here yet.", and an entry added there, typed in clear, replaced every stored one on save.

         `aria-invalid` nor the error edge every other control in error has. It has both now.
      6. **Storage that could not be read opened the theme light** (low). The boot script read
         storage and the system in one `try`, and its `catch` set light whatever the system
         asked, where `useTheme` treats the same failure as no stored choice and follows the
         system; so the reader got light on every load and dark after the system's first change.

      **Review round 2, 2026-10-20: one medium, closed** (core, with two comments in the web

      1. **Clearing a template's secret list or secret object could never be saved** (medium). The
         editor's Clear sends `null`, which `PUT /templates/{id}` documents as the way to clear a
         secret, and the core refused it every time: `mergeSecrets` kept the `null`, and the
         method's schema then met a `null` where it takes a list (`secretArgs`, *Execute
         program*) or an object (`secretHeaders`, *HTTP action*): 400, `/secretArgs must be
         array`, with the field still reading *removed on save*. Nothing else in the UI clears
         stored secret arguments, since a Replace left empty keeps them; the program's Clear was
         new in round 1's fourth fix, the webhook's older. The editor's preview of the cleared
         draft was refused the same way, and so was a create sent with a `null`. Now
         `mergeSecrets` takes an explicit `null` out before validation, with nothing carried for
         it, as the catalogue's `carryWriteOnly` does for a sensor's: the schema's default fills
         it — `[]` or `{}`, which redaction reports as no secret — and a required one (a Slack
         or Teams webhook URL) is refused as missing. A create, a draft and a change of method
         merge over nothing stored, so a `null` there is the same unset. The UI is unchanged: its
         two comments saying `null` is the API's unset are true now and say how.

        every field `templates-model.ts`'s `initial` rebuilds from the read, the secret `null` —
        answers 200 with nothing redacted, stores the default, keeps every other setting, and
        leaves the secret's value nowhere in the row; and a POST with the secret `null` creates a
        template holding none. The registry test that a cleared Slack URL is not carried now also
        asserts it is refused as required, where it asserted the `null` was kept.
        `test-send.test.ts`: a program draft and a webhook draft with their secret `null` preview.
        **Mutants 3, 3 killed**, each restored byte for byte (`shutil.copy`, `os.utime`,
        `filecmp`): the `null` kept, as before, 7 failing; a create or a draft not merged, as
        before, 3; a `null` read as absent, so the stored secret is carried and kept, 7. Core: the
        two files, 84 tests, green against the dev PostgreSQL, none skipped, and `dist` checked
        against the restored source. Web suite 95 files and 1,288 tests, green; Prettier, ESLint
        and `tsc --noEmit` clean on what changed. Not walked in a browser: the editor's request is
        the one the HTTP test sends.

        rather than the UI sending `[]` or `{}`. The API documents `null` as how any secret is
        cleared (`PUT /templates/{id}`, and `api-reference.md`), so any client following it hit the

- [x] **U-24 — the state stream does not say a probe's link or report changed** · M · B-12 ·
      Found 2026-10-02 by `B-12`. The stream carries sensor state changes only. A probe with no
      sensor the reader can see — exactly a probe getting its first sensor — sends no frame, so
      the add-sensor form's collector notice is still read once there; and a probe that
      reconnects can be asked before its first report, with nothing to prompt the form when the
      report arrives. **Done when** the stream has a frame for a probe connecting, dropping and
      reporting, sent only to a reader who may see that probe, the form follows it, and the
      subscription is the probe and not every sensor beneath it.

      **Done 2026-10-02.**

      **A second subscription, and two frames only it is sent.** `{"subscribe":{"probeId":N}}`
      watches one probe itself: the core answers `{"type":"watching","probeId":N}` and then
      sends `{"type":"probe","probeId":N}` when that probe claims its branch, when its link
      goes, and when a report differs from the last in whether it reported at all or in which
      listeners it names (`scheduled`, `flowReceived`, `syslogReceived`, `trapReceived` present
      or absent — `reportShape` in `probe-endpoint.ts`; the numbers moving is not a frame). No
      snapshot, and no sensor's state: the subscription is the probe. `objectId` and `probeId`
      together are refused by the client-frame schema. The stream's own `PROTOCOL` stays 1,
      because neither frame is ever sent on a subscription a client written before them can
      make; no probe-protocol number and no migration are involved.

      **The frame is the id and nothing else.** It means "ask `GET /probes/{id}/health`
      again", so what a reader may know about a probe is still decided on that route alone.

      **Visibility.** The frame goes through `Visibility.sees` on the probe's own root-first
      path, read with the access epoch in the query sensor frames use, at the moment it is
      sent. The route refuses a watch with one `problem` for a probe out of view, an id nobody
      used and an object that is not a probe, and confirms the epoch it judged at, as a
      snapshot's is confirmed. A reader with sensors under a probe it cannot see is sent
      nothing, not a frame with an id.

      **When a watcher is told its access moved is not a function of any probe's edges**
      (review finding, fixed in a second commit). As first written a watcher's stale view was
      re-examined by `#catchUp` from `publishProbe`, so a reader revoked mid-watch was sent
      `overflow` at the instant the now-hidden probe next connected or dropped: the time of
      the edge, in a frame that carries nothing. Now a watcher is told its view changed in one
      place, the broadcaster's sweep (`#review`), on the sweep's own five-second timer: one
      read of the access epoch per sweep while anybody watches (`accessEpoch`, wired in
      `main.ts`), and a resolution only for a view read at another epoch. `publishProbe`
      examines only that probe's watchers; one whose view is stale has it asked for again and
      the frame goes through the view the account has now, or does not go — and nothing else
      is sent to it there, whatever the answer. A watcher is no longer examined on a state
      batch either. The timer runs while there is a socket to check or a watcher to review,
      and a watch still does not hold the state publish's guard open.

      **Backpressure.** Two folds, one count. A change that arrives while that probe's place
      is being read is folded into the frame the read is about to send (one query in flight
      per probe). And a watch holds at most one frame for its socket: while one is handed to
      `ws` and not yet written out, or before `watching` has gone, further changes fold into
      it (`probeFrames` in the stream route). Nothing is lost by either, since the frame that
      arrives is read after the last change. Both are counted in `StreamStats.probeCoalesced`,
      which is the new Core Health channel `streamCoalesced` (a counter, beside
      `streamCutoffs`, and `ms_core_stream_probe_changes_coalesced_total` on the exporter). A
      probe nobody watches costs no query, and a watch does not hold the state publish's
      "anybody listening" guard open.

      **The form.** `ProbeWatch` uses `useProbeStream(probeId)`; `StateStream.watchProbe`
      sends the watch, replays it on reconnect and on `overflow`, and counts `watching` and
      `probe` for the watched probe in `frames`, so `useSettledReload` is unchanged: the
      settle, the held answer, the status region not rewritten and focus not moved are
      `B-12`'s. Both cases `B-12` could not cover pass as component tests.

      **Alarm volume is untouched.** `publishProbe` writes no state and queues no
      notification; a lost probe is still Probe Health's one alarm.

      **Tests.** `core/test/state-stream.test.ts` (+17: told and not told, a table of nine
      views, a flapping link, a failed read, a deleted probe, `canWatchProbe`; and for the
      finding — revoked, then three edges with no tree subscriber: nothing, then `overflow` on
      a sweep run by hand; the same when another probe changes and when a sensor changes
      state; a view granted mid-watch; a view that could not be asked for; a sweep that cannot
      read the epoch; the sweep's timer under a mocked `setInterval`, armed by a watcher alone
      and gone with the last; a watcher attached, and one detached, while views are asked
      for), `stream-backlog.test.ts` (+4, `probeFrames`), `object-visibility.test.ts` (+1, two
      real sockets: refused three ways, told, granted, then revoked — three edges the
      administrator hears and the reader's socket is sent nothing at, bounded by a frame it
      can be waited on, and `overflow` only on the sweep — both scopes refused),
      `probe-endpoint.test.ts` (+3: claim, report shape, drop; an unclaimed probe; the shape),
      `core-health.test.ts` and `metrics.test.ts` (the channel), `web/test/state-stream.test.ts`
      (+2), `web/test/add-sensor-live.test.tsx` (12, three new). Every socket wait is
      `waitFor`'s ten seconds or `waitUntil`'s five. **Mutations 14/14**: the visibility check
      dropped, the probe match dropped, no fold in flight, the in-flight mark never cleared,
      watchers left out of the grant check, a watch allowed on a non-probe, the horizon
      ignored, no fold per socket, both scopes accepted, a hidden probe's watch allowed, a
      frame per heartbeat, no frame on a drop, a frame for another probe counted by the page,
      the form back on the branch subscription. **And 11/11 on the finding's fix**: the sweep
      not reviewing, a changed view never sent back, a review with the epoch unmoved,
      `overflow` at the edge (the finding itself), the frame through the stale view, an
      unchanged view never brought forward, a detached watcher told, watchers not arming the
      timer, a view that could not be asked for falling back to the stale one, a change
      examining every probe's watchers, a watcher sent back and left attached.

      **Not done.** A change between the form's own `GET` and its watch standing is not
      heard, as on `B-12`'s stream: `watching` is not news, by `B-12`'s rule. A read of the
      probe's place that fails is logged and the frame is not sent; the next change sends one.
      And found by review, recorded and not fixed: the route attaches a watch before
      `canWatchProbe` answers, so a client that may not see a probe can, by subscribing
      repeatedly, have `publishProbe` run its path query for that probe during each judging
      window. No frame reaches it and subscribe pacing bounds it; judging before attaching
      needs the held-frame order worked out again, and is a follow-up.

- [x] **U-25 — a socket whose credential lapsed is closed at the next thing that happens** · M ·
      U-24, A-34 · Found 2026-10-02 by `U-24`'s second review. `publish` checks every admitted
      socket's credential before a state batch goes out, and `publishProbe` does the same at a
      watched probe's edge, and closes a lapsed one there. So an account signed out or disabled
      is told so at the instant some sensor changed state or some watched probe connected or
      dropped, including ones it could never see: one sample, inside one sweep interval. The
      check is what keeps anything committed after a sign-out from being delivered (`A-34`);
      the close is what carries the timing. **Done when** a lapsed socket is sent nothing at an
      edge and closed on the sweep's own clock, on both paths, with a test that shows the edge
      happened and the close did not come with it. Also from that review: the test that the
      sweep's timer stops with the last watcher cannot fail and needs to watch the timer; the
      route attaches a watch before it is judged, so repeated subscribes to a hidden probe cost
      a path read each; and a change between the add-sensor form's own request and its watch
      standing is not heard.

      **Done 2026-10-02.**

      **Deciding and acting are two things now.** `publish` and `publishProbe` still ask about
      every admitted socket before anything goes out, in the one query they asked before, and
      what they find lapsed they *silence*: `StreamSocket.silence` detaches the socket's
      subscription synchronously, so the batch that found it delivers nothing to it (`A-34`),
      and the route's one `send` lets nothing out afterwards: no state frame, no `probe`, no
      `overflow`, no `problem`, no snapshot. The socket stays open. `StateBroadcaster.sweep` is
      the only place such a socket is closed (`4401`, with the reason), on the interval that
      was armed when the first socket or watcher arrived and that no edge moves. A silenced
      socket stays admitted, so it holds that timer.

      **The bound.** A lapsed socket is open and silent for at most one sweep interval, five
      seconds, plus the time one credential check takes, on a busy installation as on a quiet
      one. `administration.md` (where `A-34`'s rule is written), `web-ui.md` and the route's
      description in `api-reference.md` say so.

      **Cost.** No extra credential query per edge: a silenced socket is left out of the
      question a later edge or sweep asks, so an edge asks once, about fewer sockets.
      `signedOut` (Core Health's `streamEnded` and its siblings) counts a socket once, where it
      is found, which for a silenced one is before its close.

      **A client frame, and a decision made beyond the brief.** A silenced socket may not
      subscribe, re-subscribe or be sent `watching`. The first cut closed a silenced socket at
      its next frame and went on answering a lapsed socket that had *not* been silenced, and
      that difference is the oracle again: one frame of junk after a sign-out says whether
      anything changed state since. So every frame from a signed-in socket now waits for its

      **Done 2026-10-04.**

      - **(1) A failed check at an edge.** `StateBroadcaster` remembers, per admitted socket,
        when a check last said it was signed in (the instant the question was asked, on a
        monotonic clock; admission counts, since the upgrade was just authenticated; edges,
        sweeps and a client's frame all count). Where an edge's check gives no answer,
        `#atEdge` lets the batch through to a socket vouched for less than one sweep interval
        ago and **holds back** every other: `StreamSocket.withhold` detaches its subscription
        synchronously, sends nothing and marks it owed. At the edge a held-back socket and a
        signed-out one are sent the same thing, nothing, so the edge's instant tells neither
        anything. The first sweep whose check says it is still signed in calls `resume`, and
        the route sends `overflow` ("could not confirm this session for a moment; subscribe
        again"). That is on the sweep's clock, because sent at a later edge it would tell an
        account when changes happen in branches it cannot see. A signed-out one is closed
        `4401` there, as before. A subscription the client makes of its own clears what is
        owed, so its own snapshot is not followed by a second resync. A silenced socket gets
        nothing, as before. Nothing is dropped untold, and it is counted.
      - **(2) Bounded, and one question out.** An edge waits `credentialWaitMs` (2 s) from when
        it arrived. Per check there is one edge question in the database and at most one
        more waiting to be asked. An edge that arrives while one is out does not take that
        answer, which was asked before its batch committed (`A-34`). It waits for the next
        question, asked the moment the one out comes back and shared by every edge that
        arrived meanwhile (`edgesCoalesced`). Once the question out passes its wait, the
        edges waiting on the next are decided by (1) at once, and so is every edge after
        them, asking nothing, until it answers (the sweep's rule from `U-26`). So no batch is
        held past its bound, none queues behind a hang, and a hung database holds one query
        of the edges'. The late question counts in `streamChecksOutstanding`; before its wait
        it does not, so a healthy core still reads 0.
      - **(3) Accepted as it stands**: a frame whose check never answers holds that socket's
        frames until the unread bound severs it with `1008`; nothing is sent meanwhile.
      - **(4) Accepted**: a credential that lapses and comes back inside one sweep interval
        closes a silenced socket and not one that never knew. (1) leans on the same window: a
        socket signed out within the last interval can be sent an unvetted batch.
      - **(5) Accepted**: `streamChecksOutstanding` does not count a probe watcher's
        re-resolution in flight. Each waits `credentialWaitMs` on the sweep, is asked once per
        principal and epoch (`#resolving`), and one left out is reviewed on the next tick.

        harness, larger than this ticket and unrelated to the stream. The cheaper way is to
        move the runners' wiring into a function a unit test can call; left for a ticket.

      **Found, not fixed.**
      - After an outage longer than one interval, every page with a subscription is held back
        at the first unvetted change. All of them are resumed on the same sweep tick, so N
        snapshot reads land on a database that has just come back. Spreading the resumes
        over a few ticks would soften it.

        broadcaster detaches by socket and does not know what the socket's subscription would

      **U-28 outcome. A shared question gets its own wait, an unplaced change is owed to every
      open tree, and what a sweep owes goes out paced.** All in `packages/core/src/state/stream.ts`.
      - **(1) The joiner's bound.** An edge's question now carries its own bound, from when it is
        asked: one timer per round, which also marks the round late. It is no longer
        `#within` from the edge's arrival. So the edge that asks waits `credentialWaitMs`. One
        that joins waits what is left of the question out, then `credentialWaitMs` from its own
        question, so at most twice the wait. When the question out goes late, the joiners are
        still released at once, as before.
      - **(2) The docs.** They now say that a coalesced edge released because the question before
        it went late, or because its own did, goes out by the unvetted rule and counts in
        `edgesUnvetted` as well as `edgesCoalesced`. Updated: `StreamStats.edgesCoalesced`, the
        `streamEdgesCoalesced` channel comment, and `administration.md`, which also says a
        change that waited may take up to four seconds in all.
      - **(3) A change that cannot be placed.** When `publish`'s ancestry read fails, the changes
        are counted in `StreamStats.unplaced` (Core Health `streamUnplaced`, a 64-bit counter,
        and `ms_core_stream_changes_unplaced_total`).
        - **Who is told.** Without the paths nobody can say which subscriptions the change was
          for, so every tree subscription attached at that moment is owed an `overflow`.
        - **When.** On the sweep's clock, not at the failure. Most of those subscriptions would
          never have been sent the change, and an `overflow` at that instant would tell them that
          something committed somewhere they may not see (`A-21`'s instant).
        - **Until then**, they are sent what can be placed. A subscription made after the
          failure, or detached before the sweep, is owed nothing.
        - **No limit on the channel.** It happens only while the database is failing, which the
          ingestion queue's limits already alarm on (one outage, one alarm).
        - **Probe watchers are not covered.** `publishProbe`'s own failed read, which loses a
          frame that carries no value, is left as it was.
      - **(4) Paced.** What a sweep owes now goes through one queue, `#owed`, oldest first:
        held-back sockets the sweep has vouched for, and subscriptions owed for an unplaced
        change.
        - **The pace.** The first goes on the sweep, the rest `resumeSpacingMs` apart (default
          100 ms), and at most as many as fit in one sweep interval (50 at 5 s). The rest wait
          for the next sweep.
        - **The reasoning.** A snapshot took 24–182 ms at the median and 236 ms at the worst
          90th percentile in `2026-09-28-object-visibility.md`, so one to three are read at a
          time, and a few hundred pages are back inside half a minute.
        - **Skipped when it no longer applies.** A socket signed out before its turn is closed
          by that sweep and never told. Owing twice is owing once.
        - **Counted.** The queue is counted in `StreamStats.resyncsOwed` (Core Health
          `streamResyncsOwed`, a level, and `ms_core_stream_resyncs_owed`), since CLAUDE.md
          wants a metric for every queue.
        - **What it discloses.** A page's place in the line says that other pages were owed
          before it, not whose. The stream route's API description says all of this.
      - **Tests** (`state-stream.test.ts`):
        - a joiner at a database answering in 0.6 s against a 1 s wait is vetted, with no
          failure and no unvetted edge;
        - an unplaced batch is counted and tells nobody at the edge. The sweep sends back the
          whole-tree and the other-device subscriptions, and not one made after or one
          detached. Owed once;
        - with mock timers, six held-back pages go out one at a time, a spacing apart and not
          a millisecond sooner, three to an interval, oldest first. One signed out before its
          turn is closed and never resumed;
        - `core-health.test.ts` reads both channels, and the counter list names
          `streamUnplaced`.

        The U-27 helper sends what is owed at once (`resumeSpacingMs: 0`), so its tests are
        unchanged.
      - **Mutations**, each restored byte for byte (sha checked):
        - bounding a joiner from its arrival again fails the joiner test;
        - owing nobody on a failed read fails the unplaced test;
        - sending the `overflow` at the edge fails it too;

      **U-32 outcome. Decided: record it, beside the version, and show it.**
      - **Why record it.** "When it last connected it spoke protocol 12" is advice whose weight
        depends on when: an hour ago it very likely still holds, and three months ago somebody
        may well have upgraded the machine. The reader cannot ask: `GET /probes` is `ADMIN`, and
        its `lastSeenAt` is the wrong time anyway. One nullable column costs nothing at the
        handshake, which already writes the version in that statement.
      - **Migration 072, `probe_registration.protocol_accepted_at`.** It is when the recorded
        `protocol_version` was spoken on a handshake the core accepted. A check keeps it finite
        and never beside version 0. Existing rows get NULL, because `last_seen_at` is the one
        guess known to be wrong. The rollback drops the column, and is tested. The time comes
        from the registry's clock (`now`), as `first_seen_at` does.
      - **Written where the version is, and only on acceptance.** `#speaks` takes `accepted` and
        writes the version and the time in one `UPDATE`. That covers a pending and an approved
        welcome, plus `#enrol`'s insert. **A hello refused over the version (`R-06`) still
        records the version and clears the time.** No accepted handshake spoke that version, and
        a time kept from an earlier one would put another handshake's date beside it. Every
        other refusal (key, address, revoked) writes neither. So the pair always reads as one
        fact.

        `lastProtocolVersion`. It is read-only, under the route's existing `onObject('read')`,
        and comes from one query with the version in `ProbeHealthService.lastProtocol` (which
        replaces `lastProtocolVersion`). It is `null` whenever the version is, for a revoked
        identity, beside a refused version, for a pre-072 row and when the database cannot be
        asked (`P-126`). No new route, so the runbook appendix is unchanged.

        aloud. It then gives the date and time in the reader's locale (`toLocaleString`, as the
        rest of the UI shows one). Both are in the sentence the field is described by, not in a
        tooltip, and they are marked up as the UI marks a time: `<time dateTime title>`.
        **How long ago is reckoned from the answer's `at`, not `Date.now()`.** Both times come

- [x] **U-34 — the edit form offers a mode the core will refuse** · XS · P-303 · Found 2026-10-08
      in `P-303`. `snmp.custom`'s and `snmp.table` columns' `mode` is fixed once the sensor exists
      (`409 OBJECT_CHANNEL_MODE_FIXED`), but the edit form leaves it enabled and only shows the

      **U-34 outcome. A schema annotation the catalogue and the form both read, and no type id in
      the web package.**
      - **`'x-createOnly': true`** on a parameter says it is fixed once the sensor exists;
        `snmp.custom`'s `mode` and `snmp.table`'s column `mode` carry it. Inside an array the entry
        schema also names its key, **`'x-entryKey': 'column'`**, because an entry's position is not
        its identity: columns reorder, and a column added above the others moves every one, so a
        lock by index would hold the wrong column after the first move. An entry whose key the
        sensor does not have (added, or its column retyped to a new one) stays open, as the core
        allows. The catalogue declares both keywords to Ajv (strict mode admits them and refuses a
        wrong-typed value) and refuses at registration an annotation the form could not honour:
        behind a combinator, on a `writeOnly` parameter, or in an array entry that names no key or
        a key that is not a required property of it (`CREATE_ONLY`, `ENTRY_KEY`,
        `assertCreateOnlyIsPlaced`). The sensor reference flags it (**fixed once created**), and
        `adding-a-sensor-type.md` states it beside `P-303`'s rule and in the registration table.
      - **The annotation warns; the core still decides.** The 409 is judged from the channels, so
        nothing in the core's refusal changed.
      - **The form** (`SchemaForm`'s new `existing` prop, the stored parameters, passed only by
        `ParamsForm`, so adding a sensor is unchanged). A field is `open` (not fixed, or nothing
        stored there), `locked` (stored, holding the stored value: a read-only text box) or
        `changed` (stored, holding another value, reachable only by retyping a column's key to one
        the sensor has as the other mode: left editable, saying what is stored, so it can be put
        back). A read-only `<input>`, not a disabled `<select>`: a disabled control leaves the tab
        order and some screen readers skip it with its reason, and `readonly` on a `<select>` is
        ignored. The reason, "Fixed once the sensor exists; add a new sensor to change it.", is
        tied by `aria-describedby` after the type's own description.
      - **The 409 when it still comes** (a removed column put back as the other mode, which the
        stored parameters no longer name; a stale form; another writer): a `role="alert"` block
        naming each channel and direction from `details.channels`, with the core's own sentence and
        correlation id, instead of a line of small text. Any other refusal keeps its old text and
        now also has `role="alert"`.
      - **Tests.** `packages/web/test/fixed-field.test.tsx` (20): the model's states table-driven;
        a scalar read-only, focusable, its computed accessible description the hint plus the
        reason, not changeable, and a select when adding; table columns locked, an added one open,
        the lock following the column through a reorder, a retyped key opening it, a key retyped
        to the other mode's column saying what is stored and re-locking when put back; the 409
        rendered through `ParamsForm` against a stubbed fetch; a 412 still shown. Catalogue (7):
        the shipped annotations exactly, admitted placements, each refusal, wrong-typed values.
        Mutations: the model not reading the annotation fails 13; never read-only fails 7; entries
        matched by position fails 3; reason not in `aria-describedby` fails 2; no refusal branch
        fails 1; no `changed` state fails 3; no registration check fails 4; `snmp.table` without
        the annotation fails 1.

        tells the form about a channel kept from a column an earlier edit removed, so that case is
        the 409's.
      - **Amended on review** (a second commit). **Putting a `changed` field back dropped focus to
        the page**: the select it was on became a read-only box. Focus now moves to the box when
        the change came from that field while it had focus (not when a column key typed elsewhere
        locks it), and the reason is a polite live region, so the new state is heard. **A locked
        field the form holds as absent showed an empty box**: `locked` now carries the value it

        - A version refusal writes the version and the refusal's time, and clears the accepted
          time.
        - An accepted handshake writes the version and its time, and clears the refusal's.
        - Every other refusal (key, address, revoked) writes none of the three.
        - The time is the *last* refusal's: a probe that retries reads as still trying.

        schema, as `U-33` did for the accepted time.

          `incompatible` and is no longer the upgrade's sentinel.
        - Every `incompatible` explanation now says what happens next:
          - *…older than the oldest this build understands (1), so its last hello was refused,
            and it will be refused again until it is upgraded* when a refusal is recorded;
          - *…so it will be refused when it next connects, unless it has been upgraded since*
            for a version a core with a lower floor accepted.

        read in the same query as the version, from the live identity only, under the route's
        existing `onObject('read')`.

          is still `null`, as nothing recorded.
        - It is `null` beside an accepted version, for a revoked identity, and when the database
          cannot be asked (`P-126`).
        - No new route, so the runbook appendix is unchanged. `docs/api-reference.md` is
          regenerated.
      - **What the form says.** Any recorded version this core refuses comes first, before the
        listener's version, by the handshake's own `isProtocolCompatible`:

          08:30:00), was refused over its version: it spoke protocol 0, and this core accepts

          was refused…*.

      **U-39 outcome. `removeAt` walks arrays by index, copies only what it changes, and never

        `snmp.table` column's mode saves the column without `mode`, and the core applies the
        default.
      - **What it does not remove, it hands back unchanged (the same object).** A path whose last
        segment is a position names a whole entry, and that is `ArrayField`'s Remove to do: a
        splice here would delete the entry from under a control being cleared and shift the rest,
        and deleting the slot would leave a hole that serialises as `null`. So that, an index past
        the end or into a hole, a property name or a non-digit index (`0x0`) where an array is, a
        path through a string or `null`, a key not there, and an inherited property (`toString`,
        now `Object.hasOwn`) all remove nothing.

        at every bad path. `writeAt` already built arrays where the next segment is an index; it
        leaves empty slots for an index past the end, which the form never asks for (an entry's
        controls exist only for entries the array holds, and Add appends) — said in its comment,
        pinned where the existing test already showed it, not changed.

        built it: the select becomes the read-only box showing the default it compared
        (`gauge`), focus moves from the select to the box, and the reason is the polite live
        region the box is described by.
      - **Tests.** `schema-form.test.ts`: removal table-driven over deep-frozen inputs with
        `toStrictEqual` (which tells an array from an object keyed "0" and a hole from an entry):
        7 paths that remove, 12 that remove nothing and return the same object, copy-on-write,
        a round trip with `writeAt`; and `writeAt`/`readAt` tables beside it (10).
        `repeating-field.test.tsx`: "—" inside an entry keeps the entry. `fixed-field.test.tsx`:
        "—" on a `changed` column locks at the default with focus on the box; "—" on an added
        column leaves `{}`; a `ParamsForm` save of an `snmp.table` column on "—" sends no `mode`.
        Mutations: the pre-fix `removeAt` fails 22; an emptied entry spliced out fails 3, or
        deleted to a hole fails 3; no index check fails 1; no own-property check fails 2; the

        6; checking only the last segment 2.

- [x] **U-47 — a cleared JSON entry shows `""` after it is remounted** · XS · U-44 · Found
      2026-10-09 in `U-44`. `JsonBox` sets its text from the value only on mount, so a cleared
      entry moved or remounted shows `""`, which the operator never typed. **Done when** a cleared
      entry shows an empty box after a remount, with a test.

      **U-47 outcome. A JSON box's text follows its value, and an entry's `''` is shown empty.**
      - **Worse than found: a Move did not remount at all.** Entries are keyed by position
        (`U-12`), so Move and Remove keep each box mounted and hand it another entry's value; the
        text, set only on mount, stayed where it was. After a Move the boxes showed the entries in
        the old order while the form held and would save the new one; after removing Row 1, Row 1
        still showed the removed entry. The tests written first failed that way on `e7a02393`.
      - **The fix.** `JsonBox` remembers the value its text stands for — what it was built from, or
        what the text last parsed to — and when the value it is given is a different one (same
        reference or same JSON is the same), it rebuilds the text in the same render (React's
        adjust-state-while-rendering pattern) and drops "not valid JSON". What is typed, valid in
        the operator's own spelling or unparseable, is kept through any render that leaves the
        value alone, as before.
      - **Decided: `''` in an entry is a cleared box, shown empty; anywhere else it is the string,
        shown `""`.** An entry's clear writes `''` (`U-41`), and typing `""` into a JSON entry
        stores the same `''`, so an entry cannot hold the JSON string apart from a clear; `U-44`
        already judges it as emptied (*cannot be empty*), and showing it empty shows it as the form
        treats it. Outside an entry a clear removes the value, so `''` there is only ever the
        string. `jsonTextOf(value, entry)` says this, from `FieldModel.entry`, which `SchemaControl`
        now passes down; `SettingsPanel`'s fields are never entries.
      - **Tests.** `repeating-field.test.tsx`, 6 rendered: a cleared entry moved up shows an empty
        box, the other box shows the entry now beside it, and leaving it says *cannot be empty* and
        is `aria-invalid`; a form mounted afresh on the stored `['…', '']` shows the box empty and
        says the same on leaving; Row 1 after a Remove above shows the entry now there; unparseable
        text and a valid `{"b":3}` survive a render of the other entry unchanged; `""` typed into an
        entry stays as typed and is judged emptied; a non-entry JSON field holding `''` shows `""`,
        and clearing it removes the key. Mutations, each failing: no resync 2; `''` in an entry
        serialised 2; the typed value not remembered 2; `''` shown empty outside an entry too 1.
      - **Review: entries keyed by identity, and an emptied entry keeps its whitespace.** Comparing
        values alone could not tell a box it had been handed a JSON-equal neighbour's place: Add,
        Add, half-typed JSON in Row 1, Remove Row 1 left that text and "not valid JSON" on the
        untouched `{}`. `ArrayField` now keeps a key per entry and moves it with the entry on Move
        and Remove (grown or shrunk to fit a change from outside); an entry's own fields are keyed by
        name, not by a path carrying the position. So each control lives with its entry, half-typed
        text included. Focus follows: after a Move, the moved entry's same button, or its first
        enabled one where that is disabled; after a Remove, the entry now in its place, or the last,
        or Add — and only when focus was in that list. Separately, an emptied entry's box stood for
        `undefined` while the form held `''`, so the resync rebuilt its text on every keystroke and
        ate each space or Enter typed into it; it now stands for `''`. Tests, in
        `repeating-field.test.tsx`: whitespace kept in an emptied entry; Remove above a half-typed
        `{}`; a Move past an equal neighbour carries the text, warning and textarea node; an object
        entry's field and an object inside an entry keep their nodes; a 7-row focus table and focus
        left alone from outside. Mutations, each failing: standing for `undefined` 1; keyed by
        position 3; an entry's fields keyed by path 1; an object's inside an entry 1; focus not
        followed 5; no fallback for a disabled button 2.
      - **Not done.** `touched` is keyed by path, so a problem shown on an entry stays with the
        position through a Move: the moved cleared entry says nothing until it is left again, though
        its control now moves with it. A JSON entry whose schema takes the string `""` (an untyped
        `items`) cannot be saved holding it; no shipped type has one.

- [x] **U-49 — a problem stays with the position, not the entry, after a Move** · XS · U-47 ·
      Found 2026-10-09 in `U-47`. Entries now keep stable keys, but `SchemaForm`'s `touched` set is
      keyed by path, so a moved cleared entry says nothing until it is left again. **Done when**
      touched paths move with their entry on Move and Remove, with a test.

      **U-49 outcome. `ArrayField` says how it rearranged, and `touched` is remapped by path.**
      - **Remapped, not re-keyed.** `touched` stays keyed by path, the key every check, every
        server problem and `writeAt` already use. Keying it by the stable entry keys would have
        meant a second, position-free identity for every control, threaded through `Field`,
        `Entry` and nested arrays, beside the path each of them must still carry; the array that
        rearranges already knows exactly how, in one place. So Move and Remove call
        `moveTouched(field.path, order)`, where `order[j]` is the position the entry now at `j`
        held, and `movedPaths` (`schema.ts`) rewrites `arr.i…` to `arr.j…`, drops a removed
        entry's paths, and leaves everything outside the array alone. A nested array's paths come
        along with their outer entry (`steps.0.headers.1` → `steps.1.headers.1`); a name that
        only starts the same (`rowsOld`) is not the array.

        its new place, still `aria-invalid` and described by it; the untouched entry now in its old
        place says nothing. A removed entry's "left" no longer passes to the entry that takes its
        place, so an emptied entry never left stays quiet until it is; one below a Remove keeps its
        message one place up. Add needs nothing: a Remove drops the removed entry's paths, so the
        index Add reuses is clean.

        node) keeps its message and back again, its old place says none; Remove of a touched entry
        above an emptied, never-left one; a touched entry below a Remove; a header emptied in Step
        1's own list moves with Step 1. `schema-form.test.ts`: a 12-row `movedPaths` table, each
        also checking the input set is not changed. Mutations, each failing: Move not remapping 2;
        Remove not remapping 2; a removed entry's paths kept 4; only a path naming the entry
        itself moved, not one into it 4.
      - **Not done.** Server problems are keyed by path too and stay with the position through a
        Move or a Remove: a 400 naming `steps.1.path` stays on Step 2 after Step 2 moves up, until
        the next save clears it. `replacing` is keyed by path as well, but cannot meet an entry:
        the catalogue refuses a `writeOnly` under `items`.

        the series, `SeriesLegend` lost its `retired` prop: an array that has to be kept aligned
        is one a hidden series can misalign, so there is no such array any more.
