        box says the same thing on both tabs, a link opens both the same way, and the parameter
        already survives a change of tab (`U-38`). A separate parameter would allow "hidden in
        the table, shown in the charts", which is defensible (history is where a retired
        channel's data still means something) but is a second meaning for the same words on the
        same page; the box is on the History tab, so a reader who wants them there unticks it.
        The control (`detail/HideRetired.tsx`, now shared with the channel table) sits in the
        filter row, only where a charted channel is retired, with the same live region. Hidden
        **after** `groupByUnit`, so every remaining channel keeps its colour slot; a panel left
        empty goes, the table view drops the column, and a sensor whose every channel is retired
        and hidden says so.
      - **The list re-read.** The page learns of readings only from the 15 s `/values` poll (the
        state stream carries states, not channels), and `/values` carries the list's own
        `retired` (`U-38`). So `channelListIsStale` (`detail/model.ts`) compares the two: a
        channel the list holds retired that `/values` answers `false` (a reading after the
        edit) re-reads the list. Also the other way round (retired since the page opened, by an
        edit elsewhere), which is the same staleness and was one line. Compared on `retired`, not
        on whether a reading is present: a reading taken before the edit is shown but leaves the
        channel retired, so a re-read for it would answer the same. An agreeing poll asks for
        nothing. **Bounded** to one re-read per `RELIST_MIN_MS` (60 s, `performance.now()`), so
        a flapping channel, or two answers that keep disagreeing, cannot turn each poll (or each
        return to a hidden tab, which polls at once) into a second request. While the list is
        read again the page keeps the last one it read for that object, so the table and its box

        is open is noticed when the Overview tab polls again; its history is read once per range

      - **Amended on review** (a second commit). **The held list could be another sensor's.**
        The `objects/:id` route has no key, so sensor 9 to sensor 12 keeps the view mounted, and
        on the first render after the id changes `useApi` still holds sensor 9's answer (its
        effect has not run). The held list was filed under the page's id, so it recorded sensor
        9's channels as sensor 12's: they stood under sensor 12's header (with sensor 9's hide
        box, and as the History tab's retired set) until sensor 12's list arrived, and for good if

        text node whose string did not change alone, and a live region that does not change says

        shown while the next is typed and asked about; only its answer replaces it.

      is left, never over an entry the operator has gone to, and the id's colour is left as it

      - **`useAddressLater`** (`tree/address-later.ts`): `later` (the boxes), `now` (the
        checkbox, one press being one change) and `flush` (both boxes' `onBlur`). Still `replace`,
        so still one history entry for the tree. Mouse and Tab leave the box before a link is
        pressed, so what was typed is in the address before a result is followed.
      - **What waits never lands on another entry.** A `replace` goes to the current entry, and
        the router resolves `?…` against the tree's path, so a write that waited through a
        navigation would have put the tree back over the page gone to. A write is sent only while
        the history's current entry, by `key`, is the one the page last showed or last wrote. The
        history is read through the router's navigator (`UNSAFE_NavigationContext`; `BrowserRouter`
        and `MemoryRouter` both hand it their history, which has `location`), because it has moved
        before the page draws the move. A navigation the page did not make, once drawn, drops what
        was waiting.

        (signing out) writes what was typed; taken away by one writes nothing. A navigator without
        `location` is written to as before and never on unmount.

        `REPLACE` is skipped, so a late own write is never read back. With the pause it matters
        more, not less: a write goes out while the operator may already be typing again.
      - **The lag, tested without a browser.** No real-browser runner exists in the repository (no
        Playwright or WebdriverIO configuration or dependency; vitest runs jsdom only). The lag is
        made in jsdom instead: the write's timer is run outside `act`, so the router's transition

      Suspects: `U-68`'s owed focus in `keep-focus.ts` (a microtask that clears it) racing
      `Delete`'s `focusNext` effect, or a test that reads `document.activeElement` before the
      effect has run. **Done when** the cause is found and fixed in the code or the test, and the
      file passes 50 runs in a row.

      **U-81 outcome. A real race in `Delete`, not only in the test: its focus effect is a layout
      effect now, so focus reaches *Keep it* however soon after the page drew *Delete* it is
      pressed.** Web only.
      - **The cause.** `Delete` keeps where focus goes next in a ref, set by a click handler for
        the render that click causes, and read by a passive effect. On a busy machine the passive
        effects of the commit that drew *Delete* were still waiting when the test pressed it.
        React runs those before it renders the click's update, so that stale run read `'keep'`,
        cleared it and found no *Keep it* yet; the run that followed the click found nothing to do,
        and focus stayed on the page. A light focus trace under load showed it: focus on *Delete*,
        the press, then `body`, and no focus event on *Keep it* at all. It was not `U-68`'s
        `keep-focus.ts`, which only moves focus out of a panel that held it. A fast click on a
        slow machine could meet it in a browser too.
      - **The fix** (`TemplatesView.tsx`): the effect is a `useLayoutEffect`, which runs inside its
        own commit, so none is left waiting to take the next click's intent. No other focus effect
        in the web reads a one-shot intent from a ref; the others take theirs from state, which
        belongs to a render.
      - **Test** (`templates-refused.test.tsx`), deterministic: rendered without `act`, *Delete*
        is pressed with a native click from a MutationObserver callback, the microtask right after
        the commit that drew it and before its passive effects; it asserts *Keep it* was not drawn
        yet when pressed and then has focus. **Mutation**: the effect back to `useEffect` fails it
        5 runs in 5 with the flake's own error (`expected <body> to be <button>`); the fix passes 5
        in 5. Restored byte for byte.
      - **The bar.** The whole file 52 runs in a row with four copies running at once — the load
        that reproduced it once in 48 before the fix — all passed. Full web suite 1,106 passed.

- [x] **A-42 — `http.transaction` puts a credential wherever a step's text says** · M · T-13,
      S-19, A-40 · Found 2026-09-29 by `A-40`'s inventory. `{{credential.password}}` and its
      siblings are substituted into any text a step sends: the path, every header and the body.
      The sensor's writer chooses that text, and need not be able to read the device's `http`
      credential. So they can put the credential into a query string or a custom header, where a
      server logs it or sends it back. `S-19` scrubs exact values out of the sensor's messages,
      and a re-encoded copy is not an exact value.

      Decided (WatchDog, 2026-09-29): `{{credential.*}}` is accepted in the `Authorization` header
      and the body only, and refused anywhere else when the sensor is written. An echo in a
      response is scrubbed through `S-19`'s scrub point before any message or capture carries it.

      **Done when** a sensor whose path or other header names a credential is refused, with the
      step and the field in the message, and a test shows an echoed credential absent from what
      the sensor reports.

      **A-42 outcome.**
      - **Refused when written, by a new optional member of the contract.**
        - `SensorType.paramProblems(params)` returns what the schema cannot say, as JSON
          Pointer and sentence. `SensorCatalogue.validate` asks it once the schema passes, so
          every write refuses alike: create, edit, clone, device template, discovery. It
          reaches the API as `OBJECT_INVALID` with the usual `problems`.
        - `http.transaction`'s `misplacedCredentials` finds `{{credential.*}}`, spacing
          tolerated, in a step's path or in any header not named `Authorization` (any case,
          trimmed). The message reads, for example: "step 2 (call the api) puts
          {{credential.token}} in its X-Api-Key header, and a credential may go only in the
          Authorization header or the body — a server or a proxy logs the rest, and may send it
          back", at `/steps/1/headers/1/value`.
        - A capture cannot be named `credential.*`; its schema already refuses the dot.
      - **Stored sensors refuse to run, and are not repaired.**
        - One saved before the rule stays readable and renamable, and a write of its steps is
          refused.
        - On the probe, `execute` refuses before any step is sent, not even the steps before
          the misplaced one. It goes Down with the same sentence, plus "This sensor was saved
          before that was refused: edit it to move the credential, and it runs again".
        - This is `S-19`'s `MS_VAR_` precedent. `administration.md` says it under "On
          upgrade".
      - **An echo is scrubbed as it arrives**, through `S-19`'s scrub point (`scrubberOf(context)`),
        before the content checks and the captures read the response.
        - That closes the capture route: the credential sent in `Authorization` or the body,
          echoed back, captured, and put in a later step's path. The capture now carries the
          marker. A marker in a path or header makes that step fail, because Node refuses the
          characters, so the step fails rather than sending anything.
        - It also closes a quieter oracle, found while doing this. `mustContain` over an echo is
          a yes-or-no question answered by the sensor's state, so a writer could spell the
          password out one guess at a time.
        - Messages carry an echo only through a reported redirect target or a transport error,
          and the catalogue scrubs both.
      - **`S-19` now catches re-encoded copies.** `secretsOfCheck` adds each secret's
        `encodedForms`:
        - percent-encoded, in upper- and lower-case hex, and form-encoded with `+`;
        - base64 padded, unpadded and URL-safe;
        - HTML-escaped and JSON-escaped.
        An `http` credential adds basic authentication's base64 `username:password`, the one
        secret the check itself encodes before sending. It applies to every type, not only this
        one. Values under four characters still get no forms at all.
      - **Not caught, and pinned by a test as not caught:**
        - hex;
        - a secret encoded twice;
        - base64 of a secret shifted inside a longer string;
        - a part of the secret;
        - a numeric HTML entity.
        Nor are these, untested:
        - a split, re-cased, reversed or hashed copy;
        - base64 of a longer string that contains the secret, other than basic authentication's
          pair.
        Response headers are not scrubbed except where a message reports one, since captures
        read only the body.
      - **What the rule costs.**
        - An API that takes its key in a custom header cannot be given the device's stored
          credential. The key has to be typed into the header, where anyone who can read the
          sensor reads it.
        - `{{credential.username}}` is refused in a path too, by the rule's letter.
        - Both are said in `administration.md`.
      - **Docs:**
        - `adding-a-sensor-type.md` gains `paramProblems`, and "scrub what a server sends back
          before your type reads it";
        - the S-19 paragraphs in it and in `administration.md` now state the forms and the
          limits;
        - the step schema's path and header descriptions say it.
      - **Tests:**
        - `http-transaction.test.ts`:
          - refusal at validate, with the pointers and messages;
          - `Authorization` in any case, and the body, allowed;
          - the login flow still valid, and a capture named `credential.password` refused;
          - a stored path and a stored custom header refused at run, with nothing sent;
          - captures of a raw, percent-encoded, base64 and basic-pair echo carry only the marker;
          - `mustContain` guesses fail;
          - a redirect echo is absent from the message.
        - `secrets.test.ts` covers every form caught, the basic pair, the named misses, and no
          forms under four characters.
        - Core `sensor-types.test.ts`:
          - a create refused through `ObjectService`, with the pointer and message;
          - a stored row that stays readable and renamable but is refused on a steps write.
        - Passing: 133 in the sensors and hygiene suites, 101 in the other suites that assert the
          marker, and 77 in the core sensor-type and device-template suites.
      - **Mutations 11/11.** Each was applied alone and run against the sensors and core tests
        above. Killed:
        - the catalogue not asking `paramProblems`;
        - `Authorization` misspelt, so it is no longer exempt;
        - the path not checked;
        - a stored row run anyway;
        - the response not scrubbed;
        - base64 dropped;
        - percent-encoding dropped;
        - the basic pair not added;
        - forms made for a value too short to scrub;
        - `{{ credential.x }}` with spaces not recognised;
        - the step index used as the header index in the pointer.

- [x] **A-43 — A mistyped credential key is stored in plaintext and returned** · S · A-05 ·
      Security. Found 2026-09-29 by `D-12`'s sweep of open request schemas, and split out by
      WatchDog to go first. `PUT /objects/:id/credentials/:kind` takes `values` as any object.
      `vault.write` → `splitCredential` sorts each key only by whether the kind's schema marks it
      `writeOnly`, and never applies that schema, although every kind is
      `additionalProperties: false`. So a secret under a mistyped name (`{"comunity": "…"}` on
      SNMP, `{"pasword": …}` on SSH) was stored in `public_params` in the clear, returned by
      `GET /objects/:id/credentials` to anybody who could read the object, and recorded in the
      `credential.set` audit entry's public fields. A value of the wrong type was stored too, and
      failed on the probe.

      **Done when:**
      - a write is checked against its kind before the split: an undeclared key or a wrong type
        is a 400 naming the field, `null` is still the unset, a secret the write leaves out is
        still kept, and `required` binds only on a set's first write;
      - a read returns only the keys the kind declares public, whatever is stored;
      - the sets already holding an undeclared key are counted at start-up, logged once each by
        kind and owner (never a key or a value) and counted on Core Health, and no migration
        guesses which keys were secrets;
      - the `credential.set` audit entry records only declared public keys;
      - `administration.md` says that audit entries already written may hold such a value and
        that nothing rewrites them;
      - tests: the typo refused, with nothing stored and nothing audited; a row holding an
        undeclared key neither returned nor sent to a probe, and counted.

      **A-43 outcome.**
      - **Checked before the split.** `writeSchema(definition, existing)` in
        `sensors/credentials` is the kind's own schema with a secret's type widened to take
        `null`, and with secrets dropped from `required` on a set that exists. No kind declares
        `required` today, so that rule has nothing to bind yet. The vault compiles both forms of
        each kind at construction, without defaults, so a write stores what it was sent. It reads
        the existing row first and refuses before anything is split, stored or audited. The
        refusal is `CREDENTIAL_INVALID`, a 400 like every `VaultError`. For an undeclared key it
        names the key and lists the kind's fields, since a typo is the likely cause. It never
        repeats a value.
      - **One filter for every read.** `declaredPublic` is applied in the inheritance resolver,
        which both reads go through: the API's `resolveCredentials` and the probe's
        `resolveSealedCredentials`. An undeclared key stays in the row until the set is
        re-entered, and nothing returns it. A kind this build does not know declares nothing.
      - **The audit entry** is built from the declared public keys, although the check already
        guarantees that. A key that reached the log could never be taken back.
      - **Counted, not migrated.** `CredentialVault.setsWithUndeclaredKeys` finds the sets in one
        query (`jsonb_object_keys` against each kind's declared list). At start-up
        `warnOfUndeclaredKeys` logs each set by kind, object id and number of keys. Core Health's
        new `credentialsToReenter` channel counts them at every reading, so it falls as sets are
        re-entered, and any value is a warning. It is a gap when the database cannot be read,
        as the other queue channels are.

      Tests. `credential-vault` refuses `{"comunity": …}` with a 400 whose answer does not echo
      the value, stores no row, and records no `credential.set` entry, with the value nowhere in
      the audit. It also refuses a number for `community` and `v4` for `version`, each naming the
      field; still unsets a secret with `null` and keeps one left out; and plants a row as a write
      before `A-43` could leave it. That row's key is returned neither by `resolveCredentials`
      nor to the probe, which still gets the real community. It is counted and warned of once,
      and re-entering the set clears it. `core-health` reads the count through, and reads a gap
      when the database fails.

      Mutation 6/6:
      - the write not checked (the typo test and the type test);
      - the API's read or the probe's read unfiltered (the stored-row test, one mutant each);
      - the count taking declared keys instead of undeclared ones (the stored-row test);
      - Core Health dropping the count (its count test and its gap test);
      - `null` no longer taking a secret away (three tests).
      The audit summary's own filter is belt and braces behind the check, and no test can tell
      it apart while the check stands.

        routes pass `clears(request, 'admin')`, and the default refuses. A non-admin may keep or
        remove a `user` or `userGroup` row the stored template has, and gets 403
        `AUTH_FORBIDDEN` for any other one. A row is its kind and its value, so user 7 is not
        group 7. An id that is nothing is refused the same way, or the refusal would be the
        oracle.

        list, on a failure as well as a success, and email's error is plain `nobody to send to`.

        - the test-send report names them for an administrator, and says
          `not sent to 2 recipients (1 disabled, 1 no email address)` to anybody else. The request
          field is `namesAccounts`, absent is false;
        - the log keeps names in `skipped_recipients` and counts in the new `skipped_counts`. The
          dispatcher writes both, on a failure too. `NotificationLogQuery.namesAccounts` is
          required, so a new reader of the log decides;
        - the journal keeps the names: whoever reads it runs the service.

        counts. It cannot restore names past the column's 2,000 characters. The error had no
        limit, the column has, so up keeps the first 2,000 and down returns those. The migration

      - **One scrub, in `@ms/shared`.** `scrubSecrets`, `SCRUBBED` and `MIN_SCRUBBED_LENGTH`

        - the log, named for the administrator and counted for a writer and a reader.
      - `migrator.test.ts` 065: a round trip over a failure with names (restored whole), one past
        2,000 characters (restored as clipped), a partial send, another failure and a nameless
        one. A group name with brackets in it, or with a reason in brackets inside it, does not
        miscount.
      - `email-delivery.test.ts`: the transport's plain error and structured `skipped`; the
        dispatcher's counts on a send and on a failure.
      - `test-send.test.ts`: the default counts; a program's refusal comes back scrubbed.
      - `program-delivery.test.ts`: the error and the journal scrubbed of the substituted secret;

      - `scrub.test.ts` in `@ms/shared`, and `secrets.test.ts` checks that `@ms/sensors` hands
        out the shared functions. `exe-script` and `windows-transport` pass unchanged.

      Mutation 26/26, every one caught:
      - the server rule: refusing nobody, every route caller an administrator, an edit keeping
        nothing, a row as its value alone, update comparing with nothing, create unchecked;
      - who is told: the test send and the log naming to everyone (M8 is the second finding as
        it was), the tester naming by default, the log always naming, email's error naming again;
      - the dispatcher: a failure keeping no names or no counts, a send keeping no counts;

      - 065: up leaving the names in the error, moving a nameless error, dropping a character;

- [x] **A-45 — `A-29`'s vouching: auth off still records account vouchers, a sight is cached
      under the wrong epoch, and a failed settle never retries** · M · A-29 · Found in review
      round four (`findings/2026-09-29-review-round-4.md`, `A-45`).
      - **Medium** (`authorization.ts:372`). With `requireAuthentication` off, `writerFor` treats
        only a missing principal as "the layer is off". A logged-in account's write therefore
        records an *account* voucher. When that account is disabled or deleted, or lacks read on
        what the sensor names, the sweep withholds the sensor, Core Health included. Migration
        059's backfill does the same from audit rows.
      - **Low** (`vouching.ts:335`). Concurrent sweeps can cache a pre-revoke sight under the
        post-revoke epoch, so a revoked voucher keeps publishing until the next epoch bump.
      - **Low** (`vouching.ts:281`). A settle that throws has already updated the withheld map,
        so the next sweep sees no change and never retries. A withheld sensor keeps its old
        state, Up, or Down with its alarm running.
      - **Not checked:** other places that read `principal === undefined` as "authentication is
        off".

      **Done when:**
      - a layer-off write vouches as the installation, and its audit still names the account;
      - the rows 059 backfilled as `account` on an auth-off install are re-vouched as the
        installation at startup, or the upgrade note tells the operator to do it, with the
        entry saying which and why;
      - a sight is cached only under its own epoch;
      - settle restores the maps on failure, and the next sweep retries;
      - the `principal === undefined` sweep is listed in the outcome, each site fixed or argued.
      Tests per the findings doc. Mutants as usual.

      **A-45 part 1 outcome.** Everything but the settle rollback, which waited for `A-41a`'s
      change to `settle`'s contract and is built on it (part 2).
      - **Layer off, the installation vouches.** `writerFor` asks whether the layer is off, not
        whether there is a principal: the everyone sight, or no sight at all, the test `clears`
        already made, now one function `layerOff`. A logged-in account's write vouches as the
        installation, and the audit still names the account. `A-41a`'s layer-off branch, which
        made only the credential voucher the installation's, is subsumed: `credentialVoucherOf`
        falls back to the voucher, which is now the installation's too.
      - **059's rows: neither re-vouched at startup nor left to an upgrade note.** `SensorVouching`
        takes `requireAuthentication`. With it off, `refusals` holds no account's voucher against
        a sensor and asks nothing. Nobody's grants apply to any reader then, so withholding
        protected nobody. This covers 059's backfill on such an installation, and any voucher an
        account wrote before this fix.
        - A startup rewrite would drop every account's voucher for good the first time an
          operator switched the layer off, for instance to recover a locked-out administrator. A
          revoked account's factory would then go on publishing once the layer was back on.
        - Left in place, each is held to its account again when the layer is switched on. That
          fails closed: a sensor withheld then says so, and says how to vouch for it.
        - `administration.md` says both.
      - **A sight is cached only under its own epoch.** `#readableFor` stores a resolved sight
        only when its `Visibility.epoch` is the one the caches hold. One from another epoch
        answers the call that asked and is not kept. The per-id answers need no guard: an epoch
        change empties the map they go into, so a late one lands where nothing reads it again.
      - **The `principal === undefined` sweep**, every read of `request.principal` in
        `packages/core/src`:
        - `writerFor`: the defect, fixed.
        - `clears`: already asked the layer. It now shares `layerOff`.
        - `partitionByRight` (bulk): asks `authorizing` first, so a logged-in caller with the
          layer off passes (`R10`'s fix).
        - `actorFor`: audit attribution, which should name whoever logged in, layer or not.
        - `requireRole`, and the self routes in `auth.ts`, `tokens.ts` and `access.ts`: refuse
          without a principal. That is the answer for "my account" and for the administrator
          routes, layer or not.
        - The rate limiter's key and the CSRF guard's token exemption: whoever is calling, not a
          question about the layer.
        - `viewerOf` in the maps, reports and libraries routes, and the map background route:
          argued, not changed. They refuse an anonymous caller and filter to the caller's own
          account, even with the layer off. That fails closed: an account sees what its grants
          allow rather than everything. All three are v2 features whose ownership is per
          account, and "everything, when the layer is off" there is a product decision for them,
          not a leak.
        - Stream log lines: logging only.

      **Tests (part 1).**
      - `access-matrix.test.ts` 1: a server with the layer off; a logged-in `readwrite` account
        creates a factory, which is vouched for by the installation with the account in the
        audit.
      - `sensor-vouching.test.ts` 2:
        - the layer off withholds nothing and asks nothing, for a revoked read, a deleted
          account and Core Health short of root; the control with the layer on refuses all three;
        - the race: a sweep waiting on a sight while a grant is revoked and another sweep reads
          the new epoch. The next sweep refuses; the waiting sweep's own answer is the control.

      Mutation 3/3: `writerFor` without the layer test, `refusals` without it, and the sight
      cached at any epoch. The `main.ts` line that passes `requireAuthentication` is covered by
      no unit test.

      **A-45 part 2 outcome: the settle rollback**, on `A-41a`'s per-owner contract.
      - **What happens.** A failed re-decision puts the owner's answer back: the entry it had, or
        none if it had none. It then recounts the live fact for each sensor that crossed.
      - **Why that retries.** The next settle sees the same crossings and makes the same write,
        both ways: a withheld sensor is re-decided to Unknown, and a released one back to its
        reading.
      - **Why recount rather than copy back.** Another owner that settled while this write was
        out keeps what it did, where copying the old values back would undo it. No test races
        two owners against a failed write.

      **Tests (part 2).** `sensor-vouching.test.ts` 1: a real factory, Up, and a reevaluator
      whose first write each way fails. The withholding and the release each leave the stored
      state behind (the control), and the next settle writes it. There are four calls in all,
      and nothing is withheld at the end.

      Mutation 2/2: the owner's answer not put back, and the live fact not recounted.

- [x] **A-46 — three places still show or count what the reader cannot see** · S · A-26, A-31,
      A-35 · Found in review round four (`findings/2026-09-29-review-round-4.md`, `A-46`). All
      low.
      - **Reorder** (`objects/service.ts:1951`) rewrites hidden siblings' rows, bumping their
        version, and records indices that count them.
      - **Object history** (`routes/audit.ts:138`) shows probe-trust entries (address, GID,
        allow-from, note) to anyone with read on the probe object. `GET /probes` is ADMIN.
      - **History counts** (`objects/service.ts:590`): `sensorsAffected` and `movedCount` include
        sensors hidden from the reader.
      - **Not checked:** settings edits on a container, and bulk operations other than pause,
        acknowledge and force.

      **Done when:**
      - reorder moves among visible siblings only and leaves hidden rows untouched, or the
        materialising write is shown not to bump versions;
      - probe-trust entries are an administrator's, as grants are;
      - history counts are dropped or flagged for a reader with holes under the object;
      - the unchecked writes are checked, with the outcome listing them.
      Tests in `object-visibility.test.ts`. Mutants as usual.

      **A-46 outcome (2026-09-29).** Migration 066.
      - **Reorder moves among the siblings its caller can see.** The route passes the caller's
        visibility, and `reorderAmong` reorders the visible siblings as before and puts them back
        into the places they held. Every hidden sibling keeps its index. "Up" passes the nearest
        visible sibling, and "up" and "first" stop at the top the caller can see, so a no-op there
        reads the same whether or not something hidden sits above.
        - **A hidden row is written only where it does not hold its place yet.** That happens on
          a parent nobody arranged, or one arranged in part: a NULL sorts after every place, so
          leaving the row alone would slide it to the end. The index written is the position the
          NULL ordering already gave it. The write runs under `ms.sibling_order_only`, set with
          `set_config(…, true)` and cleared straight after that one statement. Migration 066's
          `object_touch` skips the version and `updated_at` bump only while that is set and
          `sort_order` is the only column that differs. Its rollback restores 002's body, byte for
          byte.
        - **The entry still records positions among every sibling**, so an administrator's
          history is exact. The history route empties the diff for a reader with a hidden child
          of the entry's parent, whoever moved it. Positions recorded over the mover's view would
          still count, for another reader, siblings that reader cannot see (an administrator's
          reorder read by a branch account), and entries from before this fix count them anyway.
          This departs from the finding's "positions among visible siblings". The mover with the
          hole reads no positions for its own move; the tree shows it where it went.
      - **Probe-trust entries are an administrator's**, as grants are:
        `withoutCategories: ['grant', 'probe']` for anyone who does not clear `admin`, role and
        scope both. The route description and `administration.md` say so.
      - **History counts are dropped for a reader with a hole beneath the object.** That means
        `sensorsAffected`, `movedCount` and `clonedCount`. `Visibility.hidesBeneath` climbs from
        the reader's hidden boundaries and never descends a subtree. The entries stay, and filling
        the hole in brings the counts back. One bit remains, whether the count is there, which says
        a hole sits beneath the object: the bit `A-35`'s refusals already give.
      - **Checked** (the ticket's "Not checked"):
        - A setting set or reverted on a container, singly or in bulk, writes only that
          container's `object_setting` row. `object_touch_owner` bumps only the container. The
          hole inherits the value, as `A-31` decided for pauses, and the entry carries no count.
          Tested.
        - A pause or resume, singly or in bulk, writes the `object_pause` row on the container
          only. `recompute` writes `sensor_runtime`, which bumps no version. The counts are the
          history fix above.
        - A schedule or dependency setting on a container: `ScheduleSync` and `DependencySync`
          write `sensor_runtime` only.
        - A bulk move or delete is partitioned by subtree (`A-35`), so a caller with a hole
          beneath is refused before anything is written. An administrator's `movedCount` is the
          history fix.
        - A bulk clone copies only what its caller sees (`A-35`). `clonedCount` is the history
          fix, for a reader with a hole under the copy: the copy carries its source's grants.
        - **A device's new host clears the secrets in every sensor beneath it (`A-41`), hidden
          ones included**, each with a version bump and an entry of its own. Left as it is:
          otherwise the hidden sensor's secret goes to a host its writer chose, and refusing
          would say the hole is there. The device's own answer and history name none of those
          sensors.
        - **Found, and fixed here:** the answers to `PATCH /objects/:id` and to a reorder carried
          `childCount` over every child, holes included. Both now count what the caller can see,
          as a read does (`A-12`).
      - **Tests:**
        - `sibling-order.test.ts`, 5:
          - three `reorderAmong` units: up, down, first and last among the shown; the stops at
            the shown ends; and the plain move for a caller shown everything;
          - the repository writes a place quietly, and a later write in the same transaction
            bumps, even of that row;
          - the setting spares a change of place and nothing else (a rename with it, a rename
            alone, no change at all), and only in the transaction that set it.
        - `migrator.test.ts`, 1: 066 forward, back, with `pg_get_functiondef` identical to before,
          and forward again.
        - `object-visibility.test.ts`, 5:
          - an unarranged parent: the order, the hidden row's place, version, time and tag, the
            moved row's bump, the answer's count, and positions for an administrator but not for
            the operator until the sibling is granted;
          - a parent arranged in part: up, first and last, a place already written not written
            again, and no-ops under a hidden top;
          - probe trust as watcher, operator, administrator and an administrator's read token;
          - counts two levels down: an acknowledgement, a drill, a pause, a move and a clone,
            dropped for the watcher, kept for a sensor with nothing beneath, and back once the
            hole is filled;
          - settings on a container, singly and in bulk, and a PATCH's `childCount`.
        - `access-rights.test.ts`: `hidesBeneath` and `hidesChildOf` agree with the resolver on
          every container, for every role and scope, on every fixed hole shape and a quarter of
          the random seeds.
      - **Mutation 20/20.** The walk, the boundaries and the condition of both `Visibility`
        questions; the three conditions of 066's trigger; the setting left off, and not cleared
        after; the service's visibility and its unseen set; positions among the visible only;
        reorder ignoring what its caller sees (written `seen === null || seen.size >= 0`, since

- [x] **A-47 — Host, throttle, proxy range and idle timeout: four gaps in `A-36` and `A-38`** · M
      · A-36, A-38 · Found in review round four (`findings/2026-09-29-review-round-4.md`,
      `A-47`).
      - **Medium, DNS rebinding** (`hardening.ts:215`). The Origin check compares Origin with the
        request's own Host. A rebinding page sends both as its own name and passes, on the
        stream and, with authentication off, on every write. `/metrics` and the other
        unauthenticated GETs have no Host check at all.
      - **Medium, login throttle** (`auth/throttle.ts:90`). The count is keyed on the exact
        address, and the per-account delay is a sleep that parallel attempts do not wait for.
        Rotating addresses inside one IPv6 /64 gives unbounded guessing, and behind a trusted
        proxy that is per browser.
      - **Low** (`config/schema.ts:1177`). `api.trustedProxies` refuses `uniquelocal` and
        `linklocal` but accepts `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0` and `10.0.0.0/8`.
      - **Low** (`auth/sessions.ts:272`). Lowering `sessions.idleTimeoutMinutes` does not reach
        sessions already extended under the old value.

      **Done when:**
      - an `onRequest` hook, first and whether authentication is on or off, refuses a Host
        outside the bound address, loopback, `notifications.publicUrl` and
        `api.allowedOrigins`, and the Origin check compares against that set;
      - the per-login delay is a gate checked before any argon2 work, and IPv6 counts by /64;
      - a proxy range wider than a floor is refused, with the floor stated;
      - `live()` applies the current idle timeout.
      Tests per the findings doc. Mutants as usual.

      **Outcome (2026-09-29).** Migration 062.
      - **Host.** `registerHostCheck` is the API listener's first `onRequest` hook, whether
        authentication is on or off. It answers every IP literal (a strict `isIP` on the name, so
        `127.0.0.1.evil.example` is a name), `localhost` and `*.localhost`, the host of
        `notifications.publicUrl`, the host of each `api.allowedOrigins` entry, and the new
        `api.allowedHosts`. Names are compared lower-cased without a trailing dot, and ports are
        not compared. Anything else gets **421** `HOST_NOT_ALLOWED`, whose body names the Host seen
        and `api.allowedHosts`. Each name is logged once, up to a hundred. The probe endpoint is
        TLS on its own port and is not touched: a test connects a probe by a name the API
        refuses. With neither `allowedHosts` nor `publicUrl` set, startup warns once, naming both.
        `ms-setup` writes `hostname -f` into `allowedHosts` on a fresh core install, unless it is
        an address or `localhost`. Core Health's new `hostsRefused` is the count since the last
        reading. An entry that is an address, or not a plain name, is refused at startup.
        **Deviation, agreed:** the Origin check (`refusalFor`) still compares host and port with
        `Host`, or an `allowedOrigins` entry. It does not take the whole answered set as
        origins, which would let any other port on an answered name write. Tested with auth off:
        `http://localhost:3000` against `localhost:8080`, and `http://10.9.9.9:3000` against
        `10.9.9.9:8080`, are both refused.
      - **Throttle.** `admit()` replaces check-then-sleep. It reads the counts and takes the
        login's one verification together. An attempt inside the login's delay since its last
        failure is refused 429 with `Retry-After` before argon2. A second attempt while one is
        being verified gets `Retry-After: 1`. So does an attempt whose counts were read before a
        failure it did not see, since a failure landing while an admission was deciding turns it
        away. The slot goes back once a failure is recorded and before its answer is waited out.
        The answer still sleeps exactly as long as the gate it closes, so a person who waits never
        meets the gate.
        **Targeted lockout.** An attacker failing as an operator every few seconds holds that
        login's gate shut. An `address_key` that signed in successfully as that login in the last
        30 days skips the delay, though not the one-in-flight rule. The attacker is not at the
        victim's desk, so the victim signs in from where they always do. What that costs: an
        attacker at such an address, such as a shared NAT, guesses without the delay but is held to
        that address's 20 failures in 15 minutes, which is the ceiling everybody had before and is
        far below the unlimited guessing the gate replaces. The victim signing in from somewhere
        new waits like anybody. Successes are kept for those 30 days. IPv6 counts as its /64
        (`addressKey`; `::ffff:a.b.c.d` is IPv4) in the throttle and the rate limit alike. Rows
        from before 062 keep a NULL key and are not counted.
      - **Proxy floor.** `trustedProxies` refuses any range wider than /16 for IPv4 or /48 for
        IPv6, naming the floor. `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0` and `10.0.0.0/8` are refused;
        `10.0.4.0/28`, `127.0.0.1` and `loopback` are accepted.
      - **Idle.** `live()` has `last_seen_at + idle > now`, bound in `resolve` and `lapsed`, so a
        lowered idle timeout reaches sessions extended under the old one.
      Docs: `administration.md` (the names the core answers to, with an upgrade note; wrong
      passwords; the proxy floor; lowered timeouts; `hostsRefused`), `installation.md`,
      `troubleshooting.md` (every page answers 421), the regenerated API and sensor references.
      Tests: `host-check` (new), `address-key` (new), `hardening`, `accounts`, `auth-api`,
      `core-health`, `migrator` (062 up and down), `probe-endpoint`, `deploy-scripts`,
      shared `config`.
      - **Found on the way.** Fastify types `request.ip` as a string, but it is `undefined` for a
        socket that has already closed, and under `injectWS`. The rate limiter used to build the
        key `ip:undefined` from it. `addressKey` threw on it and answered 500, so it now treats
        "no address" as `''`.
      - **Mutants: 47, 45 killed on the first pass.** Two survived, and each got a test:
        - Known addresses counting failures as well as successes. The victim test now asks
          about an address that has only failed as that login.
        - The route giving the slot back before the failure is recorded. A throttle whose
          failure recording is held shows the second attempt is turned away unverified.

        Two changes were left out as equivalent: `Math.max(1, …)` on a `Retry-After` that is
        already at least 1, and dropping the deciding map's cleanup, which changes memory and
        nothing else.
      - **Full suite:** core 3,689 tests, 3,688 passing. The failure was `candidate-surface`: its
        harness must pass `ApiServer` exactly what `main.ts` passes, and now passes `publicUrl`
        too. Re-run green with `fingerprint-check`, which uses the same harness. Shared 313,
        simulators 24, sensors 1,029 (10 skipped: the MySQL and SQL Server simulators were not
        running), probe 379, web 46 files, all passing.

        Test: a comment on the hidden probe answers the watcher's `?include=ancestors` 304, a

- [x] **A-50 — a debug log line carries a probe's decrypted credentials** · S · A-05 · Found in
      review round 4b (`findings/2026-09-29-review-round-4b.md`, `A-50`). Medium.
      `MessageConnection.send` (`shared/src/protocol/connection.ts:83`) logs the whole message at
      debug when the connection is closed. A config push racing a disconnect, with `logLevel:
      debug` set to diagnose that very flapping link, therefore writes every assignment's SNMP
      community, SSH key, database password and `writeOnly` parameter to the log. pino's redact
      paths stop at depth 3, and never reach `message.sensors[i].credentials`.

      **Done when** that line logs the message type only, and the config push returns after its
      await if the session closed. A test asserts that a log captured at debug, over a push that
      races a close, contains no credential value. The critic's sweep found no other payload
      log. Say in the outcome whether redact paths should be made depth-free as defence in
      depth. Mutants as usual.

      **A-50 outcome.** Both halves.
      - **`MessageConnection.send` logs a dropped message by its type alone.** `Outbound` is
        now constrained to messages with a `type`, so the line cannot be written from anything
        else. The comment beside it says why.
      - **The configuration push returns after reading the assignments if the connection has
        closed.** It sends nothing and updates nothing. The next session asks again.

      **Depth-free redact paths: no.** pino's redaction (fast-redact) has no recursive
      wildcard. The only depth-free alternative is a formatter that walks every object on every
      line for secret-looking keys, which puts a cost on each of the core's log lines to guard
      against a payload being logged at all. The rule that prevents that is cheaper and is now
      in the code: a connection logs a message's type, never the message. The critic's sweep
      found no other payload log, and neither did a grep for `{ message }` across `shared`,
      the core's transport and the probe's.

      **Tests.**
      - `shared/test/connection.test.ts` 1, new: through the real `createLogger` at debug, a
        push carrying an SNMP community, an SSH passphrase and three `writeOnly` parameters is
        dropped on a closed connection. The line says `config-set` and none of the secrets.
      - `probe-endpoint.test.ts` 1: the probe connects, its assignment read is held, and the
        probe closes during it. With a debug log captured, no credential appears, and no
        `config-set` or `config-delta` is even attempted.

      Mutation 2/2:
      - the whole message logged (the shared test fails; the endpoint test does not, because
        the push has already returned);
      - no return after the read (the endpoint test fails).

- [x] **A-53 — a probe's honest refusal that arrives after the configuration changed reads as a
      failed scan** · S · A-41c · Found 2026-10-02 by `A-41c`'s review fixes. `reported()` honours
      `withheld` only for a sensor the probe's last configuration left to it. A refusal made just
      before a configuration stopped leaving it, and delivered after, is kept as a plain error:
      one Down where Unknown was true. **Done when** a refusal is judged against the
      configuration it was made under (a configuration generation on the result, or a short
      grace), with a scenario test that the race raises no Down.

      **Outcome.** For ten minutes after a configuration stops leaving a sensor to its probe, a
      refusal from that probe for that sensor is dropped and counted: no failed scan, no hold.
      - **No wire field, and protocol 25 is not used.** A result carries no configuration
        version, and adding one would have decided nothing: a probe that follows its
        configuration refuses only what that configuration left to it, so a refusal for a
        sensor it is no longer left was made under an earlier one, and a probe that does not
        follow it would write whatever version it liked. What the core needs is which sensors
        it stopped leaving and when, which it knows itself.
      - **The mechanism.** `CredentialVouching.withhold` records, per probe, each sensor the new
        configuration stops leaving and the time, on a monotonic clock. The time is the first
        such configuration's; a later one does not move it. `reported` drops a result that is
        marked, an error, and without readings, for such a sensor inside
        `LATE_REFUSAL_GRACE_MS` (600,000 ms, inclusive). The entry goes when the sensor is left
        again, at the first configuration after the grace, and with its probe (`reconcile`).
      - **Dropped, not held.** Held Unknown, a paused or core-withheld sensor would carry a hold
        no result will come to release. Whatever the configuration now says speaks for it. A
        dropped refusal measures nothing: it lets no hold go, this probe's or another's.
      - **Counted** as `late` on the batch, and by `IngestionService` with Probe Health's
        refused results, as a result for a sensor that moved away is.
      - **What a probe that misbehaves can do:** for ten minutes after a configuration stops
        leaving it a sensor, have its own error-with-no-readings results for that sensor
        discarded, each counted on its Probe Health. That is what not sending them does. **What
        it cannot do:** begin or prolong an Unknown with such a mark (`F5` stands: a hold is
        still only for a sensor its last configuration left to it); discard a result that is
        `ok` or has readings; use it on a sensor it was never left, or past the ten minutes,
        where the mark is unearned and the result is the failed scan it reads as; or reopen the
        window, which only a configuration change does.
      - **Not covered:** the record is in memory, so a refusal that crosses a core restart is
        judged as before. A spool replay that is still delivering refusals more than ten
        minutes after the reconnect's configuration reads them as failed scans.
      - **Alarm volume** (`credential-pinning.test.ts`): a sensor Up, a name entry added so the
        probe is left nothing, two refusals delivered after: still Up, no row in its state
        history, not held, no notification request, 2 on Probe Health's refused. Two real
        failed scans after that: Down once, one request. Past the grace, two marked results:
        Down, and counted.
      - **Tests:** 14 unit cases on the bound, where the window starts, what forgets it, what
        is and is not dropped, and that no hold moves; the scenario above. `state-machine.md`
        says the rule and the bound.
      - **Mutation:** 11 of 11 killed.

- [x] **A-54 — `A-09`'s link-local guard resolves, checks, and lets the socket resolve again** ·
      M · A-09, A-41c · Found 2026-10-02 by `A-41c`. For a request that is not pinned, the
      metadata-address guard looks the name up and checks it, and the connection then looks it up
      again: the rebinding gap `A-41c` closed for bounded sets is still open on this guard, and
      is older than that ticket. **Done when** the guard's check and the connection use one
      lookup (`pinnedLookup` already does this for a pinned target), on HTTP and mail, and a test
      with a resolver that answers differently the second time shows one lookup and a refusal.

      **A-54 outcome.** An HTTP request no credential set pins resolves its device's name once,
      checks every answer, and connects to an address that lookup answered with.
      - **Where the guard is.** One place: `fetchHttp` (`support/http/request.ts`), which every
        HTTP type goes through (`http.request`, `http.advanced`, `http.content`, `rest.custom`,
        and each step of `http.transaction`). **Mail has no such guard and never had**, so
        there was nothing there to close, and none was added: refusing a mail device on a
        link-local address is a change of policy, not this defect. The webhook client in
        `@ms/core` already pinned what it checked.
      - **`checkedTarget`** replaces `refuseBlockedTarget`. It resolves through the catalogue's
        resolver (`CheckTarget.resolve`, set where `pinTarget` is called), checks every answer
        that is an address, and hands the socket `pinnedLookup` for one of them. SNI, `Host`
        and the certificate check stay on the name. A target `A-41c` pinned is checked at that
        address and not resolved again.
      - **Lookups per request, before and after.**

        | Request | Before | After |
        | --- | --- | --- |
        | A name, no redirect | 2: the guard's, the socket's | 1 |
        | A name, n redirects followed | 2 + n | 1 |
        | `http.transaction`, s steps on a name | 2 per step, more with redirects | 1 per step |
        | An address | 1 call to `dns.lookup`, which answers an address with itself | 0 |
        | A name pinned by `A-41c` | 1, in `pinTarget` | 1, unchanged |
        | Any host under the `none` policy | 1, the socket's | 1, unchanged |

      - **Redirects and steps.** A redirect is followed only on the same host, scheme and port
        (`resolveRedirect`), so every hop goes to the address already checked and there is no
        second name to pin. A redirect to another name is reported and not followed, and that
        name is never resolved. A transaction's steps cannot name another host: each step is
        its own `fetchHttp`, resolved and checked on its own answer.
      - **A name that does not resolve fails in the guard**, in the words the request used for
        it. It used to be left to the socket, which is a second lookup. The lookup is bounded by
        `resolveBoundMs` and ends with the check's signal (`resolveWithin`, `pinTarget`'s own
        bound, now shared).
      - **No agent on any request.** `agent: false` for every one, where only a pinned request
        had it. `connection: close` was already sent.
      - **A name with several addresses** used to be walked by the socket. Now the request
        goes to the resolver's first, and to the next checked address when the connection is
        refused, has no route (`NOT_CONNECTED`), or is not made within `connectAttemptMs`: 250
        ms, Node's own `autoSelectFamilyAttemptTimeout`, which is what these requests had
        before, so a dual-stack name whose first address drops packets reads Up as it did. The
        addresses before the last share at most half the request's timeout, and time one
        spends is taken from the next, so all of them together stay inside the timeout. Only
        the connect is bounded; an address that accepted and is slow is not abandoned.
      - **The connect of the last address is bounded too**, by what is left of the timeout.
        `req.setTimeout` only counts once a socket is connected, so an address that never
        answered the SYN was left to the system's connect timeout or the runner. It now fails
        at the sensor's timeout saying the device did not answer.
      - **The policy reads the address, not its spelling** (`@ms/shared` `target-policy.ts`,
        for sensors and webhooks both). `unmapped` turns an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address into the
        IPv4 one in either spelling (`::ffff:169.254.169.254`, `::ffff:a9fe:a9fe`), and
        `refuses`, `isLinkLocal` and `isPrivate` all go through it; `isPrivate` knew the dotted
        spelling only and `isLinkLocal` neither. `isMetadataAddress` adds `fd00:ec2::254`, the
        one address the comment named that link-local does not contain, refused under
        `link-local` and compared as numbers. `fe80::/10` is read from the groups.
      - **Docs:** `administration.md` gains "HTTP sensors and the cloud metadata address"; the
        guard was not described there before. No schema or route changed.
      - **Tests:** 18 new in `pinned-transports.test.ts` and one rewritten: a resolver that
        answers 127.0.0.1 once and 169.254.169.254 after is asked once and the request arrives;
        one refused answer among several refuses the name; a redirect on the device and one to
        another name; a transaction whose second step's answer is refused; TLS with SNI, `Host`
        and a certificate for another name; the next address after a refused connection and
        never past the checked ones; a resolver that fails, answers nothing, hangs, or is
        cancelled; an address and the `none` policy; the shared agent. Then 8 more there: a
        first address whose connection is never made (a socket the test makes and leaves
        connecting) is passed in about 250 ms; three such share one timeout and no other
        address is tried; one alone has the whole timeout; a slow answer is not abandoned,
        over TLS either; the share with little time; and the mapped and `fd00:ec2::254`
        addresses as a host and as an answer. `target-policy.test.ts` in `@ms/shared`, 11, and
        2 in `webhook-delivery.test.ts` for the same addresses as an answer and in a URL.
      - **Mutation:** 36 mutants, 36 killed: 23 on the first commit and 13 on the second (6 on
        the policy, 7 on the connect bound). Three were killed by a test that then never ended
        and failed its file at the run's timeout (the retry that does not advance, the
        resolution timer that does not reject, the last address with no connect bound), the
        other 33 by an assertion.
      - **Not covered by a test:** the peer check on a guard-pinned socket and the sentence
        `describeFailure` gives it (`byGuard`): a socket handed the address cannot arrive
        anywhere else.
      - **Found, not fixed:** mail, SSH, SNMP and the port sensors have no metadata guard at
        all. Other ways to write an IPv4 address inside an IPv6 one (NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`,
        the deprecated `::a.b.c.d`) are not unwrapped; whether a probe's network routes them
        is the installation's. Metadata addresses of other providers that are not link-local
        are not on the list.
      - **Review** (four lenses, each claim put to two skeptics): no way past the guard was
        found. Three low findings were confirmed and closed in a third commit. The walk moved
        on after six listed codes where the socket's own walk moved on after any failed
        connect; it now moves on whenever the socket never connected (`NeverConnected`), with

- [x] **A-56 — the late-refusal record does not survive a core restart, and late refusals are
      counted with the rest** · S · A-53 · Found 2026-10-02 by `A-53`. The record of which
      sensors had a set narrowed, and when, is in memory: a core restarted inside the ten-minute
      grace forgets it, and a probe's honest late refusal then reads as a sensor failure again.
      A late refusal also counts into Probe Health's refused results beside the refusals that
      mean something is wrong, so the channel cannot tell the two apart. **Done when** either
      the record is rebuilt at start from what the database already holds or the runbook says
      the bound in words with a test of what a restart does, and a late refusal is counted
      where an operator can tell it from a standing one.

      **A-56 outcome.** The second way out for the restart, and a channel of its own for the
      count. No migration, no protocol number, nothing sent to or from a probe.
      - **The record is not rebuilt, because nothing stored says it.** Looked for: a timestamp
        that means "a configuration stopped leaving this sensor to its probe".
        `credential_set.updated_at` moves on any update of the row, a rotated secret included,
        and a removed set has no row. `object.updated_at` moves for anything written on the
        object or its settings, channels or credentials. Neither keeps what the targets or the
        host were before, and the history's `credential.set` entry keeps the public half after
        the write only. A pause, a move and the probe's protocol version stop leaving a sensor
        too, and what the probe was sent at the time is not stored anywhere. Rebuilt from those,
        the grace would go to every sensor near a recent change, the ones the probe was never
        left included, which `A-53` says a probe cannot have. So the bound is written down:
        `state-machine.md` (the rule, what a restart costs, why it is not stored),
        `troubleshooting.md` under "A sensor is Down and the device is fine" (the symptom and
        what to do), and the channel's row in `administration.md`.

        sensor Up, a name entry added, the configuration built, then a core with the same
        database and nothing in memory. One late refusal is one failed scan and no page; the
        second is Down in the probe's words, one Down row and one notification request; two
        more raise nothing; the next scan under the new configuration reads Up. They are
        counted as marks the probe had no claim to (`reportsRefused`), none as late.
      - **A late refusal is counted on its own Probe Health channel**: `lateRefusals`,
        "Refusals delivered late", a 64-bit counter with no limit and no lookup, so no state
        and no alarm, declared after `reportsForeign`. `ProbeRefusals.late` and `lateFor` keep
        it per probe and apart from `refused`; `IngestionService` counts `reported.late` there
        and no longer in `refused`. Absent the source, the channel gaps. An unearned mark is
        still counted in `reportsRefused`, which is now only that and what `P-228` refuses.
      - **Prometheus:** `ms_probe_late_refusals_total`. There was no series for
        `reportsRefused` to put it beside, so `ms_probe_reports_refused_total` is added with
        it. `sensor-reference.md` regenerated.
      - **Tests:** `probe-refusals` (8, one new), `probe-health` (three: the channel, the
        counter text, zero against a gap), `health-types` (the declaration and its place),

        wiring in `main.ts` (`lateRefusals` on Probe Health's sources) has no test of its own.

        `none`, in the probe's configuration file. The probe puts it in the environment its
        workers and check processes get (`MS_TARGET_POLICY`), the catalogue reads it once and
        hands it to every check as `CheckTarget.policy`, overwriting whatever the check arrived
        with. A value that is not one of the three is `link-local`. No protocol number and no
        migration: the core is not involved. A change needs a probe restart, which is also
        what closes every kept SSH connection.

        answer checked, a name that does not resolve failed there. `checkedLookup` answers a

      - **Every built-in type, and what it is held to** (44, from the catalogue):

        | Types | Held to the policy | How |
        | --- | --- | --- |
        | `http.request`, `http.advanced`, `http.content`, `http.transaction`, `rest.custom` | yes, as before | `fetchHttp`, now under the probe's setting |
        | `mail.smtp`, `mail.pop3`, `mail.imap`, `mail.roundtrip` | yes | `MailConnection.open`: the socket's lookup, per connection |
        | `ssh.load`, `ssh.meminfo`, `ssh.diskfree`, `ssh.script` | yes, when a connection is opened | the pool asks `SshTarget.guard` only to open one: a socket of the session's own (`ssh2`'s `sock`) with the lookup. A held connection is reused with no lookup, and the pool key is what it was |
        | `snmp.traffic`, `snmp.custom`, `snmp.custom.string`, `snmp.table`, `snmp.cpu`, `snmp.diskfree`, `snmp.memory`, `snmp.uptime` | yes | `snmpCheck` resolves and checks each scan; the pool, keyed as it was, keeps its session while its address is among the answers and replaces it only when it is not. IPv4 unless the device says IPv6, as before |
        | `port.tcp`, `port.range` | yes | the socket's lookup; a range resolves once for all its ports |
        | `tls.certificate`, `tls.security` | yes | the socket's lookup; one lookup for every handshake |
        | `db.postgresql`, `db.mysql`, `db.mssql` | an address only | the driver resolves a name itself and takes no lookup |
        | `windows.cpu`, `windows.memory`, `windows.service`, `windows.volume` | an address only | PowerShell resolves the name, and Kerberos wants it; the `host` parameter is checked too |
        | `icmp.ping`, `icmp.jitter` | no | see below |
        | `dns.record`, `dns.blocklist` | no | they ask a resolver, not the device; a cloud's own resolver is link-local |
        | `exe.script`, `exe.script.advanced` | no | the probe connects to nothing; the script is handed the host |
        | `snmp.trap`, `syslog.receiver`, `flow.netflow` | no | listeners: nothing is sent |
        | `ms.core.health`, `ms.probe.health`, `core.factory` | no | computed by the core |

        the largest sensor population on the probe's shared libuv thread pool, where
        `getaddrinfo` cannot be cancelled and abandoned lookups pile up uncounted during a
        resolver outage; and it lost `ping`'s own choice of address family.
      - **No transport makes an in-process lookup that made none before** (read from the
        parent, `ab55657`). Mail (`net.connect`/`tls.connect` by name), `port.tcp` and
        `port.range` (`net.connect`), and TLS (`tls.connect`) each had their socket call
        `dns.lookup` in the probe, on the same thread pool the guard's `dns.lookup` uses now, so
        the call moved and did not multiply. SNMP's `dgram` socket resolved the name for each
        datagram sent, and now there is one a scan. SSH's `ssh2` socket resolved it when a
        connection was opened, and still does only then. Only ping resolved outside the probe,
        which is why it is out.
      - **A target a credential set pinned (`A-41c`) connects exactly as it did**: one lookup,
        `pinTarget`'s, the pinned address, and `CredentialsWithheldError` with Unknown when the
        set is withheld. What is new is that the policy reads the pinned address on SNMP, SSH
        and mail as it already did on HTTP, so a set whose targets allow a link-local address
        does not make the probe connect to one; that refusal is an ordinary failed check.
      - **The refusal is an ordinary check error** (`TargetRefusedError`, no code a runner
        reads), so the sensor reads Down. Its message names the device, the address and the
        policy, and says `probe.targetPolicy` "none" refuses nothing. HTTP's sentence changed
        to the shared one.
      - **Alarm volume: a sensor on a link-local device that was Up reads Down after the
        upgrade**, ping sensors excepted. That is the intended change. One failed check a scan
        for each such sensor, by the ordinary path; no new state, no new notification.
        `probe.targetPolicy: none` on that probe, and a restart, is the way back.
        `administration.md` says so, with the cases to look for (APIPA devices, `fe80::`
        devices, a cloud's link-local DNS and time servers). **And a resolver outage raises no
        alarm it did not raise before**: SSH sensors on a kept connection ask the resolver
        nothing, and a test holds six of them Up through a resolver that fails and one that
        hangs.
      - **Lookups per scan, for a device given as a name.**

        | Transport | Before | After |
        | --- | --- | --- |
        | TCP port, TLS certificate, mail (per connection) | 1, the socket's | 1, the guard's |
        | `port.range`, n ports | n | 1 |
        | `tls.security` | 1 per version tried | 1 |
        | SNMP | 1 per datagram sent | 1 |
        | SSH | 1 when a connection is opened, 0 while it is kept | the same |
        | ping | 0 in the probe, 1 in `ping` | the same |
        | Any, device given as an address, or under `none` | as before | as before |

      - **Timeouts and readings are as before the ticket.** The lookup and the connect share
        the sensor's timeout on `port.tcp`, `port.range`, TLS and mail: what the lookup took is
        taken from the connect (on a range, from the first port each worker tries; on
        `tls.security`, from the first handshake). `port.tcp`'s connect time and
        `tls.certificate`'s handshake time include the lookup, and did before, when the socket
        made it: the clock starts before the lookup in both. SSH's connect timeout starts after
        the lookup when a connection is opened, which the first commit introduced and this
        leaves: the lookup has at most half of it more.
      - **Docs:** `administration.md` gains "The target policy: every sensor that connects, and
        the addresses it will not", beside the HTTP section; `adding-a-sensor-type.md` gains
        the rule for a transport of a type's own. No sensor schema changed, so
        `sensor-reference.md` is not regenerated.
      - **Tests:** `target-policy-transports.test.ts`, 68, none skipped, against the SNMP, SSH,
        SMTP and HTTP simulators and loopback listeners for TCP and TLS. For each transport
        held to the policy: a resolver that answers the metadata address is refused after one
        lookup; a name with one good and one refused address leaves the simulator untouched; a
        resolver that would answer differently the second time is asked once and the check
        arrives; an IPv4-mapped spelling is refused as a host and as an answer; an address and
        any host under `none` make no lookup; a pinned target makes the pin's one lookup and
        keeps its `CredentialsWithheldError`. Also: a first address that refuses the connection
        is passed (SSH, mail, TCP, TLS); SSH sensors coming due together share one connection
        and one lookup, stay Up with no lookup while the resolver fails or hangs, keep one
        connection while the name's answers change every scan, and are checked again when a
        connection has to be opened; an SNMP name whose answers rotate keeps one session, one
        that really moved is asked at the new address with the old session closed, and an
        answer set with a refused address is refused whole; the shared timeout on `port.tcp`,
        `port.range`, `tls.certificate`, `tls.security` and mail, against a loopback port that
        never answers a connection; ping is not held to the policy and makes no lookup in the
        probe; the database and Windows address-only check; the catalogue's setting and the
        environment; and one device on a link-local address whose eight sensors each fail
        once, unwithheld, with nothing resolved. Two tests in `pinned-transports.test.ts` that
        pinned "an unrestricted name makes no lookup" on SNMP and mail now pin the one. One in
        the probe's `catalogue-registry.test.ts`: the real registry refuses `port.tcp` and
        `tls.certificate` on the metadata address with no code a runner reads.
      - **Test faults closed:** the `port.tcp` case waits, with a bound, for the listener's
        accept instead of reading its counter as the client's connect resolves; the TLS suite
        skips only when `openssl` is not installed and fails on any other setup error.
      - **Mutation:** the first commit's 22 of 22, and 15 of 15 for what the review changed,
        each planted alone, built clean and failed by an assertion: the SSH pool opening
        without asking the guard, asking it and connecting by name all the same, and asking it
        before the pool is consulted; an SNMP session kept whatever the name answers, replaced
        at every scan, handed the name in place of a checked address, never closed when
        replaced, closed under the check using it, and not closed when that check is done;
        `snmpCheck` not handing the pool the checked addresses; and the whole timeout given
        after the lookup on `port.tcp`, `port.range`, the TLS handshake, `tls.security`'s first
        handshake, and mail.
      - **Not covered by a test:** the two lines in the probe's `main.ts` that put the setting
        in the environment, and no test in the core drives a Down from this refusal through
        notifications: it is a failed check like any other there.
      - **Found, not fixed:** the database and Windows sensors still connect to whatever a name
