- [x] **A-60 — no test delivers a webhook over HTTPS to an address** · S · A-58 · Found
      2026-10-02 by `A-58`. A URL whose host is an address is delivered to over HTTP in a test;
      over HTTPS it needs a certificate that names the address, and the file has none.
      **Done when** a fixture certificate with an IP subject alternative name exists and a test
      delivers to `https://127.0.0.1` and, where the machine has it, `https://[::1]`, with the
      certificate checked against the address.

      **A-60 outcome.** A webhook, Slack or Teams URL that gives an address is delivered to over
      HTTPS under a certificate that lists that address, and the test found that for an IPv6
      address it could not be. No migration, no protocol number.
      - **The defect, and it is Node's.** `https://127.0.0.1` worked as it stood.
        `https://[::1]` failed under a certificate whose subject alternative names list `::1`:
        "Host: ::1. is not cert's CN". Measured on the toolchain's Node 24.19:
        `tls.checkServerIdentity` puts the host through `domainToASCII` before it asks whether
        it is an address, an IPv6 address is not a domain and comes back empty, and the address
        is then matched as a DNS name. No certificate can pass that, so an IPv6 literal over
        HTTPS failed every attempt and was retried until they ran out.
      - **The fix** (`serverIdentity`, `http-client.ts`), passed as the request's
        `checkServerIdentity`. An IPv6 address is asked of the certificate itself by OpenSSL
        (`X509Certificate.checkIP`), not read out of the `subjectaltname` string; everything
        else — a name, an IPv4 address — is Node's check as before. Only an address the
        certificate lists as an address passes, a certificate with nothing to ask is refused,
        and the refusal reads as Node's does for IPv4 and carries its code. Whether the
        certificate is trusted is not decided there and is unchanged.
      - **The fixture** is made at test time with `openssl`, as `tls.test.ts` and
        `pinned-transports.test.ts` make theirs, and trusted through
        `tls.setDefaultCACertificates` as the second of those does; no key is committed. Five
        certificates: both loopback addresses, a DNS name only, another address, `::1` as a
        DNS name and common name, and one that names the addresses and is not trusted.
      - **What a mismatch is.** A certificate that does not name the address fails the
        handshake: `retryable: true`, the error Node's "IP: 127.0.0.1 is not in the cert's
        list", nothing sent. It is not a target-policy refusal and is retried like any failed
        attempt, as a wrong certificate for a name always was.
      - **SNI, pinned.** The server sees no server name in the hello for either address, and
        sees `webhook.test` for a name, on the same kind of server, so the empty list is the
        client's doing.
      - **Tests:** `webhook-delivery.test.ts`, eight new: delivery to `https://127.0.0.1` and
        to `https://[::1]` (skips, saying so, where `::1` cannot be listened on; it ran in the
        toolchain container); the name with its SNI; a DNS-only certificate and another
        address's refused for `127.0.0.1`; three certificates refused for `[::1]`; the check
        itself against real and empty certificates; an untrusted certificate refused. 64 in
        the file, none skipped; `chat-delivery` and `test-send`, which share the client, pass.
      - **Mutation:** 10 of 10 killed.
      - **Not done.** The same Node check is what the sensor types, the probe's connection to
        the core and mail delivery use, and none of them was looked at for an IPv6 address
        over TLS.

- [x] **A-61 — a late refusal that crosses a core restart is a failed scan** · M · A-56 · Found
      2026-10-02 by `A-56`, which wrote the bound down and pinned it because nothing stored says
      which sensors a configuration stopped leaving to a probe, or when. Inside the ten-minute
      grace, a core restart turns a probe's honest late refusals into failed scans: two of them
      are one Down and one notification for a change somebody made on purpose. **Done when**
      the record is stored (a migration, forward and back), read at start, pruned past the
      grace, and the restart scenario in `credential-pinning.test.ts` shows no Down.

      **A-61 outcome.** The record is stored, and a core restarted inside the grace takes a late
      refusal as late. Migration 067, no protocol number, nothing sent to or from a probe.
      - **The table.** `late_refusal_grace`: (probe, sensor) as the key, `stopped_at`, both ids
        cascading from `object` as `sensor_credential_voucher`'s do, an index on the sensor for
        that cascade, and a check that the time is finite. The rollback drops it.
      - **Written where the record is made, which is not where the change is decided.** A change
        is decided in its own write; what makes a refusal late is that the probe's configuration
        stopped leaving it the sensor, and the core knows that when it next builds that
        configuration (`withhold`), from what the one before left the probe, which is in memory.
        The row is written there, in one statement, waited for (within a bound, see the review
        below) before the configuration is handed over, and only when the build changed what is
        recorded: a steady build writes nothing.
        **The window that remains** is from the change's commit to that build: the notifier's
        250 ms for a connected probe, and until it redials for one that is away. A core that
        stops inside it starts with no row, and the refusal is the failed scan it was before.
        Accepted because closing it means storing what each probe was last left, which is a
        second record and a different question; it is a follow-up.
      - **Read once at start**: `restore()`, awaited in `main.ts` straight after `adopt()`, before
        the ingestion service and the probe endpoint are built. It throws when the table cannot
        be read, and the core does not start.
      - **Wall clock across the restart, monotonic after it.** At start, what has run is the wall
        clock now less the stored time, bounded both ways by `storedStop`: past the grace is
        spent and the row removed (a clock set forward lands here, and ends the grace early); a
        time later than now, a clock set back, gets the whole grace from that start and no more,
        is written down again as now so a second start does not give it twice, and is logged at
        `warn`; a time that is not finite is spent. No case gives more than
        `LATE_REFUSAL_GRACE_MS`.
      - **Pruned** on write (the statement removes every row of the probe that is no longer
        recorded: left again, or past the grace at that build), at start, and by `prune()` on a
        one-minute `PeriodicSweep` for a probe never sent another configuration. A write that
        fails is logged at `error` and made again at the next build or the next prune.
      - **What a probe that misbehaves can and cannot do is `A-53`'s, unchanged.** It can have its
        own error-with-no-readings results for a sensor discarded for ten minutes after a
        configuration stops leaving it that sensor. It cannot begin or prolong an Unknown,
        discard an `ok` or a reading, use it on a sensor it was never left or past the ten
        minutes, or reopen the window. Storing changes one thing: those ten minutes no longer
        end at a restart, and a restart does not start them again. **No result a probe sends
        writes to the table.** One thing a probe says does: the protocol version it connects
        with decides whether a named device is left to it (`boundRefusal`), so a reconnect under
        a version that changes that causes one statement, once per reconnect, of no more rows
        than the probe has sensors (a test counts both). The first outcome said "nothing a probe
        sends writes", which was wrong. A probe alternating its version re-opens the ten minutes
        each time; that is `A-53`'s in-memory behaviour and is not changed here. Besides that,
        an operator's clock set back across a restart gives a fresh ten minutes, once.
      - **Review, second commit: the write gives way and holds nobody back.** Three findings.
        (1) Every probe's write went through one chain with no bound, so one stalled write held
        back every probe's configuration. Each probe now has its own line (the write running and
        at most one behind it), the write runs in its own transaction with `lock_timeout` 300 ms
        and `statement_timeout` 2 s, and a configuration or a prune waits 3 s at most for it,
        whatever the connection does. On a timeout the configuration is returned, the probe is
        marked unsaved and the existing retry writes it; that is logged at `warn`, anything else
        at `error`. (2) The write locks its rows and then the sensors' rows in `object`; a delete
        of a device or group takes them in the other order. 300 ms is under `deadlock_timeout`
        (1 s as shipped), so the write always gives up first and the operator's delete is never
        the one aborted: that is the design, and a test on the real table holds the lock from a
        second connection, once as an update would and once as a delete, and shows the build
        returning inside the bound, the other transaction committing, and the next build or
        prune storing what is left. The statement returns the rows it wrote, and an entry whose
        sensor or probe is gone is dropped from memory, so it is not a write retried every
        minute. (3) The claim above, corrected here, in the migration's comment and in
        `state-machine.md`. 13 more unit cases and the one on the real table; mutation 10 of
        10 killed.
      - **Alarm volume** (`credential-pinning.test.ts`, the restart scenario, rewritten): a
        sensor Up, a name entry added, the row stored, then a second `CredentialVouching` on the
        same database that reads it. Four late refusals: still Up, no row in its state history,
        not held, no notification request, 4 on `lateRefusals` and 0 on `reportsRefused`. Two
        real failed scans: Down once, one request; a third beside another late refusal raises
        nothing more. Past the grace, two marked results are Down and counted as refused. Then
        the row is pruned.
      - **Tests:** `migrator.test.ts` (067 up, the key, the check, both foreign keys, both
        cascades, down, up again); 33 unit cases in `credential-pinning.test.ts` (a table of 13
        stored times through `storedStop` and through a start, what a start takes up, what is
        written and when, writes in order, pruning, and that `main.ts` reads the record before
        the endpoint is built); one case on the real table for the write, the row going when the
        sensor is left again, a start an hour behind and a start after it; the scenario above.
        `state-machine.md`, `troubleshooting.md` and `administration.md` say what holds now.
      - **Mutation:** 17 of 17 killed.
      - **Not done.** No Core Health channel for the rows held: a channel is a declaration, a
        reference regeneration and its tests, for a table that holds a handful of rows for ten
        minutes, and a failed write is logged. `main.ts` is not started by any test: its order is
        pinned by reading the source. The window above.

        table said it took neither option). Read from the installed sources:
        - `pg` 8.23, `lib/connection.js`: `config.stream`, called when it is a function, then
          `stream.connect(port, host)`; `upgradeToSSL(host)` wraps that stream with `servername`

          made it, and a client is never connected twice. Handed a socket whose `connect` goes
          to the device through the checked lookup.

          connect of the driver's own; `startTLS` wraps it with `servername` from

          already connecting.

          place of its own connect and awaited with nothing raced against it, so the connector
          ends itself at the timeout. The TLS it runs inside TDS names `config.server`

        (an address, or `none`), each driver connects exactly as before.

        server the login was routed to. That host is resolved and checked on a lookup of its
        own before it is followed; with a pinned set it is refused as
        `CredentialsWithheldError`. `tedious` passes the destination as arguments its typings

- [x] **A-64 — the target policy has no exception for one device** · M · A-57 · Found
      2026-10-02 by `A-57`. `probe.targetPolicy` is one setting for a probe, so a site with one

      exception is one device's own setting, not inherited from a group, so it can never
      exempt more than the device it names: `targetPolicyException`, the addresses of that
      device the probe may connect to although its policy refuses them. Only an administrator
      may set or clear it, every change is audited, it reaches the probe with the assignment,
      and an account that may only edit the device can neither set it nor read it changed.
      Without it a site with one link-local device turns the policy off for the whole probe,
      which is the weaker of the two.

      **A-64 outcome.** A device carries `targetPolicyException`, the addresses its probe may
      connect to although its policy refuses them; only an administrator sets it, and it is
      never inherited. Migration 070, protocol 28.
      - **Where it lives**: a column on `device_config` (070, `text[]`, at most 16, no NULL or
        empty entry), not an `object_setting`, so the resolver never sees it and a group, a
        probe or the root cannot carry one (409). Clone, template, discovery and tree-plan
        inserts name host and family only, so a new device has none. A host change does not
        clear it: it names addresses, not the host.
      - **Who**: `PUT /api/v1/objects/:id/target-policy-exception` `{ addresses }`, `ADMIN`
        (admin role, `full` token: the grant routes' bar); `[]` clears; `If-Match` taken.
        `PATCH` refuses the field (closed schema), the settings routes refuse the key. **Decided:
        readable by whoever may read the device** (on the detail, absent when empty), as the
        host is; the ticket's "nor read it changed" read as "nor change it".
      - **What**: addresses only (`exceptionProblem` in `@ms/shared`), checked by the core and
        again by the probe on every match. **Decided: no CIDR at all**, not even a /24: a range
        exempts more than the device. No names, zones, multicast/broadcast, unspecified, and
        **never a metadata service** (`169.254.169.254`, `169.254.170.2`, `fd00:ec2::254`, any
        spelling); the rest of link-local may be excepted.

        `refuseLocalSocket` (a socket path is `127.0.0.1`, so excepted where that is listed) all
        go through `judged()` → `excepts()`, after the policy refuses. It matches the address
        the lookup answered; a name passes only when every answer is allowed or listed.

        catalogue passes `CheckTarget.policyException` through. A refusal on a device with one
        names the list. The SSH pool keys a held connection by it, so withdrawing it is not
        outlived by a connection it allowed.

        upgrade. "Check now" follows the session's version.
      - **Audit**: an `object.updated` of the device, with `targetPolicyException` tracked in
        `diff.ts` (absent when empty, so no other device's diff changes); an unchanged list

        settings 400, invalid entries 400, non-device 409, clone without, If-Match, audit rows,
        assignment at 28 and not 27, check now); `shared` target-policy, messages and

- [x] **A-65 — three loose ends on the SSH and probe side of the target policy** · S · A-57 ·
      Found 2026-10-02 by `A-57` and its review. Sensors that join one connection being opened
      share the first one's lookup and its `AbortSignal`, so the first being cancelled can fail
      the others for a scan (one reviewer traced it, one found it unreachable in a running
      probe: settle which with a test). The SSH connect timeout starts after the lookup. The two

      **A-65 outcome.** One shown not to happen, one fixed, one given a function and a test.
      - **Joined SSH opens: not reachable in a running probe, and pinned.** The SSH pool is a
        module singleton, so one a worker thread; a worker has one check in hand at a time
        (the check pool holds a slot until its worker answers, a timed-out check included);
        no SSH type asks for a process of its own; and a check makes one `acquire`. So the
        second SSH sensor on a device finds the connection the first left and never one half
        open. `ssh-shared-open.test.ts` runs the shipped registry, pool and `ssh.load` in a
        real worker against the SSH simulator, six sensors on one device submitted together:
        the worker never had two checks in hand, six acquires, one open, five reused, **none
        joined**, one connection at the server. A second case holds the four SSH types to no
        `isolation`. The pool keeps the join (a caller that overlaps in one thread, which
        today is a test) and its comment now says what it shares, why that is out of reach,
        which test fails when it is not, and what to do then. No mechanism was added.
      - **The SSH connect timeout covers the lookup.** `SshSessionPool.acquire` times the
        guard and opens the session with what is left of `connectTimeoutMs` (at least 1 ms),
        as `A-57` did for port, TLS and mail. With no guard the handshake has the whole
        timeout, as before. The pool key still carries the sensor's own `connectTimeoutMs`.
        Four cases in `ssh-session.test.ts`, against a listener that accepts and never
        speaks: 1,200 ms of lookup under a 2,000 ms timeout ends at 2,000 and not 3,200.
      - **The two lines in `main.ts` are `handTargetPolicy`** (`probe/src/target-policy-env.ts`),
        which writes the setting to the probe's environment for the workers and returns it
        for `childEnv`, and writes `link-local` for anything that is not one of the three
        names. `target-policy-env.test.ts` starts a `CheckPool` and a `ProcessRunner` as
        `main.ts` does, on a registry that is a real catalogue with one type that reports
        `CheckTarget.policy`: a worker thread and a check process both run under `none`,
        `private` and `link-local` as configured; unset, empty, `None` and `off` are
        `link-local` in both, with `none` in the parent's environment for the check process;
        a check that arrives claiming `none` is told the probe's. **`main.ts` itself is still
        not run by a test**: it calls the function and spreads what comes back, and a mutant
        of those two call sites would survive.
      - **Mutation: 10/10** (five on the timeout arithmetic, five on `handTargetPolicy`), each
        failing a test, with the source restored and the rebuilt `dist` compared after each.
      - **Seen, not fixed.** `SshSession.open` takes no `AbortSignal`: a check cancelled
        during the handshake is not ended by its signal, only by the connect timeout or by
        the pool recycling the worker after its abort grace. Read from the code, not tested.

      `test:perf` has the case. The measurement is the orchestrator's, from a quiet window.
      - **Where a lookup is made, read from the code.** Every transport that connects to a
        device by name resolves it in `checkedTarget` under `link-local` or `private` (`A-57`,
        `A-62` for the databases), and a credential pin in `pinTarget` (`A-41c`): both wait in
        `resolveWithin`, bounded at `resolveBoundMs`, half the transport's timeout and 10 s at
        most (SNMP's own 5 s gives 2.5 s). Discovery's identification does the same in the main
        thread, and **Check now** in the query runner's own worker. Not through it: a socket
        that resolves the name itself (every transport under `none`), the listener types' sender
        (`sender.ts`, `P-425`), ping and PowerShell (their own processes), and the probe's link
        to the core.
      - **The thread pool, read from the code and from libuv.** The probe sets no
        `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, in `main.ts` or in `ms-probe.service`, so libuv's pool is four
        threads, one pool a process, which every check worker (worker threads share it) and the
        main thread use. libuv submits `getaddrinfo` as slow I/O and lets slow I/O hold at most
        `(threads + 1) / 2` of them, two: the file system and crypto keep the other two, and at
        most two lookups run at once on the probe, whatever its 64 workers ask. A lookup the
        resolver does not answer holds one of the two until glibc gives up on it, and every
        lookup asked after it waits, whichever device it is for. At the 5,000-sensor class a
        lookup a scan is 83 a second, which two lanes serve only from a resolver answering in
        under about 24 ms. Read, not measured against a real resolver here: the perf case
        models the lanes (below), and `P-426` is the decision the measurement is for.
      - **Counted where the check waits.** `resolveWithin` counts into `nameLookups`
        (`@ms/sensors` `support/lookups.ts`), one a thread: **in flight** from the lookup being
        asked until the resolver answers it, whether or not the check still waits, since the
        lookup and not the check holds the thread; **given up** when the check stops waiting
        first, at its bound or cancelled, as a running total. A name the resolver says does not
        exist is an answer, not a give-up.
      - **To Probe Health.** The probe's registry answers `CheckRegistry.lookupCounters`; the
        worker sends it with each result and on its idle timer when it changed (`P-256`'s 5 s
        session report), since a lookup a check gave up on settles with no check running and a
        check waiting for one has no result yet. The pool sums its workers, with a retired
        baseline for given up; a retired worker's in flight goes with it, as `sessionsOpen`
        does, which is a loss only for a worker terminated mid-lookup. The report adds what is
        made beside the scheduled pool, `lookupsBesideThePool`: the main thread's own and the
        query runner's (`QueryRunner.lookupCounters`), whose pool of one loads the same registry,
        so a named device on **Check now** resolves as on a scan. The query runner was left out
        until review.
      - **A pool fix on the way.** The pool took a worker's counters only from a result it had
        not settled yet, so a check it timed out left them on the worker, which does not send
        unchanged counters again: the lookup that check gave up on, and its sessions, stayed off
        Probe Health until something else changed. Now taken from every result.
      - **Protocol 36, `lookupCounters`**: `lookupsInFlight` and `lookupsGivenUp` on the
        heartbeat, stripped below 36, a gap for either end below it. Probe Health channels
        **Name lookups in flight** (a gauge) and **Name lookups given up** (a 64-bit counter),
        beside the sessions, **with no limits**: every check whose lookup was given up already
        fails naming the resolver, Down, or Unknown under a credential pin, so a limit would be
        a second alarm for one outage. `/metrics`: `ms_probe_name_lookups_in_flight` and
        `ms_probe_name_lookups_given_up_total`. No migration. `administration.md` has the row
        (what is counted and what is not); `sensor-reference.md` and `api-reference.md` are
        regenerated.
      - **The perf case**, `packages/probe/test/perf/name-lookups.test.ts`: a real wheel, a real
        pool at its shipped ceiling (64) and queue (1,000), and a real catalogue whose one check
        (`support/lookup-registry.ts`) is SNMP's resolution and nothing else, `checkedTarget`
        with SNMP's family and timeout, then `MODEL_CHECK_MS`. 5,000 sensors on 500 named
        devices, one minute an arm, six arms on fresh pools: addresses (no lookup, the
        baseline); the system resolver (`getaddrinfo` for `localhost` in the worker, from the
        hosts file); and four through **lanes**, every worker's lookups answered from the main
        thread `(UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE + 1) / 2` at a time, first come first served, which is
        libuv's discipline: answering (real `getaddrinfo` inside them, the model's control),
        slow (100 ms a lookup), not answering (30 s, then `EAI_AGAIN`), and one device in ten
        not answering beside the rest answering. A resolver this test controls cannot be put
        under `getaddrinfo` without changing `/etc/resolv.conf`, which is why the lanes are a
        model; they do not hold libuv's threads, so the `fs.stat` probe reads the file system's
        share unharmed in the lane arms whatever they do. Per arm it prints the results
        (answered, lookup given up, failed otherwise), refused, deferred, jitter (`P-15`'s),
        check run p95, Probe Health's `lookupsInFlight` (highest, last) and `lookupsGivenUp`
        from the real reporter, the lanes' deepest queue and what is still queued once the pool
        has drained, their p95 wait (the lookups served and those still queued, so far) and how
        busy they were (a lookup still held counted so far, from the wheel's start), the
        `fs.stat` p95 and worst from the wheel's start, and how long the pool took to drain, and
        for the zone arm how the answering devices fared. Review found the probe started before
        the workers had loaded and the lanes' busy share counting a lookup only once answered,
        so reading 66% with 44 queued; both fixed before the measurement. It asserts that
        `lookupsGivenUp` is exactly the checks that failed at the lookup's bound, and that the
        hosts-file arms give nothing up and refuse nothing. `MS_DNS_SENSORS`, `MS_DNS_MINUTES`,
        `MS_DNS_SLOW_MS`, `MS_DNS_HANG_MS`, `MS_DNS_LANES`, `MS_DNS_POOL` and `MS_DNS_ARMS`
        shape it.
      - **Measured** by the orchestrator, 2026-10-17, twice in one quiet window, at the defaults
        (`docs/findings/2026-10-17-name-lookups-a-scan.md`).
        - **A resolver that answers costs nothing measurable.** The hosts-file and answering
          arms ran all 5,000 checks at the address arm's jitter, with at most four lookups in
          flight.
        - **At 100 ms a lookup the probe goes down.** The two lanes serve 20 lookups a second
          against the 83 a scan needs. Of 5,000 scans, 58 were answered, 2,465 were given up at
          the bound and 2,477 were refused by a full queue. Median jitter was 34 s.
        - **One zone in ten silent takes the other nine with it.** 6 of the answering devices'
          2,287 lookups were answered, and 2,281 were given up.
        - **Probe Health showed both.** It read 634 lookups in flight in the slow arm and 2,500
          in the silent arms, and given up equalled the checks failed at the bound.
        - So `P-426` has its answer: the probe has to change how it resolves.
      - **Tests.** `sensors/test/name-lookups.test.ts` (11: `resolveWithin` answered, refused,
        at its bound, cancelled, cancelled before it began and many at once, each read on both
        sides of the resolver settling; then the guard, the pin and a catalogue check on the
        thread's own count). `probe/test/pool-lookups.test.ts` (11, real workers through
        `support/lookup-registry.ts`: nothing for a registry that counts nothing, an address and
        an answer and `ENOTFOUND` as neither, three workers summed, the idle report of a late
        answer and of a lookup still waited for, the pool's timeout, given up never falling
        across a shrink, and a query's lookup given up reaching the reporter beside a scan's and
        the main thread's through `lookupsBesideThePool`). One case each in `health-types`,
        `catalogue-registry`, `core/probe-health` and `metrics`, two in `probe-health-report`,
        three in `capabilities`. The perf case was smoke-run at 200 sensors for a quarter of a
        minute an arm on a pool of 8 with a 5 s hang, once before review and once after: six of six
        passed. After: the address arm made no lookup, and the hosts-file, answering and slow
        arms answered every one and gave none up, jitter p95 2 to 5 ms; the not-answering arm
        gave all 50 up, Probe Health read 44 in flight and 50 given up, the lanes were 95% busy
        with 42 still queued and a p95 wait of 15 s, and the pool took 4.1 s to drain; the zone
        arm gave up 18, 13 of them the answering devices' (32 of 45 answered) behind the 5 that
        were not. Not numbers: a smoke on a shared VM, at about 50 checks an arm.
      - **Mutation: 24 of 24 killed.** Not tracking a lookup; no give-up at the bound, on a
        cancel, or for a check already cancelled; never counting an answer down; a fresh count
        as the default; the given-up channel as a gauge; the registry answering zeros; the
        worker leaving them off its result; its idle report leaving them out; the pool ignoring
        that report; the pool fix reverted; the pool reporting one worker's in flight; no
        retired baseline; the report dropping the main thread's in flight; given up reporting
        in flight; no strip below 36; the capability at 35; the core reading in flight as given
        up; the exporter's counter reading in flight; the query runner answering nothing,
        `lookupsBesideThePool` leaving out the query runner's or the main thread's, and the sum
        both reports share dropping the second's in flight. Each built and failed its file.
      - **Not covered by a test:** the line in `main.ts` that hands the query runner to
        `lookupsBesideThePool`, which is tested.
      - **Filed:** `P-425` (the listener types resolve a sender with no bound and no signal) and
        `P-426` (the probe's two lookup lanes, decided from this measurement).

- [x] **A-67 — an IPv6 address under TLS has only been tried on webhook delivery** · S · A-60 ·
      Found 2026-10-02 by `A-60`. Node's `checkServerIdentity` (v24.19 in the toolchain) reads
      an IPv6 host as a name and refuses a certificate that lists the address; the delivery
      client now asks the certificate itself. The HTTP, `tls.certificate` and mail sensors, mail
      delivery, and the probe's connection to a core given by IPv6 address rely on the same
      check and have not been tried. **Done when** each has a test against a certificate
      listing `::1`, the ones that fail share one identity check with the delivery client, and
      a core addressed as `https://[::1]` accepts a probe.

      **A-67 outcome.** Every TLS client named above was run against `::1` under a certificate
      that lists `::1`; five failed for `A-60`'s reason and now pass one shared check. No
      migration, no protocol number.
      - **The measurement, taken again first.** On the toolchain's Node 24.19 a direct
        `tls.checkServerIdentity('::1', certificate)` refuses a certificate whose subject
        alternative names list `::1` ("Host: ::1. is not cert's CN"), accepts the same one for
        `127.0.0.1`, and `X509Certificate.checkIP('::1')` on it answers `::1`. It is a test
        (`server-identity.test.ts`), so the day Node checks an IPv6 address itself that test
        fails and says the workaround can go.
      - **One check.** `serverIdentity` moved from the delivery client to
        `packages/shared/src/net/server-identity.ts`, unchanged, and is passed as
        `checkServerIdentity` at each site. `rejectUnauthorized`, the trusted authorities and
        what is sent as the server name are as they were everywhere.
      - **Per site.**
        | Site | Tried | Before | Now |
        | --- | --- | --- | --- |
        | Webhook, Slack, Teams (`http-client.ts`) | `A-60` | fixed by `A-60` | imports the shared check |
        | HTTP sensors (`support/http/request.ts`) | yes | failed: "not valid for ::1" | fixed |
        | `tls.certificate` (`support/tls/handshake.ts`) | yes | read `trusted` 0 for a trusted certificate that lists `::1` | fixed; nothing refused, as before |
        | `tls.security` (same handshake) | yes | unaffected | not applicable: it reads protocol versions and nothing of who the certificate is for |
        | Mail sensors, implicit TLS (`support/mail/connection.ts`) | yes | failed | fixed |
        | Mail sensors, after `STARTTLS` | yes | failed, and for a second reason (below) | fixed |
        | Email delivery (`delivery/email.ts`, both modes) | yes | failed every send | fixed |
        | Probe to core (`core-client.ts`) | yes | never said hello | fixed |
        | Core's probe endpoint | yes | not applicable: it judges the probe's certificate by its CA, and listens on `::1` as on anything | a test connects to it there as the probe does |
      - **`tls.certificate` keeps its meaning.** It still verifies nothing and refuses nothing.
        `trusted` is Node's verdict on the connection, which includes who the certificate is
        for, so it read 0 on any device at an IPv6 address; it now reads as it always did for
        an IPv4 one. `hostMatches` is the sensor's own reading of names only (common name and
        DNS entries) and is 0 for a device given by address in either family, as before — pinned
        in the test, not changed.
      - **Found: after `STARTTLS` a device given by address was checked against `localhost`.**
        Not an IPv6 matter. The upgrade handed Node a connected socket and no host; with no
        server name either (none is sent for an address) Node falls back to the literal name
        `localhost`. So a mail server at any address, `127.0.0.1` included, was refused under a
        certificate that lists its address and *accepted* under any trusted certificate for
        `localhost`. The upgrade now names the host, as nodemailer's does. A sensor that
        verified a mail server by address after `STARTTLS` and was Up can only have been Up
        under a certificate for `localhost`; one that was Down for "not valid for" its own
        address comes Up.
      - **Server names, pinned as they are.** Mail and email send none for an address. The HTTP
        and TLS sensors send the address itself as the server name (`::1`), which RFC 6066
        forbids and Node warns about (`DEP0123`, "will be ignored in a future version");
        left as it is and pinned, since changing what a hello carries was not this ticket.
      - **Tests:** `server-identity.test.ts` (shared, 5), `tls-address-identity.test.ts`
        (sensors, 17: HTTP, both TLS sensors, SMTP and IMAP in both modes, each with the
        certificates that must still be refused — other addresses, `::1` as a DNS name and
        common name, a name — and `127.0.0.1` and a named device as controls),
        `email-relay-identity.test.ts` (core, 6, against a relay of the file's own because
        MailHog speaks no TLS), four in `core-client.test.ts`, two in `probe-endpoint.test.ts`.
        Certificates are made with `openssl` at test time; the `::1` cases skip, saying so,
        where it cannot be listened on, and ran in the toolchain container. The simulators
        gained `listenHost` (HTTP, mail) and `implicitTls` (mail).
      - **Mutation:** 11 of 11 killed — the option dropped at each of the seven call sites
        (two in the mail connection), the host dropped from the `STARTTLS` upgrade, and three
        in the shared check.
      - **After review, three closed.** (1) A zone-scoped address, `fe80::1%eth0` — the only way
        to reach a link-local one — is an IPv6 host to `net.isIP`, and OpenSSL calls the whole
        spelling invalid, so a certificate that lists `fe80::1` was refused. The zone is taken
        off before the certificate is asked; another address's certificate is refused with a
        zone as without, and a host that is only a zone is no address and is refused by Node as
        a name. (2) The three new test files skipped every case when certificate generation
        failed for any reason; they now skip only when `openssl version` cannot run, and
        anything else fails them (tried: with generation broken, all 30 cases are cancelled
        and none skipped). (3) The test that pins Node's defect now says what to do when it
        fails — delete the IPv6 branch of `serverIdentity` and that test — and is the only
        test that calls Node's check with an IPv6 host, so the only one that fails that day.
        Two tests more in `server-identity.test.ts` (7); mutation 2 of 2 on the zone.
      - **Not done.** The heartbeat (`health/heartbeat.ts`) uses `fetch`, which fails for
        `https://[::1]` the same way (measured) and has no `checkServerIdentity` to pass. The
        database sensors and the core's own database pool hand TLS to `pg`, `mysql2` and
        `tedious`, not tried: no simulator speaks their TLS.

- [x] **A-68 — a probe that changes its protocol version re-opens the late-refusal grace** · M
      · A-61, A-53 · Found 2026-10-02 by `A-61`'s review. A probe that reconnects announcing a
      version without `credentialAddressPinning` stops being left its named sensors, which
      begins ten minutes for them; announcing the newer one ends it, and the older one again
      begins another. The window is `A-53`'s; `A-61` made it a write a reconnect and one that
      outlasts a restart. Also left by `A-61`: a core that stops between a change's commit and
      the next configuration built for that probe has no row, which storing what each probe
      was last left would close; and a write that gives way is a log line and no number.
      **Done when** a window cannot be begun again for a sensor inside some bound of its last
      one by a version change alone, with a test; the commit-to-build window is closed or
      written down as accepted; and give-ways are a Core Health number.

      **A-68 outcome.** All three parts, one commit. Migration 068, no protocol number, nothing
      sent to or from a probe.
      - **One window an hour by the version alone.** A window is remembered for an hour from
        when it began: the ten minutes and `LATE_REFUSAL_COOL_OFF_MS`, fifty more. The entry is
        kept when the sensor is left to the probe again, which is what a probe gets by
        reconnecting under the newer version, and inside the hour a stop that only the version
        caused leaves the time where it was. So a refusal is late for what remains of the one
        window, and for nothing after it: the window is not cut short by the alternation and
        not begun again. That is "resume", where the ticket's example said "no grace". Chosen
        because it is one rule (the window is ten fixed minutes, and only a configured stop
        moves it), it gives no more than the one window either way, and it does not turn an
        honest probe's rollback, upgrade and rollback inside ten minutes into failed scans.
      - **Why an hour.** The bound is what a probe gets by reconnecting: one window in it,
        ten minutes in sixty. What it costs is an honest probe rolled back twice inside the
        hour, whose spool still holds refusals after the second: those are failed scans of a
        sensor the core is withholding, and two of them are a Down when the probe is upgraded.
        People do not roll a probe back twice in an hour often; a shorter cool-off buys that
        case and gives a reconnecting probe more.
      - **The cause is told apart, exactly.** `withhold` asks its own check a second time, for
        what this configuration would have left the probe had its version stayed
        (`#leftUnderVersionBefore`). A sensor still left under the version before was stopped by
        the version alone; one that is not was stopped by a change (targets, the device's host,
        a move, a pause, a voucher), whatever the version did beside it, and **that stop begins
        its grace at once, hour or no hour**. Asked only when the version differs and a
        remembered window could begin again, so a steady build asks nothing more. The same
        check decides both, so nothing here knows which capabilities a version carries, and
        `A-62`'s changes to `boundRefusalReason` need nothing from it. **Where they cannot be
        told apart** is when that second check fails (the database): then time alone decides,
        no remembered window is begun again, and the log says so at `warn`.
      - **Part 2 is closed, not accepted.** The same rows now say what each probe was last left
        and the version it was left it under (`left_version`), written in the one statement
        and read back by `restore()`. A core that stopped between a change's commit and the
        next configuration compares its first configuration for the probe with the last one
        the core before it built, finds the stop, and begins the ten minutes then. Storing the
        version is what lets the restarted core tell the cause too, and a time past its ten
        minutes is taken up as remembered, so the hour survives a restart as the grace does.
      - **Migration 068**: `stopped_at` nullable, `left_version integer` (positive), and a check
        that a row says one of the two. The rollback keeps exactly the rows 067's build would
        have written (not left, with a time) and removes the rest.
      - **What it writes now.** A probe's rows are written when a configuration changes what it
        is left, the version it is left it under, or a window: so once at each probe's first
        configuration on this build, and one statement for a reconnect under another version,
        of no more rows than the probe has sensors, as `A-61` already bounded it. A steady
        build still writes nothing. The version is kept only beside what the probe is left:
        a probe left nothing has no row, and nothing that could stop. The give-way case on the
        real table was moved to a sensor's first configuration, which is an insert and needs
        the lock on the sensor's row that the case holds.
      - **Part 3.** Core Health **Late-refusal record writes given up**
        (`lateRefusalWritesGivenUp`): a 64-bit counter, no limit, no lookup, so no state and no
        alarm, declared after `credentialsWithheld`. Counted once for each write that gave way
        (lock, statement timeout, a deadlock lost), was not waited for (the 3 s client bound),
        or failed, whichever came first, and not again if it then does both. Absent the
        source, the channel gaps. `ms_core_late_refusal_writes_given_up_total`;
        `sensor-reference.md` regenerated.
      - **What a probe that misbehaves can and cannot do, now.** It can have its own
        error-with-no-readings results for a sensor discarded for ten minutes after a
        configuration stops leaving it that sensor, each counted on its Probe Health. By
        reconnecting under an older protocol version it can begin those ten minutes itself,
        **once in an hour for each sensor and no oftener**, and each such reconnect costs the
        core one statement of no more rows than the probe has sensors. It cannot begin or
        prolong an Unknown with such a mark, discard an `ok` or a reading, use it on a sensor it
        was never left, use it past the ten minutes, move a window that has begun, or begin
        one inside the hour of the last by anything it says. A core restart changes none of
        that. Nothing a probe sends in a result writes to the table.
      - **Found, and not this ticket's.** Alternating versions still pages, and the grace never
        caused it: each downgrade withholds the probe's named sensors (Unknown, the Unknown
        trigger's page) and each upgrade lets them go (its recovery). Five alternations are
        three Unknown pages and two recoveries for a sensor, with or without a single refusal
        sent, where one downgrade is one. The scenario pins that the refusals add nothing to
        it. And a marked result that arrives past the window while the core is withholding the
        sensor is taken as a failed scan: two are a Down, in no words, when the sensor is let
        go, for a single downgrade as for an alternating probe.
      - **Alarm volume** (`credential-pinning.test.ts`, four scenarios on the real tables).
        Three probes, one downgraded once, two alternating five times in twelve minutes, one of
        those sending marked refusals as the single one does: late refusals 4 and 4, refused 2
        and 2, one time in the table and it is the first downgrade's, no Down for any, the
        pages of the two alternating probes identical, and after the upgrade one Down and one
        page each for the two that sent refusals and none for the one that did not. An
        operator's name entry eleven minutes after a downgrade: two late refusals, still Up,
        no transition, no page. A core restarted two minutes into a window: the next downgrade
        begins nothing, late 2 and then refused 2. A core that stops between a change and the
        next configuration: the restarted one finds the stop, two late refusals, still Up, no
        Down, no page.
      - **Tests.** 14 new unit cases (the hour and its last millisecond, five alternations, a
        change beside a downgrade, the check that fails, a restart in the middle and one past
        the grace, what is stored of what a probe is left, a refusal before the first
        configuration after a restart), 2 more rows in the table of stored times, and the
        `A-61` cases rewritten where the record now keeps a time or writes what a probe is
        left; the four scenarios; the give-way case on the real table now counts; `migrator`
        (068 up, the three checks, down to 067's rows, up again), `core-health`, `metrics`,
        `health-types`. 424 passing in the eleven files run, none skipped.
      - **Mutation:** 15 of 15 killed, one of them taken again after its line changed.
      - **Not done.** The first start of a core upgraded to this schema has no row of what any
        probe is left until it has built each a configuration, so the commit-to-build window
        is open for that one start. A write that failed or gave way, and a restart before it is
        made again, still loses what that write said; that is what the counter is for.

- [x] **A-69 — four loose ends from discovery and SSH under the target policy** · S · A-63,
      A-65 · Found 2026-10-02. The `identify-start` schema takes any 7 to 15 characters as an
      address where it means IPv4. A host the policy refused is still given a device and a
      Ping sensor by the built-in templates, and whether a site's template can add a
      connecting sensor to it was not checked. The core bounds `refused` and no other
      free-text field of a fingerprint (`sysDescr`, `sysName`, `reverseName`, `httpServer`,
      `vendor`, `evidence`), which a probe cuts and a core takes at any length.
      `SshSession.open` takes no `AbortSignal`, so a check cancelled in the handshake ends on
      the connect timeout. **Done when** each is fixed with a test.

      **A-69 outcome.** Three fixed, one decided and pinned. No migration, no protocol number.
      - **`identify-start` takes dotted-quad IPv4 by pattern** (`IPV4_ADDRESS_PATTERN` in
        `protocol/messages.ts`): four octets to 255, no leading zero, mask or space. No
        protocol number, because nothing a core sends stopped being valid. Read: the one
        dispatch (`#offerIdentify`) sends `host(address)` of `discovery_host` rows, which a
        sweep of an IPv4 range fills from `toText`. **The core could be made to send something
        else, and no longer can**: `sweep-progress` is held only to a length and the column is
        `inet`, so a probe reporting `fe80::1` got a row, which would have been offered back
        and is now a frame the probe refuses. The offer reads `family(address) = 4` rows only;
        such a row stays unidentified, which the summary says, and it could never have been
        identified, since a fingerprint's address must be IPv4. A name was never something a
        core had to send. Tests: 18 refused spellings and five taken in `messages.test.ts`,
        the pattern against `isIPv4` and against every octet value `toText` renders; in
        `discovery.test.ts` a run with IPv6 rows offers only its dotted quads, in a frame
        `parseCoreToProbe` takes, and ends.
      - **A refused host is still provisioned, and that is the rule, not a leftover.** Every
        host nothing identified gets a device and a Ping ("gives a host nothing identified a
        Ping sensor rather than nothing", `D-04`), a refused host is one of those, ping is not
        held to the policy, and the summary says why it was not identified. So it is kept, and
        pinned: the built-in set plans `ms.generic` and `icmp.ping` alone for a refused
        fingerprint with every credential kind available, the same plan as for no fingerprint.
        **A site's own template can put a connecting sensor on it** (one with no criteria
        matches every host) and the core does not stop that; a test creates one. The probe
        does: the device's host is the refused address itself, never a name, so every type
        held to the policy, the address-only ones included, refuses it at check time with
        the policy's sentence before a socket exists. That is `A-57`'s "a device on a
        link-local address" case in `target-policy-transports.test.ts`, with the database and
        Windows cases beside it, re-run here and passing. Such a sensor reads Down every scan
        until the policy is `none`: one failed check a scan, as `A-57` wrote down.

      **Decided 2026-10-04 by WatchDog**, on Roman's "you decide".
      **Damped, and withheld results do not
      count.** One outage, one alarm: a probe whose protocol version changes more than once in
      an hour stops moving its named sensors on each alternation; they hold their last state and
      Probe Health raises one warning naming the flap, cleared when the version has held for an
      hour. A result for a sensor the core is withholding is dropped and counted on Probe
      Health, never a failed scan, so a release cannot open with a Down that has no message.

        since its last change. "Check now" is judged at the floor too (`judgedVersion`). Only
        what the version decides is held: a name entry added in a flap sends the sensor at once.
        The minute `prune` ends it and asks for the probe's configuration through `main.ts`'s
        `configNotifier.flush()`, so the held sensors are let go then and not at a reconnect.

- [x] **A-83 — results that reach a restarted core before the probe's first configuration**
      · S · A-78 · Found 2026-10-11 by `A-78`. What a probe's configuration withholds is held
      in memory (`#withheldByProbe`, and `SensorVouching`'s live fact) and rebuilt by the first
      configuration the restarted core builds for it. `ProbeEndpoint.#queueResults` hands a
      batch to ingestion as soon as the probe is known, without waiting for that
      configuration. A spooled result for a sensor the core before the restart withheld (one
      a flap held, or any refusal of `A-29`'s set) is therefore taken as an ordinary result:
      it decides the sensor out of `unknown`/`access`. The first configuration then withholds
      it again, which is an Unknown page and its recovery that one outage did not earn. The
      window is the time from the probe's hello to its first build, usually under a second,
      and the sensor needs a result spooled from before it was withheld. Proposed: chain the
      session's result batches behind its first configuration, under a bound, and as before
      once the bound has passed. **Done when** fixed with a scenario test on the real tables
      (stored withheld sensor, a restart, a spooled result first) or decided to keep.

      **A-83 outcome.** Nothing to fix for a probe of ours: the premise, written in `A-78`, was
      wrong, and is pinned now. No code change, no migration, no protocol number.
      - **A batch already waits for the first build.** The probe drains its spool from the
        `welcome` (`CoreClient`, `setState('connected')`). The core sends the welcome and queues
        the first configuration in the same turn, on both admission branches, and on
        `session.pending`, the chain every batch of the session joins. So a batch sent after
        the welcome reaches ingestion only once `assignmentsFor` has returned, and with it
        `CredentialVouching.withhold`, which rebuilds what is held. Read wrongly in `A-78` as
        "as soon as the probe is known".
      - **Pinned** (`probe-endpoint.test.ts`, through the registry `main.ts` uses): a build held
        open, a batch sent the moment the welcome lands, and a heartbeat answered behind
        nothing. The batch is not taken while the build is held, and is taken after it.
        Mutation: 2 of 2 killed (the batch chained on `known` alone instead of the session's
        chain; the first build queued 30 ms after the welcome).
      - **Kept, two cases where a batch is taken without the build.**
        - **A batch sent before the welcome**, during the admission, is chained ahead of the
          build (`P-307`'s test sends exactly that). Our probe never sends one.
        - **A first build that fails**: the connection stays up and results are taken, by
          design (`could not build this probe's configuration`, at `error`). Withholding
          results until a build succeeds would stall a probe on a database fault.
        Both need a spooled result for a sensor the core before the restart withheld, which
        the probe was not sent after it was withheld.

- [x] **R-11 — a sensor re-decided when its probe comes back says nothing** · XS · R-05,
      A-78 · Found 2026-10-11 by `A-78`. Leaving `unknown`/`probe` for the state its last
      scan decided writes that state with an empty message until the next scan, as a

      own (as `RELEASED_FROM_WITHHOLDING`) with a test, or the silence is decided right.

      **R-11 outcome.** Fixed. No migration, no protocol number.
      - **The words were already there, and dropped.** Every path that lets a sensor go from
        `unknown`/`probe` passed a sentence: the probe answering again, a move to another
        probe, the probe's clock passing the sensor's last result. `SensorStateService
        .reevaluate` kept a caller's words only for an operator-decided state, and a state the
        last reading decides is not one. Now a sensor leaving `unknown`/`probe` carries the
        words of the caller that let it go, **when that caller says it speaks for the probe**
        (`sources: ['probe']`). Any other caller's words are about something else, and it
        says nothing rather than the wrong thing (`releasedMessage`, beside `A-78`'s rule for
        `access`).
      - **The probe paths say so.** `ProbeReachability` (lost, found, the tree resync and its
        retry) and `ClockFreeze` (freeze, thaw, the probe's alarm) pass `sources: ['probe']`,
        and `StateReevaluator` now requires it. A side effect, and the right one: a sensor these
        paths re-decide into a state another cause owns (a pause, a simulated error) takes that
        cause's words and not the probe's (`P-94`). The two sentences for the way back end
        "until its next result it stands where it stood before", as `A-78`'s does.
      - **Tests.** `probe-offline.test.ts`: the return carries the words on the sensor and on
        its transition, and a caller that does not speak for the probe lets go in none.
        `clock-freeze.test.ts`: every frozen row in the table reads Up with the thaw's words
        once thawed, on the real tables. `docs/state-machine.md` gains the row for leaving
        `unknown`/`probe`.
      - **Mutation:** 3 of 3 killed (a probe release silent again, any caller's words taken,
        the probe paths speaking for no cause). Core 5,274.

- [x] **A-74 — what is left of a database sensor's address, certificate and wording**
      · M · A-70 ·
      Found 2026-10-02 by `A-70` and its three reviews. (1) `db.mysql` and `db.mssql` refuse a
      device given as an IPv6 address once verification is on, because neither driver takes a
      custom identity check: fail closed today, and a sensor that cannot be made to work.
      (2) `mysql2`'s IPv4 check leans on `socket._host`, which Node reads and does not
      document. (3) The core's own pool (`db/pool.ts`) hands `pg` `rejectUnauthorized` and
      nothing else, so a core whose database is given as an address with `ssl` on checks the
      certificate against `localhost`: read, not measured. (4) A bounded database set facing
      a PostgreSQL socket path is undecided to the core and unresolvable to the probe: read,
      not tested. (5) After a SQL Server redirect, a timeout in the query phase names the
      device and not the routed server; the driver has to remember where the connector last
      connected. (6) `describeDbError` takes the first coded error out of `tedious`'s
      `AggregateError`, so a name with several addresses is diagnosed by whichever was tried
      first (`ENETUNREACH` before `ECONNREFUSED` reads as neither). (7) Nothing here has run
      against a real SQL Server: the PRELOGIN guard's 64 KiB bound, a redirect followed
      through a login with TLS on, and TDS 8 `strict`. **Done when** each is fixed with a
      test or written down as accepted, and (7) is run once against a real server.

      **A-74 outcome. Five fixed with tests, one written down, and (7) run against SQL Server's
      engine for what it can show.** No migration, no protocol number. The generated references
      are untouched.
      - **(1) and (2), `db.mysql`: an address of either family is checked by us, before the
        login.** `mysql2` sends credentials only from the callback its `startTLS` is handed
        (`lib/commands/client_handshake.js` 318-329). The driver now makes the core connection
        itself, wraps that method on it, and checks `serverIdentity(device, certificate)` in
        the callback before calling the driver's own.
        - **The chain** stays Node's to refuse under `rejectUnauthorized`. `verifyIdentity` is
          off for an address only.
        - **On a failed check** the socket is destroyed and the driver is handed the error, so
          nothing is sent.
        - **`socket._host` is gone**, and with it the reliance on something Node does not
          document. The reliance is now on `mysql2`'s `startTLS(onSecure)`, which the lockfile
          pins. It is looked for on the class before a connection is made, and a driver without
          it is refused with a sentence.
        - **IPv6 works**: `db.mysql` at `::1` passes under a certificate listing it.
        - **The fake now counts logins**, so the refusals are shown to send no password. Before,
          it recorded queries only.
      - **(1), `db.mssql` and IPv6: written down as accepted.** The reasons are in `mssql.ts`.
        - **What would be possible.** `tedious` emits `secure` before LOGIN7, and the connector
          could block non-PRELOGIN writes until a check passed, so the login could not leave
          unchecked.
        - **What blocks it.** With the driver's rejection off, whether the chain passed would be
          read off which `authorizationError` Node reports. That is its order of checks, and it
          is not documented. If the order changed, an untrusted certificate would pass.
        - **So** the refusal stays: it fails closed and says what to do. The sentence is now
          SQL Server's only.
      - **(3) The core's pool**: measured, then fixed.
        - **Measured.** `database-tls-identity.test.ts` runs a PostgreSQL of its own that
          answers `S` and counts startup messages. Against the old setting it failed 4 of 6: at
          `127.0.0.1` and `::1` alike, a certificate listing the address was refused and one for
          `localhost` accepted.
        - **Fixed.** `pool.ts` now passes `checkServerIdentity` bound to `config.host`, through
          the shared `serverIdentity`. 6 of 6 pass.
        - **An upgrade note** says that such a core must have a certificate for its address
          before upgrading, or it cannot start.
      - **(4) A socket path facing a bounded set is decided, as the probe's own machine.**
        `targetVerdict` in `@ms/shared` reads a host starting with `/` as inside exactly when
        the targets cover `127.0.0.1`, `::1` or `localhost`, and outside otherwise. It was
        undecided against address targets, so the core sent the set to be pinned and the path
        read Unknown as an unresolvable name. This matches the probe's own rule for the path
        (`A-70` F1).
        - **Not a path that begins `//` or holds a `\`** (the re-review): Windows reads those as
          a pipe on another machine. They stay names, undecided against address targets, and
          the pin that cannot resolve them withholds the set. A probe on Windows refuses every
          socket path, whatever the core decided.
        - **Tests.** Twelve rows in `allowed-targets.test.ts`, and a `boundRefusal` case in
          `credential-pinning.test.ts`: `outside` against address targets, null against
          `127.0.0.1` at any probe version, and `//10.0.0.66/pipe` left to a pin.
          `credential-vouching.ts` was not touched; it reads the verdict.
      - **(5) After a redirect, a query's failure names the routed server.** The connector
        reports where it connected (`tdsConnector`'s `connected`). `describeDbError` takes it in
        the query phase: `Microsoft SQL Server at R, where D routed the login: …`.
        - **The TDS fake** now takes a login, answers `tedious`'s batches and RPCs, and fails
          the check's query. End to end, through a redirect from `127.0.0.1` to `127.0.0.2`, the
          sentence names `127.0.0.2`.
        - **Not covered.** With nothing checked (policy `none`, no bounds, not `require`),
          `tedious` follows the redirect itself, and the device is named, as before.
      - **(6) Several addresses: the furthest attempt is the diagnosis, and every attempt is
        named.**
        - **The ranking**: refused, reset, timed out, then the unreachables. So
          `ENETUNREACH` on `::1` and then `ECONNREFUSED` on `127.0.0.1` reads `nothing is
          listening at …`, in either order.
        - **An attempt's timeout says no `within N ms`** (the re-review): among several it is
          Node giving up on one address after 250 ms for the next, or the kernel's, and never
          the connect timeout, whose timer gathers nothing.
        - **The sentence ends** with `every address it has was tried: ::1 ENETUNREACH,
          127.0.0.1 ECONNREFUSED`.
        - **Unchanged**: one attempt, and a refusal of ours, keep their class and their words.
      - **(7) Against Azure SQL Edge 15.0.2000**, the dev stack's SQL Server engine. The full
        image segfaults under emulation here, and there is no amd64 host. Three cases in
        `db-drivers.test.ts`:
        - its PRELOGIN answer to a request for encryption is 26 bytes and reads ON to the guard,
          so the 64 KiB bound is about 2,500 times what a real server sends;
        - `require` with verification off logs in through the TLS it negotiates inside TDS,
          past the guard;
        - with verification on, its self-signed certificate is refused with the self-signed
          sentence.

        **Not run, and written down:**
        - **A redirect through a TLS login.** Only Azure SQL's gateway routes.
        - **TDS 8 `strict`.** It is SQL Server 2022's, and this driver passes `tedious` a
          boolean and never asks for it.
        - **Both need** an amd64 host with SQL Server 2022, or an Azure SQL database.

        - `P-406`'s handshake assertion for an IPv6 address now covers all three engines,

        1. **A host beginning `/` was inside for every platform.** On a Windows probe Node opens

- [x] **A-75 — three small things the heartbeat and the certificate sensor still say
      wrongly** · S · A-71 ·
      Found 2026-10-02 by `A-71`. The channel is still named "Host name matches" though it
      now answers for an address: find out whether renaming touches stored channel rows
      before doing it. The mismatch note in `tls.certificate`'s message lists the
      certificate's DNS names and not its IP entries. A `101` answer to the heartbeat is
      logged as phase `request` with a sentence, not as `refused` with its status. And the
      heartbeat was never tried under `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`, which `fetch` honoured and
      `node:https` does not. **Done when** each is fixed with a test or written down.

      **A-75 outcome. Three fixed with tests, the name written down; the proxy was a real
      regression.** No migration, no protocol change.
      - **The channel keeps *Host name matches*. Written down.** A rename would reach stored rows
        only for sensors created after it. An existing sensor's channel name is written at
        creation and re-declared by an edit only when the declaration moved (`P-303`), and the
        stored parameters' declaration is computed by the running type, so after a rename both
        sides of every edit carry the new name and nothing moves. One channel would read under
        two names across an installation, which costs more than the wording: *host* is also the
        device field that holds a name or an address, and the `A-71` upgrade note says what the
        channel answers for an address.
      - **The mismatch note names the addresses too.** `addressesOf` in `support/tls/handshake.ts`
        reads the IP SANs as Node writes them, for saying what a certificate is for and never for
        deciding (that stays `certificateListsAddress`, OpenSSL on the DER). The verdict carries
        them, and the note lists up to four names and up to four addresses: *the certificate is
        for ms-a67-test, 127.0.0.2, ::2 and this sensor asked for ::1*, where it said only the
        name.
      - **A `101` is refused with its status.** The request listens for `upgrade`, so Node hands
        the `101` over instead of destroying the socket; the socket is hung up on and the status
        goes the way of any answer that is not a 2xx: phase `refused`, `status: 101`, one failure,
        the next pass sends. `close` still ends any request that ends with no answer.
      - **The proxy, measured first.** On the toolchain's Node 24.19: with `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`
        and `HTTP_PROXY` set, the global agent goes through the proxy, and both `agent: false` and
        a fresh `new Agent()` go direct; an `Agent` given `proxyEnv` goes through it. Node turns it
        on for `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` (not `true`, not `0`) and for `--use-env-proxy`. So since
        `A-71` the heartbeat went direct where `fetch` had gone through the proxy. Each request now
        has an agent of its own, `keepAlive: false`, handed the environment when
        `proxiesFromEnvironment` says Node is told to: `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`, or `--use-env-proxy`
        in `execArgv` or `NODE_OPTIONS`. Node applies `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY`.
        `administration.md` says so in the heartbeat section and the upgrade notes.
      - **Tests.**
        - `heartbeat.test.ts`: the `101` case now asserts phase `refused` and status 101 on both
          passes. The proxy rule's table, seven rows. Told to: a URL whose host resolves nowhere
          is answered by the proxy, which was asked for it as written. Not told to, with a proxy
          named, and told to with `NO_PROXY` naming the receiver: each goes direct and the proxy
          is asked nothing. HTTPS through a proxy (Node's `CONNECT` tunnel) is not tried here.
        - `tls.test.ts`: `addressesOf` reads IPv4 and IPv6 SANs and nothing from a certificate
          without them. `tls-address-identity.test.ts`: at `::1`, the note for the certificate
          for other addresses names `127.0.0.2` and `::2`.
      - **Mutation: 5/5**, each restored byte for byte and `dist` rebuilt: no `upgrade` listener,
        the proxy never handed to the agent, any value of `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` taken as on, no
        addresses in the verdict, and the note naming names only.

### Panel round two — notifications, schedules, triggers

Eight lenses over `packages/core/src/{notifications,schedules,triggers}`, merged to 34 distinct
claims, each put to three skeptics briefed to refute it; a completeness critic then named five
areas nobody had looked at and those were run and verified at the same bar. 27 + 18 confirmed.

- [x] **P-112 — A pending alarm was destroyed by any state change, restarting its latency**
      `chain.ts` tested `phase === 'pending'` before the `P-105` rule and answered `cancel`, so a
      probe blip — `down -> unknown` — deleted the alarm, and the reconnect armed a fresh one from
      the sensor's new `since`. A target down continuously behind a link flapping every three
      minutes never reached its five-minute latency: no notification, ever, and a notification
      queue that reads clean. The comment justified sending nothing, which is right; it never
      justified re-reading `since`. `P-105` had fixed the same shape for `notified` only.

      Now the only paths that cancel a pending alarm are the ones where the alarm is genuinely
      over — a recovery, or a pause — and everything else suspends, so the return picks the
      latency up where it stopped. Also fixed here: **a trigger retargeted onto the state the
      sensor is already in** now arms in the same reaction instead of cancelling and stopping.
      Reactions are driven by transitions, and a sensor Down for a week has none coming, so the
      retargeted trigger was inert and looked identical to a working one.

- [x] **P-113 — A trigger configured for `up` notified once per sensor, ever**
      `up` is an offered trigger state, and for an alarm armed on it the recovery branch is
      unreachable: `isRecovery` is true only for `up`, so leaving `up` suspended the alarm and the
      return matched `stillStanding` and took `resume` — and a resumed `notified` phase with no
      escalation and no repeat has nothing left to send. The operator who asked to be told when
      sensors come back was told once and then never again, silently, with the alarm row flipping
      suppressed true and false and nothing anywhere saying why. `endsAlarm` now takes the state
      the alarm is *about*: suspension is for an ongoing problem whose escalation must survive a
      blip, and there is no ongoing problem to escalate about a healthy sensor.

- [x] **P-114 — An unreadable trigger had its standing alarm deleted rather than skipped**
      The engine claims each trigger out of an orphan map and deletes whatever is left. It read
      the settings *before* claiming, so a trigger this build cannot parse — a downgrade, or a
      shape written by a newer build — logged a warning and then lost its alarm to the orphan
      sweep, cancelling an outage that was still happening on the strength of not understanding
      it. Claimed first now: this build cannot judge it, so it changes nothing.

- [x] **P-115 — Changing a trigger's kind orphaned the alarm and blocked the pair for ever**
      `PUT /triggers/:id` is whole-document and does not refuse a change of `kind`, so a standing
      threshold alarm can find itself under a state trigger. Its `state` is null, the engine's view
      collapses, and `reconcile` can only answer `idle` or `arm` — neither of which clears a row —
      while the trigger has already been claimed out of the orphan sweep. The row was unreachable
      by every clearing path: the state arm was swallowed by `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` while the
      counters reported it armed, so that (sensor, trigger) pair could never notify again, and the
      sweep re-read a `next_due_at` in the past at the scheduler's floor of 25 ms — forty times a
      second, for ever, each one logging that the settings were unreadable. The row is cleared now,
      and **the writes were reordered so clears land before arms**: `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` means
      a pair that is both cleared and armed in one reaction would otherwise have its insert
      swallowed by the row it is replacing and then lose that row to the delete.

- [x] **P-116 — The sweep erased an acknowledgement that landed while it was deciding**
      `due` read without a lock and `advance` wrote back blind, so an acknowledgement committing
      between the two halves was overwritten by the sweep's own `suppressed = false` and the
      escalation went out to everybody the operator had just told they were handling it. Both
      readers take the row lock now — `FOR UPDATE OF a SKIP LOCKED` on the sweep so two sweeps
      divide the work rather than queue, and `FOR UPDATE OF a` on the reaction's read, because
      they are the only two writers of the table and both are read-modify-write.

- [x] **P-117 — A resumed chain did not wake the scheduler**
      Only an arm poked it, on the reasoning that a reaction which cleared alarms has made the next
      due time later and never sooner. True of a clear; not true of a resume. A probe blip suspends
      the chain leaving nothing due, and the reconnect gives it back the escalation it had already
      earned, due at once — which the scheduler then slept straight past until the next unrelated
      event, however far away that was.

      Tests: 15 new — 9 in `notification-chain.test.ts` over the three chain rules, 5 in
      `notification-engine.test.ts` including a two-transaction test for the lock, and the resume
      poke. Mutation 7/7.

- [x] **P-118 — An HTML email inserted probe-controlled values with no escaping**
      The email transport declared no `bodyEscaping` at all, so `html: message.body` put whatever
      a device reported straight into a document. A sensor named after a tag lost a piece of its
      email; a hostile response to a `rest.custom` sensor wrote whatever it liked into the inbox
      of everybody on the notification list. The escaping machinery was already there and already
      right — `json`, `form` and `mrkdwn` all escape per *substituted value*, so the operator's
      own syntax survives — and email was simply not using it. An `html` escaping was added and
      the transport asks for it when the template's format is HTML.

- [x] **P-119 — A part-rejected email was recorded as delivered**
      `sendMail` resolves for a partial send and names the refusals in `rejected`, which was
      thrown away. An alarm that reached nobody on the list — every address unknown at the relay —
      was recorded `delivered`, counted as a success on Delivery Health and never retried; the one
      place an operator would look said it went out. Every recipient rejected is now a permanent
      failure naming them (retrying a RCPT TO rejection ten times changes nothing but how long the
      operator waits to find out), and a partial send is still delivered — somebody got it — with
      the missed addresses in the detail and a warning in the log.

- [x] **P-120 — A program template silently dropped its secret arguments**
      Two numbers for one limit: the schema allowed 32 visible arguments plus 8 secret, and the
      transport capped the concatenation at 32. A template using its full complement of visible
      arguments had every secret one dropped — so the program ran, exited non-zero for want of a
      credential nobody had removed, and the notification was recorded as a failed delivery with
      nothing anywhere to say why. The two schema limits are named constants now and the cap is
      derived from them.

- [x] **P-121 — Placeholders in a method's settings were substituted but never validated**
      A program template's arguments carry `N-06` placeholders like any other content, and
      `substitute`'s report of the ones it did not know was discarded — so a typo was neither
      refused at save, where the subject and body have been refused since `N-06`, nor reported at
      send. The program was handed the literal text `%lastvlaue` as an argument and failed for a
      reason nothing in the system could explain.

      **The fields are declared by the method rather than swept for.** A percent-encoded webhook
      URL is indistinguishable from a placeholder — `%AF` in an encoded segment is a name called
      `af` — so validating every string in a settings document would refuse templates that are
      perfectly correct. `placeholderFields` names the places an operator is invited to write one.

      Tests: 10 new — 3 on the HTML escaping, 1 on the transport's choice of it, 2 on partial
      rejection, 1 on the full argument complement reaching the program, and 3 on the settings
      walk including the encoded-URL case. Mutation 5/5.

- [x] **P-122 — One undeliverable digest window starved every other template's digests**
      A closed window whose template had since been disabled, or whose method has no transport in
      this build, holds requests the claim will never take. So it came back from `owing` on every
      pass, produced no members, and consumed one of the caller's slots for ever. Enough of them
      and no digest arrived anywhere — and nothing said so, because each pass looked like an
      ordinary quiet one. `owing` now asks the same question the claim does; the rows stay in the
      table, because re-enabling the template still owes those people the digest.

- [x] **P-123 — A failed digest came back as several fragments, each labelled part 1 of 1**
      Every member got its own jittered backoff, so a digest of forty that failed fell due at
      forty different moments. The next pass claimed whichever handful had ripened, assembled them
      into a digest of their own and labelled it complete. One outage arrived as half a dozen
      fragments, in an order the jitter chose. One delay is now drawn per part and shared.

- [x] **P-124 — Delivery Health counted failures by when they fell due**
      `notification_request.at` is when the obligation *fell due* — migration 016 says so, and
      that is the right meaning for a digest naming when an outage started. Counting failures by
      it asks a different question: `DEFAULT_RETRY` spends 45 to 90 minutes on nine backoffs
      against a 60-minute window, so a notification that exhausted its retries — the one failure
      the whole subsystem exists to prevent — usually fell due outside the window and counted
      zero. It stopped being `pending` at the same moment, so it dropped out of `oldest_retrying`
      too: **Delivery Health flipped from Down back to `ok` at the exact instant the alarm was
      abandoned**. Migration 043 adds `settled_at`, written on every terminal transition.

- [x] **P-125 — A message waiting on purpose was counted as undeliverable**
      A request collecting into an open digest window, or parked because its template is outside
      its activation schedule, is doing exactly what an operator configured. Both were counted as
