## Phase 11 — Flow monitoring (`V2-01`)

The first v2 subsystem, started 2026-09-09 with v1 complete except for `H-06` and `H-09`, both
of which need a Windows machine and a week with a hundred devices rather than any more code.

**Why this one first.** It is the top of the v2 ordering, and it is the last of the three
transports `CLAUDE.md` commits to building in-house — syslog (`T-20`) and WMI (`T-09`) shipped in
v1, and the reason is the same for all three: npm has no maintained option. It also needs no new
always-on dependency, so unlike clustering (`V2-06`) or SSO (`V2-07`) it clears the hard
constraints without an ADR.

**It follows a contract that already exists.** `T-06` built the listener shape and `T-20` proved
it transfers: one socket for the whole probe, a ring buffer, a cursor per sensor, and **nothing in
the listener that decides anything** — filtering, counting and retention are the sensor's
parameters and live in `@ms/sensors`, testable against a fabricated batch with no socket in sight.
A flow collector is the same shape with a harder decoder in front of it. Do not invent a third
arrangement.

**The tickets use the `B-` prefix** after `CAPABILITIES.MD §3.9`, "Bandwidth and traffic
analysis". `F-` is Phase 0.

- [x] **B-01 — NetFlow v5, decoded** · M · — · The fixed-layout format, as pure functions over a
      buffer: a 24-byte header and 48-byte records, no templates anywhere. Ships with a v5
      exporter in `packages/simulators` (`CLAUDE.md`: sensor types are tested against the
      simulator harness, never live network targets).

      **First because it is the format with no template cache in it.** Everything hard about flow
      collection lives in v9/IPFIX, and doing v5 first gets the decode contract, the fixtures and
      the simulator settled against a format that cannot fail in that particular way. `T-06` and
      `T-20` earned the same order.

      Things a v5 decoder gets wrong and the tests should say out loud: the counts in the header
      are records claimed rather than records present, so a truncated datagram must be refused
      rather than half-read; `sysUptime` is milliseconds since the exporter booted and the flow
      timestamps are in that same clock, so wall-clock conversion needs the header's `unix_secs`
      and is where an exporter with a wrong clock shows up; and the record's `srcaddr`/`dstaddr`
      are big-endian words, not strings.

      **B-01 outcome.** `@ms/sensors/flow` — `decodeNetflowV5` and `flowWindow` — with a v5
      exporter in `@ms/simulators` that writes the bytes out against Cisco's layout rather than
      running the decoder backwards, which is the rule `syslog-sender.ts` and `snmp-agent.ts`
      both state: a harness built from the code under test proves the decoder can read what the
      encoder wrote, and that loop closes whether or not either matches the specification.

      **The decoder is mostly its refusals, so the simulator can emit datagrams that are wrong on
      purpose** — a truncated one, a count nothing backs up, a v9 datagram at a v5 collector.
      Failures are a discriminated `FlowDecodeFailure` rather than a thrown string, because
      `B-02` counts them by kind and an operator reading a `malformed` counter needs to know
      whether the exporter is set to v9 or sending rubbish.

      **The header's `count` is a claim, not a length**, and that is the case that matters: v5
      rides UDP with no length negotiation, so a path MTU below what the exporter assumed clips
      the datagram silently. The claim is checked against the bytes present and a mismatch is
      refused whole — half a flow table is worse than none, because the missing half is invisible
      to everything downstream. Trailing bytes beyond the claim are ignored, since padding to a
      convenient size is a thing exporters do and is not a fault.

      `flowWindow` is a named function rather than three inlined lines because it is the
      arithmetic every NetFlow collector gets asked about: `first`/`last` are uptime
      milliseconds, and only the header knows what the wall clock was at that uptime. Every
      timestamp this produces inherits the exporter's opinion of the time, which nothing here can
      fix and everything here should make checkable.

      **Mutations 5/5**, each killed by exactly the case written for it: trusting the claimed
      count, reading `srcAddr` one field along, reading the sampling word without splitting mode
      from interval, adding the uptime delta instead of subtracting it, and dropping the
      nanosecond term. 12 tests; the workspace went 807 to 820 and the full suite is green at
      3,545.

- [x] **B-02 — The flow listener** · M · B-01 · The socket half: one UDP socket for the probe, the
      `NotificationRing`, a cursor per sensor, and the stats every listener reports — running,
      received, rejected, malformed, buffered, cursors, overwritten. Mechanical given `T-06` and
      `T-20`, and it should read that way; the injectable `open` is what makes it testable without
      a port.

      **The sender allow-list is a filter and not a lock**, and the comment must say so, exactly
      as the other two do. A flow exporter authenticates nothing.

      **B-02 outcome.** `openFlowReceiver` in `@ms/sensors/flow` and `FlowListener` in the probe,
      the syslog listener with a different socket in front of it. **UDP only**, unlike `T-20`:
      IPFIX over TCP and SCTP exist on paper and on essentially no switch, and offering them
      would advertise something nothing sends.

      **One notification per flow record, not per datagram.** A datagram holds one to thirty flows
      depending on how busy the exporter was, so buffering by datagram would make the ring's
      capacity mean thirty different things and a drop count uninterpretable.

      **The counter that is not like the others is `missed`** — flows the exporter's own
      `flowSequence` says it sent and this probe never received. UDP drops silently, so the
      exporter's running count is the only evidence loss exists at all; without it a link shedding
      a third of its flow export is indistinguishable from a quiet network. Kept **per exporter**,
      because two devices have unrelated sequences and one shared counter reports a loss on every
      alternate datagram. A sequence that goes *backwards* is a reboot, not a loss, and resyncs
      silently rather than reporting four billion missing flows.

      **The ticket was half the work, and a guard said so.** `probe-health-report.test.ts` scans
      `src/listeners/` and fails when something keeping counters is not named in
      `ProbeHealthSources` — the rule `P-61` bought and `P-64` widened, and it caught this
      immediately. Wiring it up meant five places, not one: the source key, the report fields, the
      channels on the Probe Health sensor type, the core's mapping (`?? null`, because absent must
      not read as a confident zero), the Prometheus names, and the wire type **and its JSON
      Schema** — without which the numbers validate away at the boundary and reach nothing, which
      is `P-61` exactly. `H-07`'s generator guard then caught `docs/sensor-reference.md` going
      stale, and it is regenerated.

      **Mutations 5/5 — and one survived first.** The case named *keeps a sequence per exporter*
      gave both exporters the same sequence numbers, which makes one shared counter and two
      separate ones behave identically, so it passed against the bug it was written for. Catalogued
      as entry 38: a fixture where every actor is identical cannot test per-actor anything. Fixed
      by putting the second exporter nine hundred ahead, and the mutation dies. 13 tests; the
      probe workspace went 285 to 298 and the full suite is green at 3,558.

- [x] **B-03 — NetFlow v9 and IPFIX, and the template cache** · L · B-01, B-02 · Where the
      difficulty actually is. A data record cannot be decoded without the template that describes
      it; templates arrive out of band, are keyed by (exporter, observation domain, template id),
      are re-sent on the exporter's own schedule, and can be redefined under a live id.

      **The case that decides the design is data arriving before its template**, which happens on
      every collector restart and after every exporter reboot. Dropping it is honest and loses the
      first interval; parking it needs a bounded buffer and an expiry, or it is a memory leak with
      a protocol in front of it. Whichever is chosen, the count of undecodable records is a
      channel — `CLAUDE.md`: backpressure is visible, never silent.

      IPFIX is not "v9 with a different version number": different set ids, enterprise-specific
      fields with a private enterprise number, and variable-length encoding v9 has no concept of.

      **B-03 outcome.** `TemplateCache` and `decodeFlowSets` in `@ms/sensors/flow`, with v9 and
      IPFIX exporters in `@ms/simulators` written against RFC 3954 and RFC 7011 rather than by
      running the decoder backwards.

      **One module for both formats, because they are one format with different constants** — and
      separating them would mean two copies of the set walk, the template parse and the record
      split, which are the three places a mistake is silent rather than loud. Every difference is
      enumerated in one `DIALECTS` table, and each is one somebody has shipped wrong: the header
      is 20 bytes against 16; v9's `count` is records where IPFIX's `length` is bytes; template
      sets are 0/1 against 2/3; only IPFIX has enterprise elements and variable-length fields; and
      **the sequence number counts packets in v9 and data records in IPFIX**, so `B-02`'s loss
      arithmetic cannot be applied to both the same way — the header says which, rather than
      leaving a caller to assume.

      **Keyed by exporter, observation domain and template id, all three.** Template 256 from one
      switch has nothing to do with 256 from another, and one switch may export several domains
      with independent ids. Keying on the id alone decodes one device's flows with another's
      layout and yields plausible, wrong numbers instead of an error — which is worse than
      dropping them, because nothing downstream can tell.

      **Data arriving before its template is dropped and counted**, which is the choice this
      ticket asked for. Parking it would need a bounded buffer and an expiry keyed the same three
      ways, and would buy one interval's flows on a path where exporters re-send templates on
      their own schedule anyway. The count is the honest part: it is the ordinary state for
      seconds after a restart and should fall to zero, and a count that *stays* above zero means
      an exporter whose template interval is longer than its data interval — a device
      misconfiguration that is invisible without it. **Templates are learnt as they are met, in
      order**, so the first datagram after a restart — template then data for that template —
      decodes fully rather than being dropped by a collector making two passes.

      **The cache is bounded and expiring because its key is attacker-influenced**: nothing
      authenticates a flow datagram, so anything that can reach the port can mint templates under
      invented domains until the process dies. Oldest-seen is evicted past the ceiling, which is
      also right for the honest case of an exporter churning ids. Expiry runs from when a template
      was last *seen*, not first learnt, or a live exporter's templates age out mid-conversation.
      Re-sending an identical template is not a redefinition, or every healthy exporter reads as
      constantly reconfiguring itself.

      **Mutations 7/7**: the IPFIX header read at v9's width (15 cases red), its template set id
      read as v9's (9), the enterprise bit ignored, the declared length ignored so padding is
      walked as sets, an unknown template decoded as empty rather than counted (6), the cache keyed
      on the id alone (7), and expiry measured from the first learn instead of the last sighting.
      38 tests; the sensors workspace went 820 to 858 and the full suite is green at 3,596.

- [x] **B-04 — The flow sensor type** · M · B-03 · Channels per protocol and per host, and the
      user-defined channel and filter rules `CAPABILITIES.MD §3.9` calls "custom flow variants".
      One file against the `SensorType` contract, per `docs/adding-a-sensor-type.md`.

      **No-data is not zero applies with force here.** An interval in which the exporter sent
      nothing is a gap, not a line drawn to the floor — and for a flow sensor that distinction is
      the difference between "the link was idle" and "the exporter stopped".

      **B-04 outcome.** `flow.netflow`, the third listener sensor on `T-06`'s contract unchanged —
      which is the return on having written a contract rather than a syslog listener.

      **Silence fails the check, and that is the one real decision in the file.** A flow exporter
      with nothing to report sends nothing at all: no heartbeat, no empty datagram, no keepalive.
      So an interval with no flows is *either* an idle link *or* an exporter that has stopped, been
      reconfigured or lost its route, and nothing in what arrived can separate them. Reporting zero
      picks the flattering reading silently and draws a confident line along the floor. Failing
      says the true thing — this sensor does not know — and `silenceIsIdle` is the escape hatch for
      a link that is quiet by nature, with the trade stated in the parameter's own description.

      **Rates, not totals**, so a limit survives a change of schedule: a sensor whose reading
      doubles when the interval doubles is one whose thresholds have to be re-derived every time
      anybody touches the scan rate.

      **Which needed a window, and finding that changed the contract.** The first version measured
      from `batch.since` to its own `Date.now()`, and every rate came out 0.1% low in a test that
      took a millisecond. On a probe that gap is the wait for a free worker — so a busy probe would
      have reported *less traffic* on the same link than a quiet one, and the dilution would have
      read as a network change. `ReceivedBatch` now carries `until`, set by the ring at the moment
      it drains, so the window is what the listener actually covered. Required rather than
      optional: a batch without a window is incomplete, and the compiler naming every fixture is
      the point. Counting sensors ignore it, which is why it arrived at the third listener sensor
      and not the first.

      **Channels**: bytes as primary, packets, flows, then per-protocol TCP/UDP/ICMP/other —
      because "the link is busy" and "the link is busy with UDP" are different findings and only
      the second says what to do next. `other` is the remainder, so a protocol nobody thought of
      lands somewhere instead of vanishing. Distinct sources is the per-host signal that fits a
      fixed channel set; a channel per host would be unbounded, and the object model has devices
      for that.

      **Custom channels are the "custom flow variants" `CAPABILITIES.MD §3.9` names**, each
      counting traffic matching **all** its rules — `T-20`'s reasoning, that "any" would widen a
      channel as rules are added. A key colliding with a built-in is dropped rather than allowed
      to shadow it in the reading array. **Rules match on CIDR rather than substring**, because
      `contains: "10.0."` also matches 110.0.4.1 and the operator who wrote it never finds out:
      the channel keeps reporting a plausible number.

      **Mutations 6/6**: silence reporting zero, rules matching any instead of all, CIDR falling
      back to a substring, the rate measured to `now()` instead of the window (7 cases red), a
      custom key shadowing a built-in, and the dropped-flows guard never firing. 25 tests; the
      full suite is green at 3,621.

- [x] **B-06 — one record shape, and the dialects actually wired to the socket** · M · B-03 ·
      **`B-03` shipped a decoder nothing calls.** `decodeFlowSets` is exported, has 26 tests and is
      reachable from `@ms/sensors/flow` — and `receiver.ts` still calls `decodeNetflowV5` and
      nothing else, so a real v9 or IPFIX exporter has every datagram refused as an unsupported
      version. The decoder is correct and unreachable, which is `P-61` again: the numbers were all
      right and they arrived nowhere. Found while starting `B-05`, by asking what the socket
      actually dispatches on.

      **The reason it needs a ticket rather than a one-line fix is that the three dialects do not
      produce the same thing.** v5 yields typed records, v9 and IPFIX yield `Map<elementId,
      Buffer>` of raw IANA elements, and `B-05`'s sFlow will yield parsed packet headers. Wiring
      them in as they are would put a per-dialect branch in the listener *and* another in the
      sensor, and the third one would be written by whoever adds `B-05`.

      So: normalise at the decoder boundary. One `FlowRecord` — addresses, ports, protocol,
      packets, octets, interfaces — that every dialect produces, and one `FlowMessage` carrying the
      exporter's sequence, what that sequence counts, and the undecodable count. The listener and
      the sensor then know nothing about dialects, which is the arrangement `T-06` already
      established for listeners and this subsystem quietly abandoned.

      **`samplingRate` belongs on the record, not the dialect.** v5 has a sampling interval in its
      header and sFlow is sampled by definition; a record that does not say what it stands for is a
      record somebody will read as an exact byte count.

      **B-06 outcome.** `FlowRecord` and `FlowMessage` in `record.ts`, `decodeFlowDatagram`
      dispatching on the version, and the receiver holding the `TemplateCache` — on the receiver
      rather than per datagram, because a cache built per message learns a template and forgets it
      before the data set three bytes later can use it.

      **Two things fell out that were wrong before and are not mutations of new code.**

      The **sequence arithmetic was one rule for three dialects**, which `B-03` had already
      established could not be right: v5 counts exported flows, IPFIX counts data records, and v9
      counts *packets* — one per datagram. `B-02`'s `missed` advanced by the record count in every
      case, so a healthy v9 exporter would have read as losing every flow but one, every datagram,
      for ever. Keyed per exporter *and* per meaning now, because one device can send both.

      And **`samplingRate` was nowhere**. A 1-in-100 sampled exporter's `octets` are a hundredth of
      the traffic; summing them unscaled under-reports by exactly N, silently, on the busy links
      somebody is watching. It is on every record, `1` where nothing samples — and an interval of
      zero reads as one, not as zero, because "not sampling" means a packet stands for itself.
      v9/IPFIX report sampling through an options template, which is a lookup this does not do
      yet; that limitation is written where the field is set rather than left to be discovered.

      **`undecodable` reaches Probe Health**, which `B-03`'s own ticket asked for and `B-03` did
      not do — through all five places again, ending at `flowUndecodable`.

      **Mutations 5/5, and one survived first.** "Elements read at a fixed 4-byte width" passed
      every test, because the 4-and-8-byte case exercises the `BigInt` branch at 8 and nothing
      touched the integer read at any other width. IPFIX §6.2 permits any reduced size and 6-byte
      counters ship. Covered at 2, 3, 5 and 6 bytes, plus a 64-bit value past 2^53, and the
      mutation dies. Full suite green at 3,638.

- [x] **B-05 — sFlow** · L · B-02, B-06 · A different protocol wearing a similar name: sampled packet
      headers and interface counters in XDR, not flow records. It shares the listener and shares
      nothing else, which is why it is last and its own ticket rather than a variant of `B-01`.

      **`B-06` was added when this ticket was started** and the socket turned out to dispatch on
      nothing: sFlow would otherwise have been the third decoder wired in by hand, and the second
      one nothing called.

      **B-05 outcome, and Phase 11 is complete.** `decodeSflow` in `@ms/sensors/flow`, producing
      `B-06`'s `FlowRecord` like every other dialect, with an sFlow agent in `@ms/simulators` that
      writes the XDR against the v5 spec rather than by running the decoder backwards.

      **Nothing in an sFlow datagram is a flow.** NetFlow reports accounting — a flow table with
      byte counts. sFlow copies the first hundred-odd bytes of one packet in N and sends that, so
      every record here is *reconstructed* from a packet header, and the only thing making it
      comparable to a NetFlow record is `samplingRate`.

      **Two fields decide whether the numbers mean anything.** `frame_length` is the length on the
      wire — 1,514 where the copied header is 128 — so reporting the copy under-reports by an
      order of magnitude and looks entirely plausible doing it. And `sampling_rate` is carried per
      *sample*, not per datagram, because an agent may sample interfaces at different rates.

      **Which found a defect in `B-04`.** The sensor summed `octets` without scaling, so an sFlow
      exporter at the ordinary 1-in-2,048 would have reported a two-thousandth of the traffic on
      the busiest link in the building. Fixed here, along with saying "estimated from N sampled" in
      the message — an operator comparing this against an interface counter needs to know why the
      two do not agree exactly.

      **Counter samples are counted and decoded no further, deliberately.** They carry lifetime
      interface counters, and putting one into a field this subsystem reads as an interval delta
      would be wrong in a way nothing downstream could see. `snmp.traffic` already covers that
      ground; making them interface sensors is its own ticket if anybody wants it.

      **The version collision is real and is handled by width.** NetFlow's version is a 16-bit word
      and sFlow's is 32-bit, so a NetFlow v5 datagram starts `00 05` and an sFlow v5 one starts
      `00 00 00 05`. A collector guessing on port number would decode one as the other on any site
      sending both to 2055.

      The packet parse handles what a real switch sends: 802.1Q and Q-in-Q tags, the IHL rather
      than an assumed twenty bytes (options would otherwise be read as ports), fragments past the
      first (no transport header, and the offset says so), and the expanded sample encoding, which
      widens the source id and both interface fields.

      **Mutations 6/6**: the header length reported instead of the wire length, VLAN tags not
      skipped, a fixed 20-byte IPv4 header, an IPv6 agent address skipped as four bytes, the
      sensor's scaling removed, and a fragment's payload read as ports. 25 tests here and 31 on the
      sensor; the full suite is green at 3,669.

      setting with no effect must not hold a v1 probe on its old version. It was first written

      **Done 2026-10-02. The arithmetic reproduces; the device behaviour is taken on trust.**
      Before any change, `flow-listener.test.ts` rendered v5 datagrams from one address as two

      the engine further on was 895 ahead of the other's count, and each of the other's was
      taken as a restart.

      counts `flow_sequence` per engine. Nothing in this repository says a device does: v5 has
      no specification, the decoder's own comments call it a layout Cisco froze in 1996 and say
      only that bytes 20 and 21 are an engine type and an engine id, and no capture of a
      two-engine exporter is here to read. The per-engine reading is this ticket's and `B-10`'s
      premise, not a cited fact. It is safe either way round only in one direction — see below.

      since an id is unique only within a type; the listener's key and `MAX_SEQUENCES` are
      `B-10`'s, unchanged. An exporter with one engine sends the same pair in every datagram
      and is followed exactly as before. `docs/administration.md` says v5 is followed per engine
      and why.

      the same id on another type, none missed across ten datagrams, then a three-flow gap
      inside one engine while the others run on, read as 3. One at the dispatch for what the
      decoder names (`0/0` by default, each byte on its own side), replacing the case that
      pinned v5's scope as absent. `probe-flow.test.ts` passes unchanged. **Mutations 10/10**:
      no scope, the id alone, the type alone, the two swapped, a constant, no separator, the
      scope out of the listener's key against the new case alone, each header byte read from
      the other's offset, and no bound.

      **Not done, and the cost if the premise is wrong.** A device that keeps *one* count for
      the address and stamps each datagram with whichever engine switched the flows would now
      be split into sequences that each see only some of the datagrams, and every datagram the
      other engine sent in between reads as a gap: false `flowMissed` in the other direction.
      Deciding between the two needs a capture from a multi-engine chassis, which the field
      test has not had.

## Phase 12 — Maps and dashboards (`V2-02`)

The second v2 subsystem, started 2026-09-09 with Phase 11 complete. `CAPABILITIES.MD §6` asks for
a drag-and-drop designer producing an HTML page: status icons, live graphs, data tables, sensor
lists, connector lines, geo maps, custom HTML and background images, publicly shareable by URL,
with 5-star maps in the Home menu.

**A map is not a tree object.** The hierarchy is Root → Probe → Group → Device → Sensor → Channel
and a map is none of those; `§9` grants access to "tree, libraries, maps and reports" per group,
which makes it a first-class entity with its own storage, its own API and its own RBAC surface.
That is why `G-01` exists before any pixel does.

**Three of these were gated on a decision rather than on effort, and all three are now settled.**
`ADR-002` was written before any code because two of them change the widget model: public share
links exist as per-map revocable bearer tokens with an expiry, and custom HTML runs in a sandboxed
iframe. The third, geographical maps, is `ADR-004`: the product ships no tiles and no default
provider, takes a URL template an operator configures, and draws the widgets over the `G-05`
background when there is none — so a tile provider is an operator's choice rather than a network
dependency in a product whose whole architecture is "one service an operator installs". None of
the three was built merely because it is on a capability list.

**The tickets use the `G-` prefix** for the graphical views `CAPABILITIES.MD §6` describes. `M-` is
the state machine and `U-` is the Phase 5 UI.

- [x] **G-01 — The map entity** · M · — · Storage, migration with a tested rollback, CRUD API, and
      access by group the way `§9` grants it. No widgets and no canvas: this is the thing every
      other ticket here needs, and the one that decides whether a map is versioned, how it is
      scoped, and what happens to it when an object it points at is deleted.

      **That last question is the interesting one.** A map holds references to sensors that can be
      deleted underneath it. A dangling reference must render as a visibly broken widget rather
      than an empty space — an operator looking at a map with a hole in it should be told the
      sensor is gone, not shown a dashboard that quietly stopped mentioning the thing that failed.

      **G-01 storage landed 2026-09-09; the CRUD API is still open.** Migration 044 creates `map`
      and `map_access`, and `migrator.test.ts`'s existing "forward and all the way back" case
      covers the rollback.

      **The dangling-reference question is answered by the storage shape, not left to the API.**
      Widgets live in a `jsonb` layout, so a foreign key is not available — and that is the right
      outcome rather than a limitation. Rows in a child table would have to choose between
      `ON DELETE CASCADE`, where the widget silently disappears and the dashboard stops mentioning
      what failed, and `RESTRICT`, where deleting a sensor fails because somebody once put it on a
      map. A document keeps the reference, the object goes, and **`G-02` must render a widget that
      says so** — a requirement this schema creates rather than a detail it leaves open. Asserted:
      a widget naming a deleted object is still on the canvas afterwards, still naming it.

      The cost is that "which maps reference sensor 42?" is a document scan. Deferred on purpose:
      the index wants the shape `G-02` settles on, and building one now would index a guess.

      **Access is flat, unlike `object_access`.** That table walks ancestors because objects nest
      and maps do not, so a grant is a grant. Both share migration 033's `access_right` enum and
      `access_rank` ordering rather than declaring a second copy that would eventually disagree
      about what `write` means. A map carries a `version` for optimistic concurrency, because a
      designer is the place where silently discarding somebody's work is most visible.

      **Mutations 5/5** — a case-sensitive name index, the priority range dropped, the
      `updated_at` trigger never created, a group's grants outliving the group, and a nullable
      layout. 10 tests; the full suite is green at 3,679.

      **The repository, service and routes landed the same day, and G-01 is done.**

      **Access is resolved in `MapService` and nowhere else**, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s rule for
      inheritance applied to the thing that will have two callers: the authenticated API, and
      `G-06`'s public route, which arrives with no principal at all. The route-level `onObject(...)`
      helper resolves against the *object tree* and could not have been reused — pointing it at a
      map id asks the wrong table a question it cannot answer — so every route is `READS` and the
      real decision happens one layer down.

      Four rules, each asserted rather than described: an administrator group short-circuits the
      lookup, because "may do anything, including to things that do not exist yet" must not depend
      on a row somebody can delete; the account's role caps what its groups granted (`A-04`) and a
      token's scope caps its owner (`A-06`), both only ever lowering; granting needs `full`, so a
      `write` holder may edit the canvas without deciding who else sees it; and **a map the caller
      cannot read answers 404 rather than 403**, because distinguishing them turns the error into
      an oracle for enumerating which ids exist.

      **A creator's primary group is granted `full` in the same transaction as the insert.**
      Without it a non-administrator creates a map and immediately loses it — access is per group
      and a new map has no grants — which is the kind of thing a user finds rather than a test.

      **The version goes in the `WHERE` clause, not a comparison before the write**, so the
      zero-row result *is* the conflict and there is no window for the other designer to commit
      into. `If-Match` is required on a PATCH: last-write-wins on a canvas is somebody's afternoon
      disappearing without a message.

      **Two guards caught things on the way.** `listFor` used `SELECT DISTINCT` with an ordering
      expression outside the select list — rewritten as `EXISTS`, which avoids the duplicate rows
      a two-group grant produces rather than de-duplicating after the fact. And `H-07`'s API
      reference generator **refused to run**: it derives its route list from `server.ts` and will
      not produce a reference that silently omits a gated group, so `mapRoutes` had to be given a
      stub before it would write. That is the guard doing exactly what it was built for.

      **Mutations 6/6 on the access decisions** — an unreadable map answering forbidden instead of
      absent, the role ceiling dropped, the token scope dropped, the creator's grant removed (8
      cases red), granting needing only `write`, and the version leaving the `WHERE` clause. 25
      tests across the schema and the service; the full suite is green at 3,694.

- [x] **G-02 — Widgets, and where their data comes from** · L · G-01 · The widget model — status
      icon, sensor list, data table — and one resolver that fills them, in the core rather than in
      the browser. A map with forty widgets must not be forty round trips, and a widget must not be
      able to read an object the viewer cannot see: the resolver is the one place that can enforce
      both.

      **Landed 2026-09-09.** `widgets.ts` reads a `jsonb` layout into `Widget`s and `resolver.ts`
      fills them: one object lookup and one access resolution for the whole canvas, whatever the
      widget count.

      **Correcting this row, written the same day.** It first said "one history read for the whole
      canvas", and that is not true: `#data` calls `latestForSensor` once per table widget and runs
      the sensor-list subtree query once per list widget, sequentially. The object lookup and the
      access resolution are one pass and are the two the test counts; the per-widget reads are not,
      and forty table widgets are roughly a hundred and twenty round trips. Found by `G-03` looking
      for the route that would serve this, which is why that route is `G-10` and not part of the
      designer — exposing an N+1 as an endpoint is a worse thing to ship than not having the
      endpoint yet.

      **The audience is a choice at the call site, not an absent principal.** `MapAudience` is a
      discriminated union — `{ kind: 'viewer', viewer, holdsFull }` or `{ kind: 'public' }` — so
      `G-06`'s share link cannot be built by passing `undefined` and hoping the resolver treats it
      as anonymous. An optional viewer would have made "nobody is looking" and "I forgot to thread
      the principal through" the same value, and the second one fails open. The public branch
      returns every requested id as visible because the token already decided which map may be
      seen; that decision belongs to the route that minted it, not to a null check here.

      **A widget naming something gone stays on the canvas** — `G-01`'s requirement, now asserted
      from the rendering half. It resolves to `state: 'unavailable'`, keeps its title and its
      position, and carries a `reason` only when the viewer holds `full`. Everyone else, the public
      audience included, is told the tile is unavailable and not whether the id is deleted or
      merely invisible to them: the same oracle `G-01` closed by answering 404 for an unreadable
      map, closed again one layer in, because a map anybody may embed is a place to ask that
      question forty times a second.

      **Forty widgets are one object lookup, counted rather than timed.** The test wraps the
      `Queryable` and counts the queries matching the object lookup, so a slow machine cannot make
      it pass or fail for the wrong reason. Table widgets read through `HistoryService`'s
      `latestForSensor` instead of querying the readings directly — it applies a staleness window
      that is a multiple of *this sensor's* interval, so a sensor Down for a day shows a gap rather
      than yesterday's healthy figure. `no-data is not zero` is easiest to break in a new reader.

      **Malformed widgets are kept as problems, not dropped**, and the layout is capped at
      `MAX_WIDGETS = 200`: a document a user can grow without limit is a document that can be made
      to cost the server an unbounded resolve.

      **Mutations 6/6, and the sixth is why this ticket has a catalogue entry.** The forty-widget
      case originally pointed all forty widgets at one sensor — and the resolver de-duplicates ids
      before it queries, so one lookup and forty lookups behaved identically and the case passed
      against exactly the bug it exists to catch. Found by the mutation surviving, fixed with forty
      distinct ids, and written down as entry 39 of
      `docs/findings/2026-09-04-tests-that-passed-for-the-wrong-reason.md` — the same shape as
      entry 38, four hours earlier, in a different subsystem: a fixture where every actor is the
      same actor. 15 tests; the full suite is green at 3,709.

- [x] **G-03 — The designer canvas** · L · G-02 · Drag, drop, resize, snap, undo. Keyboard-operable
      throughout, per `U-11` — a designer that can only be used with a mouse fails the same WCAG
      criteria the tree did, and for the same reason.

      **Landed 2026-09-09.** `maps/canvas.ts` is the geometry, the undo stack and the keyboard,
      decided without a DOM; `MapDesigner.tsx` is the surface; `/maps` lists and creates and
      `/maps/:id` opens one.

      **The first thing this ticket found had nothing to do with the canvas: `G-01`'s routes were
      never mounted.** `ApiServer` takes `maps` as an option and declines to register the routes
      without one — the right shape, so that a build without maps has no maps API rather than an
      empty one — and the only caller passing a service was a test. Every route `G-01` shipped
      answered 404 in the binary anybody actually runs. One line in `main.ts`.

      **Every pointer gesture has a key, because 2.1.1 has no exception for a canvas.** Tab reaches
      a widget, arrows move it, Shift and an arrow resizes it, Delete removes it, Ctrl or Cmd with
      Z steps back and Escape abandons a drag in progress. One decision table — `canvasCommand` —
      serves both the keyboard and the toolbar, so Undo and Ctrl+Z cannot drift apart. Each edit is
      announced in a live region: on a canvas the result of a key press is a *position*, and there
      is nothing for a screen reader to read unless the position is said out loud.

      **A tab stop per tile, which is `U-11`'s own lesson deliberately reversed.** The tree's
      15,000 stops were on a navigation surface where Tab was a wrong turn; here every tile is a
      thing being edited, the ceiling is 200, and a roving tab stop would need arrow keys to change
      the selection — which is what moves a tile.

      **A drag is one undo entry, not one per frame**, which is why `draft` (canvas only) and
      `record` (one entry for the gesture) are separate calls; and a drag that ends where it began
      records nothing, because an undo button that visibly does nothing reads as broken. The
      dragged box is computed from the origin every frame rather than accumulated, so the rounding
      happens once per drag instead of once per pointer move — the classic snapping drift, and
      invisible to a test that moves the pointer once.

      **Overlap is allowed, and refused in exactly one place.** A map is a picture: a label over a
      background, a legend across a group box. What is refused is a *new* tile landing on top of
      the last one, because that looks like the Add button did nothing.

      **The object picker is a search, not a dropdown**, for the same reason the tree is virtual: a
      `<select>` holding the first two hundred of 5,000 sensors is a control that quietly cannot
      reach most of the estate.

      **A refused save keeps the work.** `If-Match` carries the version; a `MAP_CHANGED` answer
      leaves the canvas exactly as it is and says somebody else saved, because that is the one
      moment an afternoon exists only in this tab.

      Two things deliberately left: the API does not tell a client what right it holds on a map, so
      the designer offers editing to everybody and surfaces the core's 403 if it comes — adding a
      `right` to the map response is a `G-01` change and belongs with `G-06`'s sharing work; and
      nothing here resolves widget data, which is `G-10`.

      **`fit` was wrong and a test caught it**: it capped the width against the tile's own x, which
      is right for a resize handle and wrong for a document that put the tile at column 999 — where
      x is the thing that is broken. A tile written off-canvas came back 2 units wide.

      **Mutations 8/8** — truncating the pointer distance, dropping the no-op guard on `record`,
      swapping move and resize on Shift, putting the accelerators behind the selection check, the
      old `fit`, a selection that survives its tile, an unbounded history, and recording every
      pointer move. The last one **survived**: "one Ctrl+Z puts the tile back" is true whether the
      drag recorded one step or five, because the entry pushed at the end of the drag is the origin
      either way. Asserting that nothing is left to undo kills it — entry 40 of
      `docs/findings/2026-09-04-tests-that-passed-for-the-wrong-reason.md`. 59 tests; the web
      workspace went 357 to 416, and the backend suite is unchanged and green at 3,709 — this
      ticket adds no backend logic beyond the one line in `main.ts`.

      **Not verified in a browser.** The dev core requires authentication and reaching the designer
      means logging in, which is a credential this session does not enter. The keyboard, the drag,
      the undo stack and the save are covered by the 59 tests above, including a real `PointerEvent`
      — jsdom ships none, so `fireEvent.pointerDown` builds a bare `Event`, every property the
      handler reads arrives `undefined`, and the drag case silently exercised nothing until a
      `MouseEvent` subclass was put in its place.

- [x] **G-04 — Live graphs on a map** · M · G-02, U-05 · The uPlot charts the sensor detail page
      already draws, at a size somebody chose, updating from the same WebSocket stream rather than
      polling per widget.

      **Landed 2026-09-09, on top of `G-10`**, which is the same day's other ticket and had to come
      first: a live graph on a map needs a map you can look at, and until the view route existed
      the only way to see one was the designer.

      **`/maps/:id` is now the map and `/maps/:id/design` is the designer**, the other way round
      from how `G-03` shipped it. Opening a map to find an editing surface is the same mistake as a
      document that opens in a form.

      **One socket and one clock for the whole canvas.** Every tile showing a state reads it from a
      single `useStateStream(null)` — the whole tree, because a map's widgets can name anything and
      a subtree subscription would silently stop updating the tiles pointing outside it — and every
      graph refreshes on one shared interval. The failure this avoids is the one a widget-shaped
      codebase drifts into: twenty tiles with twenty timers and twenty sockets, a page that never
      settles. A tile owns no schedule of its own.

      **A tile prefers the stream to the map it was loaded with**, which is the whole of "live". A
      resolved map is a snapshot taken when the request was made; a wall display left open for a
      day would show that snapshot for ever otherwise.

      **The series are fetched per graph tile and are not in the resolved map.** One request brings
      back every tile's identity, state and channels; a week of buckets for every graph on a canvas
      is not a thing to fold into it, and each tile draws a range its author chose. Ranges are per
      tile — the point of a week beside an hour is the comparison — which is the opposite of the
      sensor page's one control for the whole tab, and safe here only because every tile is
      labelled with its own period.

      **One chart per tile, not one per unit.** `U-05` splits a sensor's channels into a chart per
      unit because a shared y-axis across units is the dual-axis lie. A tile has room for one
      chart, so it draws the group the primary channel is in — keeping the one-axis rule rather
      than bending it to fit.

      **Mutations 7/7** across both tickets — the widest staleness window applied to every sensor,
      the subtree answers keyed by sensor instead of by root, the `MapError` translation removed,
      an unclamped graph range, every viewer reduced to `read`, the snapshot preferred over the
      stream, and a range running forward from now. 7 web tests and 12 core; the web workspace goes
      416 to 423 and the backend 3,709 to 3,721.

      **What is not covered: the drawn chart.** `uPlot` does not mount under jsdom — it needs a
      canvas and a `ResizeObserver` — so what these tests assert is which sensor, which period and
      which refresh, not the pixels. The drawing itself is `U-05`'s component, unchanged. Together
      with `G-03`'s note about the browser, the visual half of Phase 12 is still unverified.

- [x] **G-05 — Connector lines and background images** · M · G-03 · The part that makes a map a
      map rather than a grid of tiles. An uploaded background is a file this system stores on
      behalf of an operator, which is a first for it — where it lives and what bounds it are part
      of the ticket.

      **Landed 2026-09-09, and the file question got an ADR.** `ADR-003` settles where an
      operator's uploaded file lives, because more of them are coming — `G-07`'s custom HTML,
      report templates, the inevitable device photograph — and deciding it per feature is how a
      system ends up with three answers.

      **The bytes live in PostgreSQL, and the deciding argument is backup.** An operator who backs
      up the database has backed up their maps; the moment a background is a file under the data
      directory that stops being true, and nobody discovers it until the day they restore. One
      thing to install has a matching rule: one thing to back up. Deletion becomes a foreign key
      rather than a reaper, and `V2-06`'s clustering replicates rows but not one node's disk. The
      cost — large objects in a relational database — is bounded by 2 MiB and by what this is for;
      a feature wanting hundreds of megabytes gets its own ADR rather than being smuggled in under
      this one.

      **A table of its own, not a column on `map`.** `map` is read on every list and every view,
      and a row carrying two megabytes of TOASTed image is a cost paid by every caller who did not
      want it.

      **The declared `Content-Type` is never consulted.** `images.ts` reads the file's own header —
      PNG's IHDR, JPEG's segment walk, WebP's three forms — and a file whose bytes are not one of
      those three is refused whatever it is called. The dimensions come from the same read, because
      asking the client for them is the same claim again and decoding the image to learn them means
      running a decoder over hostile bytes. Every read is bounds-checked: a truncated header is a
      400, never an exception.

      **The JPEG reader walks segment lengths rather than scanning for a frame marker**, which is
      not fussiness: an Exif segment routinely contains a whole second JPEG, and a scan finds the
      thumbnail's header first and reports a 160×120 background.

      **SVG is refused, and `ADR-002` is why.** An SVG is a document that can carry script, and
      Decision 2 there already settled that operator-supplied documents run in a sandboxed iframe
      and never in the application's own page — which is exactly where a background is drawn. The
      response carries `nosniff`, `default-src 'none'` and no filename regardless.

      **The bytes are addressed by content**: the SHA-256 is the strong `ETag`, so a wall display
      re-opens with a 304 instead of the floor plan. Not immutable caching — the URL is stable
      across a replacement, and a long max-age would leave somebody looking at the plan they had
      just replaced.

      **Connectors are widget ids in the same document, not a table.** A line is a statement about
      the picture, and the same sensor can be on a canvas twice — a connector to *the sensor* would
      be ambiguous about which tile it meant. Removing a tile takes its lines with it, because a
      connector whose endpoint is missing has no geometry: it cannot be drawn as a broken line the
      way a widget is drawn as a broken tile, so the core reports it and the designer never saves
      one.

      **The lines are drawn once and said twice.** The SVG is `aria-hidden` — a `<line>` has no
      name worth announcing — and the same connections are a list of text: visually hidden on the
      board, and visible in the designer where each row carries the button that cuts that line.
      One list, both jobs, and it is also the only way to remove a connector without deleting a
      widget.

      **Two things this ticket found in code that was already green.** A Fastify reply is
      thenable, so `await reply.header(...)` waits for a response nobody has sent yet — every
      conditional request for a background hung until a test sat on it for two minutes. And the
      security-headers hook overwrote whatever a route had set, so the stricter
      `default-src 'none'` on an operator's uploaded image was being widened to the application's
      own `'self'` on the way out; every header there is a floor, and the hook now says so.

      **The API reference had been missing `GET /maps/:id/view` since `G-10`** — the generator
      builds a server from stubs and had no resolver, so the route was never registered and the
      hygiene check compared two documents that agreed with each other. One line in the generator.

      **Mutations 8/8** — a JPEG scan instead of a segment walk, no ceiling on claimed dimensions,
      the header hook overwriting a stricter policy, an upload needing only `read`, a connector to
      a widget that is not there, a deleted tile leaving its lines, lines drawn centre to centre,
      and A→B and B→A as two different lines. 15 image tests, 9 API tests, 2 resolver tests and 22
      in the browser; the web workspace goes 423 to 445 and the backend 3,721 to 3,748.

      Deliberately not built: connector styling. A line is a line until somebody asks for more, and
      a colour or a dash pattern in the document is a thing every later renderer has to keep
      honouring.

- [x] **G-06 — Public share URLs** · M · G-02 · **Decided 2026-09-09: build it, token-gated —
      `ADR-002` Decision 1.** A per-map bearer token, revocable, with a mandatory expiry, on one
      unauthenticated route that serves that map's widgets and nothing else: no object id, no tree
      walk, no drill-through, no object API. The blast radius of a leaked link is exactly what the
      person who made it was looking at. What it still leaks — hostnames, sensor names, what is
      failing — the sharing UI says at the point of sharing. **The resolver must therefore work
      with no principal at all**, which is a constraint on `G-02` rather than a detail of this
      ticket. The original framing follows.

      **Gated: this is a security posture, not a feature.** PRTG offers it and the capability list carries it, and it means an unauthenticated
      route returning live monitoring data — topology, hostnames, what is failing — to anybody with
      a link. Phase 9 spent a lot of effort making every read answer to a principal. Before any
      code: decide whether this exists at all, and if it does, whether the link is a bearer token
      with an expiry and a revocation list, whether it is per-map, and what it may show. Write it
      down as an ADR; `A-11` is the precedent for treating an access decision that way.

      **Landed 2026-09-09.** `GET /api/v1/public/maps/:token` serves a map to somebody with no
      session; `/shared/:token` is the page they open. Migration 046 stores the links, and the
      whole public surface is one file — `api/routes/public-maps.ts` — under one path prefix.

      **The token is stored as a SHA-256 and nowhere else**, the same as `api_token`. The
      consequence is that the URL is shown once and can never be shown again, which is a property
      rather than an inconvenience: a link that can be re-read from the system is a link that
      leaks with a database backup. The sharing panel says so at the moment it shows the URL,
      because somebody who loses it will otherwise hunt for a button that cannot exist.

      **An expiry is required and bounded at both ends.** In the past is a link that never works,
      which reads as a bug; past a year is the permanent unauthenticated route `ADR-002` refuses to
      allow. `expires_at` is `NOT NULL` here where `api_token`'s is nullable, and that difference
      is the decision: an API token at least belongs to an account somebody can be asked about.

      **Expired, revoked and never-existed are one answer, in one wording.** Telling them apart
      would tell a guesser which of their attempts was once a real link, which is the only useful
      signal this route could give them. Revocation and expiry are in the `WHERE` clause rather
      than checked afterwards, so a row that comes back *is* a link that works — no second step
      anybody can forget, and no window where two queries disagree.

      **Making, listing and revoking need `full`, not `write`.** `write` moves a widget; `full`
      decides a map's audience, and a public link is the largest audience there is.

      **Rate limited per link, and only per link.** The global limiter already bounds every
      unauthenticated caller by address, so a second per-address bucket here would be a second
      policy to keep in step with the first. What that limiter cannot see is the *link*: a URL
      posted somewhere public is hit from a thousand addresses, each comfortably within its own
      budget. The bucket map is bounded and evicts the oldest window, because the caller chooses
      the keys — an unbounded map of counters is a memory leak with a remote control.

      **Every method on `MapService` is either viewer-gated or token-gated.** Serving a shared
      map's background could have taken a map id one query more cheaply; it takes the token
      instead, because a `backgroundOfShared(mapId)` is a method that hands an operator's uploaded
      image to anybody who can call it, and the invariant is worth more than the query.

      **`ADR-002` has two amendments, written rather than diverged from.** There are two public
      routes, not one — the second serves the map's background, which did not exist when the ADR
      was written, and the alternative was two megabytes of base64 in every poll. And the paths
      differ: the API is `/api/v1/public/maps/:token`, where the authentication hook can exempt
      exactly one namespace, while the page a person is given is `/shared/:token`, which the app
      shell has to serve. The rule that survives is the one that mattered: the public surface is a
      token-scoped namespace, and reading one file answers "what can a stranger reach?".

      **A shared map's graphs show current readings rather than history**, for the ADR's own fourth
      reason: an unauthenticated range query per graph tile is exactly the work that has to be
      bounded. The page shares the *same canvas component* as the signed-in board — a second
      renderer would drift the first time a widget kind was added, and the person who made the link
      is the one person who cannot see what a stranger sees.

      **Mutations 8/8, and the ninth is a finding rather than a defect.** Killed: a revoked link
      still opening, an expired one still opening, `write` being enough to publish, no ceiling on
      the expiry, the token stored as itself, a rate limit that never refuses, an exemption
      narrowed to an exact path, and `last_used_at` never written. The one that *survived* widened
      the exemption to every path under `/api/` — and every route still answered 401, because
      authentication and authorization are separate hooks and the second refuses an anonymous
      caller on anything not marked `PUBLIC`. The path exemption cannot open a route on its own.
      That is the defence in depth working, and it is worth knowing that a test asserting "still
      needs a session" cannot see the difference.

      7 unit tests for the token and the limiter, 10 API tests, 9 in the browser; the web workspace
      goes 445 to 454 and the backend 3,748 to 3,765.

- [x] **G-07 — Custom HTML widgets** · M · G-02 · **Decided 2026-09-09: sandboxed iframe —
      `ADR-002` Decision 2.** `<iframe sandbox srcdoc>` with no `allow-same-origin` and a
      restrictive CSP: safe by construction rather than by a sanitiser being complete and staying
      complete. It costs theming and layout freedom, which is the right cost. **Sharper because
      `G-06` exists**: operator HTML on a public map is arbitrary content served to strangers from
      this system's origin, so without the sandbox a map author who is not an administrator could
      publish script under the monitoring domain. The two features are individually defensible and
      together are a phishing kit unless the sandbox is non-negotiable. The original framing
      follows.

      **Gated: arbitrary operator HTML in the application is XSS by design.** The honest options are a sandboxed iframe with no same-origin
      access, a strict sanitiser with a small allowlist, or not building it. Which one changes the
      widget model, so it is decided before `G-02` finalises and not after. Note the interaction
      with `G-06`: custom HTML on a publicly shared map is operator-supplied content served
      unauthenticated, which is a different question again.

      **Landed 2026-09-09.** A `html` widget kind whose markup renders inside
      `<iframe sandbox srcdoc>` — and `sandbox=""`, no tokens at all, which is stricter than the
      ADR asked for.

      **The markup is never cleaned, and that is the decision rather than an omission.** Nothing
      between the textarea and the frame rewrites what an operator typed: a sanitiser is safe for
      as long as it is complete and stays complete against the whole history of browser parsing
      quirks, while an opaque-origin frame with no script, no forms and no navigation is safe by
      construction. A half-cleaner in front of that would be a weaker second defence somebody
      eventually leans on.

      **`srcdoc`, never a served URL.** A route serving operator markup from this origin is a page
      somebody can open in a tab, and an operator-authored page on the monitoring domain is exactly
      the phishing kit `ADR-002` refuses — sharper still now that `G-06` exists and the map may be
      public. The same component draws the tile on the shared page, so there is one sandbox rather
      than two.

      **Why no scripts at all, when the ADR only refused `allow-same-origin`.** A `srcdoc` document
      inherits the embedding page's content security policy, which is `default-src 'self'` with no
      `unsafe-inline` — so inline styles, style attributes and third-party images are inert in
      there whatever the sandbox says, and granting `allow-scripts` would have been a promise the
      policy breaks. **A custom widget is markup and text**, and the designer says so under the
      textarea rather than leaving somebody to spend an afternoon on a stylesheet that cannot load.
      Recorded as an amendment to `ADR-002`. The safety argument rests on the sandbox attribute,
      which is well defined; the inheritance is read from the specification and is not verified in
      a browser here.

      **A widget that draws no object no longer has to name one.** `objectId` is `number | null`,
      required for the four kinds that read something and dropped for the one that does not —
      because a sensor id a widget never reads is a field a later ticket starts believing, and
      inventing one would eventually block that sensor's deletion. The resolver skips such a widget
      entirely: no lookup, no visibility decision, no place in either batched read. A canvas of
      nothing but custom HTML now costs **zero** queries, which it did not before — `#objects` was
      asking `ANY('{}')` for the privilege of being told so.

      Bounded at 4 KiB of markup per widget, truncated rather than refused: a tile showing the
      first few kilobytes is a better answer than a map that will not open. The layout as a whole
      is bounded again by the request body limit.

      **Mutations 8/8** — the sandbox attribute removed, the sandbox widened to
      `allow-scripts allow-same-origin`, the markup sanitised on the way in, the 4 KiB cap dropped,
      `html` added to the kinds that must name an object, an object id kept on a widget that draws
      none, the empty-lookup guard removed, and `html` dropped from the saved document.

      **What the tests cannot say, said here.** jsdom does not enforce a sandbox, so nothing in the
      suite proves a script fails to run — a test that claimed to would be proving nothing. What is
      asserted is the three things that have to hold for the browser's guarantee to apply: the
      markup reaches a frame, the frame carries `sandbox=""`, and what arrives is byte-for-byte
      what was typed. The guarantee itself is the browser's.

      5 core tests and 8 in the browser; the web workspace goes 454 to 462 and the backend 3,765 to
      3,770.

- [x] **G-08 — Geographical maps** · L · G-02 · **Still gated, and `ADR-002` Decision 3 says only
      what the eventual answer must satisfy**: whatever is chosen degrades to a plain background
      when no provider is configured, so an air-gapped installation gets a map without tiles rather
      than a map that does not load. Deciding it properly wants its own ADR and is not on the path
      of any other Phase 12 ticket. **Gated: it needs map tiles from somewhere.** A
      tile provider is a network dependency in a product that installs as one service and is
      expected to run in a NOC that may not reach the internet. Bundling tiles is gigabytes;
      requiring an API key makes an operator sign up for something; a self-hosted tile server is
      another thing to install, which `CLAUDE.md`'s third hard constraint has an opinion about.
      Decide, and if the answer is "configurable provider, degrade to a plain background without
      one", say so in the ADR rather than discovering it at install time.

      **`ADR-004` is written and is `Proposed`, 2026-09-09.** It says: ship no tiles and no default
      provider, take a URL template an operator configures, render the widgets over the `G-05`
      background when there is none, keep coordinates on the widget rather than on the object, draw
      no tiles on a `G-06` share link unless somebody opts in, and write the projection and the
      tile grid rather than taking a mapping library. **This ticket stays blocked until that ADR is
      accepted**, and it carries two open modelling questions the ADR deliberately left to `G-08`:
      whether a map's extent is per map or per viewer, and whether geo widgets share a canvas with
      box-positioned ones or a geo map is a different kind of map.

      **Landed 2026-09-09, and both open questions were answered by noticing the same thing.** The
      extent is **per map**: where a map opens is part of what its author arranged, so a wall
      display comes back to the same place after a reboot rather than to wherever a passer-by left
      it — panning is local to a browser and nothing persists it. And there is **one kind of map**,
      with widgets that may carry a coordinate: a geographical map needs box-positioned widgets
      anyway — a legend, a status list, a note — so the tile layer is a property of the map exactly
      as `G-05`'s background is, and a widget without a coordinate keeps its box on a geo map.
      Turning the map geographical and back again therefore loses nothing.

      **The projection is ours, and that is the whole argument for not taking a library.**
      `packages/web/src/maps/geo.ts` is two formulae, their inverses, and a loop that says which
      tiles cover a rectangle. Its tests assert properties rather than magic numbers — the round
      trip, the corners of the world, the direction each axis runs, that the grid covers every
      corner of the viewport and never asks for a tile outside the world, and that the tile count
      follows the screen rather than the coordinate, so a caller cannot make it expensive by
      panning. A library would have brought several hundred kilobytes, its own event model and its
      own theming for one screen, and would still have had to be taught `ADR-004` Decision 2.

      **The defect this ticket found was in itself, between its two readers.** The core clamped an
      out-of-range centre while the designer refused it, so a document the editor treats as a plain
      canvas would have come back from the view route as a geographical map opening at the pole —
      and the core's own comment claimed the designer applied "the same rule". Both now refuse a
      centre that is not a coordinate; zoom stays clamped, because a scale is not a place. The
      view route also stopped naming the installation's tile source on a map that has none to draw
      under, which is one fewer thing said to a client that cannot use it.

      Nine mutations were applied and all nine were caught: centring a pinned widget, an unpinned
      one keeping its box, the `{y}` placeholder, the world clamp on the tile grid, the provider's
      attribution, the designer's default for the share opt-in, clamping instead of refusing a
      centre, the widget coordinate's range guard, and the `ADR-004` Decision 4 gate on both the
      opt-in's reading and the public route's use of it.

- [x] **G-09 — 5-star maps in the Home menu** · S · G-01 · `§2` says priority sorts objects and
      five-star maps surface in Home. Small, and last, because it is a presentation rule over
      whatever `G-01` decides a map is.

      **Landed 2026-09-09, and it needed two halves rather than one.** The presentation rule is
      four lines; what made it reachable is the control that sets a priority. `map.priority` has
      existed since `G-01` and `PATCH /maps/:id` has always accepted it, but nothing in the product
      could change it — every map was created at three stars and stayed there, so the rule would
      have shipped as a card that was empty on every installation forever.

      **Five stars, not four or more.** `§2` says five-star maps surface in Home, and a friendlier
      threshold would be a different rule: the point of the top of the scale is that reaching it is
      a decision somebody took.

      **The order is the core's.** `GET /maps` already answers priority-first and then by name, and
      a second ordering in the browser is a second thing that eventually disagrees with the first —
      the same reasoning `CLAUDE.md` applies to inheritance.

      **One request, filtered in the browser.** A `?priority=` this page would be the only caller
      of is a wider API for no gain: the list is already ordered, an installation has tens of maps,
      and the card needs to know whether *any* map exists to say the right thing when none are
      starred. Bounded at eight with the remainder counted, because a list that stops without
      saying so is one somebody trusts to be complete.

      **The card is absent, not empty, when there are no maps at all.** A card explaining a feature
      nobody has reached for is a card everybody reads past; once maps exist, "none of them is
      starred" is a status report.

      **The priority control lives with the designer and shares its version.** A priority change
      bumps the map's version, so it writes back through the same ref the canvas saves against — a
      stale copy would turn the operator's next layout save into a conflict with their own edit.
      It carries `If-Match` like every other change: the rule is not about the size of the field.
      A refused change puts the number back, because a select still showing five stars is a map
      somebody believes is on the home screen.

      **Mutations 7/7** — the threshold lowered to four, the ceiling removed, the remainder
      reported as zero, the order re-sorted by name, the failed change left on screen, `If-Match`
      dropped, and the card rendered on an installation with no maps.

      9 tests of the model and the control, 3 more on the Overview; the web workspace goes 462 to
      474. **Phase 12 is done apart from `G-08`, which `ADR-002` Decision 3 still gates.**

- [x] **G-10 — Serving a resolved map, in one pass for real** · M · G-02 · The route that hands a
      client a map with its widgets filled in, and the batching that has to exist before it can be
      one. `G-02`'s resolver is one pass for the two things it counts — the object lookup and the
      access resolution — and an N+1 for the rest: `latestForSensor` runs per table widget (three
      queries each, in its own transaction) and the subtree query runs per sensor-list widget, all
      sequentially. At the 200-widget ceiling that is a single request costing several hundred
      round trips, which is why the endpoint is here rather than in `G-03`.

      Wants a `latestForSensors(ids)` on `HistoryService` — the store's `latestValues` already
      takes many channel ids, and the awkward half is the lookback, which is a multiple of *each*
      sensor's own interval — and one recursive query over every list widget's root at once. Both
      are measurable: put the query count for a forty-widget map in `docs/findings/`, the way
      `P-15` did for the scheduler, rather than asserting it got better.

      `G-04`, `G-06` and `G-07` all need this route. `G-03` deliberately does not: a designer edits
      the document and shows the tiles it holds, which needs no resolution at all.

      **Landed 2026-09-09, and measured: a forty-table canvas costs four statements.** The object
      lookup, one channel lookup for every sensor at once, one `resolveForObjects` for their
      effective intervals, and one newest-per-channel scan. A viewer who is not the public audience
      costs a fifth, for the access resolution. Before this it was 1 + 40 × 3 = 121, sequentially.
      Forty sensor lists are one recursive query ranked per root, so the hundred-sensor limit stays
      a property of one widget rather than of the request. The counts are asserted, not asserted
      about: `maps-resolver.test.ts` watches the real `Database` — including `HistoryService`'s own
      handle, which the earlier counting stub could not see — and pins the number at four.

      **One query, but every sensor keeps its own window.** `latestValues` takes a single
      `notBefore`, so `latestForSensors` asks it the widest question and holds each sensor's rows to
      its own cut-off afterwards. A daily check and a minute-interval sensor cannot share a
      staleness window: widening the *query* is free, and widening the *rule* would let a
      day-old reading through as current.

      **`GET /maps/:id/view` resolves the widgets and answers 404 for a map the caller may not
      read**, the same as every other map route, so the view cannot be used to enumerate ids. The
      audience is built here: `withRight` resolves the caller's right once and `holdsFull` decides
      whether a broken tile explains itself.

      **Two things were found by writing the first HTTP test against these routes.** The first is
      why there was none: `G-03` had only just mounted them. The second is entry 41 of the
      catalogue — **every map error reached the client as a 500**. `MapError` extends `AppError`,
      `api/errors.ts` had no branch for it, and the careful 404-not-403, the 409 from `If-Match`
      and the 400 for a bad name all fell through to the catch-all with their messages replaced.
      The service was right about all of them and the wire said "the request could not be
      completed". A claim about what the API answers has to be asserted where the API answers.

      6 API tests, and the resolver's own file goes 15 to 21.

## Phase 13 — Reporting (`V2-03`)

The third v2 subsystem, started 2026-09-11 with Phase 12 complete. `CAPABILITIES.MD §6` asks for
report templates, scheduling, time spans with rules, four output formats, three delivery modes and
a security context — and §14 gives stored reports a home of their own.

**The tickets use the `E-` prefix**, for the exported documents `§6` calls reports: `G-` is the
graphical half of the same section and `R-` is remote probes.

**Three of these were gated on a decision rather than on effort, and the gate is the same one
`ADR-001` Decision 1 sets for everything else: production is a standalone native service.**
`ADR-005` settled the third on 2026-09-11 and **`ADR-006` settled the first two on 2026-09-12**, so
nothing in this phase is gated on a decision any more.

1. **A PDF without a browser.** The obvious way to render one is to drive headless Chromium, and
   that is a several-hundred-megabyte dependency an operator has to install, patch and supervise —
   on Windows too, where `H-06` is already the hard half. A PDF library is small and cannot lay out
   HTML. Which of those this project accepts is an ADR, not a preference.
2. **A graph without a browser**, and it is not the same question. The UI draws with uPlot in a
   canvas; a report needs the same series as an image on the server. That is either a second
   renderer to keep in step with the first — `CLAUDE.md`'s "inheritance is resolved in one place"
   applied to charts — or a decision that a report's graph is deliberately a different picture.
3. **Where a generated report lives.** `ADR-003` put uploaded files in PostgreSQL as `bytea` and
   justified the 2 MiB bound by the feature being small — one background per map. Reports are the
   opposite shape: produced on a schedule, retained, potentially large, and `§14` names a
   `\Report PDFs` directory as though they are files. That decision has to be made again rather
   than inherited.

**Every ticket in this phase has landed**: graphs and data tables as HTML, CSV, XML and PDF, on a
schedule, delivered by email, rendered without a browser. `ADR-006` Decision 4 put `E-07` ahead of
the two `L` tickets, `E-06` took the PDF, and `E-05` the graphs. `E-12` — scripts the report font
did not cover — was the one follow-up it opened, and it has landed too.

- [x] **E-01 — The report entity** · M · — · Storage, migration with a tested rollback, CRUD API,
      and access by group the way `§9` grants it — the same shape `G-01` gave a map, and for the
      same reason: a report is not a tree object. It holds a template kind, an object set, a time
      span, a security context, a schedule and a set of outputs. No rendering and no scheduling
      here.

      **The question this ticket settles is what a report points at.** `G-01` chose a document over
      a foreign key so that deleting a sensor leaves a tile saying so rather than a canvas that
      quietly stopped mentioning it. A report has the same problem and a worse version of it: a
      monthly report whose sensor was deleted on the 3rd must say so in the output, because a
      report is read by somebody who was not there.

      **Landed 2026-09-11.** Migration 047 creates `report` and `report_access`; `subjects` is a
      `jsonb` document for the reason above, and the rollback is covered by `migrator.test.ts`'s
      forward-and-all-the-way-back case — mutation-proved by removing `DROP TYPE IF EXISTS
      report_kind`, which fails the re-up with `type "report_kind" already exists`.

      **The security context turned out to be the substantive decision, not the object set.**
      `§6` says a report renders under a named account's visibility, which is an "act as" path
      granted to whoever can edit a report. Two rules follow, and both are in `reports/service.ts`
      rather than the schema, because neither can be written as a `CHECK`:

      - **Changing it needs `full`, not `write`.** Everything else `update` touches is a document;
        this field decides whose data the output contains, which is the same class of act as
        granting access. A `write` holder may change what a report measures and not as whom.
      - **Losing the account must stop the report, not unscope it.** The reference is
        `ON DELETE SET NULL` *and* the login is snapshotted beside it, so a deleted account leaves
        a readable broken state — the API answers `runAs: { login, available: false }` and
        `E-03` refuses to run it. The alternative, a null column and nothing else, reads as "run as
        nobody", and nobody in a scheduler with no session is one careless join from everybody.

      Routes mirror `G-01`'s: `READS` with the right resolved per report, 404 rather than 403 for
      one the caller may not see, `If-Match` on the write, 204 from the grant routes. `ReportError`
      got its branch in `api/errors.ts` **in the same commit as the routes** — the catalogue's
      entry 41 is `G-10` discovering that every `MapError` had been reaching the wire as a 500 for
      months because that branch was missing. Mounted in `main.ts` at the same time for the other
      half of that story: `G-01`'s routes existed and nothing passed the service.

      18 service tests and 14 API tests.

- [x] **E-02 — Time spans, and the rules that bound them** · S · E-01 · Day, week, month, quarter,
      year, and custom start and end. **`§6`'s three rules are the ticket**: a span over 500 days
      is rejected and shortened to 365, and a span of 40 to 500 days forces averaging of at least
      60 minutes. Pure logic, property-tested, no database.

      The averaging rule is not cosmetic — it decides which rollup tier answers, so it belongs
      beside `tiers.ts` rather than in a renderer. **And `CLAUDE.md`'s "no-data is not zero" is the
      case to get right here**: a span with a gap in it must render a gap, in CSV as much as in a
      graph, or a report becomes the most durable way this system can tell a lie.

      **Landed 2026-09-11, and the ticket was wrong about what the work was.** All three rules
      were already written — `planSeries` in `timeseries/query.ts` has had them since `M-13`,
      because the history API and the sensor detail page need exactly the same bounds. A second
      copy beside a renderer is the duplication `CLAUDE.md` forbids for inheritance, and the
      failure mode is worse here than for a graph: two copies that drift mean a report and the
      graph a user checks it against are drawn from different data and neither says so. So
      `reports/span.ts` calls `planSeries` and imports its constants.

      **What was actually missing is the calendar**, which `planSeries` cannot do because it takes
      two instants. "Last month" is 28 to 31 days long, starts at local midnight in a zone somebody
      chose, and in that zone one of its days may have had 23 or 25 hours. Three things fell out of
      writing it that were not in the ticket:

      - **A day does not start at midnight.** `Asia/Beirut` and `America/Santiago` change their
        clocks *at* 00:00, so that wall time does not exist twice a year and the first instant of
        the day is 01:00. Resolution takes two offset samples and picks the earlier of two valid
        instants, the only valid one, or — when the clock jumped over the time entirely — the
