        later, which is the first instant that exists. Property-tested over eight zones including
        `Australia/Lord_Howe`, whose shift is 30 minutes.
      - **`offset` defaults to 1, the last complete period.** A monthly report fires on the 1st at
        02:00, and one covering "this month" would cover two hours — every month, without
        complaint. `0` is offered for month-to-date and is the only span whose end is clamped to
        now.
      - **The 500-day rule is applied to the window before it is labelled**, rather than left to
        `planSeries`. A 600-day custom span would otherwise be planned over 365 days while the
        report's own header still said 600. A graph that shortens its x-axis is self-evident; a
        PDF in a compliance folder is read by somebody who cannot check.

      The resolved window is on the API response as `resolved` — the interval, the bucket width,
      the rollup tier that will answer, and every adjustment — so an author who pins five-minute
      averaging over a quarter is told it will be hourly **while they are still looking at the
      form**. `unresolvable` carries the one refusal a read must not fail on: a month-to-date span
      fetched at 00:00:00 on the 1st.

      "No-data is not zero" is `E-04`'s to keep, not this ticket's: a span is a window, and nothing
      here reads a sample. What `E-02` owes `E-04` is that the window is honest — it never covers
      more than it says, and `to` is exclusive so consecutive periods tile without an overlapping
      instant. Both are property-tested.

      22 span tests (three of them property-based over 8 zones × 5 kinds), plus 5 API and 3
      service tests for the wiring.

- [x] **E-03 — The security context** · M · E-01 · A report runs under a named user's visibility
      scope, so what it contains is what that person could see — not what the person who scheduled
      it could see, and not everything.

      **This is the ticket with a security property to prove rather than a feature to build.** It
      is a deliberate "act as" path, and the rules it must not break are already written:
      credentials are never returned by any route to anyone (`CLAUDE.md`), and access is resolved
      in one place. A report that renders a sensor's `writeOnly` parameters, or that widens scope
      because the scheduler runs as nobody, is the failure. Scenario tests, not unit tests.

      **Landed 2026-09-11.** `reports/context.ts` resolves a report's account into a principal and
      answers what that principal can see, through the same `AccessService` the object API uses —
      the rule `G-10` applied to the map resolver, for the same reason: a report must not become a
      second, more permissive way to read a sensor. Inheritance, explicit-beats-inherited,
      highest-across-groups and the role ceiling all arrive for free and cannot drift.

      Three things came out of writing it, and two were holes rather than decisions:

      - **`E-01` closed only one of the two ways to lose a security context.** A deleted account
        nulls `run_as_user_id`; a **disabled** one keeps its row, so the reference stays valid and
        nothing would have noticed. Disabling is how `031` says this system revokes an account —
        it is what an operator does when somebody leaves — so ignoring it made revocation not work
        for the one path that runs unattended, and a departed colleague's scope would have gone on
        publishing monthly. Both now refuse with `REPORT_NO_CONTEXT`, and `runAs.available` on the
        API counts both. A *locked* account is deliberately not refused: lockout is `A-08`'s
        brute-force defence, it clears on its own, and stopping a monthly report for one would be
        a denial of service anybody could trigger from the login form.
      - **Telling "deleted" from "forbidden" would have been an existence oracle.** A `write`
        holder on a report needs no access to the object tree at all, so a subject list that said
        which unavailable ids existed would let anyone who can edit a report enumerate every id in
        the installation — add ids, run it, read which came back forbidden. `unavailable` is a
        bare list of numbers with nowhere to put the distinction; the split is written to the core
        log, which only an administrator reads.
      - **A principal cannot be fabricated.** `ReportPrincipal` carries a branded symbol no other
        module can produce, so the only way to obtain one is `resolve()`, which is also the only
        place the refusals are applied. A future caller cannot hand `subjectsFor` an ad-hoc
        `{ userId, role }` and skip them — it does not typecheck. `ApiServer` takes the service and
        the context as **one option** for the same reason: a build that mounted the routes without
        a context would not be a reduced API, it would be an unscoped one.

      The credential rule is kept structurally rather than by redaction: the subject projection is
      `{ id, kind, name }` and has no field a `writeOnly` parameter could ride out on. An
      installation report needs configuration and must get it from `ObjectService`, whose `#redact`
      is the one boundary that strips them — never from the repository, and never by widening that
      shape. A test asserts the key list, so widening it later fails there rather than in a PDF.

      `GET /reports/:id/subjects` answers what a report would contain, which makes every property
      above checkable over HTTP and gives an operator the way to see what granting a report would
      hand somebody. **The asymmetry is documented rather than fixed**, because it is the feature:
      `read` on a report is `read` on everything its account can see. `administration.md` says to
      grant a report the way you would grant the account it runs as.

      Not here: the audit row. An act-as that runs is an auditable event, and nothing runs a report
      until `E-08` — resolving a context on an API read is not the event. `E-08` adds `report.ran`
      to the audit union; until then the refusals and the visibility split are structured log lines.

      12 scenario tests over a real tree with real grants, plus 4 API tests.

- [x] **E-04 — Data-table rendering, HTML and CSV** · M · E-02, E-03 · The two outputs that need no
      new dependency, and the two that make a report useful before any picture exists. Channel
      values over the span, per sensor, with gaps as gaps.

      **Landed 2026-09-11.** `reports/table.ts` is pure — a document in, a string out — and
      `reports/render.ts` assembles that document from `E-02`'s window, `E-03`'s subjects and
      `HistoryService`'s readings. **One document formatted twice**, not two renderers reading the
      database: the two formats have to agree about every number and every gap, and a test asserts
      cell-for-cell that they do.

      **Gaps survive, and the pipeline is where they would have died.** `HistoryService` already
      returns dense arrays with `null` for an empty bucket, so the rule was never about inventing
      it — it was about not losing it. Three places could have: building rows from "the buckets
      that have data" (the arrays are dense precisely so that cannot be written), dropping a row
      whose channels are all empty (which compresses time and makes the table claim a shorter
      period), and CSV. A gap is an empty field in CSV and `—` in HTML, and a **measured** zero is
      `0` — the fixture has a channel reading zero in every hour that has data, so a rendering that
      collapsed the two fails rather than looking right.

      **The security issue here is the spreadsheet, and it is not obvious.** Device and sensor
      names are typed by users, a report is emailed, and Excel evaluates a cell beginning `=`, `+`,
      `-`, `@`, tab or carriage return — `=cmd|'/C calc'!A0` is the classic. Every *text* field is
      quoted and prefixed with an apostrophe. **Numbers are deliberately exempt, and that is the
      half that is easy to get wrong**: `-5` begins with `-`, so a guard applied to every field
      would write `'-5` and turn every negative measurement into text in every spreadsheet that
      opened the file. Numbers here are produced by the formatter from a `number` and are never
      user-typed, so there is nothing to escape. Both halves are tested. The HTML document escapes
      the same names and **fetches nothing from anywhere** — a remote stylesheet would fail in an
      air-gapped NOC and a remote asset in an emailed document is a read receipt nobody agreed to.

      **Refused rather than truncated.** `planSeries` bounds buckets per sensor; nothing bounded
      the product of sensors, buckets and channels, and a year of hourly data over five hundred
      sensors is tens of millions of cells built in memory. `MAX_CELLS` is 200,000 and a document
      over it answers 422 with the count and what to narrow. `CLAUDE.md`'s "backpressure is
      visible, never silent" decides the direction: a report quietly missing its last four hundred
      sensors is the failure this whole surface exists to avoid.

      Timestamps are the span's wall clock **with the offset attached**, so the hour that repeats
      in October is two distinct correctly-labelled rows rather than one ambiguous pair. Writing
      that found a real bug: `Intl`'s `longOffset` renders UTC as `GMT` on some ICU builds and
      `GMT+00:00` on others, so two installations on different Node versions would have produced
      different bytes for the same report. Both normalise to `Z`.

      `GET /reports/:id/render?format=html|csv` is the surface, registered separately for the
      response-schema exemption the way `mapBackgroundRoute` is — it answers text, which the guard
      cannot filter.

      Not here, and deliberate: `HistoryService.forSensor` is called once per subject,
      sequentially. A batched query would be a second implementation of `segmentsFor` — the
      stitching of a rollup tier with everything newer than its watermark — and the first sign of a
      disagreement would be a report and the sensor page showing different numbers for the same
      hour. The cost is real and noted in `P-203`, with a measurement, because `CLAUDE.md` does not
      allow the claim without one.

      18 rendering tests, 8 against real readings with a deliberate hole in the middle, 5 API.

- [x] **E-05 — Graphs in a report** · L · E-04 · **`ADR-006` Decision 3**: the
      chart's geometry is computed in `@ms/shared` and drawn twice — SVG for the HTML report,
      `pdfkit` primitives for the PDF. No browser, no `node-canvas`, no raster.

      **The move matters more than the drawing.** `packages/web/src/charts/groups.ts` already holds
      every charting *decision* — one chart per unit, colour by entity, what an all-gap channel
      means — and uPlot only draws pixels. That file moves to `@ms/shared` so the core and the web
      app read one copy, and it lands with this ticket rather than after it. What is duplicated is
      a drawing routine, which is the cheap half; a report's graph is static, paged and printed,
      and matching uPlot pixel for pixel would be an expensive way to be wrong.

      The expensive part is axis tick selection, label collision and the null-gap path — all of
      them assertable from an SVG string, which is why this is drawn rather than rasterised.

      **Landed 2026-09-13, and Phase 13 with it.** The charting decisions moved first:
      `@ms/shared/charts` now holds unit grouping, extents, colour slots and the palette, and the web
      app imports them from there. **The web app had never depended on `@ms/shared`**, whose entry
      point is service code, so the charts are their own browser-safe subpath with a test that
      nothing in the directory imports outside it; the web bundle grew by 0.09 kB, and its scripts
      build shared themselves so a fresh `npm run dev:ui` works. **Moving the palette found drift
      already there**: the web app's JavaScript copy of the light palette had kept the eight hues and
      lost the stylesheet's neutrals. One palette now, and a test holding the stylesheet to it.

      Then the geometry, in the same package: a y-axis at 1, 2 or 5 × 10ⁿ that starts at zero for a
      magnitude and still draws a flat series; lines broken at every gap, a lone reading drawn as a
      dot rather than lost, the min–max band only where both edges are known; and time labels chosen
      so that none overlaps another and none leaves the chart. **The candidates for the time axis
      come from the core**, because which instants are round in a zone is `span.ts`'s calendar —
      local midnights, the first of the month, and no tick for the hour the clocks skipped. The core
      draws the one layout twice, as SVG in the HTML and as `pdfkit` primitives in the PDF, where a
      chart is an atomic block; `graph_only` has no table in either, and CSV and XML carry the data
      whatever the template says.

      **Two layout bugs were found by looking and are now tests**: the last date of every chart was
      clipped to `09-0`, and a legend drew its swatches over the dates. Sixteen mutations were run;
      the first pass caught twelve, and the four that were not caught were weak tests rather than
      correct code — including the legend test, whose first version would not have caught the very
      overlap it was written for. All sixteen are caught now. **Measured**: at the value limit an
      HTML report is 7.3 MiB as a table, 13.9 MiB with graphs and 6.5 MiB as graphs alone; a month of
      hourly data over fifty sensors is 5.1 MiB of HTML with graphs, and **its PDF with tables is
      refused at about 700 pages while `graph_only` is under a megabyte** — so for a PDF over many
      sensors, the graph template is usually the report that was wanted.


- [x] **E-06 — PDF output** · L · E-04 · **`ADR-006` Decisions 1 and 2**: `pdfkit`, laying the
      document out ourselves, with DejaVu Sans embedded.

      A fourth renderer over `E-04`'s `ReportDocument`, beside HTML, CSV and XML. Chromium is
      refused — measured at 195 MB for `linux64` and 205 MB for `win64`, per platform, to lay out a
      table we generated ourselves. **The font is not optional**: the standard PDF fonts encode
      WinAnsi, and `pdfkit` asked for `Маршрут` emits truncated code points without throwing, so a
      Cyrillic sensor name would reach a filed document as mojibake with nothing having failed.

      The work is pagination: repeating column headers, column widths from the content, and a page
      break that does not separate a row from its own timestamp.

      **Landed 2026-09-13.** Split in two, which is the whole reason the ADR could refuse a
      browser: **`paginate` is pure** — document in, pages out, with a measuring function the
      caller supplies — and **`draw` is dumb**, walking those pages and issuing `pdfkit` calls with
      no decision left in it. So the layout rules are unit tests rather than something to look at:
      headings repeat on every page, every row is placed exactly once, a section that does not fit
      the remainder starts a new page unless it does not fit a whole one either (then it flows,
      marked `(continued)`), small sections pack together, and **columns too wide for the page are
      carried to a following page group with the time column repeated rather than clipped** —
      clipping being the one way this layout could have lost a measurement silently. The finished
      PDF is then read *back* in the tests through its own `ToUnicode` map, which is how a reader
      copies text out of one, so the assertions are about what a person sees.

      **The font is committed to the repository** (`packages/core/assets/fonts`, Debian's
      `fonts-dejavu-core 2.37-6` build with its checksum and licence recorded); `scripts/package.sh`
      now stages a package's `assets` directory, and the package smoke test asserts the font is
      installed. `ADR-006` said OFL-1.1 and that was wrong — DejaVu is under the **Bitstream Vera**
      licence, corrected in the ADR.

      **And the first rendered CJK name found the gap the ADR left.** DejaVu has no CJK glyphs, and
      a font without a glyph draws an empty box without anything failing — the same silent mojibake
      the decision embedded a font to prevent, one alphabet further out. Characters the font cannot
      draw are now written as their Unicode notation (`U+6771`) with a line in the document's
      header saying so; `E-12` is the ticket for covering those scripts properly. Bounds are
      measured: 10,000 rows over two channels is 185 pages, 0.43 MiB and 1.5 s, and `MAX_PDF_PAGES`
      refuses beyond 400 pages with the count and the suggestion to take CSV instead. Migration 051
      admits `pdf` to `report_output_format`, which is the reopening `ADR-005` Decision 3 asked for
      and was done the way it asked — against a real rendered PDF.

- [x] **E-12 — A report in a script DejaVu does not cover** · M · E-06 · Japanese, Chinese and
      Korean device names in a PDF. `E-06` made the failure visible — a character the font cannot
      draw is written `U+6771` and the document says so — which is honest and is not a report
      somebody in Tokyo wants to file.

      **The decision is which font, and what it costs the installer.** Noto Sans CJK is tens of
      megabytes per weight against the 760 KB `ADR-006` Decision 2 weighed, and the alternatives —
      a subsetted build, a per-installation font path in the configuration, or a fallback chain —
      each trade size for a different failure. `ADR-006`'s own numbers are the starting point, and
      the ticket is a decision before it is an implementation. The machinery is already there:
      `Typesetter.has` asks the font whether it can draw a character, and a second font is a second
      answer to that question.

      **Landed 2026-09-13** — `docs/findings/2026-09-13-report-cjk-fonts.md`, and `ADR-006`
      Decision 2 extended. Measured three candidates from Debian's packages: Noto Sans CJK (19.5 MB,
      every set, regional shapes, 80 MiB once opened), Droid Sans Fallback (4 MB, **no Korean**) and
      WenQuanYi Micro Hei (5.2 MB, all of JIS X 0208, GB 2312, Big5 and KS X 1001, 22 MiB). **The
      decision, the project owner's: bundle WenQuanYi and let an operator name a font ahead of it**
      — +2.3 MB on the tarball against Noto's +15.5 MB — with `reports.pdfFonts` for the regional
      shapes WenQuanYi does not draw (Noto's Japanese and Simplified Chinese faces differ on 8,638
      ideographs). A font chain in `reports/fonts.ts` draws each character with the first font that
      has it, opening the second only when needed; text in two fonts is drawn in runs on one
      baseline, and right-aligned headings end on the column edge. The pool passes the fonts to
      its workers; a configured font that cannot be opened is logged at startup with the faces it
      has, not fatal. **A Latin-only PDF is byte-identical to the previous commit's**, and renders
      within 3–4% (noise on a busy machine) after an ASCII fast path took the first version's 13%
      away. `readPdf` decodes per font and reports positions — one merged `ToUnicode` map read the
      title as `東京nthly` — and glyphs were checked by rendering with macOS's own PDF renderer, since
      a text round-trip cannot see a blank glyph. Still written as notation: 〜 (U+301C) and CJK
      Extension B, which need a configured font. Eleven mutations, all caught.

- [x] **E-07 — XML output** · S · E-04 · The fourth format `§6` lists. Cheap once the data layer
      exists, and worth doing with CSV rather than after the pictures. **`ADR-006` Decision 4 says
      it goes first** — a third formatting of a document model that already exists, with no
      dependency, no font and no geometry, against two `L` tickets.

      **Landed 2026-09-12.** `renderXml` beside `renderHtml` and `renderCsv` over the same
      `ReportDocument`, and the cell-for-cell parity test now covers all three. **A gap is
      `xsi:nil="true"`, not an empty element** — `Number(node.textContent)` on `<value/>` is `0`,
      which is the one reading this whole surface exists to make impossible, so the element is
      always emitted and always says it has no value. Characters XML 1.0 cannot carry are dropped
      rather than escaped, because `&#1;` is equally illegal and a control byte in an SNMP
      `sysName` would otherwise produce a document no parser will read; tab, newline and return
      inside an attribute are escaped numerically, which is what survives attribute-value
      normalisation. Migration 050 adds `xml` to `report_output_format` before `zip`, with a
      rollback that deletes the documents it cannot keep and says so (`ADR-005` Decision 3 amended
      rather than reopened). Tests parse the output with a real parser rather than with the
      regexes that wrote it; seven mutations were run and all seven were caught.

- [x] **E-08 — Scheduling** · M · E-04 · One-off "run now", and hourly, daily, weekly, monthly,
      quarterly or annual. **Two constraints decide the design.** `CLAUDE.md` says nothing blocks
      the scheduler, and a report is the longest-running thing this system will ever do — so it
      runs where a check does not, and its progress is visible. And `§4` says a Schedule's
      inactive periods pause reports as well as monitoring, so this reuses the existing schedule
      resolution rather than growing a second idea of "is it office hours".

      **Landed 2026-09-11.** Migration 048 adds `report_run` and `report.next_run_at`;
      `reports/cadence.ts` answers when; `reports/runs.ts` runs it on its own `PeriodicSweep`, two
      at a time, nowhere near the timing wheel. `§4`'s window is honoured by asking `isActiveAt`,
      which is `M-09`'s own evaluator — a cadence says when, a window says whether, and neither
      learned the other's job.

      **Three of the six frequencies could reuse `D-07`'s cadence and three could not**, for a
      mechanical reason rather than a preference: that module finds the next firing by scanning
      forward a minute at a time, bounded at a week. A year is half a million minutes and half a
      million calls into the zone database. Hourly, daily and weekly delegate to it unchanged;
      monthly, quarterly and annual compute the civil date and resolve it through `E-02`'s
      `instantOf`, so "the 1st at 00:00 in Beirut" lands on the morning that has no midnight.
      **It moved to `schedules/cadence.ts` to make that honest** — it was never about discovery,
      and it is the event twin of the window in `definition.ts`.

      Writing the tests found **four defects, three of them in code that was already green**:

      - **`nextRun` can book the instant it was given.** `Math.ceil` on a minute boundary returns
        it unchanged, so a scheduler re-booking from the instant it just fired books the same
        instant, finds it due, and runs every minute for ever. Rediscovery never hit it because
        `tick` passes `now`, which has milliseconds. **The fix is not in the shared module**: a
        pre-existing test says "at or after" is deliberate there, so a sweep waking a moment early
        does not skip the occurrence it was woken for. `reports/cadence.ts` asks for strictly-after
        explicitly, and says why.
      - **A one-day window grace skips most months.** A monthly report on the 1st with an
        office-hours window would have run only in months whose 1st is a weekday. The grace is a
        week, because a `M-09` window *is* a week: seven days covers every minute it has, so if
        none is open the answer is "never" rather than "later", and seven days cannot reach the
        next firing of a monthly report.
      - **`started_at` was never written**, so every run's duration was null and the history could
        not answer "is this report getting slower".
      - **The `queued` state was a lie.** Nothing could produce one — a render starts the moment
        its slot is claimed — and the API schema would have promised a state it never answers.
        Removed; `E-09` can add one with its own migration when delivery is the thing that waits.

      **One run at a time, and the database says so.** `report_run_active_idx` is a partial unique
      index over `running`, so a double-clicked button loses on an insert rather than in the window
      between a check and an insert, and answers 409. `recover()` clears runs abandoned by a core
      that stopped mid-render — without it that index keeps the report unrunnable for ever, which
      is what a `kill -9` would have left behind.

      The next run is booked **before** the render, so a render that throws does not leave the
      report due for ever; `D-07` arrived at the same rule the same way. A report more than six
      hours behind is skipped with a log line rather than run, so a core that was down for two days
      does not produce a burst of runs each covering a period the next one also covers.

      **The audit row `E-03` deferred is here**, because an act-as that actually happened is the
      auditable event. It names *both* accounts: who asked, and whose visibility it rendered
      through. Those are routinely different and the second is the one that decides what left the
      building. `reportAuditSinks` is the record and nothing else — a report that ran changed no
      configuration, so none of the caches or synchronisers the other sets fan out to want it.

      Core Health gains `reportsDeferred` and `reportsFailed`, because a subsystem with a pool and
      a queue reports here (`CLAUDE.md`). Two lines rather than one: a rising `reportsDeferred` is
      an installation that has scheduled more than it can render, a rising `reportsFailed` is one
      report that is broken, and collapsing them would name neither fix.

      Not here: what happens to the document. `E-09` decides that, and `ADR-005` has not settled
      where a generated report lives — storing it now to save it for later would be deciding that
      question in a migration. A run records that it rendered, what period it covered, how large it
      was, and why it failed. **That is not a wasted render**: a scheduled run that finds a
      disabled security context or a document over the cell limit records the failure at 03:00,
      which is the point of scheduling something.

      17 cadence tests, 13 runner tests against a real database, 7 API.

- [x] **E-09 — Delivery** · M · E-08 · Store, store and email, or email only, with optional ZIP.
      The email half is `N-07`'s transport unchanged — a report is an attachment, not a new
      channel. **The failure to design against is one this project already has a rule for**: a
      scheduled report that cannot deliver must not retry into an alarm storm, and must not fail
      silently either.

      **Landed 2026-09-11, and it needed an ADR first.** `ADR-003` Decision 1 put uploaded files in
      PostgreSQL and explicitly refused to cover this case — *"if a later feature wants files
      measured in hundreds of megabytes — packet captures, report archives — that is a different
      question and it gets its own ADR"*. `ADR-005` is that ADR, and it settles **only Phase 13's
      third question**: a stored report lives in PostgreSQL as `bytea`, bounded by `E-04`'s cell
      limit rather than a second number, compressed by TOAST rather than by the application, and
      admitting `html`, `csv` and `zip` only. The PDF and graph questions stay open, and the ADR
      says it is reopened when they are answered rather than treating this as a precedent.

      **`ADR-005` Decision 4 is the one that was not obvious.** Email-only still stores, and then
      deletes: a delivery that fails is retried, a retry needs the bytes, and the alternatives are
      re-rendering — minutes of work, and a *different document* once a rollup has moved underneath
      it — or holding megabytes in memory across an outage. A delivery that has **permanently
      failed keeps its output**, because deleting the evidence of a failure is the opposite of what
      somebody investigating one needs.

      The failure rule is kept with four things rather than one: bounded attempts (five, over about
      ninety minutes) with a growing delay; **a permanent rejection that is not retried at all**,
      using the retryable/permanent distinction `N-07` already draws between an address the relay
      refused and a relay that timed out; one row holding one state, so a relay down for an hour is
      one failed report rather than sixty log lines; and a terminal `failed` that nothing re-arms
      on a timer. Core Health gains `reportsUndelivered` — **a gauge, not a counter**, because the
      question is how many are stuck *now*.

      **`N-07`'s transport did need a second entry point**, and pretending otherwise would have
      meant fabricating an eighteen-field `MessageContext` about a sensor that does not exist.
      `EmailTransport.sendDocument` shares the relay selection, the fallback, the header
      sanitising and `P-119`'s partial-send detection; `send` is unchanged from the outside and the
      alarm-shaped `OutgoingMessage` is untouched. The `X-MS-Sensor` header is now omitted rather
      than claiming sensor 0.

      The ZIP writer is ~140 lines over `node:zlib`, for the reason this project writes its own
      syslog and NetFlow: a small, completely specified slice of a format against a dependency tree
      inside a service whose premise is that an operator installs one thing. It is checked against
      the specification byte by byte **and handed to a real `unzip`**, which verifies every entry's
      CRC — an implementation that satisfies only its own reader is worth very little.

      Three defects found while writing it, all by the tests:

      - **`0o100644 << 16` is negative.** The Unix file mode in the central directory overflows a
        signed 32-bit shift, so `writeUInt32LE` refused it and *every* archive threw. `>>> 0`.
      - **Two clocks in one comparison.** `place` wrote `delivery_next_at` with SQL's `now()` while
        `tick` compared it against the runner's injected clock. Fine until they differ, and then
        nothing is ever due.
      - **An enum column orders by declaration, not alphabet.** `ORDER BY format` gives
        `html, csv, zip`, which is what was wanted and not what the test assumed.

      8 ZIP tests (one against a real `unzip`), 14 delivery tests against a real database, 6 API.

- [x] **E-10 — Retention of stored reports** · S · E-09 · What the housekeeper does with old
      output. Follows `S-14`'s shape — a bound an operator sets, enforced by the same loop that
      drops chunks, counted where somebody can see it. Blocked with `E-06` only in so far as the
      ADR decides what is being retained.

      **Landed 2026-09-11.** `ADR-005` settled what is retained, so this was unblocked: a
      `report-retention` step in the housekeeping pass, bounded per statement and per pass like the
      audit prune, counted in the housekeeping report and logged.

      **Two horizons rather than one**, and that is a judgement rather than an oversight.
      `reportDays` (90) bounds the documents and `reportRunDays` (730) bounds the record that a
      report ran. The two are different sizes and answer different questions — a rendered report is
      kilobytes and is what grows a backup, a run row is a few hundred bytes and is what answers
      "has this been failing since August". The config already draws exactly this distinction six
      times over, and `auditDays` is twice `rawDays` for the same reason. A run horizon set below
      the document horizon makes the shorter one win, because deleting a run cascades — coherent
      rather than contradictory, and it needs no cross-field validation to be safe.

      **The interesting part is the two refusals.** Retention must not delete the bytes under a
      delivery that is still queued: `E-09` treats missing bytes as a *permanent* failure —
      correctly, since there is nothing left to send — so pruning them would be this system
      manufacturing the one outcome it cannot recover from. And it must not delete a run that is
      still rendering, which would free `report_run_active_idx` and let a second render start
      beside the first. Both cases wait for the next pass, which costs five minutes; both are
      tested.

      The per-statement bound is 200, not the audit prune's 5,000, and the difference is the point:
      an audit row is a few hundred bytes and a report document is kilobytes to megabytes of
      TOASTed `bytea`, so the same number would be a transaction holding megabytes of dead tuples
      and a lock while it ran.

      8 tests, including both refusals and the backlog draining across passes.

- [x] **E-11 — The reports UI** · M · E-08 · List, create, edit, run now, download, and see what a
      schedule will do next. Follows the maps views: the designer half is behind write access and
      the reading half is not.

      **Landed 2026-09-11.** `/reports` lists and creates; `/reports/:id` is the report, its runs
      and its settings. **Both halves on one page**, which is where this departs from `/maps/:id`
      and its separate designer — a map's editing surface is a canvas that needs the viewport, a
      report's is eight fields, and splitting them would make an operator checking why last night
      failed navigate away to fix it.

      Nothing here decides whether the caller may write. The core refuses with a message and the
      message is shown, which is the choice `MapView` makes about its Edit link and the reasoning
      `Layout` records about showing the role beside the name: a button that explains why beats one
      whose absence is a support conversation.

      **The logic that had to be right is which schedule fields a frequency uses.** The core refuses
      a weekday on a monthly report outright, so a form offering the control produces a 400 nobody
      can explain — and worse, a frequency changed in the form must not leave a `weekday` behind
      from the one before it. `scheduleFields` mirrors `validateSchedule` and `scheduleFrom` builds

      Four things are said where somebody can act on them rather than discovered by running one:
      **a template that does not render yet** (only two of the seven do), **a lost security
      context** — shown in the *list*, not only on the report's own page, because the failure to
      prevent is an operator scanning twenty reports and seeing nothing wrong with the one that has
      been silently refusing since August — **what the averaging rule changed**, and **a bad
      recipient named individually** rather than twelve addresses coming back as one error about
      the field.

      **Not verified in a browser, and the reason is worth recording.** The dev installation
      requires a login, and entering a password into a form is something this assistant does not
      do. The substitute is stronger rather than weaker: 13 rendered tests against stubbed API
      responses, committed and run by CI, asserting behaviour rather than appearance — including
      the one assertion a manual look would most likely miss, that the weekday control is absent
      for a monthly report.

      21 model tests and 13 rendered tests.

## Phase 14 — Libraries (`V2-04`)

The fourth v2 subsystem, scoped 2026-09-27 with Phase 13 complete and nothing built yet.
`CAPABILITIES.MD §6` asks for "alternate device-tree views assembled from filter rules (by type,
status, tag) across unrelated branches", whose sensors "don't double-count". §10 grants access to
"tree, libraries, maps and reports" per group, and §1 says tags are "used for filtering and library
rules".

**The tickets use the `L-` prefix.**

**Blocked, on purpose, behind `A-12`…`A-15`.** Scoping read the code this phase would build on and
found that every route returning many objects ignores per-object rights (`A-12`). It also found
three holes in the map and report entities whose shape a library copies (`A-13`, `A-14`, `A-15`).
A library is one more list of sensors assembled across branches and one more flat entity with
grants, so building it first would copy the holes into a third place. `L-01` starts once `A-14`
has landed; `L-02` needs `A-12`.

**No ADR, and the reason is worth stating.** Phases 12 and 13 were gated on decisions that changed
the product's security posture or added a dependency: public links, custom HTML, a PDF without a
browser, where a generated file lives. A library does neither. It is stored the way a map is,
evaluated by queries that exist, and drawn by UI that exists. The four decisions it does need follow
from rules already written, and are settled here so that no ticket re-derives them:

1. **A library holds rules, never sensors.** A node names roots (objects, by id), sensor types,
   tags and states, and what it shows is evaluated whenever it is read. Without a licence to count
   against, that is what "don't double-count" means: a sensor in three libraries is checked once,
   stored once and alarms once. `CLAUDE.md`'s "one outage, one alarm" holds by construction,
   because nothing about a library reaches the scheduler, storage or notifications. It is also
   why a sensor added under a linked group appears without anybody editing the library, and why a
   moved root is followed rather than lost: rules refer to ids.
2. **A library is evaluated through its viewer's eyes, and never acts as anyone.** `read` on a
   library grants the arrangement, not the contents. It shows only sensors the viewer can read in
   the tree, and says nothing about matches it withheld, not even a count, because "4 hidden" on a
   node filtering for tag `customer-b` is the oracle `G-01` and `E-03` closed. That is the
   opposite of a report, deliberately. A report is read later by people who were not in the room,
   so it needs a fixed account (`E-03`); a library is looked at by whoever opens it.
3. **Tags mean what the tree's tag box means**: effective (inherited from ancestors), compared
   folded, several ANDed, and evaluated through `ObjectRepository.list`'s walk, not a new one. Tag
   inheritance already lives in two places — that walk, and `notifications/context.ts`'s
   `%objecttags`, which does not fold — and a library must not become the third. Types and states
   are sets matched any-of, and the fields of a rule combine all-of.
4. **A library view is the server's answer, and the stream only decides when to ask again**, the
   rule the Alarms view already follows (`web-ui.md`). A node filtering on state changes as
   sensors change state, and only the core can evaluate a rule with rights applied. The browser's
   rollup (`tree/model.ts`) colours what it is given.

- [x] **L-01 — The library entity** · M · A-14 · Storage, a migration with the generic
      forward-and-back rollback test, a CRUD API, and access by group: the shape `G-01` gave a map
      and `E-01` a report. Three things are different this time:

      - **The third copy of flat-entity access is where the copying stops.** `MapService` and
        `ReportService` carry `rightFor`, `withRight`, the administrator check and the group
        lookup line for line, with a third copy of the administrator query in `AccessService`.
        `V2-17` records the rule for this: the third instance is where the shape becomes known.
        Extract it, move maps and reports onto it, and build libraries on it, so that
        `A-13`…`A-15`'s fixes live in one place.
      - **Nodes are one `jsonb` document, capped in count and depth**, for `G-01`'s reason
        unchanged. A root deleted under a node has to leave a node that says so, which neither
        `ON DELETE CASCADE` nor `RESTRICT` allows. `MAX_WIDGETS` is the precedent for the cap.
      - **Its mutations are audited.** Maps record nothing in the audit log and reports record
        only `report.ran` — their create, edit, delete and grants are log lines — which is a gap
        of its own. A third entity should not join it.

      From the first commit: a `LibraryError` with its own branch in `api/errors.ts` (catalogue
      entry 41), a stub in the API reference generator, and a place in the access-matrix harness,
      which is the lesson of `A-14`.

      **L-01 outcome.** Migration 053 (`library`, `library_access`), `packages/core/src/libraries/`,
      `auth/flat-access.ts`, and seven routes under `/libraries`. What is worth knowing:

      **The extraction found that only the error varies.** `FlatAccess` holds the administrator
      short-circuit, both ceilings (`A-04`, `A-06`), `A-13`'s "an administrator is a group, and a
      token below `full` is not one", the creator's grant, and the grant SQL, keyed by a closed
      union of three table names so the identifiers it interpolates cannot be anything else. Maps
      and reports moved onto it in their own commit with their suites unchanged. **The third copy
      of the administrator query, in `AccessService`, was left where it is**: `A-12` is rewriting
      `auth/access.ts`, and editing it under that ticket would be merging into a moving file.
      When `A-12` lands, `FlatAccess.#isAdmin` should ask whatever it exposes.

      **A library is refused at the write, where a map is not.** A map keeps a widget it cannot
      parse as a broken tile (`G-02`); a library node that did not parse would not look broken, it
      would answer a different question — a misspelt `rule` reads as a heading, a string where
      `states` wants a list reads as every state. So `validateNodes` refuses the whole document
      and names the node (`nodes[1].children[0].id`). The JSON Schema is built from the same
      exported limits and says what a schema can; the validator says the rest (count across
      levels, depth, an id used twice, a tag listed twice in different case). Nodes are capped at
      200 and six levels. Rules are checked for shape only: whether a type is registered and
      whether a root still exists is `L-02`'s to report at read time.

      **Audited from the first commit, in the transaction.** `library.created`, `.updated` and
      `.deleted`, under a new `library` category, with the nodes rendered one line per node —
      `Customer A › Routers: types snmp.traffic; states down` — because a person reads the diff.
      `libraryAuditSinks` is the database and the log and nothing else, asserted beside
      `reportAuditSinks`, which had no assertion either. A refused edit writes no row, and a test
      says so. **Grants are logged and not audited**, as every grant is: closing that for one
      entity of four would be a fourth inconsistency, so it is `A-17`'s, which also takes map and
      report create, edit and delete.

      **Found in passing:** the doc comments above `report.ran` and `schedule.created` in
      `objects/audit.ts` had been swapped; they are back where they belong.

      Tests: `library-nodes` (table-driven, every refusal naming its path), `libraries-service`
      (the map service's access cases asked of a third entity, plus the audit), and
      `libraries-api` over HTTP — a 404 rather than a 403 or a 500 on every route for an account
      that cannot read, 428 and 409 on `If-Match`, the validator's 400 reaching the wire, and
      every level of a nested document surviving the response schema. The access matrix sweeps
      the new routes, and `POST /libraries` joins its list of routes an unwired module would take
      with it. The web Logs view's category chips do not list `library` yet — nor `report` or
      `credential`, which the server already has — and `L-03` adds the navigation it would sit
      beside.

- [ ] **L-02 — Rules, and the resolver that evaluates them** · L · L-01, A-12 · The rule model, and
      one resolver for all of a library's nodes. What it must do:

      - **Refuse invalid rules at the boundary**: types must be registered in the catalogue,
        states must be `sensor_state_kind` values, and tags must fit the objects' own limits.
      - **Keep a type the catalogue later drops**: it matches nothing, and says so to anyone who
        can write the library.
      - **Resolve in a fixed, counted number of statements, whatever the node count** — `G-10`'s
        lesson, counted rather than timed, with a fixture of distinct roots so the count means
        something (catalogue entry 39).
      - **Apply rights through `A-12`'s primitive**, never a second walk.
      - **Bound each node**, and say `truncated` when it hits the bound.
      - **Treat a root that is gone or unreadable as a broken node**, and follow whatever `A-15`
        decides about telling the two apart. A library's author holds `full` on it, which is
        exactly the position `A-15` is about.

      `GET /libraries/:id/view`. Measure statements and latency for a library of twenty nodes over
      the 5,000-sensor target, and put the numbers in `docs/findings/`.

- [ ] **L-03 — The library view** · M · L-02 · `/libraries` and `/libraries/:id`:
      - **A keyboard tree to the ARIA pattern**, with each node's sensors written out with their
        path, the way the tree's search results are.
      - **Each node coloured the worst of what it shows.**
      - **Acknowledge, pause and resume from the row**, under the sensor's own rights, as the
        Alarms view does.
      - **One tree implementation, not two.** `TreeView`'s rows and keyboard handling are private
        and hard-wired to `GET /objects?parentId=`; extract them so the device tree and a library

      Live by decision 4 above. A navigation entry, a `web-ui.md` section, and WCAG 2.1 AA.

- [ ] **L-04 — The library editor** · M · L-03 · Everything an editor has to do:
      - **Arrange nodes**: add, remove, reorder and nest them.
      - **A rule form**:
        - roots from `ObjectPicker`, which offers only probe, group and device roots today, where
          a node may name a single sensor;
        - types from the catalogue;
        - tags and states.
      - **A preview of what a draft node matches before it is saved**, through a `COMPUTES` route,
        the way the report form shows the period it works out to while it is still being edited.
      - **An `If-Match` conflict that says so** rather than overwriting.
      - **The grants UI maps and reports already have.**

- [ ] **L-05 — From the tree into a library** · S · L-04 · PRTG builds a library by dragging
      branches into it. Here that is "Add to library…" on a tree row and on an object's detail
      page, creating a node rooted there. It is its own ticket because it is the only one that
      changes the device tree's UI.

- [x] **L-06 — Library, map and report hardening, before anything is built on them** · M ·
      L-01 · Found by review round 1 on 2026-09-28. Six things `L-01` left, each small, and
      each one `L-02`…`L-05` would otherwise build on. Maps and reports share most of them.
      Some may already be done at HEAD by other work: the outcome says which.

      1. **No params schema on any library, map or report route.** So `GET /libraries/abc` is a
         500: `Number('abc')` reaches PostgreSQL as `NaN` (22P02), and an id past bigint does
         the same. Give each route an integer id, and a group, share or run id where it has
         one, as the object routes' `idParams` does.
      2. **The library audit diff compares `describeNodes`' lossy text**
         (`audit/store.ts:471-476`). Two different documents can render the same line:
         `['core','berlin']` and `['core, berlin']`, a changed node id, or a name containing
         ` › `. A real change is then recorded with `diff: []`. Diff the structured document,
         and keep the one-line-per-node text for a person to read.
      3. **Bound the depth before the recursive schema runs.** `ms:libraryNode` refers to itself
         and AJV runs before `validateNodes`. So a body nested a few thousand levels deep is
         walked by the schema, one stack frame per level, before the six-level bound is
         asked, and it answers 500.
      4. **`LIBRARY_NAME_TAKEN`, `MAP_NAME_TAKEN` and `REPORT_NAME_TAKEN` are existence
         oracles.** Each name is unique across the installation, so a writer on one branch
         learns what another branch's libraries, maps and reports are called by trying names.
         A name becomes unique among what the caller can read: migration **064** drops the
         three unique `lower(name)` indexes for plain ones. Conditions (WatchDog):
         - a transaction-scoped advisory lock on (kind, `lower(name)`), with a test of two
           concurrent creates;
         - nothing resolves one of the three by name, and the outcome says what was checked;
         - administrators' lists and pickers show enough, the owning group or the id, to tell
           two of the same name apart;
         - the down migration suffixes duplicates with " (#id)", and that is documented.
      5. **"records nothing for a change that was refused"** (`libraries-service.test.ts:408`)
         cannot fail: the version check throws before the audit is written, so an entry written
         outside the transaction would pass it too. Make it fail after the entry is written.
      6. **A stale version is a 412, as HTTP defines it**, not the 409 maps, reports and
         libraries answer today while objects and rediscovery rules answer 412. The `*_CHANGED`
         codes stay in the body, reads carry an `ETag` if they lack one, and `api-reference.md`
         is regenerated. The web's `isStale()` narrows to 412, and `ReportSettings`, the map
         editor and the library editor are each tested against it. Added 2026-09-28 by
         WatchDog when `D-11` chose 412.

      **Done.** None of the six was done at HEAD by other work; each was checked before it was
      written.

      1. **Params schemas.** Every library, map and report route with an id in its path declares
         one — 30 routes: 6 library, 13 map, 11 report. The shapes shared by all three files are
         in `api/params.ts`, bounded as `objects.ts`' `idParams` is (1 to 2^53−1). `abc`, `0`,
         `1.5`, 2^53 and 10^20 are a 400 on every route. A download's `format` is one a run can
         store, so a name PostgreSQL cannot take as text is refused too. The handlers take the
         coerced number.
      2. **The audit diff compares the document.** `LibraryAudit` carries `document` beside the
         text, and `library.updated` asks `isDeepStrictEqual` of the documents, which ignores the
         key order `jsonb` changes. The entry keeps the text when the text differs. When the two
         documents render alike, it records the documents instead, so the entry still says what
         moved. Tested with the finding's tags and with a changed node id; each recorded
         `diff: []` before.
      3. **Depth before schema.** `refuseTooDeep` walks the body on its own stack and stops at
         the first node deeper than six, naming the path `validateNodes` names. A route
         `preValidation` hook on POST and PATCH runs it after the authorisation hook and before
         AJV. A body 10,000 levels deep is a 400 `LIBRARY_INVALID` at the seventh level on both
         routes. Every node in that test has one id, so only the early bound can name the
         seventh level; past the schema the duplicate id would be named first.
      4. **Names unique among what the caller can read** (migration **064**).
         `FlatAccess.nameTaken` is the one check for all three. It takes
         `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('ms:<kind>-name'), hashtext(lower(name)))`, then asks

         three unique `lower(name)` indexes for plain ones. Its down migration leaves the oldest

         and moves its version on. A name that still clashes fails the rollback whole.
         `installation.md` says so beside `migrate down`. The conditions:
         - **The lock**, with a test that makes the race happen: the first create is held after
           its row is written until the second is seen waiting on the lock (`pg_blocking_pids`),

         - **Nothing resolves one of the three by name.** Checked: the core's SQL on `map`,

         - **Lists tell two apart.** There is no picker for any of the three. The maps list,

         - **The rollback's renaming is documented** (`installation.md`, and 064's comment).

         - **The library editor does not exist yet.** It is `L-04`'s, and should be tested the

      **Mutations caught: 16 of 17.** The one that lived locks on the name without the kind,

**Not in this phase**: a library as a report's subjects or as the source of a map widget (both

## Phase 16 — Directory sign-in (`V2-07`)

LDAP / Active Directory and OIDC sign-in, scoped 2026-09-28 and reviewed the same day.
`CAPABILITIES.MD` marks both `[V2]` and says where PRTG falls short: domain membership, one
domain, whole groups only, no nesting, an hourly cache. SAML stays out, as PRTG leaves it.

**The tickets use the `X-` prefix.**

**Reviewed before it was placed, and amended.** A design review read the draft against the code
and upheld 21 amendments. Three were blocking because the draft's decisions contradicted the
code, and those decisions would have gone into the ADR as written: directory deprovisioning never
reached unattended authority, admin authority is the role *and* the group, and `A-07`'s per-group
MFA requirement was either bypassed or a permanent lockout. They are folded into the decisions
below. The rest are in the tickets' text and done-when lists.

**What v1 has already provided.** `A-34` closes a socket whose credential lapses for any reason,
expiry included, so a refresh or a lifetime that ends a session ends its stream too. `A-38` gave
session lifetimes a `sessions` section of their own. `A-18` audits identity changes. `M-19` and
`M-20` resolve user and group recipients, and list accounts. `A-36` refuses a stream opened from
another origin.

**The decisions, before the tickets.** They go into `ADR-007-directory-sign-in` (`X-01`) before
anything else starts. They change who an account is, and every rule about rights rests on that.

1. **A directory feeds group membership. It never grants rights.** Rights stay on local groups
   (`object_access` → `user_group`), where `A-03`'s inheritance, `A-12`'s visibility and the
   access epoch already work.
   - An admin writes **mapping rules**: a directory group, or a claim value, maps to a local
     group and carries a role.
   - **Rules key an LDAP group by its `objectGUID` or `entryUUID`.** The DN is shown, not
     matched. Name matching would let a delegated OU admin create a same-named group and inherit
     an admin rule. DN matching silently breaks on a rename.
   - **Only issuer-asserted claims drive a rule**: `groups`, `roles`, or a claim name the admin
     declares. `email`, `preferred_username`, `upn`, `unique_name` and `name` are refused as rule
     sources, because a user controls them or they change. That is the reasoning decision 2
     applies to accounts, and a rule can map into admin. Claims come from the `id_token`.
   - A login replaces the account's *directory-sourced* memberships with what the rules give, as
     a diff. Local memberships are never touched.
   - **A login that matches no rule is refused.** It does not get an empty account.
   - **There are two admin authorities, and a rule can grant either.** `role = 'admin'` passes
     every ADMIN route: groups, memberships, grants, audit, probes, and this phase's directory
     configuration. Membership of an `is_admin` group gives `full` on every object. An **admin
     rule** is one that carries role admin or maps into a group whose *current* `is_admin` is
     true, and the rules UI flags both kinds.
   - **A directory account's role is derived, and only derived.** It is the highest role any
     matched rule carries, recomputed at every login and every refresh by the same function. A
     hand-added membership of an `is_admin` group is refused for a `source = directory` account.
     Otherwise such an account could add itself to Administrators as a local row that no refresh
     removes.
   - **Statement order**, because `A-04`'s triggers are not deferrable: lowering a role deletes
     directory memberships first and then changes the role; raising it changes the role first
     and then inserts memberships. A conflict refuses the login with the reason in the log, not a
     500. The refresh runs one transaction per account, so one bad account does not stop the run.
   - Nested groups are resolved. On AD that is `LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_IN_CHAIN` in one query. On
     plain LDAP it is a bounded walk (`MAX_WALK_DEPTH`) with cycle detection.
   - Any number of directories may be configured, each with its own rules.
2. **An account is keyed by the directory's stable id, not by its login.**
   - The key is (directory, `objectGUID` or `entryUUID`) for LDAP, and (directory, `iss` + `sub`)
     for OIDC. A rename in the directory renames the account and does not create a second one.
     `objectGUID` is read as a buffer and escaped byte by byte, since decoding it as a string is
     lossy and it is the key.
   - Accounts are provisioned just in time at the first successful login, with `email` and
     `display_name` from a configured attribute or claim. They have no password.
   - **The login is derived and namespaced.** Each directory names the attribute or claim that
     becomes the login, fitted to `LOGIN_PATTERN` and 64 characters, and namespaced per directory,
     since `lower(login)` is unique across the installation and two directories with a `jsmith`
     are expected.
   - **A collision is refused, never merged.** A collision is a match with any existing account
     not keyed by this (directory, external id), local or not. It covers a re-created entry with
     a new `objectGUID`, a rename into a login that is taken (the old login is kept, and the case
     is reported), and one person arriving through two directories. Otherwise whoever controls a
     directory entry named `admin` holds the local `admin`. An admin may link two identities
     explicitly (`X-04`), and the link is audited.
   - **A typed login reaches exactly one directory.** Accounts with `source = local` are settled
     without contacting any directory, which keeps break-glass independent of them. A directory
     login goes to one LDAP directory, chosen by a per-directory suffix or domain (`jsmith@corp`,
     `CORP\jsmith`) or by a picker. A failed login never falls through to another directory, and a
     search that returns more than one entry is refused. Otherwise the obvious implementation
     tries directories in turn and binds a corporate password against a partner's server.
3. **A directory change reaches every authority the account holds, within a bounded time.**
   Sessions are only part of it: an API token, a report's run-as account and a map share link
   each act for an account with nobody signed in.
   - **LDAP: the refresh reads every enabled directory-sourced account**, not only those with a
     live session. It uses the service bind, every 15 minutes by default, and the interval is a
     setting.
   - **OIDC: an account that has not authenticated at its IdP recently is stale.** OIDC has no
     general way to ask afterwards, so `last_directory_auth_at` records the last IdP
     authentication. Past a setting's worth of hours, the account's tokens are refused (in the
     token lookup's single `WHERE`), its reports refuse to run and its share links resolve blank.
     An `offline_access` refresh grant on the refresh interval may be added on top, and a refused
     refresh then counts as deprovisioned (OIDC Core §12).
   - **An OIDC session has an absolute lifetime, 8 hours by default**, as
     `sessions.oidcAbsoluteTimeoutHours` in `A-38`'s section. A `ruleProblems` rule refuses it
     longer than `sessions.absoluteTimeoutHours`. At the end the browser re-authenticates, silently
     if the IdP session is still live, and the claims are read again.
   - **Deprovisioning is its own state.** A refresh that finds an account gone, disabled or
     matching no rule sets `directory_disabled`, removes its directory memberships and sets its
     role to `readonly`. Sessions end and sockets close (`A-34`). A later confirmed-enabled read or
     login clears it. The admin's own `disabled` flag is separate and sticky, and sessions and
     tokens refuse either.
   - **Only a definitive answer deprovisions.** That means a service bind proven authenticated
     (WhoAmI, RFC 4532, returns the configured DN and the service account resolves itself) and a
     positive "disabled" (`userAccountControl` 0x2 on AD, a per-directory rule elsewhere, since
     OpenLDAP has no standard attribute). An empty or implausible result, an error, a timeout, a
     size limit or a referral fails the run, which is counted, and every session stays. One run
     may disable at most a capped share of accounts. Above the cap it stops and warns on Core
     Health. A narrowed base DN or a lost ACL returns success with zero entries, and that must not
     disable every administrator.
   - A changed membership moves the access epoch through the existing trigger, so open streams
     resync (`A-12`). Only a non-empty diff is written, and no transaction is held open across
     directory or IdP I/O.
4. **API tokens stay local.** They are issued here, to an account, and checked here.
   - A token's authority is its account's rights now. So an LDAP refresh that narrows or
     disables the account narrows or disables its tokens within one interval, and an OIDC
     account's tokens stop when it goes stale (decision 3), not before.
   - IdP-issued tokens are **not** accepted as API bearer credentials. That would be a second
     token model, with its own revocation story, for automation that a local token already
     serves.
5. **Break-glass is a local admin account that works with the directory down.**
   - Local password login stays enabled for `source = local` accounts.
   - An admin may switch local login off for everybody except accounts flagged break-glass.
   - **The invariant is a state rule, held on every write that can break it**: there is always
     an account that is `source = local`, enabled, flagged break-glass, role admin, and TOTP
     enrolled with recovery codes left. Role admin is what reaches every ADMIN route, and an
     account that has it can repair its own admin-group membership. One service method enforces
     it, raising the unused `ACCOUNT_LAST_ADMIN`. It is called from account disable, role change
     and delete, unflagging, TOTP disable (refused outright for a break-glass account), the
     local-login switch, and linking (a break-glass account cannot be linked to a directory).
   - **Each break-glass login is counted on Core Health**, and an ordinary trigger and template
     deliver it. It needs no new notification path, and it reaches somebody during the outage it
     exists for.
6. **The directory's secrets are write-only, and bound to where they are sent.** The LDAP bind
   password and the OIDC client secret are stored like device credentials: encrypted at rest
   (`A-05`'s vault), `writeOnly`, absent from every read, which shows only whether each is set.
   - **Changing an endpoint clears its secret.** A change to the host, port, TLS mode, bind DN,
     issuer or token endpoint clears the stored secret, which must be entered again in the same
     request, and "test connection" never pairs a stored secret with an unsaved endpoint. The
     vault keeps a secret the caller leaves out, so re-pointing the URL and pressing test would
     otherwise send the service password anywhere (Keycloak CVE-2024-5967 is this case).
   - **The configuration is trusted with domain credentials**, and the ADR says so: an admin who
     re-points search-then-bind can collect users' passwords.
7. **Neither the IdP nor the directory is a dependency of ours.** They are the operator's, and the
   feature is off by default. The ADR argues directly that hard constraint 3 is not engaged, and
   amends Phase 11's preamble, which reads SSO as not clearing the constraints without an ADR.
   The cost is that logins depend on something outside us, and (5) is the answer to that.
   - **Two libraries and `jose`, no service.** `ADR-001` already names `ldapts` and
     `openid-client` (Decision 9). The work is to update the versions (`ldapts` 9.2.0,
     `openid-client` 6.8.8, both MIT and pure JS) and to add `openid-client` and `jose` to
     Decision 6's table.
   - **The full profile only** (`H-12`). None of this is constructed in the v1 build, whose
     unauthenticated surface `H-13` asserts is exactly `auth/{login,logout,session}`. Its Core
     Health channels read as gaps where no directory is configured. The shared session and token
     path refuses a non-local account whose directory is not present, enabled and constructed.
     That one rule covers a v1 core started against a database a full build has touched, and a
     deleted or disabled directory.
8. **The test directories are dev-only** (`X-02`). The compose file gains an OpenLDAP, a Samba AD
   DC and Dex. Nothing in `packages/` reaches for any of them at runtime, suites that need them
   skip when they are absent, and CI asserts that they ran.
9. **A group's MFA requirement holds for a directory login.** `A-07` promises that joining a
   group never quietly relaxes a requirement, and today the second-factor gate exists only inline
   in `POST /auth/login`, after the local password check.
   - LDAP: the gate runs after this login's memberships are written, in the same flow.
   - OIDC: either the same local TOTP step after the callback, or a per-directory required
     `acr`/`amr` checked in the `id_token` (OIDC Core §2, §3.1.2.1). The ADR chooses.
   - A just-in-time account in a `requires_mfa` group enrols on its first login, through a
     half-open state scoped to enrolment only (`X-07`). An admin cannot pre-enrol an account that
     does not exist yet.
   - Routes that re-check a local password, `/auth/mfa/disable` among them, get a
     re-authentication path for directory accounts, which have no local password.
10. **A directory login may lock, deliberately.** `A-01`'s throttle delays and never locks. Put in
    front of a directory, that makes the login form a domain-wide AD lockout tool: 20 failures per
    address per 15 minutes, a delay spent after the bind, against a Microsoft baseline threshold of
    10 and 5 on hardened domains. So failed binds are capped per resolved entry (`objectGUID` or
    `entryUUID`), configurable per directory below the domain threshold. Past the cap the login is
    refused without a bind and answered as a wrong password, and those refusals are counted. AD FS
    Extranet Lockout is the precedent. The ADR states that this breaks `A-01`'s rule, and why.

**Tickets**

      - **A fresh `ldapts` client per login and per refresh batch, `autoRebind` off.** Before
        every bind, assert that the socket is a `TLSSocket` with `authorized === true`, and fail
        closed otherwise. A StartTLS failure never falls back to plain. `ldapts` 9.2.0's
        `_sendBind` reconnects over plain TCP without StartTLS, and AD's default `MaxConnIdleTime`
        of 900 s equals the refresh interval, so a reused client would send a password in clear
        with no attacker needed.
      - Filter input is escaped per RFC 4515.
      - **An empty password is refused before any bind**, because an unauthenticated bind succeeds
        on many servers and that is the classic bypass.
      - The bind cap from decision 10. **Enumeration parity:** a search miss spends a floor delay
        or a decoy bind, and a miss, a wrong password, a collision and no matching rule give the
        same code and words, with the reason in the log only, as a disabled local account is answered today.

        precedent). The MFA gate runs after this login's memberships are written.
      **Done when** tests against the dev directories pass for injection, an empty password,
      nested and cyclic groups, a collision, a disabled user, a directory rename and a
      `requires_mfa` group without a second factor (no session). N+1 bad attempts send at most N
      binds. A password is bound against exactly one server. A proxy that drops the connection
      between StartTLS and the bind sees no cleartext bind.

        with a stated reason, and the guidance to use app roles. Only tenant-specific issuers are
        supported.
      - **A mix-up defence** where more than one OIDC directory is configured (RFC 9700 §4.4.2): a
        server-side pending-authorization record, bound to the pre-authorization cookie, carries
        the directory, and a callback for another directory is refused. Each directory has its own
        redirect path, and the RFC 9207 `iss` is validated where it is advertised.

        a disabled user whose socket closes;
      - a user removed from the AD admin group losing role admin at the next refresh.

- [ ] **X-13 — OIDC back-channel logout** · M · X-09, X-02 · OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout
      1.0. It ends *sessions*, not accounts, and works only with an IdP that implements it and can
      reach the core inbound. Entra's discovery document does not advertise
      `backchannel_logout_supported`. The `logout_token` is validated with `jose`, since
      `openid-client` has none: signature, `iss`, `aud`, `iat` and `exp`, the `events` claim,
      `nonce` absent, `sub` or `sid`, and `jti`. A route-scoped
      `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` parser is needed (BCL §2.5). **Done when** the pinned
      Dex's (or Keycloak's) logout reaches a live session and closes its socket in a test.

**Exit criteria.** One installation logs in through AD (the dev Samba AD DC; a real domain
controller stays a field-test item until there is hardware) and through OIDC. A group change
reaches a live session within one refresh. A directory-side disable ends every authority the
account holds within its bound: sessions, sockets, tokens, reports and share links. With the DC
blackholed and the IdP down at startup, not merely refusing connections, the break-glass admin
can still log in. No route returns a directory secret.

### V2-17 — One session pool for every transport

`support/snmp/pool.ts` and
      `support/ssh/pool.ts` share their lease counting, idle eviction, LRU room-making and
unref'd sweeper, and differ in async open, in-flight sharing and liveness checking.
**Added by `T-07`:** extracting it at two instances would have guessed which half varies;
`T-09`'s WinRM transport is the third and the point at which the shape is known. **`T-09`
landed and is not a third instance** — it is a shell-out with no session to keep, so the two
pools are still two and this ticket's trigger never fired. Whoever picks it up decides on
that basis: either two instances are enough to see the shape, or this waits for a third
transport — which is `V2-08`, and therefore v2. See the re-check below. Keep the SNMP pool's synchronous `acquire` working or update its 21 tests
deliberately, not incidentally.

**Decided 2026-09-03: wait for `D-05`, and here is the evidence so nobody re-derives it.**
The shape *is* now visible without a third instance — the two pools differ on exactly one
axis, `open`: SNMP's is synchronous, SSH's is `async` with in-flight sharing (`#opening`),
a liveness check and an `#attach` step. Everything else is shared, and it is not
approximately shared:

| Method | Difference |
| --- | --- |
| `sweep()` | **byte-identical** but for `sessions` / `connections` |
| `#makeRoom()` | byte-identical but for the same rename and one word of prose |
| `#lease`, `#startSweeping`, `#stopSweeping`, `stats()`, `closeAll()` | same |

**And that is the argument for waiting rather than against it.** Byte-identical after
months means the duplication has cost nothing — no fix has landed in one and missed the
other, which is the failure extraction prevents. Against that: the shared code is
credential-keyed session handling, the stat names `sessions` and `connections` are not
interchangeable prose, and a third transport is the instance that would say whether the
varying half is "async open" or something wider. Refactoring working, tested, undrifted code
in that area for tidiness alone is a bad trade; refactoring it when a third caller forces the
shape is a good one.

**The re-check this ticket asked for has been done, and its trigger was pointing at the wrong
thing** (2026-09-04). It said "re-check the diff when `D-05` lands", and named "`D-05`'s
VMware transport" as the third instance. `D-05` is *Default master dependency*; it landed and
has no transport in it. Virtualisation sensors are **`V2-08`**, which is v2 — so the third
caller this ticket waits for **cannot arrive in v1**, and the instruction to re-check had
silently come due without anyone noticing, because it named a ticket that was never about
what it claimed.

**The re-check itself says: still no drift.** Neither `support/snmp/pool.ts` nor
`support/ssh/pool.ts` has been touched since 2026-08-27 — nine days, one commit each, the
ones that created them — and the only difference in their method sets remains SNMP's
`acquire` against SSH's `#attach`. So the "waiting has cost nothing" argument holds on its
own evidence; what has changed is that waiting now means waiting for v2.

**Moved here on 2026-09-04, by the operator's decision**, of the two options this ticket had
narrowed itself to: extract at two instances and accept the guess `P-19` warns about, or follow
the trigger to where it actually lives. The trigger is a third transport, the third transport is
`V2-08`, and the two now sit in the same backlog — which is the point, since the extraction is a
good trade exactly when that third caller forces the shape and a bad one until then.

**It keeps the name `P-24` as well as its new one.** `P-36`, `T-01`, `T-07`, `T-09`, `T-20`,
`P-54` and a comment in `support/windows/powershell.ts` all cite it by that name; renumbering live
cross-references in order to record a scope move would trade one kind of staleness for another.

**Whoever picks this up starts by re-running the diff above.** It was byte-identical on
2026-08-27 and again on 2026-09-04. If the two have drifted by then, that changes the answer on
its own and the argument for waiting is void.

### (unnumbered) — A check worker that runs more than one check at a time

Filed 2026-09-29 by `P-216b`, without a number; the scheduler allocates one. **Not v1: it changes
the runner contract, and needs an ADR.**

A worker runs one check at a time, so an I/O-bound check holds a whole worker for as long as it
waits. `P-216b` measured what that costs: a `port.tcp` check against a port that never answers
holds 35–40 MiB for its 5 s timeout, and 5,000 of them a minute wanted about 540 workers, about
20 GiB, to wait on sockets that one event loop could hold by the thousand
(`docs/findings/2026-09-29-probe-starvation-b.md`). `P-236` bounds the pool by memory, which stops
the probe dying; it does not make waiting cheap. A worker that runs several asynchronous checks at
once would, by about an order of magnitude for checks that mostly wait.

What an ADR has to settle: which checks may share a worker (`costHint`, or a new declaration on
`SensorType`), how `ctx.signal` and a timeout abandon one check without taking its neighbours, what
a worker crash now costs, and how `P-34`'s sizing counts a worker that holds more than one check.
